chunks.page: The agent workspace at a glance
chunks.text: A tour of the agent desktop: four chat columns, each with client information, the conversation, AI support, and controls.

chunks.page: The agent workspace at a glance
chunks.heading: Layout
chunks.text:
The agent workspace is a browser application that shows up to four simultaneous client conversations side by side. Each conversation occupies a column (sometimes called a slot). A column has four parts, from top to bottom:
1. Client info panel: the client's name, the AI-generated intent label, their accounts and balances, and other profile details. See The client info panel.
2. Chat thread: the full conversation, including what the client said to the virtual assistant before you joined, live messages, typing indicators, and green confirmation cards for completed actions.
3. AI support panel: the suggested reply, predicted topics and questions, relevant client-safe resources, and autopilot controls. See The AI support panel.
4. Composer: where you type or edit messages. While autopilot is running, the composer is replaced by the Pause Autopilot control.
Above the columns, incoming contacts arrive as alert cards with a countdown. See Incoming contacts and the alert card.

chunks.page: The agent workspace at a glance
chunks.heading: Display modes
chunks.text: The workspace offers several layouts. The grid shows all four columns at once. Focus layouts enlarge one conversation and shrink the others to summaries, which is useful during a complex chat. Every layout shows the same information; choose the one you work best in. Some controls (for example, pagination of long chat histories) appear only in the grid layout.

chunks.page: The agent workspace at a glance
chunks.heading: Connection to the phone system
chunks.text: The workspace connects to our contact center platform through the Contact Control Panel (CCP). Your availability status (Available, Busy, Offline) controls whether new chats are routed to you. Set yourself to Busy before a break so no contact is routed to an empty desk. If the workspace loses its connection, a banner appears; refresh the page, and in-progress chats will reattach.

chunks.page: The agent workspace at a glance
chunks.heading: Build stamp
chunks.text: The browser console shows a "build" identifier for the version of the workspace you are running. Support may ask for it when you report a technical issue. See Chat and workspace technical problems.

chunks.page: Incoming contacts and the alert card
chunks.text: How new chats arrive, what the alert card shows, and when to accept or skip.

chunks.page: Incoming contacts and the alert card
chunks.heading: The alert card
chunks.text:
When a client is routed to you, an alert card appears with:
- The client's name.
- The intent summary, a one-line AI description of what the client wants, written from their conversation with the virtual assistant (for example, "Wants to roll over a 401(k) from a former employer into a new IRA").
- The account types the client holds.
- A countdown showing how long you have to accept.
- A bonus opportunity badge, when the contact qualifies for a team incentive (for example, a new-account or rollover conversation).

chunks.page: Incoming contacts and the alert card
chunks.heading: Accepting
chunks.text: Click Accept to take the contact. It opens in your first free column with the transcript of the client's virtual-assistant conversation already loaded and a suggested greeting drafted. Read the intent and the transcript before sending your first message so the client does not have to repeat themselves. See First-contact checklist.

chunks.page: Incoming contacts and the alert card
chunks.heading: Skipping
chunks.text: You may skip a contact only when you genuinely cannot take it: all four columns are busy, you are about to go on a scheduled break, or your team lead has asked you to hold. A skipped contact is re-offered to another agent. Skipping to avoid difficult topics is a quality issue.

chunks.page: Incoming contacts and the alert card
chunks.heading: Continued conversations
chunks.text: If the client chose "Continue this chat" to return to a conversation from the last 7 days, the alert indicates a continued chat. If the client asked for you specifically and you are available, the contact is routed to you first. See Continued chats.
What each field in the client info panel means and how to use it during a chat.

chunks.heading: What it shows
chunks.text:
The client info panel at the top of each column summarizes the client's profile:
- Name and preferred pronouns, if the client has provided them. Use the client's pronouns when you refer to them in after-chat notes or to another agent.
- Intent label: the AI's short description of why the client is here. Treat it as a starting hypothesis, not a fact; confirm it with the client.
- Accounts: each account's type (Roth IRA, Traditional IRA, SEP-IRA, Taxable, and so on), its account ID (for example acc-302), and its total value. The total includes uninvested cash; where cash is shown separately (for example "total incl. $877 cash"), the remainder is invested in funds.
- IRA contributions summary (for clients with IRAs): contributions made at Bob's for the current and, during January to April, the prior tax year, against the client's personal limit. See The IRA contributions summary.
- Contact details on file: email, phone numbers and whether each is verified, mailing address.

chunks.heading: Account values and cash
chunks.text: A client's account value equals their cash plus the market value of their fund holdings. When a client asks "how much cash do I have", quote the cash figure, not the total. When a client funds a purchase "from my account", the available amount is the cash, not the total; to use invested money they must sell or exchange first. See Funding sources for purchases.

chunks.heading: When the panel and the client disagree
chunks.text: If the client describes an account or balance that does not match the panel (for example, "my $50,000 IRA" when the panel shows $41,200), do not argue. Values change daily with the market, pending transactions may not be reflected yet, and the client may be remembering a statement value. Explain the difference neutrally and check pending activity. See "My balance looks wrong".

chunks.heading: Privacy
chunks.text: The panel shows sensitive information. Never read out a full account number, Social Security number, or full date of birth in chat. Confirm details by asking the client to provide them, not by stating them. See Protecting client information.
The suggested reply, predicted topics, predicted questions, and relevant resources: what each is and how to use it responsibly.

chunks.heading: Components
chunks.text:
The AI support panel sits beneath the chat thread in each column and contains:
- Suggested reply: a draft of your next message, written from the whole conversation and the client's profile. See Suggested replies, Change to, and Magic.
- Predicted topics: buttons for the topics the client is most likely to need next, drawn from our knowledge base and the page the client was on.
- Predicted questions: the three questions the client is most likely to ask next. One click puts a question's text into your composer so you can answer it proactively.
- Relevant resources: up to three client-safe help articles chosen for this conversation. Each has a Send button that posts the link to the client as a formatted message. Sending a resource does not change the suggested reply.
- Autopilot controls: start, pause, resume, and exit autopilot, and choose its scope. See Autopilot: what it is and when to use it.

chunks.heading: How to use it well
chunks.text:
- Read every suggestion before sending. The AI is usually right about tone and often right about content, but it can be wrong about facts. Check account-specific details against the info panel and policy details against this library.
- Prefer sending resources for depth. A short answer plus a link to the full article is better than a long chat message.
- Use predicted questions to anticipate. If the client asked about RMDs and the panel predicts "When is my RMD due?", answer it before they ask.

chunks.heading: What the AI cannot do
chunks.text: The AI support panel does not know about anything that happened outside the conversation and the profile (for example, a phone call the client made yesterday, or a form in the mail room). It may not know about very recent rule changes. When in doubt, this library is authoritative.

chunks.page: Suggested replies, Change to, and Magic
chunks.text: How to send, edit, browse, and reshape the AI-suggested reply.

chunks.page: Suggested replies, Change to, and Magic
chunks.heading: Sending and editing
chunks.text:
The Suggested reply box shows a draft of your next message. You can:
- Send it as written. It goes to the client immediately.
- Edit it in place by clicking into the text, then send your edited version.
- Ignore it and type your own message in the composer.
After you send any message, a fresh suggestion is written for your next turn.

chunks.page: Suggested replies, Change to, and Magic
chunks.heading: Browsing history
chunks.text: The suggestion box keeps a history of every suggestion in the conversation. Use the ‹ and › arrows to step through earlier suggestions. A spinner shows while the next one is being written, and a small dot indicates a newer suggestion arrived while you were reading an older one.

chunks.page: Suggested replies, Change to, and Magic
chunks.heading: Change to
chunks.text: The Change to menu offers a few alternative directions that change the meaning of the reply: ask a clarifying question instead of answering, lead with empathy, give a different answer. Picking one writes a new reply along that direction.

chunks.page: Suggested replies, Change to, and Magic
chunks.heading: Magic
chunks.text: The Magic menu keeps the meaning and restyles the wording: more concise, more detailed, more casual, more formal, or a custom instruction you type ("mention the April 15 deadline"). Use it to fix tone without retyping.

chunks.page: Suggested replies, Change to, and Magic
chunks.heading: Feedback loop
chunks.text: The workspace records how each of your messages was produced (sent as suggested, edited, restyled, replaced, or written freehand). This helps improve suggestions over time. It is not used to judge you for editing; editing a suggestion to make it right is exactly what we want.

chunks.page: Autopilot: what it is and when to use it
chunks.text: How autopilot carries routine parts of a conversation, its scopes, and the situations where you should never use it.

chunks.page: Autopilot: what it is and when to use it
chunks.heading: What autopilot does
chunks.text: Autopilot lets the AI send messages in your column on a timer, so routine work continues while you focus on another conversation. When a column is on autopilot, each drafted reply waits through a short countdown before it sends, and the client sees a normal typing indicator. You can pause, edit, or send immediately at any point. See Autopilot controls: pause, resume, exit, send now.

chunks.page: Autopilot: what it is and when to use it
chunks.heading: Scopes
chunks.text:
Autopilot runs in a scope that defines its job:
- Task collection (get-intent): identifies the service task the client wants, then a task expert collects the required details one question at a time. When every detail is collected and confirmed, a Proposed Action card appears for your review. See Task experts and the task menu and The Proposed Action card.
- Callback: arranges a phone callback at a time the client chooses, checking availability. Requests for financial advice are routed here, because a callback can be fulfilled by a licensed professional. See Scheduling callbacks.
- Idle check: sends a gentle check-in when the client has gone quiet.
The scope recommendation in the AI support panel suggests which scope fits the current moment.

chunks.page: Autopilot: what it is and when to use it
chunks.heading: When to use autopilot
chunks.text:
- Collecting routine details for a well-understood task (an automatic investment, a tax form request, a contact update).
- Scheduling a callback.
- Keeping a quiet conversation alive while you handle a more urgent column.

chunks.page: Autopilot: what it is and when to use it
chunks.heading: When not to use autopilot
chunks.text:
- Bereavement conversations, complaints, fraud reports, or any emotionally charged chat.
- When the client is confused or the request is ambiguous.
- When the client is asking for advice, other than routing them to a callback.
- When you are unsure what the client needs.

chunks.page: Autopilot: what it is and when to use it
chunks.heading: Safeguards built in
chunks.text: Autopilot never submits a task on its own. Every task ends in a Proposed Action that you must approve (or, for client-submitted tasks, that the client must approve). Autopilot will not give investment advice, will not discuss topics outside the task, and will tell the client when it cannot help with something. Even so, you remain responsible for every message sent from your column.

chunks.page: Autopilot controls: pause, resume, exit, send now
chunks.text: Exactly how the autopilot control bar works so you can intervene in time.

chunks.page: Autopilot controls: pause, resume, exit, send now
chunks.heading: While autopilot is running
chunks.text:
The composer is replaced by a large Pause Autopilot button. The pending reply shows a live countdown to auto-send. In the final 10 seconds the countdown flashes red, which is your cue to read the reply if you have not already.
Clicking elsewhere in the column, or dragging the resize handle on the AI panel to read a longer draft, does not stop autopilot. Only the controls do.

chunks.page: Autopilot controls: pause, resume, exit, send now
chunks.heading: Pausing
chunks.text:
Pause freezes the countdown without exiting autopilot. While paused, the pending reply becomes a compact control bar:
- ‹ › arrows flip between alternative drafts.
- Send now sends the reply shown immediately.
- Magic and Change to reshape the reply in place, exactly as on the Suggested reply.
- Resume ▶ continues the countdown from where it stopped.
- Exit ends autopilot for that column and returns the normal composer.
Editing the pending reply automatically pauses autopilot, and your edited version is the one that sends.

chunks.page: Autopilot controls: pause, resume, exit, send now
chunks.heading: Recovery
chunks.text: If the AI has a temporary error, autopilot retries once. If it still cannot continue, it stops and posts a note in the column explaining what happened; you can resume once the issue clears. A client message that arrives while you are editing will never cause a duplicate send.

chunks.page: Autopilot controls: pause, resume, exit, send now
chunks.heading: When the client leaves
chunks.text: If the client closes the chat, autopilot stops immediately and the column shows "Client closed the chat." See When the client disconnects.

chunks.page: Task experts and the task menu
chunks.text: The service tasks that can be completed through chat, how a task expert collects details, and how to start one manually.

chunks.page: Task experts and the task menu
chunks.heading: What a task expert is
chunks.text: A task expert is an AI specialist for one service task. When autopilot identifies a task (or you pick one), the expert asks the client for each required detail, one at a time, checks the answers against the client's profile, and recaps everything for confirmation. When the client confirms, the expert produces a Proposed Action for your approval.

chunks.page: Task experts and the task menu
chunks.heading: The tasks
chunks.text:
Task: Update Contact Information; What it does: Phone, email, or mailing address; Procedure page: Procedure: Update Contact Information
Task: Change Beneficiary Designations; What it does: Add, update, or remove a beneficiary; Procedure page: Procedure: Change Beneficiary Designations (chat)
Task: Add Authorized Account User; What it does: Grant view-only, limited, or full access (client approves); Procedure page: Authorized users and access levels
Task: Open a New Account; What it does: Roth IRA, Traditional IRA, SEP-IRA, or Taxable; Procedure page: Procedure: Open a New Account (chat)
Task: Buy / Make a Contribution; What it does: Purchase fund shares; Procedure page: Procedure: Buy / Make a Contribution (chat)
Task: Sell Fund Shares; What it does: Sell part or all of a holding; Procedure page: Procedure: Sell Fund Shares (chat)
Task: Exchange Between Funds; What it does: Move money between funds in one account; Procedure page: Procedure: Exchange Between Funds (chat)
Task: Change Dividend Reinvestment; What it does: Turn DRIP on or off for a fund; Procedure page: Procedure: Change Dividend Reinvestment (chat)
Task: Set Up Automatic Investment; What it does: New recurring purchase; Procedure page: Procedure: Set Up Automatic Investment (chat)
Task: Modify Auto-Invest Schedule; What it does: Change amount, frequency, or day; Procedure page: Procedure: Modify an automatic investment
Task: Pause or Resume Auto-Invest; What it does: Suspend or restart a schedule; Procedure page: Procedure: Pause or resume an automatic investment

chunks.page: Task experts and the task menu
chunks.heading: The tasks
chunks.text:
Task: Request a Distribution; What it does: One-time withdrawal; Procedure page: Procedure: Request a Distribution (chat)
Task: Set Up Recurring Distributions; What it does: Systematic withdrawal plan; Procedure page: Procedure: Set Up Recurring Distributions (chat)
Task: Update RMD Settings; What it does: RMD delivery, frequency, withholding; Procedure page: Procedure: Update RMD Settings (chat)
Task: Roll Over From Another Institution; What it does: Start an incoming rollover; Procedure page: Procedure: Roll Over From Another Institution (chat)
Task: Convert to Roth IRA; What it does: Traditional or SEP to Roth; Procedure page: Procedure: Convert to Roth IRA (chat)
Task: Request Tax Document; What it does: Copy of a 1099 or 5498; Procedure page: Procedure: Request Tax Document (chat)
Task: Cancel or Reschedule Callback; What it does: Change an arranged callback; Procedure page: Procedure: Cancel or Reschedule Callback (chat)
Task: Update Security Settings; What it does: Password, 2FA, trusted devices; Procedure page: Procedure: Update Security Settings

chunks.page: Task experts and the task menu
chunks.heading: Starting a task manually
chunks.text: If autopilot misidentifies the task, or you want a specific expert, open the task menu (the ✈ icon) in the AI panel and choose the task. Your choice overrides the AI's identification. The expert then begins collecting details.

chunks.page: Task experts and the task menu
chunks.heading: What experts will not do
chunks.text: Task experts stay on their task. They will not recommend funds, comment on whether a transaction is wise, or answer unrelated questions; they will tell the client you can help with other topics once the task is done. If a client asks for advice mid-task, the expert pauses the task and offers a callback with a licensed professional.
How to review, edit, and submit the structured action a task expert prepares.

chunks.heading: What appears
chunks.text:
When a task expert has collected and confirmed every required detail, a Proposed Action card appears in the AI panel. It lists the task name and each field with the value collected, for example:
Field: Account; Value: Roth IRA (acc-301)
Field: Fund; Value: BF500
Field: Purchase amount; Value: $2,000.00
Field: Funding source; Value: Linked bank account

chunks.heading: Your review
chunks.text:
Before you submit, check every field:
1. Is the value what the client said? Use the locate button (⌖) beside each field to jump to the place in the transcript where it was established. See Evidence highlighting.
2. Did the client confirm the recap? There should be a clear "yes" after a full recap.
3. Does the action make sense for this account? For example, an IRA contribution that would exceed the client's remaining limit, a sale larger than the holding, or a purchase funded from cash larger than the cash balance. Check the relevant procedure page.
4. Is anything missing? Optional details (like tax withholding on a distribution) may matter to the client.
You can edit any field directly on the card. If you change a value, tell the client what you changed and why, and get confirmation.

chunks.heading: Submitting
chunks.text:
For most tasks, click Submit Action. The action executes, a reference number in the format REF-XXXXXX is generated, and the client receives a green confirmation card describing what was done. Give the client any next steps (for example, when the money will arrive).
For tasks the client must approve themselves, the button reads Send to client. See Actions the client must submit.

chunks.heading: If something goes wrong
chunks.text: If the submission fails, the card shows an error. Do not resubmit repeatedly. Check whether the action partially completed (look at the client's recent transactions), then try once more. If it fails again, tell the client you will complete it and escalate to your team lead with the reference details. See Transaction statuses.
How the transcript highlights show where each Proposed Action value came from, and what "not located in transcript" means.

chunks.heading: How it works
chunks.text:
When a Proposed Action card is showing, the transcript highlights the exact words where each value was established: either the client's own statement ("put $2,000 into the 500 index fund") or an agent recap that the client explicitly confirmed. Later echoes ("great, the $2,000 is all set") are not used as evidence.
Each field on the card has a locate button (⌖). Clicking it scrolls the transcript to that field's highlighted span and flashes it.

chunks.heading: "Not located in transcript"
chunks.text:
If a field shows "not located in transcript", the system could not find where that value came from. This is a signal to scrutinize the field. Common reasons:
- The value was inferred from the profile (for example, the only account the client has) rather than stated. That may be fine; confirm it with the client.
- The client gave the value in an unusual form ("two grand") that the locator could not match. Confirm the exact amount.
- The value is wrong. Correct it on the card and reconfirm with the client.
If the highlighting service is unavailable, the card simply shows no highlights. Review the transcript manually.

chunks.heading: Why it matters
chunks.text: Most service errors are transcription errors: the wrong fund, the wrong account, an extra zero. Evidence highlighting lets you verify each value in seconds. Use it on every card.
Tasks that only the account owner may authorize, how "Send to client" works, and what the client sees.

chunks.heading: Submission types
chunks.text:
Every task has a submission type:
- Agent-submitted (Type 1): any agent may submit on the client's behalf after the client confirms. Most tasks are Type 1.
- Licensed-agent (Type 2): reserved for tasks that will require a licensed representative. No tasks use this type yet.
- Client-submitted (Type 3): only the account owner can authorize the action. Adding an authorized account user is the current Type 3 task, because granting someone access to an account is a decision only the owner can make.

chunks.heading: How Send to client works
chunks.text:
For a Type 3 task, the Proposed Action button reads Send to client. When you click it:
1. A card titled "Your approval is required" appears in the client's chat window, showing the same fields. The client can edit the fields.
2. Your panel shows "Waiting for client to submit…".
3. The client clicks Submit action or Decline.
4. If submitted, the action executes and the client receives the same green confirmation card as any other action. If declined, nothing changes, and you should ask whether they would like to adjust anything.

chunks.heading: Guidance
chunks.text: Explain to the client before you send it: "For your security, adding someone to your account has to be approved by you. I'm sending a card to your chat window; please review it and click Submit if it looks right." If the client does not see the card, ask them to scroll down in the chat window. If they are not the account owner, they cannot approve it; see Authorized users and access levels.
What the system writes for you when a chat ends, what you must review, and how to submit.

chunks.heading: What is generated
chunks.text:
When a chat ends, the column moves to after-chat work. The system automatically drafts:
- A wrap-up code from the standard list. See Wrap-up codes.
- A summary of three to five factual sentences: what the client asked, what was done, and the outcome.
- Coaching: one sentence of specific positive feedback and, where useful, one actionable improvement point, written to you.

chunks.heading: What you must do
chunks.text:
Review and submit. You do not write ACW by hand, but you are responsible for it being correct:
- Is the wrap-up code the most specific one that fits the main topic?
- Does the summary accurately state what was done, including reference numbers and any promised follow-up?
- If you promised a callback, a secure message, or a specialist contact, is it in the summary?
Edit anything that is wrong before submitting. Accurate summaries matter because the next agent, and the client's "Continue this chat" recap, depend on them.

chunks.heading: Timing
chunks.text: Submit ACW promptly. A column in ACW is not available for a new contact. Aim to finish within one minute of the chat ending.

chunks.heading: Example summary
chunks.text: "Client asked to add her daughter as a view-only user on her Roth IRA. Agent explained access levels; client chose View-only. Agent sent the action for client approval; client submitted (REF-48231). Daughter will receive an email invitation."

chunks.heading: Wrap-up code for that example
chunks.text: Access Authorization.
The standard wrap-up codes, what each means, and how to choose the most specific one.

chunks.heading: Choosing a code
chunks.text: Choose the single most specific code that describes the primary reason for the chat. If a client asked a quick balance question and then changed beneficiaries, the code is Beneficiary Change. The summary records secondary topics.

chunks.heading: The codes
chunks.text:
Code: Access Authorization; Use when the primary topic was: Adding or changing an authorized user or power of attorney
Code: Account Inquiry; Use when the primary topic was: General questions about an existing account (balance, holdings, activity)
Code: Address Update; Use when the primary topic was: Changing a mailing address
Code: Beneficiary Change; Use when the primary topic was: Adding, updating, or removing beneficiaries
Code: Complaint Filed; Use when the primary topic was: The client made a formal complaint that was logged
Code: Contribution Question; Use when the primary topic was: IRA or account contributions, limits, deadlines
Code: Distribution Request; Use when the primary topic was: A one-time withdrawal from any account
Code: Estate Planning; Use when the primary topic was: Death of an account holder, inherited accounts, estate questions
Code: Fee Dispute; Use when the primary topic was: The client disputed a fee
Code: Fund Comparison; Use when the primary topic was: Comparing funds factually
Code: Fund Switch; Use when the primary topic was: An exchange between funds
Code: General Information; Use when the primary topic was: Questions not tied to the client's own account
Code: Grievance; Use when the primary topic was: Dissatisfaction expressed without a formal complaint
Code: Investment Advice; Use when the primary topic was: The client sought advice and was referred
Code: IRA Inquiry; Use when the primary topic was: IRA rules not covered by a more specific code

chunks.heading: The codes
chunks.text:
Code: Market Question; Use when the primary topic was: Market movements, news, volatility
Code: New Account; Use when the primary topic was: Opening an account
Code: Password Reset; Use when the primary topic was: Login, password, or 2FA issues
Code: Performance Question; Use when the primary topic was: Fund or account performance
Code: Portfolio Review; Use when the primary topic was: Client wanted their holdings reviewed (referred)
Code: RMD Calculation; Use when the primary topic was: RMD amounts, timing, settings
Code: Rebalancing Discussion; Use when the primary topic was: Rebalancing questions or requests
Code: Referral; Use when the primary topic was: The client was referred to a specialist team
Code: Retirement Planning; Use when the primary topic was: Retirement planning questions
Code: SEP-IRA Question; Use when the primary topic was: SEP-IRA specific questions
Code: Systematic Withdrawal; Use when the primary topic was: Recurring withdrawal plans
Code: Tax Information; Use when the primary topic was: Tax forms, cost basis, tax questions
Code: Technical Issue; Use when the primary topic was: Website, app, or login technical problems
Code: Transfer Request; Use when the primary topic was: Rollovers, ACATs, transfers between institutions
Code: Withdrawal Processing; Use when the primary topic was: Status or processing of a withdrawal already requested

chunks.heading: Complaint versus grievance
chunks.text: Use Complaint Filed only when a complaint was logged following Handling complaints. A client who is unhappy but does not want to file a complaint is a Grievance. When unsure, log the complaint; under-recording complaints is a compliance failure.
How "Continue this chat" works for clients and what you see when a client returns.

chunks.heading: The client side
chunks.text: If a client spoke with a live agent within the last 7 days, opening chat shows a card with the date and a one-sentence recap of that conversation and a Continue this chat button. Clicking it checks whether the same agent is available. The client can wait for that agent or take the first available agent.

chunks.heading: Your side
chunks.text: When you accept a continued chat, the previous transcript loads into your column, marked as a continued conversation. Read the recap and skim the transcript. Open with continuity: "Welcome back, Maria. Last time we set up your monthly investment into BF500. How can I help today?"

chunks.heading: If you were not the original agent
chunks.text: You inherit the previous agent's commitments. If they promised a follow-up, check whether it happened. Do not contradict a prior agent in front of the client; if you believe something was handled incorrectly, correct it calmly and note it in ACW.

chunks.heading: Privacy
chunks.text: The recap is written in second person for the client ("You granted your wife limited access..."). It is shown only to the client in their authenticated session and to agents.

chunks.heading: Example
chunks.text: The previous agent set up an automatic investment and promised to email a confirmation. When the client continues the chat, you check: the confirmation was sent. You open with: "Welcome back! I see you set up your $200 monthly investment last week; that confirmation went to your email on file. What can I help with today?"
What clients can see of past chats, how transcripts are saved, and how to handle transcript requests.

chunks.heading: What is saved
chunks.text: When a chat with a live agent ends, the full transcript is saved with a short recap. Conversations with only the virtual assistant (that never reached an agent) are not saved as transcripts.

chunks.heading: What the client can see
chunks.text:
- At the end of a live chat the client sees "Chat ended." and a Download transcript button that saves a plain-text copy (date, agent, duration, timestamped messages).
- The chat menu shows a history of the client's live-agent chats from the last 3 months, newest first, each with date, start time, duration, and recap. Clicking one opens the read-only transcript.

chunks.heading: Requests for older transcripts
chunks.text: If a client needs a transcript older than 3 months, or a certified copy for legal purposes, take the request and route it to Client Records through your team lead. Records requests from attorneys or courts must go to the Legal department; do not provide transcripts to third parties from chat. See Recordkeeping and retention.

chunks.heading: Your conduct
chunks.text: Assume every word you type will be read by the client, a quality reviewer, and possibly a regulator. Never type internal opinions about the client.

chunks.heading: Example
chunks.text:
Client: "Can you send me the transcript of my chat from last month?"
Agent: "You can view and download it any time: open the chat menu (the icon at the top left of the chat window), choose 'Chat history', and select the chat from last month. There's a Download link on the transcript."
What happens when a client closes the chat, and how to wrap up correctly.

chunks.heading: What you see
chunks.text:
If the client closes or ends the chat on their side, the column does not jump straight to after-chat work. Instead:
- The AI support area is replaced by a notice: "Client closed the chat."
- The composer is disabled.
- Any running autopilot stops.
- An End chat button appears.
Click End chat to move the column into after-chat work.

chunks.heading: Unfinished tasks
chunks.text:
If the client disconnects before confirming a Proposed Action, do not submit it. A task without the client's confirmation is not authorized. Note in ACW where the conversation stopped. If the client returns through "Continue this chat", you or the next agent can pick up where it left off.
If the client disconnects after you submitted an action, the action stands, and the confirmation remains visible in their chat history.

chunks.heading: Minimized chats
chunks.text: Clients can minimize the chat to a docked bar without disconnecting. A minimized chat is still live. Messages you send appear with an unread badge. Do not treat a slow reply as a disconnect; use the idle check-in.

chunks.heading: If the client reconnects
chunks.text: A client who closed the chat accidentally can open a new chat; if they spoke with you, "Continue this chat" will offer to reconnect them. The previous transcript loads into the new column.

chunks.heading: Partial tasks
chunks.text: If the client disconnected mid-collection, autopilot stops. Note in ACW what had been collected so the next agent can resume quickly.
How to arrange a phone callback from a chat and what happens after you do.

chunks.heading: When to offer a callback
chunks.text:
Offer a callback when:
- The client asks for investment advice, which must come from a licensed professional.
- The request requires a phone conversation with a specialist (complex estate, some trades by phone).
- The client would rather talk than type, or must leave now.
- You need time to research and want to give the client a definite follow-up.

chunks.heading: How to arrange it
chunks.text: Switch the column's autopilot to the callback scope, or use the scheduling flow yourself. The client chooses a day and time; the system checks availability, converts the time correctly from Eastern Time, and confirms. Clients can also schedule a callback themselves from the virtual assistant.

chunks.heading: What happens next
chunks.text: When a callback is scheduled, the system prepares a call dossier for the phone agent: a summary of the client's goal written from the real conversation, research on the question, a guided script, and the transcript that led to the callback. The phone agent sees it in the callback console at the scheduled time. See The phone callback console.

chunks.heading: Changing a callback
chunks.text: Clients can cancel or reschedule through chat. See Procedure: Cancel or Reschedule Callback (chat).

chunks.heading: Example
chunks.text:
Client: "I'd like someone to look at my whole portfolio and tell me if I'm on track."
Agent: "That's a great question for one of our licensed professionals, who can review your full situation. I can schedule a call. What day and time works for you?"
What phone agents see when they handle a scheduled callback, for chat agents who set callbacks up.

chunks.heading: Purpose
chunks.text: The callback console is the workspace for agents who make scheduled outbound calls. Chat agents do not use it directly, but understanding it helps you set up callbacks well.

chunks.heading: The dossier
chunks.text:
For each scheduled callback, the system researches the client's request and builds a dossier:
- The intent: a summary of the client's underlying goal, taken from the real chat that led to the callback.
- A worked answer with findings and any gaps that need confirmation.
- Coaching for the call.
- An editable guided script with branches for likely responses.
- The originating transcript, with the key passages highlighted.
- A client snapshot: accounts, balances, and recent performance.

chunks.heading: Helping the phone agent
chunks.text: The better the chat that leads to a callback, the better the dossier. Before scheduling, make sure the chat states clearly what the client wants ("Client wants to discuss whether to convert part of her Traditional IRA to Roth this year; she has questions about the tax impact") and any facts you have already confirmed. Promise the client only what the callback can deliver.

chunks.heading: What chat agents should include
chunks.text:
- Any facts already verified with the client.
- The client's preferred callback number and best times.
- Sensitivities (recent bereavement, hearing difficulty, preference for Spanish).

chunks.heading: Example dossier intent
chunks.text: "Client wants to discuss whether to convert part of her $310,000 Traditional IRA to Roth before retiring in 2027; concerned about tax bracket and Medicare premiums."
Who counts as verified, when to re-verify, the questions to ask, and what to do when verification fails.

chunks.heading: Why verification matters
chunks.text: Every action we take on an account and every piece of account information we share assumes we are talking to the account owner or someone the owner has authorized. Verification failures are how fraudsters steal money. Treat verification as a non-negotiable step, explained to the client as protection for them.

chunks.heading: Authenticated chats
chunks.text: Most clients reach a live agent from inside the logged-in client portal. These clients have already signed in with their password and two-factor authentication, so the chat is authenticated: the system knows which client profile the chat belongs to, and the client info panel shows it. You do not need to ask an authenticated client verification questions for routine requests.

chunks.heading: When to verify again
chunks.text:
Even in an authenticated chat, perform additional verification when:
- The person says they are someone other than the account owner ("I'm calling for my mother").
- The writing style, name, or details suddenly change partway through the conversation.
- The request is high risk: changing the email or phone number and requesting a withdrawal in the same chat, adding a new bank and immediately redeeming, sending money to a new address, or adding an authorized user with full access.
- The client cannot describe their own accounts in basic terms.
- Anything feels wrong.

chunks.heading: How to verify
chunks.text:
Ask the client to provide (never read out to them) two or more of:
- The last four digits of their Social Security number.
- Their date of birth.
- The ZIP code of their mailing address on file.
- The type of an account they hold and its approximate value.
- A recent transaction (approximate amount and date).
Compare their answers with the profile. Do not reveal which answer was wrong. For high-risk requests, you may also send a one-time code to the verified email or phone on file through the security tools and ask the client to read it back.

chunks.heading: When verification fails
chunks.text: Do not process the request and do not share account information. Say: "For your security I'm not able to make changes to this account in chat right now. Please call us at 1-800-BOB-FUND so we can verify your identity by phone." Note the attempt in ACW. If you suspect fraud, follow Suspected account takeover or unauthorized activity and notify your team lead immediately.

chunks.heading: Unauthenticated contacts
chunks.text: If a contact reaches you without an authenticated session (for example, a prospect asking general questions), you may answer general questions about products and rules but must not discuss any specific account. Direct them to sign in or call.

chunks.page: What you can discuss with whom
chunks.text: A matrix of what information you may share with account owners, authorized users at each level, and unverified people.

chunks.page: What you can discuss with whom
chunks.heading: The matrix
chunks.text:
Person: Verified account owner; General product and rule questions: Yes; Account balances and activity: Yes; Changes and transactions: Yes
Person: Joint owner (verified); General product and rule questions: Yes; Account balances and activity: Yes, for the joint account; Changes and transactions: Yes, for the joint account (some actions need both owners)
Person: Authorized user, Full access; General product and rule questions: Yes; Account balances and activity: Yes; Changes and transactions: Yes, including withdrawals to outside accounts and closing the account
Person: Authorized user, Limited access; General product and rule questions: Yes; Account balances and activity: Yes; Changes and transactions: Trades and money back to the owner only; no ownership, beneficiary, or account opening/closing changes
Person: Authorized user, View-only; General product and rule questions: Yes; Account balances and activity: Yes; Changes and transactions: No
Person: Agent under power of attorney (on file); General product and rule questions: Yes; Account balances and activity: Yes; Changes and transactions: As permitted by the POA document
Person: Spouse or relative not on file; General product and rule questions: Yes; Account balances and activity: No; Changes and transactions: No
Person: Unverified person; General product and rule questions: Yes; Account balances and activity: No; Changes and transactions: No

chunks.page: What you can discuss with whom
chunks.heading: Common situations
chunks.text:
- "I'm her husband; she asked me to check." Unless he is an authorized user or joint owner, you cannot share anything about her account. Offer to explain how she can add him as an authorized user. See Authorized users and access levels.
- "My father has dementia and I handle his finances." Ask whether a power of attorney is on file. If not, explain the POA process. See Power of attorney.
- The owner is in the chat and asks you to talk to their daughter. With the owner present and consenting in the chat, you may discuss the account; note the consent in ACW. Transactions still require the owner's confirmation.

chunks.page: What you can discuss with whom
chunks.heading: Deceased account holders
chunks.text: When the account owner has died, information may be shared only with the executor, administrator, or named beneficiaries, and only after documentation. See When someone reports a death.

chunks.page: Third parties, advisors, and family members
chunks.text: How to handle requests from people who are not the account owner, including financial advisors, accountants, and attorneys.

chunks.page: Third parties, advisors, and family members
chunks.heading: The default
chunks.text: We serve the account owner. Anyone else must be authorized by the owner through a documented relationship on file: joint owner, authorized user, power of attorney, trusted contact (limited purpose), or court-appointed guardian or conservator.

chunks.page: Third parties, advisors, and family members
chunks.heading: Financial advisors and accountants
chunks.text: Outside advisors and CPAs often contact us for clients. They may receive information only if the client has added them as an authorized user (usually view-only) or provided a signed authorization on file. Otherwise, explain that the client can grant them access online at My Account → Account Access, and offer to send the client a link.

chunks.page: Third parties, advisors, and family members
chunks.heading: Attorneys
chunks.text: Attorneys representing a client in a legal matter, or an estate, must provide documentation to the Legal department or Estate Services. Do not provide information in chat. Subpoenas and court orders go to Legal.

chunks.page: Third parties, advisors, and family members
chunks.heading: Family members in an emergency
chunks.text: If a family member says the client is in hospital or incapacitated and money is needed urgently, be compassionate but do not make exceptions. Explain the options: the client may add them as an authorized user if able; a power of attorney can be submitted; in an emergency, the family can contact Estate Services or ask for a specialist. Watch for exploitation signals. See Elder financial exploitation and vulnerable clients.

chunks.page: Third parties, advisors, and family members
chunks.heading: Trusted contact person
chunks.text: A trusted contact is someone the client authorizes us to contact if we suspect exploitation or cannot reach the client. A trusted contact cannot transact or see balances. See Trusted contact person.
Privacy rules for chat: what never to type, how to handle sensitive data the client sends, and our privacy obligations.

chunks.heading: Our obligations
chunks.text: Bob's Mutual Funds is required by federal privacy rules (including Regulation S-P) to protect clients' nonpublic personal information: names combined with account numbers, Social Security numbers, balances, transactions, and similar data. Clients receive our privacy notice when they open an account and annually. We do not sell client information.

chunks.heading: What never to type in chat
chunks.text:
- A full Social Security number or taxpayer ID.
- A full account number or bank account number. Use the last four digits or the account type and ID shown in the portal (for example "Roth IRA, acc-301").
- A full date of birth.
- Passwords, one-time codes, or security answers. We never ask for a client's password.

chunks.heading: When a client sends sensitive data
chunks.text: Clients sometimes paste a full SSN or bank account number into chat. Do not repeat it. Say: "Thank you. For your security, please don't share full account or Social Security numbers in chat; I have what I need." Report it per your team's procedure so the transcript can be redacted.

chunks.heading: Sharing information
chunks.text: Share account information only with people entitled to it (see What you can discuss with whom). Never confirm whether a person is a client to someone who is not authorized. "I'm not able to discuss whether someone has an account with us" is the correct answer.

chunks.heading: Screens and workspace
chunks.text: Lock your screen whenever you step away. Do not copy client data into personal notes, email, or messaging apps. Use only approved tools.

chunks.heading: Privacy questions from clients
chunks.text: Clients can read the privacy notice in the portal footer. Requests to change marketing preferences can be handled at My Account → Preferences. Questions about data deletion or legal privacy rights go to the Privacy Office through your team lead.

chunks.page: Suspected account takeover or unauthorized activity
chunks.text: Recognizing account takeover, what to do immediately when a client reports unauthorized activity, and how to escalate.

chunks.page: Suspected account takeover or unauthorized activity
chunks.heading: Warning signs
chunks.text:
- A client reports a transaction, login, or change they did not make.
- Contact details (email, phone, address) changed shortly before a withdrawal or new bank link.
- A new bank account was linked and an electronic redemption followed within days.
- The person in chat cannot answer basic questions about the account.
- The person pressures you to rush ("I need this wired today, it's an emergency").
- Requests to send money to an address or bank that does not match the owner's name.

chunks.page: Suspected account takeover or unauthorized activity
chunks.heading: If the client reports unauthorized activity
chunks.text:
1. Stay calm and reassuring. "Thank you for telling us right away. I'm going to help you secure your account now."
2. Verify the client's identity (see Verifying client identity).
3. Do not process any other transactions in the chat.
4. Escalate immediately to the Fraud team via your team lead. The Fraud team can place a protective hold, block online access, cancel pending transactions, and investigate.
5. Advise the client to change their password and confirm 2FA is on, using a device they trust. See Password resets and Two-factor authentication (2FA).
6. If the client's email account may be compromised, suggest they secure it too, because password reset links go there.
7. Document everything in ACW, including times and what the client reported.

chunks.page: Suspected account takeover or unauthorized activity
chunks.heading: If you suspect the person in chat is not the client
chunks.text: Do not accuse. Decline politely: "I'm not able to complete that request in chat. Please call us at 1-800-BOB-FUND." Notify your team lead immediately so the Fraud team can contact the real owner through verified contact details.

chunks.page: Suspected account takeover or unauthorized activity
chunks.heading: Reimbursement questions
chunks.text: Clients often ask whether they will be reimbursed. Do not promise reimbursement. Explain that the Fraud team will investigate and contact them, typically within 2 business days, and that protective measures are already in place.
The scams that target our clients, what we never ask for, and how to help a client who may have been contacted by a fraudster.

chunks.heading: What Bob's Mutual Funds never does
chunks.text:
Tell clients plainly: we will never
- Ask for their password or one-time security code by phone, email, text, or chat.
- Ask them to move money to a "safe account" to protect it.
- Change our wire instructions by email.
- Ask them to pay a fee to release funds.
- Call them to recommend a specific investment or "special opportunity".

chunks.heading: Common scams
chunks.text:
- Phishing emails and texts that imitate our logo and link to a fake sign-in page. Our emails come only from noreply@bobsmutualfunds.com and never ask for credentials.
- Impersonation calls: someone claiming to be from Bob's, the bank, or a government agency, warning of a problem and asking for codes.
- Tech-support scams: a pop-up claims the computer is infected and asks the client to install remote-access software.
- Romance and friendship scams: an online acquaintance gradually asks for money, often for an emergency or an "investment".
- Investment fraud: promises of guaranteed high returns, crypto "platforms", or pressure to act fast.

chunks.heading: Helping a client
chunks.text:
If a client describes any of these:
1. Tell them not to provide any further information to the contact and not to click links.
2. If they shared their password or a code, help them reset their password immediately and check their 2FA settings. See Password resets.
3. Review recent activity with them for anything unfamiliar.
4. Escalate to the Fraud team if any information was shared or any activity looks wrong.
5. Encourage them to report scams to the appropriate authorities; their bank can also help.
Phishing reports (forwarded suspicious emails) can be sent to the security mailbox listed on the portal's Security page.
How clients reset their password, the rules for new passwords, and what to do when the reset email doesn't arrive.

chunks.heading: Self-service reset
chunks.text:
1. On the sign-in page, the client clicks Forgot Password.
2. They enter the email address on file.
3. A reset link arrives from noreply@bobsmutualfunds.com. The link is valid for 30 minutes.
4. They create a new password: at least 8 characters, with at least one uppercase letter, one number, and one symbol. It cannot match any of their last five passwords.
5. They sign in with the new password and complete two-factor authentication.

chunks.heading: Changing a password while signed in
chunks.text: Clients can change their password at My Account → Security. In chat, you can process a password change request through the Update Security Settings task, which sends the client a secure link to set the new password; you never see or set it. See Procedure: Update Security Settings.

chunks.heading: The email didn't arrive
chunks.text:
- Ask the client to wait 5 minutes and check spam or junk folders.
- Confirm they are using the email address on file (ask them to tell you the address; do not read it out).
- If the email on file is out of date, they cannot reset by email. The email can be updated only after identity verification; for a locked-out client, that means a phone call to 1-800-BOB-FUND.
- Reset links expire after 30 minutes and only the latest link works.

chunks.heading: We never ask for passwords
chunks.text: Never ask a client to tell you their password, and stop them if they start to. See Phishing and investment scams.
How 2FA works on our accounts, enabling and changing methods, and recovering when a client loses their device.

chunks.heading: Requirement
chunks.text: Two-factor authentication is required for every online account. After entering their password, the client must confirm a one-time code sent by text message or generated by an authenticator app, or approve a sign-in prompt in the mobile app.

chunks.heading: Methods
chunks.text:
Method: Text message; How it works: A 6-digit code is texted to a verified mobile number; Notes: Most common; requires a verified phone
Method: Authenticator app; How it works: A rotating code from an app the client sets up with a QR code; Notes: Most secure; works without cell service
Method: Mobile app approval; How it works: A push prompt in the Bob's Mutual Funds app; Notes: Requires the app on a trusted device

chunks.heading: Changing methods
chunks.text: Clients can add or change methods at My Account → Security. Through chat, the Update Security Settings task can enable 2FA or remove a trusted device. Because 2FA is required, a request to "disable 2FA" is processed only as replacing one method with another; we do not leave an account without a second factor. Explain this to the client.

chunks.heading: Lost device
chunks.text:
If a client has lost access to their 2FA device and cannot sign in:
1. They must call 1-800-BOB-FUND; this cannot be completed in chat because the client cannot authenticate.
2. They will need the last four digits of their SSN, their account number, and their security question answers.
3. A 2FA reset takes up to 1 business day.
If the client is already signed in (for example, they have a new phone but the old one still works), they can switch methods themselves at My Account → Security.
Why online access locks, how long the lock lasts, and how clients regain access.

chunks.heading: Automatic lockout
chunks.text: After 5 failed sign-in attempts, the online login locks for 30 minutes. This protects the client from password-guessing attacks. The account itself (holdings, scheduled transactions) is unaffected; only online access is paused.

chunks.heading: Regaining access
chunks.text:
- Wait 30 minutes and try again, or
- Use Forgot Password to reset; a successful reset unlocks the login. See Password resets.
- If they cannot reset (for example, the email on file is outdated), they should call 1-800-BOB-FUND.

chunks.heading: Security holds
chunks.text: A login can also be locked by the Fraud team as a protective measure. A client in this situation sees a message asking them to call. Chat agents cannot lift a security hold. Route the client to the phone line, and do not speculate about why the hold was placed.

chunks.heading: If a client did not trigger the lockout
chunks.text: If a client says they did not attempt to sign in, someone else may have. Recommend a password reset and review recent activity together. See Suspected account takeover or unauthorized activity.

chunks.heading: Example
chunks.text:
Client: "It says my account is locked."
Agent: "That happens after five unsuccessful sign-in attempts, to protect your account. It unlocks automatically after 30 minutes, or right away if you reset your password using 'Forgot Password' on the sign-in page. Would you like me to walk you through the reset?"

chunks.heading: Repeated lockouts
chunks.text: If a client is locked out repeatedly without trying to sign in, someone may be attempting to access the account. Recommend a password change and review recent activity. See Suspected account takeover or unauthorized activity.
What a trusted device is, how clients manage them, and when to remove one.

chunks.heading: Definition
chunks.text: When a client signs in and completes 2FA on a device, they can mark it as trusted. For 30 days, sign-ins from that device skip the 2FA prompt. Trusted status ends after 30 days, or immediately if removed.

chunks.heading: Managing devices
chunks.text: Clients can see and remove trusted devices at My Account → Security → Trusted Devices. Through chat, the Update Security Settings task includes "Remove trusted device". See Procedure: Update Security Settings.

chunks.heading: When to recommend removing devices
chunks.text:
- A device was lost, stolen, sold, or given away.
- The client signed in on a shared or public computer.
- The client suspects someone else has accessed the account.
In a suspected compromise, remove all trusted devices and reset the password.

chunks.heading: How clients see their devices
chunks.text: The Trusted Devices list shows each device's type (for example "iPhone, Bob's app" or "Windows, Chrome"), the approximate location of its last sign-in, and when it was last used. Clients who don't recognize a device should remove it and reset their password.

chunks.heading: Example
chunks.text:
Client: "I sold my old phone. Should I do anything?"
Agent: "Good thinking. Since that phone was a trusted device, I'd recommend removing it so it can't skip the security code. You can do it at My Account → Security → Trusted Devices, or I can remove it for you now."

chunks.heading: Shared computers
chunks.text: Clients should never mark a shared or public computer as trusted, and should sign out fully when finished.

chunks.heading: Relationship to 2FA
chunks.text: Removing a trusted device does not disable 2FA; it means that device must complete 2FA again at the next sign-in. See Two-factor authentication (2FA).
Chat procedure for password changes, enabling 2FA, changing 2FA methods, and removing trusted devices.

chunks.heading: What the task collects
chunks.text: Field: What to update; Options: Change password; Enable 2FA; Disable 2FA (processed as a method change); Remove trusted device

chunks.heading: Procedure
chunks.text:
1. Confirm the client is authenticated and the request is coming from the owner. Security changes are high risk; if anything seems off, re-verify. See Verifying client identity.
2. Let the task expert collect the action, or choose it from the task menu.
3. Review the Proposed Action and submit.
4. Explain what happens next:
- Change password: a secure link is sent to the email on file; the client sets the new password themselves. We never see it. - Enable 2FA: the client completes setup at My Account → Security (scan a QR code or verify a phone number). - Disable 2FA: 2FA is required, so explain that we can switch the method rather than remove it, and guide them to My Account → Security. - Remove trusted device: the device must complete 2FA on its next sign-in.

chunks.heading: Things to watch for
chunks.text:
- A request to change security settings immediately before or after a request to change contact details or move money is a fraud signal. Pause and verify.
- If a client says they are locked out, they are not authenticated, so they cannot use this task. Direct them to Password resets or Locked accounts.
Helping clients who forget their username or cannot sign in for other reasons.

chunks.heading: Forgotten username
chunks.text: Most clients sign in with their email address. If the client created a separate username, they can click Forgot Username on the sign-in page and enter their email address and the last four digits of their SSN; the username is emailed to them.

chunks.heading: Other sign-in problems
chunks.text:
Symptom: "Incorrect password" repeatedly; Likely cause: Wrong password, caps lock, saved old password; Fix: Reset password
Symptom: Locked out; Likely cause: 5 failed attempts; Fix: Wait 30 minutes or reset; see Locked accounts
Symptom: No 2FA code; Likely cause: Wrong phone, carrier delay, number changed; Fix: Wait 2 minutes, request a new code; if the number changed, call to update it
Symptom: Page won't load; Likely cause: Browser cache, unsupported browser, network; Fix: Clear cache, try another browser; see Website and app errors
Symptom: "Account under review" message; Likely cause: Protective hold; Fix: Call 1-800-BOB-FUND

chunks.heading: New clients
chunks.text: Clients who opened an account but have not enrolled for online access can enroll from the sign-in page with their account number, SSN, and date of birth.

chunks.heading: Example
chunks.text:
Client: "I don't remember my username."
Agent: "No problem. On the sign-in page, click 'Forgot Username' and enter your email address and the last four digits of your Social Security number. We'll email your username to you. Most clients sign in with their email address, so try that first."
The automatic security notifications we send and what to tell a client who received one they don't recognize.

chunks.heading: Alerts we send
chunks.text:
We automatically notify clients by email (and text if they opt in) when:
- Their password is changed.
- Their email address, phone number, or mailing address is changed (the notice goes to both the old and the new address).
- A new bank account is linked.
- 2FA settings change or a trusted device is added.
- A new authorized user is added.
- A sign-in occurs from a new device.
- A withdrawal or outgoing transfer is requested.

chunks.heading: A client didn't make the change
chunks.text: If a client receives an alert for something they did not do, treat it as possible account takeover. Follow Suspected account takeover or unauthorized activity: verify identity, secure the login, escalate to the Fraud team, and review recent activity.

chunks.heading: A client wants fewer alerts
chunks.text: Security alerts for changes to credentials, contact details, banks, and access cannot be turned off. Marketing and informational emails can be managed at My Account → Preferences.

chunks.heading: Example
chunks.text:
Client: "I got an email saying my phone number was changed. I didn't do that."
Agent: "Thank you for telling us right away. Let's secure your account. First, I need to verify a few details..." Then follow Suspected account takeover or unauthorized activity: verify identity, escalate to Fraud, reset the password, review recent activity, and remove unknown devices.

chunks.heading: Alerts and joint accounts
chunks.text: Changes made by one joint owner to the shared account (for example, adding a bank) generate alerts to both owners.

chunks.page: Elder financial exploitation and vulnerable clients
chunks.text: Recognizing signs of exploitation or diminished capacity, what you may do, and how to escalate.

chunks.page: Elder financial exploitation and vulnerable clients
chunks.heading: Why this matters
chunks.text: Older clients and clients with diminished capacity are targeted by scammers and sometimes by people close to them. Federal and state rules allow, and our policy requires, that we act when we see red flags, including placing a temporary hold on a disbursement and contacting a trusted contact person.

chunks.page: Elder financial exploitation and vulnerable clients
chunks.heading: Red flags
chunks.text:
- A sudden, unexplained large withdrawal, especially to a new bank or a person.
- A new "friend", caregiver, or relative directing the conversation or answering for the client.
- The client seems confused about their accounts, repeats questions, or does not understand a transaction they are requesting.
- The client mentions an online romance, a lottery win that requires fees, or someone who needs urgent help.
- The client is afraid, secretive, or says they were told not to tell anyone.
- Changes to beneficiaries or authorized users that benefit a new person.

chunks.page: Elder financial exploitation and vulnerable clients
chunks.heading: What to do
chunks.text:
1. Stay patient and kind. Ask open questions: "Can you tell me what this money is for?"
2. Do not process a suspicious disbursement in the chat. You do not need to accuse anyone; say you need to complete an additional review.
3. Escalate to your team lead and the Senior Investor Protection team immediately. They can place a temporary hold, contact the trusted contact person, and if needed report to Adult Protective Services.
4. Document the specific observations in ACW (quotes, behaviors, amounts).

chunks.page: Elder financial exploitation and vulnerable clients
chunks.heading: Diminished capacity
chunks.text: If a client appears unable to understand a transaction, do not proceed with it, even if no one else is involved. Offer a callback and escalate. A trusted contact, power of attorney, or guardian may need to be involved. See Trusted contact person and Power of attorney.
What a trusted contact is, what they can and cannot do, and how clients add one.

chunks.heading: Definition
chunks.text: A trusted contact person is someone a client authorizes us to contact if we cannot reach the client, if we suspect financial exploitation, or if we have concerns about the client's health or capacity. We ask every client aged 18 and over to name one when opening an account, and periodically afterward. It is optional.

chunks.heading: What a trusted contact can and cannot do
chunks.text:
Can: Be contacted by us about our concerns; Cannot: See balances or activity
Can: Confirm the client's contact details or health status; Cannot: Place transactions
Can: Help identify a legal guardian, executor, or POA; Cannot: Change anything on the account
A trusted contact is not an authorized user and not a power of attorney.

chunks.heading: Adding or changing a trusted contact
chunks.text: Clients can add, update, or remove a trusted contact at My Account → Profile → Trusted Contact, providing the person's name, relationship, and phone or email. The trusted contact must be at least 18. Clients can ask in chat; guide them to the page or note the request for the Account Services team if they cannot do it online.

chunks.heading: Talking to clients about it
chunks.text: Frame it positively: "Many clients name a trusted contact so that if we ever can't reach you or have a concern, there's someone we can check with. They can't see your accounts or make changes."
The firm's history, philosophy, product lineup, and regulatory status, for answering "who are you" questions.

chunks.heading: Who we are
chunks.text:
Bob's Mutual Funds is a mutual fund company and brokerage serving individual investors. We offer a lineup of 36 low-cost BobsFunds mutual funds and the accounts to hold them in: individual and joint taxable accounts, custodial accounts for minors, trust accounts, Traditional, Roth, SEP, and inherited IRAs. Clients invest online through the client portal, by phone, and through chat with our virtual assistant and service agents.
The firm was founded by Bob, an investor with sixty years in the markets whose views appear in the "Bob's View" opinion columns in the client Library. Our philosophy is straightforward: low costs, broad diversification, and patience are the most reliable drivers of long-term results.

chunks.heading: What we offer
chunks.text:
- 36 mutual funds across U.S. stocks, sector stocks, international stocks, and bonds, nearly all index funds with expense ratios from 0.03% to 0.13%. See The BobsFunds lineup.
- No account fees: no maintenance fee, no IRA custodial fee, and $0 to buy, sell, or exchange BobsFunds funds.
- Self-service tools: online account opening, automatic investing, dividend reinvestment, beneficiary management, tax documents, an RMD calculator, and a retirement calculator.
- Education: the Library of how-to guides and opinion columns, and a podcast.

chunks.heading: What we do not offer
chunks.text: We do not offer individual stocks, ETFs, options, other firms' mutual funds, bank accounts, credit cards, loans, insurance, 401(k) plan administration, 529 plans, or HSAs. We do not provide individualized investment advice through service channels. See Products and services we don't offer.

chunks.heading: Regulatory status
chunks.text: Bob's Mutual Funds is a registered broker-dealer and a member of FINRA and SIPC. The BobsFunds funds are registered investment companies. Our service is subject to FINRA rules, SEC regulations, and federal privacy and anti-money-laundering laws. For SIPC questions see SIPC and the safety of client assets.

chunks.heading: Answering "are you a real company / are you safe?"
chunks.text: Clients sometimes ask whether their money is safe with us. You can say: client assets are held in the client's name, separate from the firm's own assets; fund assets are held by an independent custodian; we are a FINRA and SIPC member. Do not say investments are "safe" or "guaranteed": fund values go up and down with markets.
Every way a client can reach Bob's Mutual Funds, what each channel is best for, and how to refer clients between channels.

chunks.heading: Channels
chunks.text:
Channel: Virtual assistant (chat); Availability: 24/7; Best for: Quick answers, links to self-service pages, starting a task, scheduling a callback
Channel: Live chat with an agent; Availability: Monday–Friday 8:00 AM–8:00 PM ET; Best for: Account questions and service tasks
Channel: Phone: 1-800-BOB-FUND (1-800-262-3863); Availability: Monday–Friday 8:00 AM–8:00 PM ET; Saturday 9:00 AM–5:00 PM ET; Best for: Anything, including identity problems and locked-out clients
Channel: Licensed brokerage desk (phone; say "place a trade"); Availability: Monday–Friday 8:00 AM–7:30 PM ET; Best for: Trades by phone with a licensed broker
Channel: Estate Services (phone; say "inherited account"); Availability: Monday–Friday 8:00 AM–7:30 PM ET; Best for: Reporting a death, inherited accounts
Channel: Scheduled callback; Availability: Booked through chat; Best for: Advice-related conversations, specialist calls, follow-ups
Channel: Secure message; Availability: Sent any time from My Account → Messages; Best for: Non-urgent requests with attachments; reply within 1 business day (3 for complex)
Channel: Mail; Availability: See Mailing addresses; Best for: Checks, forms with original signatures, legal documents

chunks.heading: Choosing a channel for the client
chunks.text:
- If the client is locked out of online access, chat cannot help them authenticate. Give them the phone number.
- If the client needs to send documents (death certificate, trust certification), they can upload through a secure message or the document upload page, or mail certified copies.

- The request needs research that will take longer than a chat.

chunks.heading: Limits
chunks.text: Secure messages are not for urgent matters. Fraud reports, locked-out clients, and time-sensitive trades should use chat or phone. We never ask for passwords by secure message.

chunks.heading: Example uses
chunks.text:
- Sending a copy of a divorce decree for an IRA transfer.
- Asking for a cost basis history that requires research.
- Following up on an open request with a written trail.

chunks.text: Secure messages arrive in a separate service queue. If a client mentions in chat that they sent a secure message, you can check whether it has been answered and summarize the reply.

chunks.page: SIPC and the safety of client assets
chunks.text: What SIPC protects and does not protect, and how to answer questions about the safety of client assets.

chunks.page: SIPC and the safety of client assets
chunks.heading: What SIPC is
chunks.text: The Securities Investor Protection Corporation (SIPC) protects customers of member broker-dealers if the firm fails financially and client securities or cash are missing. Coverage is up to $500,000 per customer per capacity, including up to $250,000 for cash.

chunks.page: SIPC and the safety of client assets
chunks.heading: What SIPC does not cover
chunks.text: SIPC does not protect against market losses. If a fund's value declines, that is investment risk, not a loss covered by SIPC. SIPC also does not cover fraud by third parties outside the firm.

chunks.page: SIPC and the safety of client assets
chunks.heading: How client assets are protected
chunks.text:
- Client fund shares are registered in the client's name on the fund's records.
- Fund assets are held by an independent custodian bank, separate from Bob's Mutual Funds' corporate assets.
- Our broker-dealer is subject to SEC customer protection rules that require segregation of client assets.

chunks.page: SIPC and the safety of client assets
chunks.heading: How to answer
chunks.text: "Your fund shares are held in your name, and the funds' assets are held by an independent custodian, separate from our company's money. We're also a member of SIPC, which protects customers if a brokerage firm fails, up to $500,000. SIPC doesn't protect against market ups and downs." Provide the SIPC website (sipc.org) if they want more detail.

The basic brokerage account owned by one person: features, taxes, and common questions.

chunks.heading: What it is
chunks.text: An individual account is a taxable account owned by one person. It is the most flexible account we offer: no contribution limits, no income limits, no age restrictions on withdrawals, and no required distributions. The portal labels it "Taxable" or "Individual Taxable".

chunks.heading: Taxes
chunks.text:
Because the account is taxable, the owner pays tax each year on:
- Dividends paid by the funds, whether received in cash or reinvested. Many are "qualified dividends" taxed at lower capital-gains rates. See Qualified dividends.
- Capital gain distributions paid by the funds.
- Capital gains or losses when the owner sells or exchanges shares. See Cost basis methods.
We report this income on the consolidated Form 1099 each year. See Form 1099-DIV and Form 1099-B.

chunks.heading: Transfer on death
chunks.text: An individual account can carry a transfer-on-death (TOD) registration naming beneficiaries, so the assets pass directly to them without probate. See Transfer on death (TOD) for taxable accounts.

chunks.heading: Common questions
chunks.text:
Can I take money out any time?:
Yes. Sell shares and have the proceeds sent to the linked bank by ACH, by wire, or by check. Selling may create a taxable gain or loss.
Is there a limit on how much I can put in?:
No. Daily ACH deposits are limited to $100,000 per account; larger deposits can be made by wire. See Transfer limits.
Can I convert it to an IRA?:
No. An individual account cannot be converted into an IRA. The client can sell shares and use the cash to make an IRA contribution, subject to IRA limits, but the sale may be taxable.
Can I add my spouse?:
Adding an owner is a registration change, effectively moving the assets to a new joint account. See Registration changes.
Joint registrations we offer, how ownership passes at death, and what each owner can do.

chunks.heading: Registrations
chunks.text:
Registration: Joint Tenants with Rights of Survivorship (JTWROS); At the death of one owner: Passes automatically to the surviving owner(s); Notes: Our default and most common joint registration
Registration: Tenants in Common (TIC); At the death of one owner: The deceased owner's share passes to their estate; Notes: Shares may be unequal; must be specified
Registration: Community Property; At the death of one owner: Per state law; Notes: Available only for married owners in community-property states

chunks.heading: Who can do what
chunks.text:
- Either owner can view the account, buy, sell, and exchange.
- Redemption proceeds are paid to all owners jointly, or to a bank account registered to at least one owner.
- Changes to the registration (adding or removing an owner), closing the account, and adding an authorized user require all owners' consent.
- Each owner signs in with their own credentials.

chunks.heading: Taxes
chunks.text: The account is reported under the primary owner's Social Security number (the first owner listed). Owners may split the reported income between themselves on their own returns; that is a matter for their tax advisor.

chunks.heading: Death of a joint owner
chunks.text: For JTWROS, the survivor sends a certified death certificate and the account is re-registered in the survivor's name. See Surviving joint owners.

chunks.heading: Divorce
chunks.text: Removing an ex-spouse requires the consent of both owners or a court order. See Divorce and account transfers.

chunks.heading: Common questions
chunks.text:
Can a joint account have a beneficiary?:
A JTWROS account can have a TOD registration that takes effect after the last surviving owner dies. See Transfer on death (TOD) for taxable accounts.
Can one owner remove the other?:
Not alone. Both owners must sign, unless a court order directs the change.
Accounts held for a minor under the Uniform Transfers/Gifts to Minors Acts: ownership, control, taxes, and the age of termination.

chunks.heading: What they are
chunks.text: A custodial account holds assets that legally belong to a minor, managed by an adult custodian until the minor reaches the age of termination set by their state (usually 18 or 21; some states allow up to 25). We open these under the Uniform Transfers to Minors Act (UTMA) or, in states that use it, the Uniform Gifts to Minors Act (UGMA).

chunks.heading: Key rules
chunks.text:
- Gifts are irrevocable. Money put in belongs to the child. The custodian cannot take it back.
- The custodian controls the account and must use it only for the minor's benefit (not for basic support the parent is legally obligated to provide).
- One minor, one custodian per account. A successor custodian can be named.
- At the age of termination, the custodian must transfer the account to the former minor. See When a custodial account's minor comes of age.
- Taxes: income is reported under the minor's SSN. The "kiddie tax" may tax a child's unearned income above a threshold at the parents' rate; refer specifics to a tax professional.

chunks.heading: Who can do what
chunks.text: The custodian signs in and manages the account. The minor has no online access until the account is transferred. Grandparents or others may contribute by check or by bank transfer arranged with the custodian.

chunks.heading: Common questions
chunks.text:
Can a custodial account be a Roth IRA?:
