A minor with earned income can have a Roth IRA managed by a custodian. That is a custodial Roth IRA, opened as a Roth IRA with a minor owner. Contributions cannot exceed the minor's earned income for the year.
Can I move UTMA money into a 529 plan?:
We do not offer 529 plans. A custodian can liquidate a UTMA and move proceeds to a UTMA-owned 529 at another firm; this is a sale and may be taxable.
The custodian died. What happens?:
The successor custodian, if named, takes over. Otherwise a successor is appointed under state law. Route to Account Services.
How the Traditional IRA works: contributions, deductibility, tax-deferred growth, withdrawals, and RMDs.

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text: A Traditional IRA is an individual retirement account where investments grow tax-deferred. Contributions may be tax-deductible depending on income and workplace plan coverage. Withdrawals are taxed as ordinary income. Most money rolled over from pre-tax 401(k) and 403(b) plans goes into a Traditional IRA.

chunks.heading: Contributions
chunks.text:
- Anyone with earned income (or a spouse with earned income) can contribute; there is no upper age limit.
- Annual limit for 2026: $7,500, plus a $1,100 catch-up at age 50 or older. The limit is shared with Roth IRA contributions. See IRA contribution limits.
- Contributions for a tax year can be made until the tax-filing deadline of the next year (April 15). See Contribution deadlines.
- Deductibility depends on income if the client or their spouse is covered by a workplace plan. See Traditional IRA deductibility.

chunks.heading: Withdrawals
chunks.text:
- Withdrawals are taxed as ordinary income (except any nondeductible "basis", which the client tracks on IRS Form 8606).
- Withdrawals before age 59½ incur a 10% additional tax unless an exception applies. See The 10% early-withdrawal penalty and Exceptions to the early-withdrawal penalty.
- We withhold 10% federal tax by default unless the client elects otherwise. See Federal tax withholding on IRA distributions.

chunks.heading: Required minimum distributions
chunks.text: Owners must begin RMDs at age 73 (born 1951–1959) or 75 (born 1960 or later). See RMDs: overview.

chunks.heading: Converting to Roth
chunks.text: All or part of a Traditional IRA can be converted to a Roth IRA; the converted pre-tax amount is taxable income. See Roth conversions: overview.

chunks.heading: Common questions
chunks.text:
Is a Traditional IRA better than a Roth?:
That is a planning question. Explain the difference (tax break now versus tax-free later) and refer to a licensed professional for a recommendation.
Can I have both a Traditional and a Roth IRA?:
Yes. The annual contribution limit applies to the combined total.
How the Roth IRA works: after-tax contributions, income limits, tax-free qualified withdrawals, and no RMDs for the owner.

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text: A Roth IRA is funded with after-tax money. Qualified withdrawals, including all earnings, are completely tax-free. The original owner never has to take required minimum distributions.

chunks.heading: Contributions
chunks.text:
- Requires earned income (or a working spouse for a spousal Roth).
- 2026 limit: $7,500, plus $1,100 catch-up at 50+; shared with Traditional IRA contributions.
- Eligibility to contribute directly phases out at higher incomes. See Roth IRA income limits.
- No age limit for contributions.

chunks.heading: Withdrawals
chunks.text:
Roth withdrawals follow ordering rules: contributions come out first, then conversions, then earnings.
- Contributions can be withdrawn at any time, for any reason, with no tax or penalty.
- Earnings are tax-free and penalty-free in a qualified distribution: the client is 59½ or older (or disabled, or the distribution is to a beneficiary, or up to $10,000 lifetime for a first home purchase) and the first Roth IRA was opened at least five tax years ago.
- Non-qualified withdrawals of earnings may be taxed and penalized.
See Roth IRA distribution rules and Roth five-year rules.

chunks.heading: No RMDs
chunks.text: Roth IRA owners are never required to take RMDs. Beneficiaries who inherit a Roth IRA are subject to inherited IRA rules. See Inherited IRA.

chunks.heading: Common questions
chunks.text:
My income is too high. Can I still have a Roth?:
They cannot contribute directly above the phase-out range, but they can convert Traditional IRA money to Roth regardless of income. Some clients use a "backdoor Roth"; see The "backdoor Roth" strategy for the factual explanation and the advice boundary.
When does my 5-year clock start?:
On January 1 of the tax year of the first contribution to any Roth IRA. A 2025 contribution made in March 2026 starts the clock on January 1, 2025.
The Simplified Employee Pension IRA for self-employed people and small businesses: who can open one, contribution rules, and deadlines.

chunks.heading: Who it is for
chunks.text: A SEP-IRA lets self-employed individuals and small-business owners make tax-deductible retirement contributions for themselves and their eligible employees. Freelancers, consultants, sole proprietors, partners, and owners of small corporations use them.

chunks.heading: Contributions
chunks.text:
- Contributions are made by the employer (for a sole proprietor, that is the client acting as their own employer).
- The maximum is 25% of compensation (for a self-employed person, effectively about 20% of net self-employment earnings after the deduction for half of self-employment tax), up to $72,000 for 2026 ($70,000 for 2025). Compensation above $360,000 (2026) is disregarded.
- If the business has eligible employees, it must contribute the same percentage of pay for each eligible employee as for the owner.
- Contributions are discretionary: the business can contribute nothing in a lean year.
- The deadline is the business's tax-filing deadline, including extensions. See SEP-IRA contributions.

chunks.heading: Other rules
chunks.text:
- Withdrawals, taxes, the 10% early-withdrawal penalty, and RMDs work the same as a Traditional IRA.
- SEP-IRA balances can be converted to Roth.
- A SEP-IRA owner may also have a Traditional or Roth IRA and make regular IRA contributions to it, subject to the regular limits.

chunks.heading: Opening a SEP-IRA
chunks.text: The client opens a SEP-IRA for themselves online or through chat. Businesses with employees must also adopt a SEP plan document (IRS Form 5305-SEP); employees each open their own SEP-IRA. See Opening IRAs.

chunks.heading: Common questions
chunks.text:
How much can I put in my SEP?:
The calculation depends on the client's net self-employment income and is a tax question. Explain the 25%-of-compensation rule and the dollar cap, and suggest they confirm the exact figure with their tax preparer.
Should I use a SEP or a Solo 401(k)?:
We do not offer Solo 401(k) plans. The client Library has a factual comparison article (SEP-IRA vs. Solo 401(k)); you may send it, but the choice is a planning decision.
How a spouse without earned income can contribute to an IRA based on the working spouse's income.

chunks.heading: The rule
chunks.text: Normally an IRA contribution requires earned income. A married couple filing a joint return can make IRA contributions for a spouse with little or no earned income, based on the working spouse's income. This is commonly called a spousal IRA. It is not a separate account type: it is a regular Traditional or Roth IRA owned by the non-working spouse.

chunks.heading: Limits
chunks.text:
- Each spouse may contribute up to the annual limit ($7,500 in 2026, plus $1,100 catch-up if 50+).
- The couple's combined IRA contributions cannot exceed the couple's combined taxable compensation.
- Roth eligibility uses the couple's joint modified adjusted gross income. See Roth IRA income limits.

chunks.heading: Ownership
chunks.text: The IRA belongs entirely to the spouse in whose name it is opened, even though the money came from the working spouse. The account owner names their own beneficiaries.

chunks.heading: How to open
chunks.text: The non-working spouse opens a Traditional or Roth IRA in their own name. The working spouse can fund it from a joint bank account. When contributing, the client should designate the tax year.
The account that holds IRA assets for a beneficiary after the owner dies, and how its distribution rules depend on the beneficiary type.

chunks.heading: What it is
chunks.text: When an IRA owner dies, beneficiaries usually move their share into an inherited IRA (sometimes called a beneficiary IRA) titled, for example, "Jane Smith, deceased (date), FBO John Smith, beneficiary". The assets stay tax-deferred (or tax-free for an inherited Roth) while the beneficiary takes distributions under special rules. No new contributions are allowed.

chunks.heading: Distribution rules depend on the beneficiary
chunks.text:
Beneficiary: Surviving spouse; Main options: Treat as their own IRA, roll over to their own IRA, or keep as an inherited IRA
Beneficiary: Eligible designated beneficiary (minor child of the owner, disabled, chronically ill, or not more than 10 years younger than the owner); Main options: Distributions over life expectancy (a minor child switches to the 10-year rule at 21)
Beneficiary: Other individual (designated beneficiary); Main options: Must empty the account by the end of the 10th year after death; annual RMDs in years 1–9 if the owner had started RMDs
Beneficiary: Estate, charity, or non-qualifying trust; Main options: 5-year rule if the owner died before RMDs began; otherwise over the owner's remaining life expectancy
Details: Options for a surviving spouse, Options for non-spouse beneficiaries, Eligible designated beneficiaries, Inherited IRA RMDs.

chunks.heading: Taxes and penalties
chunks.text: Distributions from an inherited Traditional IRA are taxable income but are never subject to the 10% early-withdrawal penalty, whatever the beneficiary's age. Inherited Roth distributions are generally tax-free if the original owner's Roth had met the five-year requirement.

chunks.heading: Setting one up
chunks.text: Inherited IRAs are set up by Estate Services after the death is reported and documentation is received. Chat agents should not open inherited IRAs through the regular account-opening task. See When someone reports a death.
Accounts owned by a trust: what we need to open one, who can act, and how trust accounts are taxed.

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text: A trust account is registered in the name of a trust, for example "Margaret Lee and David Lee, Trustees of the Lee Family Trust dated 03/14/2019". The trustees manage the account according to the trust document. Most trusts we see are revocable living trusts used in estate planning.

chunks.heading: Opening
chunks.text:
To open a trust account we need:
- A Certification of Trust (also called Trustee Certification), or the trust document's pages showing the trust's name and date, the trustees' names and powers, and the signature pages.
- Identification for each trustee.
- The trust's taxpayer ID: for a revocable trust, usually the grantor's SSN; for an irrevocable trust, an EIN.
Trust accounts cannot be opened through the chat account-opening task. Clients start the application online (Open an Account → Trust) or by form, and Account Services reviews the documents. See Opening trust accounts.

chunks.heading: Who can act
chunks.text: Trustees named on the account act for the trust. If there are co-trustees, the trust document says whether one can act alone or all must sign. Account Services records this when the account is opened. Beneficiaries of the trust have no access unless they are also trustees.

chunks.heading: Taxes
chunks.text: A revocable trust's income is usually reported under the grantor's SSN and taxed to them. An irrevocable trust files its own tax return. This is a question for the client's tax advisor.

chunks.heading: Trust as an IRA beneficiary
chunks.text: A trust can be named as the beneficiary of an IRA, which raises complex distribution rules. See Trusts, estates, and charities as beneficiaries.

chunks.heading: Changing trustees
chunks.text: If a trustee dies, resigns, or is added, Account Services needs an updated Certification of Trust or amendment. See Retitling accounts to a trust.
Accounts opened in the name of a deceased person's estate to settle their affairs.

chunks.heading: When an estate account is used
chunks.text: When an account owner dies without a surviving joint owner, TOD registration, or named beneficiary (for non-IRA accounts), the assets pass through the estate. The executor (named in the will) or administrator (appointed by the court) opens an estate account, registered for example "Estate of Robert Chen, Linda Chen, Executor", to collect and distribute the assets.

chunks.heading: Requirements
chunks.text:
- Certified death certificate.
- Letters Testamentary (for an executor) or Letters of Administration (for an administrator), issued by the court, usually dated within the last 60 days.
- An EIN for the estate.
- Identification for the executor.
Smaller estates may qualify for a simplified process using a small-estate affidavit. See Small estates and affidavits.

chunks.heading: Handling
chunks.text: Estate accounts are opened and managed by Estate Services. Chat agents should express condolences, explain the general process, and connect the executor with Estate Services. See When someone reports a death and Documents needed after a death.

chunks.heading: Example
chunks.text: A client's mother died without a will naming beneficiaries on her taxable account. The court appoints the client as administrator. The client provides Letters of Administration, the death certificate, and an estate EIN; Estate Services opens an estate account, moves the shares into it, and the client later distributes the assets to heirs as the court directs.

chunks.heading: Taxes
chunks.text: Income earned by the estate account after death is reported under the estate's EIN and on the estate's tax return.

chunks.page: Products and services we don't offer
chunks.text: What Bob's Mutual Funds does not offer, and how to respond when a client asks for it.

chunks.page: Products and services we don't offer
chunks.heading: Not offered
chunks.text:
Product or service: Individual stocks, ETFs, bonds, options; What to tell the client: We offer BobsFunds mutual funds only. Many of our funds track the same indexes as popular ETFs.
Product or service: Other companies' mutual funds; What to tell the client: We hold only BobsFunds funds. If a client transfers in other funds, they must be sold at the other firm first. See Incoming ACAT transfers.
Product or service: Money market fund / cash sweep with interest; What to tell the client: Uninvested cash is held in the account without interest. Our Short-Term Treasury fund (BFST) is a low-risk bond fund, but it is not a money market fund and can lose value.
Product or service: Bank accounts, debit cards, checkwriting; What to tell the client: Not offered.
Product or service: 401(k) plan administration, Solo 401(k); What to tell the client: Not offered. We accept rollovers from 401(k) plans.
Product or service: SIMPLE IRA; What to tell the client: Not offered. A SIMPLE IRA can be rolled to a Traditional IRA after the 2-year participation period.
Product or service: 529 education plans, Coverdell ESAs; What to tell the client: Not offered.
Product or service: HSAs; What to tell the client: Not offered.
Product or service: Annuities, insurance; What to tell the client: Not offered.
Product or service: Margin loans, borrowing against an account; What to tell the client: Not offered. IRA assets can never be pledged as collateral.
Product or service: Managed accounts, financial planning; What to tell the client: Not offered through service channels; clients who want advice are referred to a licensed professional by callback.
Product or service: Cryptocurrency; What to tell the client: Not offered.

chunks.page: Products and services we don't offer
chunks.heading: How to respond
chunks.text: Be direct and helpful. "We don't offer individual stocks; our accounts hold BobsFunds mutual funds. If you're looking for broad stock market exposure, I can tell you about our index funds." Describe our funds factually; do not suggest that a fund is a good substitute for the client's specific goal (that would be advice).

chunks.page: Talking about which account to open
chunks.text: How to help a client compare account types without crossing into advice.

chunks.page: Talking about which account to open
chunks.heading: The situation
chunks.text: Clients often ask "Should I open a Roth or a Traditional IRA?" or "What account should I use to save for my kids?" These are planning questions. You can help a great deal without making a recommendation.

chunks.page: Talking about which account to open
chunks.heading: What you can do
chunks.text:
- Explain each account type's rules factually: who can contribute, limits, tax treatment, access to money.
- Ask neutral questions that help the client apply the rules themselves: "Do you have earned income this year?" "Are you covered by a retirement plan at work?" These clarify eligibility, not suitability.
- Point out eligibility facts: "Based on the income you mentioned, a direct Roth contribution would be limited this year."
- Send the relevant client-facing articles.

chunks.page: Talking about which account to open
chunks.heading: What you cannot do
chunks.text:
- Say which account is better for the client.
- Predict their future tax bracket or say "you'll save money" with one option.
- Recommend a split between account types.

chunks.page: Talking about which account to open
chunks.heading: Script
chunks.text: "Both are great tools, and the right one depends on your tax situation now versus in retirement, which is a planning question I'm not able to answer for you. I can walk you through how each one works, or I can set up a call with a licensed professional who can look at your situation. Which would you prefer?" See Declining advice requests.
The ways to open an account, which account types can be opened where, and the typical timeline.

chunks.heading: Ways to open
chunks.text:
Path: Online (Open an Account); Account types: Individual, joint, custodial, Traditional IRA, Roth IRA, SEP-IRA, trust; Notes: About 10 minutes; most approved instantly
Path: Chat (Open a New Account task); Account types: Roth IRA, Traditional IRA, SEP-IRA, Taxable (individual) for existing clients; Notes: The client must already have a verified profile
Path: Paper application; Account types: All types; Notes: Mailed to the PO Box; slowest
Path: Estate Services; Account types: Inherited IRA, estate accounts; Notes: Opened as part of settling a death

chunks.heading: Timeline
chunks.text: Most online applications are approved immediately after automated identity verification. A small number need more documentation and take 1–3 business days after the documents arrive. Paper applications take 5–7 business days after receipt.

chunks.heading: Minimums and fees
chunks.text: The minimum to open any account is $1, and a client may open an account with $0 and fund it later. There are no account opening fees, maintenance fees, or IRA custodial fees.

chunks.heading: Existing clients versus new clients
chunks.text: An existing client with a verified profile can open an additional account in minutes, through the portal or chat, because we already have their identity information. A brand-new client must complete the full online application, including identity verification. Prospects who ask in chat should be sent to Open an Account.

chunks.heading: Related pages
chunks.text:
- What's needed to apply
- Identity verification for new accounts (CIP)
- Funding a new account
- Opening IRAs
- Procedure: Open a New Account (chat)
The information and documents an applicant needs, by account type.

chunks.heading: Every applicant
chunks.text:
- Full legal name, date of birth, residential street address (a PO Box alone is not accepted as a residential address).
- Social Security number or Individual Taxpayer Identification Number.
- U.S. citizenship or residency status.
- Employment status and employer name (and whether they are affiliated with a brokerage firm or are a senior officer of a public company).
- Email address and mobile phone number.
- A trusted contact person (optional, requested). See Trusted contact person.

chunks.heading: By account type
chunks.text:
Account: Joint; Additional requirements: All of the above for each owner; choice of registration (JTWROS or tenants in common)
Account: Custodial; Additional requirements: Custodian's information plus the minor's name, date of birth, SSN; state of the UTMA/UGMA
Account: Traditional / Roth IRA; Additional requirements: Beneficiary designations (name, relationship, date of birth; SSN optional but recommended)
Account: SEP-IRA; Additional requirements: As an IRA; employer name; whether a SEP plan document is in place
Account: Trust; Additional requirements: Certification of Trust, trustee IDs, trust taxpayer ID
Account: Estate; Additional requirements: Letters Testamentary or Administration, death certificate, estate EIN

chunks.heading: Funding information
chunks.text: To fund electronically, the applicant links a bank account (routing and account numbers, or instant verification). They can also fund by check, wire, transfer from another firm, or rollover. See Funding a new account.

chunks.heading: Who may not open an account online
chunks.text:
- Applicants under 18 (they need a custodial account opened by an adult).
- Non-U.S. persons without a U.S. taxpayer ID and address. See Non-U.S. persons and clients living abroad.
- Applicants whose identity cannot be verified automatically (they may be asked for documents).
Why we verify the identity of every new client, how automated verification works, and what documents we request when it fails.

chunks.heading: The Customer Identification Program
chunks.text: Federal anti-money-laundering rules require every financial firm to verify the identity of anyone opening an account. Our Customer Identification Program (CIP) collects name, date of birth, address, and taxpayer ID, then verifies them against independent data sources.

chunks.heading: Automated verification
chunks.text: For most applicants, verification happens in seconds during the online application. The applicant may be asked a few knowledge-based questions drawn from public records (for example, a previous street address).

chunks.heading: When automated verification fails
chunks.text:
If verification fails, the application is pended and the applicant is asked to upload:
- An unexpired government-issued photo ID (driver's license, state ID, or passport), and
- A document showing their residential address if it differs from the ID (a recent utility bill, bank statement, or lease).
Once documents are received, Account Services reviews them within 1–3 business days.

chunks.heading: Common causes
chunks.text:
- A recent move, so records show an old address.
- A name change (marriage, divorce) not yet reflected in records.
- A typo in the SSN or date of birth.
- A credit freeze: some identity checks use credit bureau data. A freeze does not prevent verification but may require documents.
- Thin records for young applicants or recent immigrants.

chunks.heading: Talking to applicants
chunks.text: Do not say "you failed verification". Say: "We need a little more information to confirm your identity, which we do for everyone's protection. Please upload a copy of your photo ID through the link in your application." We cannot override CIP or open an account without verification.
The ways to put money into a newly opened account and when the money is invested.

chunks.heading: Funding options
chunks.text:
Method: Bank transfer (ACH) from a linked bank; Timing: 2–3 business days; Notes: Most common; up to $100,000 per day
Method: Wire; Timing: Same day if received before 4:00 PM ET; Notes: No limit; free incoming
Method: Check; Timing: When received at the processing center; Notes: Payable to Bob's Mutual Funds
Method: Transfer from another firm (ACAT); Timing: 5–7 business days; Notes: Taxable or IRA to like account
Method: Rollover from an employer plan; Timing: 5–15 business days after the plan releases funds; Notes: Into a Traditional or Roth IRA
Method: Exchange or transfer from another Bob's account; Timing: Same day; Notes: Between accounts with the same owner and tax type; see below

chunks.heading: Is the money invested automatically?
chunks.text: At account opening the client chooses one or more funds and the amount for each. Money that arrives is invested at the NAV on the day it arrives in good order. If the client does not choose a fund, the money is held as uninvested cash in the account until they place a purchase. Remind clients who fund without choosing a fund that cash does not earn a return here.

chunks.heading: IRA funding
chunks.text: For an IRA, the client must say whether a deposit is a contribution (and for which tax year), a rollover, or a transfer. Contributions are subject to annual limits; rollovers and transfers are not. See IRA contribution limits and Rollovers and transfers: overview.

chunks.heading: Moving money between the client's own accounts
chunks.text: Money can move between two of the client's taxable accounts of the same ownership by journal. Money cannot move from a taxable account into an IRA except as a contribution (subject to the limit), and from an IRA to a taxable account only as a distribution (taxable).
Specific steps and checks for opening Traditional, Roth, and SEP IRAs, including beneficiaries and funding.

chunks.heading: Choosing the type
chunks.text: The client must choose Traditional, Roth, or SEP. If they are unsure, explain the differences factually and avoid recommending. See Talking about which account to open.

chunks.heading: Steps
chunks.text:
1. Choose the IRA type.
2. Name beneficiaries: primary and contingent, with percentages totaling 100% at each level. Beneficiaries can be added later, but we strongly encourage naming them at opening. See Beneficiaries: overview.
3. Choose funding: contribution (with tax year), rollover, or transfer.
4. Choose investments.
5. Review and sign electronically.

chunks.heading: Checks before funding a contribution
chunks.text:
- Eligibility: does the client have earned income (or a working spouse)?
- Limit: will the contribution, added to the client's other IRA contributions for the year at any firm, stay within the limit? The contributions summary shows contributions at Bob's only. See The IRA contributions summary.
- Roth income: is the client within the Roth income limits? We do not verify income; the client is responsible, but you should mention the limits if the client raises income.
- Tax year: between January 1 and April 15, ask which year the contribution is for.

chunks.heading: SEP-IRAs
chunks.text: A self-employed client opens a SEP-IRA for themselves like any IRA. If the business has employees, it must also adopt a SEP plan (Form 5305-SEP) and contribute for eligible employees. Each employee opens their own SEP-IRA. Contributions are made by the business, not as personal contributions.

chunks.heading: Inherited IRAs
chunks.text: Not opened through the regular IRA flow. See Inherited IRA.
Steps and requirements specific to joint accounts and custodial accounts for minors.

chunks.heading: Joint accounts
chunks.text:
- Both (or all) owners must provide their personal information and pass identity verification.
- The first owner listed is the primary owner for tax reporting.
- Choose the registration: JTWROS (default) or tenants in common with percentages. See Joint accounts.
- The first owner starts the online application and invites the second owner, who receives an email to complete their part and sign. The account opens when both have signed.
- Each owner creates their own login.

chunks.heading: Custodial accounts
chunks.text:
- Opened by an adult custodian for one minor.
- The custodian provides their own information and the minor's name, date of birth, and SSN. The minor must have an SSN.
- The state's UTMA or UGMA law applies, usually the minor's state of residence; this determines the age of termination.
- The custodian may name a successor custodian.
- Explain that gifts to a custodial account are irrevocable and belong to the child. See Custodial accounts (UTMA/UGMA).

chunks.heading: Custodial Roth IRA
chunks.text: A minor with earned income can have a Roth IRA with a parent or guardian as custodian. The custodian opens it through the IRA flow, indicating the owner is a minor. Contributions cannot exceed the minor's earned income for the year. Keep records of the child's earnings (pay stubs, a log of babysitting or yard-work income).
How trust accounts are opened, the documents we need, and why they can't be opened in chat.

chunks.heading: Process
chunks.text:
1. The trustee starts the application online (Open an Account → Trust) or downloads the trust account application.
2. They provide trust details: exact trust name, date of the trust, type (revocable or irrevocable), taxpayer ID, and each trustee's information.
3. They upload a Certification of Trust or the relevant pages of the trust document: the first page (name and date), pages naming trustees and their powers, and the signature pages.
4. Account Services reviews the documents, usually within 1–3 business days, and the account opens.

chunks.heading: Why not in chat
chunks.text: The chat account-opening task opens individual accounts and IRAs for the client's own profile. Trust registrations need document review, which the chat task cannot perform. Send the client to the online trust application and explain the timeline.

chunks.heading: Moving existing assets into a trust
chunks.text: Clients who create a revocable living trust often want to retitle their existing taxable accounts in the trust's name. This is a registration change, not a sale, and is not a taxable event for a revocable trust where the grantor's SSN is used. See Retitling accounts to a trust. IRAs cannot be retitled to a trust; instead, a trust can be named as IRA beneficiary.
How to check an application's status and the common reasons applications are held.

chunks.heading: Checking status
chunks.text:
Applicants can see their application status by signing in with the credentials they created. Statuses:
Status: Submitted; Meaning: Received; automated checks running
Status: Action needed; Meaning: We need documents or a signature from the applicant (or a joint owner)
Status: Under review; Meaning: Account Services is reviewing documents
Status: Approved; Meaning: The account is open; funding can proceed
Status: Declined; Meaning: We were unable to open the account

chunks.heading: Common reasons for delay
chunks.text:
- Identity verification needs documents. See Identity verification for new accounts (CIP).
- A joint owner has not signed.
- Trust documents are incomplete or the trustee names don't match.
- The applicant reported affiliation with a brokerage firm, which requires a letter from their employer's compliance department.
- The residential address is a PO Box or commercial mail drop.
- The applicant is on a sanctions or watch list match that must be cleared (we cannot tell the applicant this). See Sanctions screening (OFAC).

chunks.heading: Declined applications
chunks.text: If an application is declined, the applicant receives a letter. Agents cannot discuss reasons that relate to AML or sanctions screening. For other reasons (incomplete information), help the applicant reapply.

chunks.page: Non-U.S. persons and clients living abroad
chunks.text: Who can open an account, and what happens when an existing client moves outside the United States.

chunks.page: Non-U.S. persons and clients living abroad
chunks.heading: Eligibility
chunks.text: We open accounts only for U.S. citizens and resident aliens with a U.S. residential address and a valid SSN or ITIN. We do not open accounts for non-resident aliens.

chunks.page: Non-U.S. persons and clients living abroad
chunks.heading: Clients who move abroad
chunks.text:
Existing clients who move outside the United States:
- Must update their address. A foreign address may restrict the account: depending on the country, purchases (including automatic investments) may be blocked because the funds are not registered for sale there. Existing holdings may be held and sold.
- U.S. citizens abroad remain subject to U.S. tax reporting. Non-U.S. residents may be subject to different withholding.
- Military and diplomatic personnel with APO/FPO/DPO addresses are treated as U.S. addresses and are not restricted.
Route clients moving abroad to Account Services for a review of what their account can do. Do not promise that purchases can continue.

chunks.page: Non-U.S. persons and clients living abroad
chunks.heading: Tax forms
chunks.text: U.S. persons certify their status on Form W-9 at account opening. A change to non-resident status requires a Form W-8BEN and is handled by Account Services.

chunks.page: Non-U.S. persons and clients living abroad
chunks.heading: Example
chunks.text:
Client: "I'm moving to Portugal next year. Can I keep my account?"
Agent: "Yes, you can keep your account and your existing investments. Depending on your new country, new purchases, including automatic investments, may be restricted. Once you have your new address, our Account Services team will review what your account can do. You'll also want a U.S. bank account for transfers."
Chat procedure for opening a Roth IRA, Traditional IRA, SEP-IRA, or taxable account for an existing client.

chunks.heading: What the task collects
chunks.text:
Field: Account type; Options or format: Roth IRA, Traditional IRA, SEP-IRA, Taxable (individual)
Field: Initial contribution; Options or format: Dollar amount; $0 is allowed
Field: Funding source; Options or format: Bank transfer (ACH), Check, Rollover

chunks.heading: Before you start
chunks.text:
- The client must be an existing, authenticated client. New clients use the online application.
- Joint, custodial, trust, and inherited accounts cannot be opened with this task.

chunks.heading: Checks while the details are collected
chunks.text:
- Roth IRA: if the client mentions their income, check it against Roth IRA income limits. If they are above the limit, explain that a direct contribution is not allowed; do not recommend a backdoor strategy.
- Any IRA with a contribution: check the contribution against the client's remaining limit (see the contributions summary in the info panel) and ask which tax year it is for, if between January 1 and April 15.
- SEP-IRA: confirm the client is self-employed or their employer has a SEP plan.
- Rollover funding: the initial amount is an estimate; the rollover itself is started with Procedure: Roll Over From Another Institution (chat) after the account opens.
- Check funding: give the mailing address and tell the client to write the new account number on the check.

chunks.heading: After submitting
chunks.text:
- The new account appears in the client's portfolio, usually immediately.
- Remind the client to name beneficiaries for an IRA (link: My Account → Beneficiaries) and to choose investments. Money that arrives without fund instructions is held as cash.
- For ACH funding, the transfer takes 2–3 business days.

chunks.heading: Common mistakes
chunks.text:
- Opening a second Roth IRA when the client already has one. This is allowed, but ask whether they meant to contribute to the existing one.
- Recording a rollover as a contribution, which could create an excess contribution. Be clear about the source of the money.
Chat procedure for changing a client's phone number, email address, or mailing address, with the fraud checks that go with it.

chunks.heading: What the task collects
chunks.text:
Field: What to update; Options or format: Phone number, Email address, Mailing address
Field: New value; Options or format: The new phone number, email address, or full mailing address

chunks.heading: Why contact changes are sensitive
chunks.text: A change of email, phone, or address is the first step in most account takeovers: a fraudster changes the contact details so that security alerts and password reset links go to them, then moves money. That is why we send a notice to both the old and the new contact point, and why some money movement is restricted for a short period after a change.

chunks.heading: Procedure
chunks.text:
1. Confirm the chat is authenticated and nothing suggests a third party. If the client is also asking to move money or add a bank in the same conversation, re-verify identity first. See Verifying client identity.
2. Let the task expert collect what to update and the new value, or start the task from the task menu.
3. Read the new value back exactly as collected:
- Phone: all ten digits, and whether it is mobile (needed for text-message 2FA). - Email: spell out unusual parts. A typo means the client stops receiving statements and reset links. - Address: street, unit, city, state, ZIP. A PO Box can be a mailing address but not a residential address.
1. Get a clear confirmation, review the Proposed Action, and submit.
2. Tell the client what happens next (below).

chunks.heading: What happens next
chunks.text:
- Email: a verification code is sent to the new address. The client confirms it at My Account → Profile; until verified, statements and alerts continue to the old address. A notice of the change goes to the old address.
- Phone: the new number must be verified by a code before it can be used for 2FA text messages.
- Address: takes effect immediately for mail. A notice goes to both the old and new addresses.

chunks.heading: Restrictions after a change
chunks.text:
- For 15 days after an address change, redemption checks cannot be mailed to the new address without a medallion signature guarantee. See Medallion signature guarantees.
- For 10 days after an email or phone change, a newly linked bank account cannot receive electronic redemptions without a verification call.
These rules protect clients. Explain them as protection: "Because your address just changed, for the next 15 days we'll need extra verification to mail a check there. That protects you if someone else ever tried to change your address."

chunks.heading: Moving between states
chunks.text: An address change to a new state can affect state tax withholding on IRA distributions and the account's state of residence for UTMA accounts. Mention this if the client has scheduled distributions. See State tax withholding.
Seasonal addresses, temporary addresses, returned mail, military addresses, and moves abroad.

chunks.heading: Seasonal and temporary addresses
chunks.text:
Clients who split the year between two homes (for example, summer in Maine, winter in Florida) can add a seasonal address with start and end dates at My Account → Profile. Mail goes to the seasonal address during those dates and reverts automatically. The legal (residential) address does not change, so state tax withholding follows the legal address.
A temporary address for a single month (travel, hospital stay) can be set the same way.

chunks.heading: Returned mail
chunks.text:
If mail is returned as undeliverable, the account is flagged "address unknown":
- Further mail is suspended.
- Checks are not mailed.
- After a long period of returned mail and no client contact, the account may become subject to state unclaimed property rules. See Dormant accounts and unclaimed property.
When a flagged client contacts us, verify identity and update the address; the flag clears.

chunks.heading: Military addresses
chunks.text: APO, FPO, and DPO addresses are accepted as U.S. addresses. They do not restrict purchases. Service members may also keep a stateside legal address.

chunks.heading: Moving abroad
chunks.text: A foreign address may restrict new purchases. See Non-U.S. persons and clients living abroad. Route to Account Services.

chunks.heading: Multiple accounts
chunks.text: An address change applies to all of the client's accounts where they are the owner. For joint accounts, changing the address changes it for all owners; confirm that is intended, and if the joint owners now live apart, the account can only have one address of record. Each owner's own profile address is separate.
Verification of new email addresses and phone numbers, and what goes to each contact point.

chunks.heading: Email
chunks.text:
The email address on file is used for:
- Sign-in (most clients sign in with their email).
- Password reset links.
- Security alerts.
- Statement, confirmation, and tax form notifications for paperless clients.
- Secure message notifications.
When the email changes, a code is sent to the new address and must be confirmed. Until it is confirmed, the old address remains active. A change notice goes to the old address. If a client receives a change notice they did not request, see Suspected account takeover or unauthorized activity.

chunks.heading: Phone
chunks.text: Clients may have several phone numbers (mobile, home, work). The mobile number marked for security is used for 2FA codes. Each number shows a verified or unverified status in the client info panel. A new number must be verified by a one-time code before it can receive 2FA codes.

chunks.heading: The client lost access to their old email or phone
chunks.text: If the client is signed in, they can update details themselves and verify the new ones. If they are locked out because codes go to an old phone or reset emails go to a closed email account, they must call 1-800-BOB-FUND to verify their identity by phone. Chat cannot authenticate a locked-out client.

chunks.heading: Communication preferences
chunks.text: Email and text notification preferences (which messages to receive by text, for example trade confirmations) are at My Account → Preferences. Security alerts cannot be turned off. See Communication preferences.
How clients change their name after marriage, divorce, or court order, and why it isn't a chat task.

chunks.heading: Requirements
chunks.text:
A name change must match the client's legal name on file with the Social Security Administration, because we report tax information under name and SSN. The client must provide:
- A completed Name Change form (from the Forms page), and
- A copy of the legal document: marriage certificate, divorce decree that restores a former name, or court order.
Some registrations (trusts, custodial accounts) may need additional paperwork.

chunks.heading: Process
chunks.text:
1. The client uploads the form and document through a secure message or the document upload page, or mails them.
2. Account Services updates the name on all of the client's accounts, usually within 3 business days.
3. The client receives confirmation; their sign-in does not change.

chunks.heading: Why it cannot be done in chat
chunks.text: Updating the name requires reviewing a legal document. The Update Contact Information task does not handle names. Explain the steps and send the link to the form.

chunks.heading: Tips for clients
chunks.text:
- Update their name with the Social Security Administration first. A mismatch between our records and the SSA can cause a TIN-mismatch notice and backup withholding. See Form W-9 and backup withholding.
- Linked bank accounts must still be in the client's name; if the bank account name changes too, they may need to re-link it.
- Beneficiaries the client named are unaffected, but a client changing their name after marriage or divorce often wants to review beneficiaries too. See Reviewing beneficiaries after life events.
The three access levels, what each allows, and the chat procedure for adding an authorized user (which the owner must approve).

chunks.heading: Access levels
chunks.text:
Level: View-only; Can see accounts: Yes; Can trade and exchange: No; Can move money: No; Can change ownership, beneficiaries, open or close accounts: No
Level: Limited access; Can see accounts: Yes; Can trade and exchange: Yes; Can move money: Only back to the owner's linked bank; Can change ownership, beneficiaries, open or close accounts: No
Level: Full access; Can see accounts: Yes; Can trade and exchange: Yes; Can move money: Yes, including to outside accounts; Can change ownership, beneficiaries, open or close accounts: Yes, including closing accounts
Authorized users sign in with their own credentials. They can be added to some or all of the owner's accounts. For joint accounts, all owners must approve.

chunks.heading: Typical uses
chunks.text:
- View-only: an accountant, an adult child keeping an eye on a parent's accounts, a financial advisor at another firm.
- Limited access: a spouse who manages investments.
- Full access: rarely appropriate; usually someone with legal authority anyway. Mention a power of attorney as an alternative for someone who will manage finances if the owner becomes incapacitated. See Power of attorney.

chunks.heading: Chat procedure (Add Authorized Account User)
chunks.text:
Field: Person's full name; Format: First and last name
Field: Person's email address; Format: Used to invite them to create a login
Field: Access level; Format: View-only, Limited access, Full access
1. The account owner must be the one in the chat. A request from the would-be user ("add me to my mother's account") cannot proceed.
2. Explain the three levels clearly. The task expert explains them too, but make sure the owner understands what Full access allows.
3. When the Proposed Action appears, click Send to client. This is a client-submitted task: the owner must approve it in their own chat window. See Actions the client must submit.
4. When the owner submits, the invited person receives an email to create their login and verify their identity. Access starts once they finish.

chunks.heading: Red flags
chunks.text: Be alert if the owner seems pressured, if the new user is someone the owner met recently, or if Full access is requested for a new acquaintance. Ask open questions and escalate if concerned. See Elder financial exploitation and vulnerable clients.

chunks.heading: Removing or changing access
chunks.text: The owner can remove an authorized user or change the level at My Account → Account Access at any time. Removal is immediate.
Accepting a power of attorney, what the agent under a POA can do, durable versus springing POAs, and how to handle requests.

chunks.heading: What it is
chunks.text: A power of attorney (POA) is a legal document in which a person (the principal) authorizes another person (the agent or attorney-in-fact) to act for them. Our clients most often use a POA so a trusted person can manage their finances if they become unable to.

chunks.heading: Types
chunks.text:
Type: Durable; Effective: Immediately, and continues if the principal becomes incapacitated; Notes: Most common for financial planning
Type: Springing; Effective: Only when a stated event occurs (usually incapacity, certified by a physician); Notes: We also need the certification that the event occurred
Type: Non-durable (general or limited); Effective: Immediately; ends if the principal becomes incapacitated; Notes: Often for a specific transaction
Every POA ends when the principal dies. After death, only the executor or administrator can act.

chunks.heading: Submitting a POA
chunks.text:
The agent submits:
- A copy of the signed and notarized POA document, and
- Our POA Acceptance form, signed by the agent, and
- The agent's identification.
Account Services reviews the document (typically 3–5 business days) to confirm it grants authority over brokerage or investment accounts. Once accepted, the agent can obtain their own login with permissions matching the POA.

chunks.heading: What the agent can do
chunks.text: Whatever the document authorizes, usually: view accounts, trade, take distributions, and move money for the principal's benefit. Most POAs do not allow the agent to change beneficiaries or make gifts to themselves unless explicitly stated. Account Services records limits when accepting the POA.

chunks.heading: In chat
chunks.text:
- If the agent's POA is on file and they are signed in with their own credentials, treat them as the authorized party within the POA's limits.
- If the POA is not on file, you cannot act on the agent's instructions. Explain the submission process.
- Watch for exploitation: a newly submitted POA followed by large withdrawals to the agent is a red flag. See Elder financial exploitation and vulnerable clients.

chunks.heading: IRAs
chunks.text: An agent under a POA can request IRA distributions for the principal if the POA allows it. Distributions are taxed to the principal.
How clients link a bank account for transfers, the two verification methods, ownership rules, and timing.

chunks.heading: Why link a bank
chunks.text: A linked bank account lets the client move money electronically: purchases funded by ACH, automatic investment plans, redemptions sent by ACH, and IRA distributions by direct deposit.

chunks.heading: How to link
chunks.text:
At My Account → Linked Bank Accounts → Add Account, the client either:
1. Instant verification: signs in to their bank through a secure connection service; the account is verified immediately. Available for most U.S. banks.
2. Micro-deposits: enters the routing and account numbers; we send two small deposits (under $1) within 1–2 business days; the client confirms the amounts in the portal. The deposits are then withdrawn.

chunks.heading: Ownership rules
chunks.text:
- The bank account must be in the name of at least one owner of the Bob's account. We do not link third-party bank accounts.
- For joint Bob's accounts, a bank account in either owner's name is acceptable.
- For trust accounts, the bank account should be in the trust's name or a trustee's name.
- For custodial accounts, the custodian's or the minor's bank account.

chunks.heading: Limits and timing
chunks.text:
- ACH transfers take 2–3 business days and are limited to $100,000 per day per account.
- For 10 calendar days after a bank is linked, electronic redemptions to that bank require a verification call. Purchases from it are allowed.
- A client can have up to five linked bank accounts.

chunks.heading: Troubleshooting
chunks.text: See "I can't link my bank" and Bank verification methods.

chunks.page: Removing or replacing a linked bank account
chunks.text: What happens when a client removes a bank account, and how to avoid breaking automatic plans.

chunks.page: Removing or replacing a linked bank account
chunks.heading: Before removing
chunks.text:
Check whether the bank account funds anything:
- Automatic investment plans.
- Systematic withdrawals or RMD direct deposits.
- Dividend payments in cash to the bank.
If it does, those plans must be moved to another linked bank first, or they will fail. The portal warns the client before removal.

chunks.page: Removing or replacing a linked bank account
chunks.heading: Steps
chunks.text:
1. Link and verify the new bank account. See Linking bank accounts.
2. Update each automatic plan to use the new bank (My Account → Automatic Investments; RMD Settings; Dividend Preferences).
3. Remove the old bank at My Account → Linked Bank Accounts.

chunks.page: Removing or replacing a linked bank account
chunks.heading: Closed bank accounts
chunks.text: If a client closed their bank account without updating us, the next ACH debit or credit will be returned. Returned purchases are reversed and may incur a $20 returned-payment fee; returned redemption proceeds come back to the account as cash and are re-sent once a new bank is set up. See Returned payments and items.

chunks.page: Removing or replacing a linked bank account
chunks.heading: In chat
chunks.text: Removing a bank account is done online by the client. If a client cannot access the portal, Account Services can remove it after verification. Changing banks is a common precursor to fraud; if a client is changing banks and requesting a large redemption in the same chat, re-verify identity.
How e-delivery works for statements, confirmations, tax forms, and regulatory documents, and the paper statement fee.

chunks.heading: What goes paperless
chunks.text:
Clients can choose electronic delivery for:
- Account statements
- Trade confirmations
- Tax forms
- Fund reports and prospectuses
- General correspondence
Each can be set separately at My Account → Preferences, but most clients choose "all documents".

chunks.heading: How it works
chunks.text: When a new document is ready, we email a notification (from noreply@bobsmutualfunds.com) with no personal information in the email. The client signs in to view the document at My Account → Statements & Documents. Documents stay online for 7 years.

chunks.heading: Benefits to mention
chunks.text:
- Documents arrive about 5–7 days sooner than mail.
- The $2 per month paper statement fee is waived.
- Less risk of mail theft.

chunks.heading: Paper statement fee
chunks.text: Clients who receive paper statements are charged $2 per month per account. The fee is waived for clients who choose paperless, for clients aged 75 and older, and for accounts with balances above $250,000. See Paper statement fee.

chunks.heading: Switching back to paper
chunks.text: Clients can switch back to paper at any time. Tax forms requested by mail are sent within 5 business days.

chunks.heading: Bounced emails
chunks.text: If notification emails bounce, we switch the client back to paper automatically and notify them by mail, so they do not miss documents.
How a client can have copies of statements sent to an accountant, advisor, or family member.

chunks.heading: Interested parties
chunks.text: A client can name an interested party to receive copies of statements and confirmations by mail or email. Common interested parties are accountants, attorneys, outside financial advisors, and adult children. An interested party receives copies only; they cannot see the account online or act on it.

chunks.heading: How to set up
chunks.text: The client adds an interested party at My Account → Preferences → Duplicate Statements, providing the person's name and mailing or email address. In chat, explain where to do this. For a person who needs online visibility, suggest a view-only authorized user instead. See Authorized users and access levels.

chunks.heading: Removal
chunks.text: The client can remove an interested party at any time; it takes effect for the next statement.

chunks.heading: One-time copies
chunks.text: For a one-time copy of a past statement, the client can download it at My Account → Statements & Documents (7 years available). Older copies can be requested from Client Records through your team lead.

chunks.heading: Example
chunks.text:
Client: "My accountant wants copies of my statements."
Agent: "You can set her up as an interested party at My Account → Preferences → Duplicate Statements, and she'll get a copy of each statement automatically. If she needs to log in and see your accounts herself, you could add her as a view-only authorized user instead."

chunks.heading: Privacy
chunks.text: Interested parties receive the full statement, including balances and transactions. Make sure the client understands what will be shared.
Changing how an account is owned: adding or removing owners, retitling to a trust, and why most changes require a new account.

chunks.heading: What a registration is
chunks.text: The registration is the legal ownership of an account: who owns it and in what capacity (individual, joint, custodian, trustee, IRA owner). It determines who can act, how it is taxed, and what happens at death.

chunks.heading: Common changes
chunks.text:
Change: Individual to joint (add a spouse); How it is done: Open a joint account; transfer shares in kind from the individual account by journal
Change: Joint to individual (remove an owner); How it is done: All owners sign a transfer instruction (or provide a court order)
Change: Individual to trust; How it is done: Open a trust account; transfer shares in kind. See Retitling accounts to a trust
Change: Custodial to the former minor; How it is done: At the age of termination. See When a custodial account's minor comes of age
Change: Joint to survivor after death; How it is done: Death certificate. See Surviving joint owners
Change: IRA to another person; How it is done: Not possible except in divorce (transfer incident to divorce) or death. See Divorce and account transfers

chunks.heading: Taxes
chunks.text: Moving shares in kind between registrations with the same tax owner (for example, individual to a revocable trust using the same SSN) is not a sale. Moving shares to a different person is a gift and not a sale either, but gift-tax rules may apply; refer the client to a tax professional. Selling and repurchasing would be a taxable sale, so in-kind transfer is the norm.

chunks.heading: In chat
chunks.text: Registration changes are not chat tasks because they need signatures and often documents. Explain the process, send the client the Account Registration Change form, and route to Account Services if the client has questions about documents.
How a client closes an account, what happens to the money, taxes and penalties, and retention conversations.

chunks.heading: How to close
chunks.text:
1. The client sells all holdings in the account (a full redemption) or transfers them to another account or firm.
2. The proceeds are paid out by ACH, check, or wire, or moved to another Bob's account.
3. Once the balance is zero and no transactions are pending, the client requests closure at My Account → Account Settings → Close Account, or Account Services closes it on request.
Accounts with a zero balance for 12 months are closed automatically.

chunks.heading: IRAs
chunks.text: Closing an IRA means taking a full distribution (taxable, possibly penalized) or transferring it to another IRA custodian (not taxable). Make sure the client knows the difference. A client moving their IRA to another firm should start the transfer from the new firm rather than taking a distribution. See Outgoing transfers to another firm and IRA distributions overview.

chunks.heading: Things to check
chunks.text:
- Pending automatic investments or withdrawals: they should be cancelled.
- Dividends declared but not yet paid: a small residual may arrive after closing; we mail a check for it.
- Taxes: a sale in a taxable account may produce a gain or loss; the client will receive a 1099-B. IRA distributions produce a 1099-R.
- Tax forms for the year will still be produced and delivered.

chunks.heading: Retention conversations
chunks.text: It is appropriate to ask, once and without pressure, why the client is leaving, and to address any service issue. Do not argue, delay, or make closing difficult. If the client is leaving because of a complaint, handle it as a complaint. See Handling complaints.

chunks.heading: Fees
chunks.text: We do not charge an account closing fee or an outgoing transfer fee. An outgoing wire for the proceeds costs $25.
When accounts become dormant, how state unclaimed property laws apply, and how clients reclaim escheated assets.

chunks.heading: Dormancy
chunks.text: An account is considered dormant when the owner has had no contact with us for a period set by state law, usually three to five years. Contact includes signing in, placing a transaction, calling, or responding to mail. Automatic investments and dividend reinvestments generally do not count as owner contact.

chunks.heading: Escheatment
chunks.text: Each state requires financial firms to turn over (escheat) dormant property to the state's unclaimed property program. Before escheating, we mail a due-diligence letter to the last known address. If the owner does not respond, the shares are liquidated or transferred to the state.

chunks.heading: Preventing it
chunks.text: Clients prevent dormancy simply by signing in at least once a year or by keeping their address current. Returned mail accelerates the process. See Address changes: special situations.

chunks.heading: Reclaiming
chunks.text: A client whose assets were escheated can reclaim them from the state's unclaimed property office (searchable at missingmoney.com). If the shares were liquidated, the state returns the cash value at the time of liquidation, not current value. We can provide documentation of the escheatment through Account Services.

chunks.heading: Retirement accounts
chunks.text: IRAs are escheated less often because of their long-term nature, but the same contact rules apply in most states.
Which notifications clients can control, how to change them, and which ones are mandatory.

chunks.heading: What clients can control
chunks.text:
At My Account → Preferences, clients choose:
- Delivery method for documents: paperless or paper. See Paperless delivery.
- Text alerts for trade confirmations, deposits, and withdrawals.
- Marketing and educational emails: the newsletter, Library articles, the podcast.
- Seasonal address for mail.
- Interested parties for duplicate statements.

chunks.heading: Mandatory communications
chunks.text:
The following cannot be turned off:
- Security alerts (password, contact detail, bank, and access changes).
- Trade confirmations (they can be delivered electronically but not suppressed).
- Regulatory notices, privacy notices, and prospectuses (deliverable electronically).
- Tax forms.

chunks.heading: Do-not-contact requests
chunks.text: Clients who do not want marketing calls or emails can opt out of all marketing. We do not make sales calls. A client who received an unexpected call from someone claiming to be from Bob's should be warned about impersonation scams. See Phishing and investment scams.

chunks.heading: Example
chunks.text:
Client: "I get too many emails from you."
Agent: "I can help with that. Marketing emails like our newsletter and podcast announcements can be turned off at My Account → Preferences. Security alerts and document notices will still come, because they protect your account and tell you when statements are ready."

chunks.heading: Text alerts
chunks.text: Clients can opt in to text alerts for trades, deposits, and withdrawals. Standard message rates may apply. Texts never include full account numbers.
How a fund purchase works from order to settlement, the ways to place one, and the information every purchase needs.

chunks.heading: The basics
chunks.text:
A purchase buys shares of a BobsFunds fund in one of the client's accounts. Every purchase needs four things:
1. Account: which of the client's accounts the shares go into.
2. Fund: which of the 36 funds. See The BobsFunds lineup.
3. Amount: in dollars (most common) or shares.
4. Funding source: where the money comes from (linked bank, cash already in the account, a check, or a wire).
For IRAs, a purchase funded with new money from outside is also a contribution, and needs a tax year. See Purchases in IRAs.

chunks.heading: Ways to buy
chunks.text:
Channel: Online; Notes: Account page → Transactions → Buy
Channel: Mobile app; Notes: Trade → Buy
Channel: Chat; Notes: The Buy / Make a Contribution task; agent approves the Proposed Action. See Procedure: Buy / Make a Contribution (chat)
Channel: Phone; Notes: The licensed brokerage desk or a service representative
Channel: Automatic investment plan; Notes: Recurring purchases. See Automatic investment plans
Channel: Mail; Notes: A check with instructions. See Purchases by check

chunks.heading: Lifecycle
chunks.text:
1. Order received. If received in good order before 4:00 PM ET on a business day, it is priced at that day's NAV; otherwise at the next business day's NAV. See Trade cutoff and NAV pricing.
2. Priced. After the close, the NAV is calculated and shares are credited to three decimal places.
3. Confirmed. A trade confirmation is available the next business day. See Purchase confirmations.
4. Settled. Mutual fund trades settle T+1. For ACH-funded purchases, the bank debit occurs within 2–3 business days.

chunks.heading: Costs
chunks.text: There is no purchase fee, no sales load, and no minimum beyond $1. See Investment minimums.

chunks.heading: What "in good order" means
chunks.text: An order is in good order when it includes everything needed to process it: a valid account, a valid fund, a clear amount, an available funding source, and, for IRAs, the contribution type and year. Orders missing information are not priced until the information is supplied.
The 4:00 PM Eastern cutoff, how weekends and holidays affect pricing, and how to answer "what price will I get?"

chunks.heading: The rule
chunks.text:
Mutual funds are priced once per business day at the close of the New York Stock Exchange, normally 4:00 PM Eastern Time.
- Orders received in good order before 4:00 PM ET on a business day receive that day's NAV.
- Orders received at or after 4:00 PM ET, or on a weekend or market holiday, receive the next business day's NAV.
- On early-close days (the day after Thanksgiving and Christmas Eve), the cutoff is 1:00 PM ET. See Holiday calendar 2026.
This is called forward pricing and is required by SEC rules: no one can buy or sell at a price that is already known.

chunks.heading: What counts as "received"
chunks.text:
- Online and app: the timestamp when the client clicks Confirm.
- Chat: the time the agent submits the approved Proposed Action, not when the client first asked. If a client asks at 3:52 PM, tell them the order must be submitted before 4:00 PM to get today's price, and work promptly; do not rush the confirmation steps.
- Phone: when the representative enters the order.
- Mail: when the check and instructions arrive at the processing center.
- Wire: when the wire is received and matched to the account.

chunks.heading: Common questions
chunks.text:
"What price will I get?":
"Your order will be priced at the closing NAV calculated after 4:00 PM Eastern today, which isn't known until after the close. You'll see the exact price on your confirmation tomorrow."
"Can I buy at today's lower price?":
Only if the order is received before the cutoff. There is no way to lock in a price earlier in the day.
"Can I cancel an order?":
An order can be cancelled before the 4:00 PM ET cutoff of the day it will be priced. After that, it is final; an unwanted purchase must be sold as a separate transaction (which may be subject to the frequent-trading policy). Online orders can be cancelled from the Pending Orders view; chat or phone orders by contacting us before the cutoff.
Time zones:
Always convert: 4:00 PM ET is 1:00 PM in California and 10:00 AM in Hawaii (during daylight saving time; 11:00 AM in standard time).

chunks.heading: Worked timeline
chunks.text:
Order placed: Monday 10:00 AM ET; Priced at: Monday's NAV; Shares visible: Monday evening; Settles: Tuesday
Order placed: Monday 4:15 PM ET; Priced at: Tuesday's NAV; Shares visible: Tuesday evening; Settles: Wednesday
Order placed: Friday 5:00 PM ET; Priced at: Monday's NAV; Shares visible: Monday evening; Settles: Tuesday
Order placed: Saturday; Priced at: Monday's NAV; Shares visible: Monday evening; Settles: Tuesday
Order placed: Thanksgiving Thursday; Priced at: Friday's NAV (cutoff 1:00 PM ET that day); Shares visible: Friday evening; Settles: Monday

chunks.heading: Exchanges
chunks.text: Both sides of an exchange use the same day's NAVs, so the client is never out of the market.
The ways a purchase can be paid for, how cash in the account works, and the checks to make before choosing a source.

chunks.heading: Sources
chunks.text:
Source: Linked bank account (ACH); When the money is used: Shares priced on trade date; bank debited within 2–3 business days; Notes: Most common; $100,000 daily limit
Source: Cash in the account; When the money is used: Immediately; Notes: Only the uninvested cash portion is available
Source: Wire; When the money is used: When the wire arrives; Notes: See Purchases by wire
Source: Check; When the money is used: When the check arrives; Notes: See Purchases by check
Source: Proceeds of a same-day sale; When the money is used: Exchange instead; Notes: Moving money between funds in one account is an exchange. See Exchanges overview

chunks.heading: Cash in the account
chunks.text:
An account's total value is its uninvested cash plus the market value of its fund holdings. Cash comes from deposits not yet invested, dividends paid in cash, and sale proceeds left in the account. The client info panel and the portal show cash separately (for example "total incl. $877 cash").
When a client says "use the money in my account", check what they mean:
- If they mean the cash, confirm the cash balance covers the purchase. A $2,000 purchase from cash fails if the account holds only $877 in cash, even if the total value is $4,800.
- If they mean money that is invested in another fund, that is an exchange, not a cash purchase.
Uninvested cash earns no return in the account. Clients sometimes leave cash by mistake after a deposit; point it out neutrally.

chunks.heading: Linked bank
chunks.text: The bank account must be linked and verified. If the client has several, confirm which. Purchases from a bank linked in the last few days are allowed. If the client has no linked bank, they must link one first (see Linking bank accounts) or use a check or wire.

chunks.heading: IRAs
chunks.text: Money from a bank into an IRA is a contribution. Cash already in the IRA (from earlier contributions, dividends, or sales) can be invested without counting again toward the limit. See Purchases in IRAs.
Minimums for opening accounts, buying funds, automatic investments, and other transactions.

chunks.heading: Minimums
chunks.text:
Item: Open an account; Minimum: $0 (fund later)
Item: Initial purchase in any fund; Minimum: $1
Item: Additional purchases; Minimum: $1
Item: Automatic investment plan; Minimum: $50 per fund per investment
Item: Exchange; Minimum: $1
Item: Systematic withdrawal plan; Minimum: $50 per withdrawal
Item: Outgoing wire; Minimum: $1,000

chunks.heading: Fractional shares
chunks.text: Purchases are made in dollars and credited in fractional shares to three decimal places, so the client never needs to buy whole shares.

chunks.heading: Older documents
chunks.text: Some older materials quoted $1,000 or $3,000 minimums for certain funds. Those minimums no longer apply; all BobsFunds funds have a $1 minimum.

chunks.heading: Why the minimums are so low
chunks.text: Bob's Mutual Funds set $1 minimums so that anyone can start investing and so that small amounts (for example, leftover cash after a sale) can be fully invested. Clients sometimes ask whether a small purchase is "worth it"; there are no transaction fees, so a small purchase costs nothing extra.

chunks.heading: Automatic investment minimum
chunks.text: The $50 minimum for automatic plans exists because each plan runs an ACH debit; very small recurring debits have a higher rate of returns and errors.

chunks.heading: Outgoing wire minimum
chunks.text: Wires cost $25 and are intended for larger amounts; smaller withdrawals go by ACH (free) or check.

chunks.heading: Questions
chunks.text:
"Can I buy a fraction of a share?":
Yes. Purchases are made in dollars and credited to three decimal places.
"Is there a minimum balance to keep the account open?":
No. Only an account with a zero balance for 12 months is closed automatically.
Acceptable checks, how to send them, when they are invested, and the hold on redeeming shares bought by check.

chunks.heading: Acceptable checks
chunks.text:
- Personal checks drawn on a U.S. bank in U.S. dollars, payable to Bob's Mutual Funds.
- Cashier's checks and official bank checks payable to Bob's Mutual Funds.
- Checks from another financial institution payable to Bob's Mutual Funds for the benefit of the client (for rollovers and transfers).

chunks.heading: Not accepted
chunks.text:
- Cash, money orders, traveler's checks, and starter checks (checks without a preprinted name and address).
- Third-party checks (a check made out to the client and endorsed over to us).
- Checks drawn on foreign banks.
- Credit card convenience checks.
Unacceptable checks are returned to the sender.

chunks.heading: How to send
chunks.text: Mail to Bob's Mutual Funds, PO Box 2025, Malvern, PA 19355 (or the overnight address). Include the account number on the memo line and a note saying which fund(s) and amounts. For IRAs, the note must say contribution and tax year, rollover, or transfer. Without fund instructions, the money is held as cash in the account.

chunks.heading: When it is invested
chunks.text: At the NAV on the business day the check is received in good order at the processing center (before 4:00 PM ET).

chunks.heading: Redemption hold
chunks.text: Shares bought by check can be sold immediately, but the proceeds of that sale are not paid out until the check has cleared, up to 7 business days after purchase. This prevents losses from bad checks. Exchanges within the account are allowed during the hold. See Holds on redemption proceeds.
Wiring money to buy shares: the instructions, timing, and what the client must tell their bank.

chunks.heading: Instructions
chunks.text:
The client gives their bank:
Field: Receiving bank; Value: First National Bank of Funds (FNBF)
Field: ABA routing number; Value: 031000503
Field: For credit to; Value: Bob's Mutual Funds
Field: Beneficiary account; Value: The client's Bob's account number
Field: Beneficiary name; Value: The client's full name as registered on the account
Field: Reference; Value: Fund ticker(s), and for IRAs "contribution 2026" (or the year), "rollover", or "transfer"
Wire instructions never change by email. If a client receives an email with "updated" wire instructions, it is fraudulent. See Phishing and investment scams.

chunks.heading: Timing
chunks.text: Wires received and matched to an account before 4:00 PM ET are invested at that day's NAV. Wires that arrive after 4:00 PM ET, or that cannot be matched (wrong account number, name mismatch), are invested on the next business day once matched. We do not charge for incoming wires; the client's bank may.

chunks.heading: Large or urgent purchases
chunks.text: Wires have no dollar limit and are the fastest way to deposit large amounts or to meet a deadline (for example, an IRA contribution on April 15). Suggest the client call their bank early in the day.

chunks.heading: Advance notice
chunks.text: For wires over $250,000, ask the client to notify us in advance (a secure message or chat) with the amount and expected date, so Money Movement Operations can watch for it.
How ACH-funded purchases work, the timing between order and bank debit, limits, and the redemption hold.

chunks.heading: How it works
chunks.text:
When a client buys with a linked bank account:
1. The order is priced at the NAV for the trade date (that day if before 4:00 PM ET).
2. The shares are credited to the account right away.
3. The bank account is debited within 2–3 business days.
The client sees the shares immediately, even before the money leaves their bank.

chunks.heading: Limits
chunks.text: $100,000 per day per account. Larger purchases can be split across days or made by wire.

chunks.heading: Redemption hold
chunks.text: Shares bought by ACH can be sold or exchanged at any time, but the proceeds of a sale are not paid out of the account until the ACH debit has cleared, up to 7 business days after the purchase. See Holds on redemption proceeds.

chunks.heading: Insufficient funds
chunks.text: If the bank returns the debit (insufficient funds, closed account), the purchase is cancelled and any loss from a decline in NAV is charged to the account. A $20 returned-payment fee applies. Repeated returns can lead to ACH purchases being restricted. See Returned payments and items.

chunks.heading: Example
chunks.text: Monday 2:00 PM ET: a client buys $5,000 of BFTM from their linked bank. The purchase is priced at Monday's NAV; shares appear Monday evening. The bank is debited by Wednesday or Thursday. If the client sells those shares on Tuesday, the sale is processed but the proceeds stay in the account until the ACH clears (up to 7 business days from the purchase).

chunks.heading: Several purchases in one day
chunks.text: Each purchase counts toward the $100,000 daily limit for the account.
How buying in an IRA differs: contributions versus investing existing cash, tax years, limits, and rollovers.

chunks.heading: Two kinds of IRA purchase
chunks.text:
1. Investing cash already in the IRA, from earlier contributions, rollovers, dividends, or sales. This is not a new contribution and does not count toward the annual limit.
2. New money from outside (a bank, a check, a wire). This is a contribution (or a rollover or transfer, if the money comes from another retirement account). Contributions count toward the annual limit and need a tax year.
When a client says "buy $3,000 of BF500 in my Roth", ask where the money is coming from.

chunks.heading: Checks for contributions
chunks.text:
- Limit: the 2026 limit is $7,500 ($8,600 at 50+), shared across all Traditional and Roth IRAs at every firm. The contributions summary in the info panel shows contributions at Bob's for the year. See The IRA contributions summary.
- Tax year: from January 1 to April 15, a contribution can be for the current or the prior year. Ask. See Prior-year contributions (January to April).
- Roth income limits: if the client mentions income above the phase-out, a direct Roth contribution may not be allowed. See Roth IRA income limits.
- Age: there is no maximum age for contributions; the client needs earned income (or a working spouse).
If a proposed contribution would exceed the remaining limit, tell the client before submitting. Excess contributions incur a 6% excise tax each year until corrected. See Excess contributions and how to fix them.

chunks.heading: SEP-IRAs
chunks.text: New money into a SEP-IRA is an employer contribution, which has different limits (25% of compensation up to $72,000 for 2026) and deadlines. See SEP-IRA contributions.

chunks.heading: Rollovers and transfers
chunks.text: Money from a 401(k) or another IRA is not a contribution and is not limited. It must be coded correctly. See Rollovers and transfers: overview.
What a trade confirmation shows, when it is available, and how clients find it.

chunks.heading: Timing
chunks.text: A confirmation is produced for every purchase, sale, and exchange, available the business day after the trade is priced. Paperless clients get an email notification; others receive it by mail within a few days.

chunks.heading: Contents
chunks.text:
- Trade date and settlement date.
- Account and fund.
- Dollar amount, NAV (price per share), and shares bought.
- Funding source.
- For IRAs: whether it was a contribution (and the tax year), a rollover, or a transfer.
- A reference number.

chunks.heading: Chat confirmations
chunks.text: When an agent submits a purchase in chat, the client immediately sees a green confirmation card with a reference number (format REF-XXXXXX). This confirms the order was placed. The formal trade confirmation with the NAV follows after pricing.

chunks.heading: Automatic investments
chunks.text: Automatic investments are confirmed on the quarterly statement rather than with individual confirmations, unless the client chooses individual confirmations in Preferences.

chunks.heading: Corrections
