chunks.text: If a confirmation is wrong (wrong fund, wrong amount, wrong tax year on a contribution), the client should tell us right away. See Correcting errors (as-of trades).

chunks.heading: Example
chunks.text: "Bought 4.579 shares of BobsFunds 500 Index (BF500) at $218.40 on 09/15/2026 for $1,000.00 in Roth IRA (2026 contribution), funded from bank ••4421. Settlement 09/16/2026. Confirmation 2026091500418."

chunks.heading: Questions
chunks.text:
"Why don't I have a confirmation for my automatic investment?":
Automatic investments appear on statements, unless the client opts in to individual confirmations.
"Can I get a confirmation reissued?":
All confirmations are at My Account → Statements & Documents.
Why purchases fail or are reversed, what happens to the shares, and what the client owes.

chunks.heading: Reasons
chunks.text:
- The bank returns the ACH debit (insufficient funds, closed account, account not authorized for debits).
- A check is returned unpaid.
- The order was not in good order and could not be completed (for example, an IRA contribution without a tax year).
- The purchase would have exceeded a limit (such as the daily ACH limit).

chunks.heading: What happens
chunks.text:
When a payment is returned:
1. The purchase is cancelled and the shares removed.
2. If the NAV fell between the purchase and the cancellation, the loss is charged to the client's account. If it rose, the gain stays with the fund.
3. A $20 returned-payment fee is charged.
4. The client receives a notice.
5. After two returned payments in 12 months, ACH and check purchases may be restricted for 90 days, leaving wires as the purchase method.

chunks.heading: Automatic investments
chunks.text: A returned automatic investment is cancelled the same way. The plan stays active, so the next investment will be attempted. If the bank account is closed, the client should update the plan. See When an automatic investment doesn't run.

chunks.heading: Talking to clients
chunks.text: Be matter-of-fact and nonjudgmental: "The bank returned the payment for your March 3 purchase, so that purchase was reversed." Offer to help them place the purchase again once funds are available.
Step-by-step chat procedure for a fund purchase, every field the task collects, and the checks to make before approving.

chunks.heading: What the task collects
chunks.text:
Field: Account; Options or format: One of the client's accounts (asked only if they have more than one)
Field: Fund; Options or format: Any of the 36 BobsFunds tickers
Field: Purchase amount; Options or format: Dollar amount
Field: Funding source; Options or format: Linked bank account, or Cash in account

chunks.heading: Procedure
chunks.text:
1. Confirm what the client wants in one sentence: account, fund, amount.
2. Let the task expert collect the details, or choose "Buy / Make a Contribution" from the task menu.
3. Watch for these issues while details are collected:
- Unclear fund: "the S&P fund" means BF500; "the bond fund" is ambiguous (there are eight). Confirm the ticker and name. - Advice requests: if the client asks which fund to buy, the expert offers a callback. Do not suggest a fund. - Amount format: amounts such as "$4,800" or "4.8k" must be read correctly. Confirm the exact figure in the recap.
1. When the Proposed Action appears, check:
- The account is the one the client named (use the locate button). - The fund ticker matches the fund the client described. - Cash funding: the amount is no more than the account's cash balance (not the total value). - IRA with bank funding: this is a contribution. Is it within the remaining limit? Which tax year (January–April)? If the task did not capture the tax year, ask and note it. - Time: if close to 4:00 PM ET, tell the client which day's NAV applies.
1. Submit. The client receives a green confirmation card with a reference number.
2. Close the loop: "Your $2,000 purchase of BF500 in your Roth IRA is placed. It will be priced at today's closing NAV, and the money will come from your bank in 2–3 business days."

chunks.heading: Common errors to avoid
chunks.text:
- Funding a purchase from "cash" when the client meant to move money from another fund (that's an exchange).
- Treating a rollover deposit as a contribution.
- Placing the order in the wrong account when the client has two accounts of the same type.

chunks.heading: When the purchase fails
chunks.text: If submission returns an error, check the account's recent transactions to see whether it was placed before retrying. See Transaction statuses.
How a sale (redemption) works, the information it needs, where the proceeds go, and how it differs in IRAs.

chunks.heading: Terms
chunks.text: "Selling" and "redeeming" mean the same thing for a mutual fund: the fund buys back the client's shares at that day's NAV. Use whichever word the client uses; default to "sell".

chunks.heading: What every sale needs
chunks.text:
1. Account and fund.
2. Amount: a dollar amount, a number of shares, or "all shares" (a full redemption). See Partial and full redemptions.
3. Where the proceeds go: stay in the account as cash, go to the linked bank by ACH, by wire, or by check. See Where sale proceeds go.

chunks.heading: Lifecycle
chunks.text:
1. The order is priced at the NAV for the trade date (that day if received in good order before 4:00 PM ET).
2. Proceeds settle T+1 into the account's cash.
3. If the client asked for the money to be sent out, it leaves the account: ACH arrives in the bank in 2–3 business days, wires the same day if requested before 2:00 PM ET, checks by mail in 5–7 business days.

chunks.heading: Ways to sell
chunks.text: Online (Account → Transactions → Sell), mobile app, chat (the Sell Fund Shares task; see Procedure: Sell Fund Shares (chat)), phone, or a written request with a signature (required in some cases; see Medallion signature guarantees).

chunks.heading: IRAs are different
chunks.text: Selling inside an IRA does not, by itself, take money out: proceeds stay in the IRA as cash and there is no tax. Taking money out of an IRA is a distribution, with tax withholding and possible penalties. See Selling in IRAs and taking money out.

chunks.heading: Costs
chunks.text: No redemption fees and no transaction fees on any BobsFunds fund. Outgoing wires cost $25; overnight check delivery costs $25.
Selling a dollar amount, a number of shares, or everything, and what to watch for with each.

chunks.heading: Dollar amount
chunks.text:
The most common sale. The client names an amount ("sell $5,000"); the number of shares is calculated at the NAV. Because the NAV is not known in advance, the client receives exactly the dollar amount requested, and the number of shares varies.
If the client needs a specific net amount from an IRA after tax withholding, the gross sale must be larger. For example, to receive $9,000 after 10% federal withholding, the gross distribution must be $10,000. See Federal tax withholding on IRA distributions.

chunks.heading: Number of shares
chunks.text: The client names a share count ("sell 50 shares"). The dollar amount depends on the NAV.

chunks.heading: Full redemption
chunks.text:
"Sell everything" or "full redemption" sells all shares of that fund in that account. Notes:
- Any dividend declared but not yet paid at the time of sale arrives later as a small cash amount.
- Automatic investments into that fund continue unless cancelled; ask whether the client wants to stop them.
- If the fund is the last holding, the account will hold only cash; ask what the client wants to do with it.

chunks.heading: Selling more than the holding
chunks.text: A dollar sale larger than the holding's value cannot be processed. If the client asks to sell "$10,000 of BFBI" and holds $8,250, tell them the current value and ask whether they want a full redemption instead.

chunks.heading: Selling from several funds
chunks.text: Each fund is a separate sale. If a client says "take $10,000 out of my account", ask which fund(s) to sell, or whether to sell proportionally across all holdings. Choosing which fund to sell is the client's decision; do not recommend.
The options for receiving proceeds (cash in account, ACH, wire, check), timing, and the rules for each.

chunks.heading: Options
chunks.text:
Option: Keep as cash in the account; Timing: Available T+1; Cost: Free; Notes: Can be reinvested later
Option: ACH to linked bank; Timing: 2–3 business days after the trade; Cost: Free; Notes: Bank must be linked and verified; 10-day rule for newly linked banks
Option: Wire to linked bank; Timing: Same day if requested before 2:00 PM ET (after the sale settles); Cost: $25; Notes: Minimum $1,000
Option: Check by standard mail; Timing: 5–7 business days; Cost: Free; Notes: Mailed to the address of record
Option: Check by overnight delivery; Timing: 1–2 business days; Cost: $25; Notes: Street address required

chunks.heading: Rules
chunks.text:
- Proceeds go only to the account owner: their linked bank or their address of record. Payment to a third party, or to an address that is not the address of record, requires a written request with a medallion signature guarantee. See Medallion signature guarantees.
- Checks are payable to the registered owner(s). For a joint account, the check is payable to all owners.
- If the address changed in the last 15 days, a check can't be mailed there without a signature guarantee.
- If the bank was linked in the last 10 days, an electronic payment needs a verification call.

chunks.heading: Timing from sale to cash
chunks.text: A sale placed before 4:00 PM ET on Monday prices Monday, settles Tuesday, and an ACH lands in the bank about Wednesday or Thursday. A wire requested Tuesday before 2:00 PM ET arrives Tuesday. Tell clients realistic dates and to allow for bank holidays.

chunks.heading: Holds
chunks.text: If the shares were bought recently by ACH or check, proceeds may be held until the purchase payment clears. See Holds on redemption proceeds.

chunks.page: Settlement and when money is available
chunks.text: What T+1 settlement means, when sale proceeds become available, and how to give clients realistic dates.

chunks.page: Settlement and when money is available
chunks.heading: Settlement
chunks.text: Mutual fund trades settle on T+1: one business day after the trade date. Settlement is when the trade is final and the cash or shares officially change hands.

chunks.page: Settlement and when money is available
chunks.heading: Availability
chunks.text:
Event: Sale priced; When: Trade date (T)
Event: Cash available in account for reinvestment; When: T (exchanges) or T+1 (purchases with sale proceeds)
Event: Cash available to send out; When: T+1
Event: ACH arrives at bank; When: About T+3 to T+4
Event: Wire arrives; When: T+1 if requested before 2:00 PM ET on T+1
Event: Check arrives; When: About T+6 to T+8 by mail

chunks.page: Settlement and when money is available
chunks.heading: Business days
chunks.text: Weekends, market holidays, and bank holidays are not business days. A sale placed Friday after 4:00 PM ET is priced Monday. On bank holidays when markets are open (Columbus Day, Veterans Day), trades price but ACH and wires do not move.

chunks.page: Settlement and when money is available
chunks.heading: Giving dates
chunks.text: Give a range and say "business days". "If you sell today before 4 PM Eastern, the money should reach your bank by Thursday or Friday." Never promise a specific date for money arriving at another institution; we control when it leaves, not when the bank posts it.
Why proceeds from recently purchased shares may be held, for how long, and other holds that can affect a sale.

chunks.heading: Uncollected funds hold
chunks.text:
When shares are purchased by ACH or check, the payment takes time to clear. If the client sells those shares before the payment clears, the sale is processed, but the proceeds are held in the account until the payment clears, up to 7 business days after the purchase. This protects the funds and other shareholders from losses on returned payments.
During the hold:
- The client can exchange into another fund in the same account.
- The client cannot withdraw the proceeds.
- Wire purchases are not subject to this hold.

chunks.heading: Other holds
chunks.text:
Hold: Newly linked bank; Cause: Bank linked within 10 days; How it is lifted: A verification call
Hold: Recent address change; Cause: Address changed within 15 days; How it is lifted: Signature-guaranteed request, or wait
Hold: Protective/fraud hold; Cause: Suspected fraud or exploitation; How it is lifted: Fraud or Senior Investor Protection team
Hold: Estate hold; Cause: Death of the owner reported; How it is lifted: Estate Services, after documentation
Hold: Legal hold; Cause: Court order, levy, garnishment; How it is lifted: Legal department

chunks.heading: Talking to clients
chunks.text: Explain holds as protection, give the expected release date, and do not speculate about fraud or legal holds. For protective, estate, or legal holds, route to the responsible team. See Protective holds on money movement.
When a medallion signature guarantee is required, what it is, and where clients can get one.

chunks.heading: What it is
chunks.text: A medallion signature guarantee is a special stamp from a bank, credit union, or broker-dealer that guarantees a signature is genuine and the signer has authority. It protects against forged instructions. It is not the same as a notary stamp; a notarization is not accepted in place of a medallion guarantee.

chunks.heading: When it is required
chunks.text:
- A redemption paid by check for more than $100,000.
- Proceeds payable to anyone other than the registered owner(s), or sent to an address other than the address of record.
- Proceeds sent to a bank account not in the owner's name.
- A check mailed to an address changed within the last 15 days.
- Transfers of shares to another person or a different registration (for example, from a deceased owner's account to beneficiaries in some cases).
- Some registration changes and estate transactions.

chunks.heading: Where to get one
chunks.text: Clients can get a medallion guarantee at their own bank, credit union, or brokerage where they have an account. They should bring photo ID and the unsigned document, and sign in front of the officer. Some banks provide them only to existing customers or above a minimum relationship; advise clients to call ahead.

chunks.heading: Alternatives
chunks.text: Often there is an easier path: sending proceeds to a verified linked bank by ACH or wire does not require a guarantee, and waiting out the 15-day address-change window avoids it for checks.
Handling sales of large amounts: verification, delivery, and the fund's right to pay in kind.

chunks.heading: Extra care
chunks.text:
For sales over $250,000, or that would sell most of the client's assets:
- Re-verify identity even in an authenticated chat, especially if the request comes with recent contact or bank changes. See Verifying client identity.
- Confirm the purpose if the client volunteers it; be alert for scams ("my new friend needs help", "I'm moving it to a safe account"). See Elder financial exploitation and vulnerable clients.
- Confirm delivery: wire or ACH to a long-standing linked bank is safest.

chunks.heading: Redemptions in kind
chunks.text: The funds reserve the right, described in the prospectus, to pay very large redemptions (over $250,000 or 1% of a fund's assets in a 90-day period) partly in securities instead of cash, to protect remaining shareholders. In practice this is rarely used for individual clients. If asked, explain it factually and refer to the prospectus.

chunks.heading: Timing
chunks.text: Large sales are processed like any other; the NAV and settlement rules are the same. ACH is limited to $100,000 per day, so larger amounts should go by wire.

chunks.heading: Taxes
chunks.text: A large sale in a taxable account can produce a large capital gain. Do not discourage the sale, but if the client asks about taxes, explain how gains are calculated and suggest they consult a tax professional. See Taxes on sales in taxable accounts.

chunks.page: Selling in IRAs and taking money out
chunks.text: The difference between selling inside an IRA (no tax) and withdrawing from an IRA (a distribution), and how to handle each in chat.

chunks.page: Selling in IRAs and taking money out
chunks.heading: Selling inside the IRA
chunks.text: When a client sells a fund in an IRA and keeps the proceeds in the IRA as cash, or exchanges into another fund, nothing is taxed. There is no 1099-B for IRA trades. Clients sometimes worry that selling in their IRA triggers taxes; reassure them it does not.

chunks.page: Selling in IRAs and taking money out
chunks.heading: Taking money out
chunks.text: Moving money from an IRA to the client's bank or a check is a distribution. Distributions from a Traditional or SEP IRA are taxable income, may be subject to a 10% penalty before age 59½, and have federal withholding of 10% by default. Roth distributions follow different rules. Use the Request a Distribution task, not the Sell task, when the client wants the money out. See Procedure: Request a Distribution (chat) and IRA distributions overview.

chunks.page: Selling in IRAs and taking money out
chunks.heading: Combining the two
chunks.text: If the IRA holds no cash, a distribution requires selling shares first. The distribution task handles this: the client says how much they want and from which account, and shares are sold as needed. If the client wants a specific fund sold for the distribution, note it.

chunks.page: Selling in IRAs and taking money out
chunks.heading: Moving IRA money to another IRA
chunks.text: Transferring to another IRA custodian is neither a sale for tax purposes nor a distribution if done as a direct transfer. See IRA-to-IRA transfers.
Step-by-step chat procedure for a sale, the fields collected, and the checks before approval.

chunks.heading: What the task collects
chunks.text:
Field: Account; Options or format: One of the client's accounts (asked if more than one)
Field: Fund to sell; Options or format: A fund the client holds in that account
Field: Amount or shares; Options or format: A dollar amount, or "full redemption"
Proceeds stay in the account as cash unless the client asks for them to be sent out.

chunks.heading: Procedure
chunks.text:
1. Confirm the request: account, fund, amount, and what should happen to the money.
2. If this is an IRA and the client wants the money out, use Request a Distribution instead. See Selling in IRAs and taking money out.
3. If the client wants to move the money into another fund in the same account, use Exchange Between Funds. See Procedure: Exchange Between Funds (chat).
4. Let the task expert collect details. The expert offers only funds the client actually holds in that account.
5. Check the Proposed Action:
- The fund is held in that account, and the amount is no more than its value. - "All" or "everything" is recorded as a full redemption. - Account and fund match the transcript (use the locate buttons).
1. Submit. The client receives a green confirmation card.
2. If the client wants proceeds sent out, explain the delivery and timing (ACH 2–3 business days after settlement, wire, or check). See Where sale proceeds go.

chunks.heading: Things not to do
chunks.text:
- Do not ask the client why they are selling. It is their decision, and asking can feel intrusive. Only ask if needed to choose the right task (distribution versus sale) or if you see exploitation red flags.
- Do not comment on whether selling is wise, even in a falling market. If the client asks, see Talking with clients during market downturns.

chunks.heading: After submission
chunks.text: Point out anything that continues: an automatic investment into the fund just sold, for example. Offer to pause or change it.

chunks.page: Taxes on sales in taxable accounts
chunks.text: How capital gains and losses arise when a client sells in a taxable account, and how much you may explain.

chunks.page: Taxes on sales in taxable accounts
chunks.heading: The basics
chunks.text:
In a taxable account, selling or exchanging shares realizes a capital gain or loss: the sale proceeds minus the cost basis of the shares sold.
- Shares held more than one year produce long-term gains or losses, taxed at lower rates (0%, 15%, or 20% depending on income, plus 3.8% net investment income tax for some high earners).
- Shares held one year or less produce short-term gains, taxed as ordinary income.

chunks.page: Taxes on sales in taxable accounts
chunks.heading: Cost basis
chunks.text: Basis is what the client paid for the shares, including reinvested dividends. We track basis for shares bought since 2012 (covered shares) and report it on Form 1099-B. Our default method is average cost; clients can choose FIFO or specific identification before a sale. See Cost basis methods.

chunks.page: Taxes on sales in taxable accounts
chunks.heading: Exchanges are sales
chunks.text: An exchange in a taxable account is a sale of one fund and a purchase of another, so it can produce a gain or loss. See Tax effects of exchanges.

chunks.page: Taxes on sales in taxable accounts
chunks.heading: Losses
chunks.text: Losses offset gains, and up to $3,000 of net loss a year can offset ordinary income, with the rest carried forward. Buying the same fund within 30 days before or after a loss sale can trigger the wash-sale rule. See The wash-sale rule.

chunks.page: Taxes on sales in taxable accounts
chunks.heading: What you can and cannot say
chunks.text: You may explain these rules and show the client their unrealized gain or loss and cost basis in the portal (Account → Holdings → Cost Basis). You may not tell the client how a sale will affect their taxes or whether they should sell for tax reasons. See Tax information versus tax advice.
What an exchange is, how it is priced, what it can and cannot do, and how it differs from a sale and a purchase.

chunks.heading: Definition
chunks.text: An exchange moves money from one BobsFunds fund to another within the same account. It is a sale of the first fund and a purchase of the second, processed together at the same day's NAVs, so the money is never out of the market overnight.

chunks.heading: Rules
chunks.text:
- Both funds must be in the same account. Moving money between two accounts (for example, from a taxable account to a Roth IRA) is not an exchange. See Exchange rules and limits.
- The exchange is priced at both funds' NAVs for the trade date (that day if before 4:00 PM ET).
- There is no fee and no minimum beyond $1.
- An exchange can be for a dollar amount, a number of shares, or all shares of the "from" fund.
- An exchange into a new fund opens a new position; an exchange into a fund already held adds to it.

chunks.heading: Taxes
chunks.text:
- IRAs: an exchange has no tax effect.
- Taxable accounts: an exchange is a sale and can create a capital gain or loss. See Tax effects of exchanges.

chunks.heading: Channels
chunks.text: Online (Transactions → Exchange), mobile app, chat (see Procedure: Exchange Between Funds (chat)), or phone.

chunks.heading: Exchanges and the frequent-trading policy
chunks.text: Exchanges count toward round trips. See Frequent trading (market timing) policy.
What can be exchanged, between which accounts, and the situations where an exchange isn't possible.

chunks.heading: Allowed
chunks.text:
- Any BobsFunds fund to any other BobsFunds fund in the same account.
- Partial or full exchanges.
- Several exchanges on the same day (each is a separate transaction).

chunks.heading: Not allowed or not an exchange
chunks.text:
Request: Move money from a taxable account to an IRA; Why not: Different accounts and tax types; What to do instead: Sell in the taxable account and make an IRA contribution (subject to limits)
Request: Move money from an IRA to a taxable account; Why not: That is a distribution; What to do instead: Request a distribution
Request: Move from a Traditional IRA to a Roth IRA; Why not: That is a conversion; What to do instead: See Roth conversions: overview
Request: Move between two of the client's taxable accounts; Why not: Different accounts; What to do instead: A journal transfer between accounts (Account Services), or sell and buy
Request: Exchange into another company's fund; Why not: We hold only BobsFunds; What to do instead: Not available
Request: Exchange while purchase payment is pending; Why not: Allowed within the account; What to do instead: The redemption hold still applies to withdrawals

chunks.heading: Restrictions
chunks.text: A client restricted under the frequent-trading policy cannot exchange into the restricted fund for 30 days. A foreign address can block exchanges into funds as new purchases. See Non-U.S. persons and clients living abroad.
How the funds limit short-term round trips, what counts, the 30-day block, and what's exempt.

chunks.heading: Why the policy exists
chunks.text: Frequent short-term trading in and out of a fund raises costs for long-term shareholders and can dilute their returns. The funds' prospectuses describe a policy to discourage it.

chunks.heading: The rule
chunks.text: A round trip is a purchase or exchange into a fund followed by a sale or exchange out of the same fund within 30 calendar days. After a round trip, the client is blocked from buying or exchanging into that fund for 30 calendar days (in that account and any account with the same owner).

chunks.heading: What is exempt
chunks.text:
- Automatic investment plans and systematic withdrawal plans.
- Dividend and capital gain reinvestments.
- Required minimum distributions.
- Redemptions to pay account fees.
- Transactions in BFST (Short-Term Treasury), which is designed for short-term use.
- Corrections of errors made by Bob's Mutual Funds.

chunks.heading: In chat
chunks.text:
If a client asks to buy back into a fund they sold within 30 days, check whether the earlier trade created a round trip. If the system blocks the purchase, explain:
"Our funds limit short-term trading to protect long-term shareholders. Because you bought and then sold this fund within 30 days, new purchases into it are paused until [date]. You can still buy any other fund."
Do not help clients work around the policy (for example, buying in a different account). Repeated attempts to time the market may lead to wider trading restrictions.

chunks.heading: Talking about market timing
chunks.text: Clients who trade frequently in response to news may be anxious. Avoid commentary on their strategy; if they want guidance, offer a callback. See Talking with clients during market downturns.
Why exchanges in taxable accounts are taxable sales, and how to explain this without giving tax advice.

chunks.heading: Taxable accounts
chunks.text:
An exchange is treated as a sale of the "from" fund. If the shares are worth more than their cost basis, the client realizes a capital gain; if less, a loss. The exchange appears on Form 1099-B for the year. See Taxes on sales in taxable accounts.
Clients are often surprised by this, because the money stayed invested. Explain it before submitting an exchange in a taxable account if the client seems unaware: "Just so you know, in a taxable account an exchange counts as a sale for tax purposes, so it may result in a capital gain or loss."

chunks.heading: IRAs
chunks.text: Exchanges inside a Traditional, Roth, SEP, or inherited IRA have no tax effect.

chunks.heading: Wash sales
chunks.text: If an exchange sells shares at a loss and the client buys the same fund (or a "substantially identical" one) within 30 days before or after, part or all of the loss may be disallowed under the wash-sale rule. Whether two different index funds are substantially identical is a tax question for the client's advisor. See The wash-sale rule.

chunks.heading: Cost basis method
chunks.text: The cost basis method chosen (average cost by default) determines which shares' basis is used. Clients who want to choose specific lots must set specific identification before the exchange. See Cost basis methods.
Step-by-step chat procedure for an exchange, the fields collected, and the checks before approving.

chunks.heading: What the task collects
chunks.text:
Field: Account; Options or format: One of the client's accounts (asked if more than one)
Field: Fund to exchange out of; Options or format: A fund held in that account
Field: Fund to exchange into; Options or format: Any BobsFunds fund
Field: Amount to exchange; Options or format: A dollar amount, or the full balance of the "from" fund

chunks.heading: Procedure
chunks.text:
1. Confirm the request in one sentence: "You'd like to move $3,000 from BFGR into BFBI in your Traditional IRA. Is that right?"
2. Let the task expert collect the details, or choose Exchange Between Funds from the task menu.
3. Check the Proposed Action:
- "From" fund is held in the account and the amount is no more than its value. - "To" fund is the one the client described. Watch out for similar names (BFST Short-Term Treasury versus BFSTC Short-Term Corporate versus BFSTP Consumer Staples). - "From" and "to" are not the same fund. - In a taxable account, the client knows an exchange is a taxable sale. See Tax effects of exchanges. - The exchange does not violate the frequent-trading policy. See Frequent trading (market timing) policy.
1. Submit. The client receives a green confirmation card.
2. Tell the client the exchange will be priced at today's NAVs (if before 4:00 PM ET).

chunks.heading: Requests that aren't exchanges
chunks.text:
- Moving between accounts: see Exchange rules and limits.
- "Rebalance my account": see Rebalancing requests.
- "Move everything to safety": an emotional request in a falling market. Process it if it is clearly what the client wants, without commentary; if they ask your opinion, see Talking with clients during market downturns.
How to help a client who wants to rebalance: what you can calculate, what you can't recommend, and how to process the exchanges.

chunks.heading: What rebalancing means
chunks.text: Rebalancing is selling some of what has grown and buying some of what has lagged, to return a portfolio to a chosen mix (for example, 60% stock funds and 40% bond funds). See Rebalancing for the educational explanation.

chunks.heading: What you can do
chunks.text:
- If the client states their own target mix, you can show them their current mix from the holdings and calculate the exchanges needed to reach their target. That is arithmetic, not advice.
- Process the exchanges they choose, one exchange per Proposed Action.
- Explain that exchanges in a taxable account can create capital gains.

chunks.heading: What you cannot do
chunks.text:
- Choose the target mix for them, or say whether their mix is appropriate.
- Recommend which funds to rebalance into.
- Recommend how often to rebalance.

chunks.heading: Example
chunks.text: The client says: "I want to be 70% BF500 and 30% BFBI. I have $85,000 in BF500 and $15,000 in BFBI." Total $100,000; target $70,000 and $30,000. You can say: "To reach 70/30, you'd exchange $15,000 from BF500 into BFBI. Would you like me to set that up?"

chunks.heading: Wrap-up
chunks.text: Use the Rebalancing Discussion wrap-up code. If the client wanted advice on the mix, offer a callback and use Investment Advice.
How recurring purchases work, minimums, frequencies, and what clients can set up online versus in chat.

chunks.heading: What it is
chunks.text: An automatic investment plan (also called a systematic investment plan or "auto-invest") buys a fixed dollar amount of a fund on a regular schedule, funded from the client's linked bank account. It is the simplest way to invest consistently, and it applies dollar-cost averaging automatically. See Dollar-cost averaging.

chunks.heading: Plan details
chunks.text:
Setting: Fund; Options: Any BobsFunds fund; one fund per plan (a client can have several plans)
Setting: Amount; Options: Minimum $50 per investment
Setting: Frequency; Options: Online: weekly, every two weeks, monthly, or quarterly. Chat: monthly or quarterly
Setting: Day; Options: Day of the month 1–28 for monthly and quarterly plans (29–31 are not offered so plans run every month)
Setting: Funding; Options: A linked, verified bank account
Setting: Start date, optional end date; Options: Set by the client

chunks.heading: How it runs
chunks.text: On the scheduled day (or the next business day if it falls on a weekend or holiday), the purchase is placed and priced at that day's NAV. The bank is debited 2–3 business days later. Automatic investments appear on statements rather than in individual confirmations unless the client opts in.

chunks.heading: Changes and cancellations
chunks.text: Changes, pauses, and cancellations must be made at least 3 business days before the next scheduled date to affect that investment. See Procedure: Modify an automatic investment and Procedure: Pause or resume an automatic investment.

chunks.heading: IRAs
chunks.text: Automatic investments into an IRA are contributions for the year in which they are made, counted toward the annual limit. See Automatic investing in IRAs.

chunks.heading: In chat
chunks.text: Three tasks cover automatic investing: Set Up Automatic Investment (Procedure: Set Up Automatic Investment (chat)), Modify Auto-Invest Schedule (Procedure: Modify an automatic investment), and Pause or Resume Auto-Invest (Procedure: Pause or resume an automatic investment). Weekly and every-two-weeks plans must be set up online.
Step-by-step chat procedure for creating a recurring investment, the fields collected, and the checks before approval.

chunks.heading: What the task collects
chunks.text:
Field: Account; Options or format: One of the client's accounts (asked if more than one)
Field: Fund; Options or format: Any BobsFunds fund
Field: Investment amount; Options or format: Dollar amount, at least $50
Field: Frequency; Options or format: Monthly or Quarterly
Field: Day of month; Options or format: 1–28

chunks.heading: Procedure
chunks.text:
1. Confirm the client has a linked, verified bank account. Without one, the plan cannot run. See Linking bank accounts.
2. Let the task expert collect the details.
3. Check the Proposed Action:
- Amount is at least $50. - Day is between 1 and 28. If the client asks for the 30th or "the last day", explain the 1–28 range and ask them to choose. - For quarterly plans, confirm which months the client expects: quarterly plans run every three months starting with the first scheduled date. - For IRAs: annualize the plan (monthly × 12, or quarterly × 4) plus any other contributions this year. If the plan would exceed the client's limit, say so. See Automatic investing in IRAs. - If the client already has a plan into the same fund, ask whether they want a second plan or to change the existing one.
1. Submit. The plan is saved immediately; tell the client the first investment date.

chunks.heading: What to tell the client
chunks.text: "You're set: $200 into BF500 in your Roth IRA on the 15th of every month, starting October 15. The money comes from your linked bank, and you can change or pause it any time at least three business days before an investment date."

chunks.heading: If the client wants weekly or every two weeks
chunks.text: Explain that those frequencies can be set up online at My Account → Automatic Investments, or offer a monthly plan instead.
Changing the amount, frequency, or day of an existing plan, and how to identify which plan the client means.

chunks.heading: What the task collects
chunks.text:
Field: Which schedule; Options or format: A description of the existing plan ("the monthly $500 into BF500 in my Roth IRA")
Field: New investment amount; Options or format: Dollar amount, at least $50
Field: New frequency; Options or format: Monthly, Quarterly, or Keep the same
Field: Day of month; Options or format: 1–28, or keep the current day

chunks.heading: Identifying the plan
chunks.text: Clients often have more than one plan. Before the task is approved, make sure the plan being changed is the one the client described: match the account, fund, amount, and frequency against the client's plans (visible at My Account → Automatic Investments, and in the profile). If the description fits more than one plan, ask. Changing the wrong plan is a serious error.

chunks.heading: Timing
chunks.text: Changes made at least 3 business days before the next scheduled investment apply to that investment. Changes made later apply from the following investment. Tell the client which.

chunks.heading: Checks
chunks.text:
- New amount at least $50.
- For IRAs, the new annualized amount plus other contributions stays within the limit. See Automatic investing in IRAs.
- If the client wants to change the fund, the plan must be replaced: set up a new plan into the new fund and cancel (or pause) the old one. Explain this.
- If the client wants to change the bank account, that is done online at My Account → Automatic Investments.

chunks.heading: After submitting
chunks.text: Confirm the full new schedule in plain words, including the next date.

chunks.page: Procedure: Pause or resume an automatic investment
chunks.text: Temporarily stopping or restarting a plan, the difference between pausing and cancelling, and timing.

chunks.page: Procedure: Pause or resume an automatic investment
chunks.heading: What the task collects
chunks.text:
Field: Which schedule; Options or format: A description of the plan
Field: Pause or resume; Options or format: Pause, or Resume

chunks.page: Procedure: Pause or resume an automatic investment
chunks.heading: Pause versus cancel
chunks.text:
- Pausing stops investments but keeps the plan's settings so it can be resumed with one step. Use it for temporary needs (a tight month, a job change).
- Cancelling deletes the plan. Use it when the client does not intend to restart.
If the client says "stop my auto-invest", ask whether they want to pause it or cancel it.

chunks.page: Procedure: Pause or resume an automatic investment
chunks.heading: Timing
chunks.text: A pause takes effect for investments at least 3 business days away. An investment within 3 business days may still occur. When resuming, the next investment occurs on the plan's next scheduled day that is at least 3 business days away.

chunks.page: Procedure: Pause or resume an automatic investment
chunks.heading: Identifying the plan
chunks.text: As with modifications, match the plan description against the client's actual plans and ask if more than one fits. Pausing the wrong plan means a missed investment the client expected.

chunks.page: Procedure: Pause or resume an automatic investment
chunks.heading: Skipping a single investment
chunks.text: To skip one investment, the client can pause and then resume after the date passes, or skip it online at My Account → Automatic Investments, which offers a one-time skip.

chunks.page: When an automatic investment doesn't run
chunks.text: Why scheduled investments fail or are reversed, and how to fix the cause.

chunks.page: When an automatic investment doesn't run
chunks.heading: Common causes
chunks.text:
Cause: The plan is paused; What the client sees: No investment; Fix: Resume the plan
Cause: The bank returned the debit (insufficient funds); What the client sees: The purchase appears, then is reversed; a $20 returned-payment fee; Fix: Ensure funds are available; the plan continues next period
Cause: The bank account was closed; What the client sees: Purchase reversed; the plan keeps failing; Fix: Link a new bank and update the plan
Cause: The change was made fewer than 3 business days before the date; What the client sees: Old amount invested; Fix: Explain timing; the new amount applies next time
Cause: The scheduled day fell on a weekend or holiday; What the client sees: The investment ran the next business day; Fix: Explain the rule
Cause: IRA contribution limit reached; What the client sees: Investment rejected; Fix: Explain the limit; pause until the next tax year
Cause: Frequent-trading block; What the client sees: Rare; automatic plans are exempt; Fix: Escalate if it occurs
Cause: Foreign address on file; What the client sees: Investment blocked; Fix: See Non-U.S. persons and clients living abroad

chunks.page: When an automatic investment doesn't run
chunks.heading: Diagnosing
chunks.text:
1. Check the plan's status and settings.
2. Check recent transactions for a reversal.
3. Check the bank link status.
4. Check the IRA contributions summary for IRAs.

chunks.page: When an automatic investment doesn't run
chunks.heading: Talking to the client
chunks.text: Explain the cause simply and fix what can be fixed in the chat. If a returned payment caused a fee and the cause was our error (for example, a plan that should have been paused), escalate for a fee reversal. See Fee disputes and adjustments.
How recurring IRA investments count toward contribution limits, what happens at the limit, and the tax year of each investment.

chunks.heading: Each investment is a contribution
chunks.text: Every automatic investment into a Traditional or Roth IRA from a bank is a contribution for the current calendar year. Automatic investments made between January 1 and April 15 count toward the current year, not the prior year. Clients who want to make prior-year contributions must make a separate one-time contribution designated for the prior year.

chunks.heading: Limits
chunks.text:
The 2026 limit is $7,500, or $8,600 at age 50 or older, across all of the client's IRAs. Common plans:
Plan: $625 monthly; Annual total: $7,500
Plan: $716 monthly (50+); Annual total: $8,592
Plan: $1,875 quarterly; Annual total: $7,500
Plan: $500 monthly; Annual total: $6,000

chunks.heading: What happens at the limit
chunks.text: When an automatic investment would take the client's contributions at Bob's over their limit for the year, the investment is rejected and the client is notified. We can only see contributions at Bob's; contributions at other firms also count, and the client is responsible for the total. See Excess contributions and how to fix them.

chunks.heading: Mid-year starts
chunks.text: A client starting in July with $625 monthly will contribute only $3,750 this year. If they want to reach the full limit, they can add a one-time contribution. Explain the arithmetic; do not tell them they should max out.

chunks.heading: SEP-IRAs
chunks.text: Automatic investments into a SEP-IRA are uncommon because SEP contributions are employer contributions that depend on business income. Clients usually make one or a few contributions per year.
How recurring withdrawals work, frequencies, delivery, which shares are sold, and taxes.

chunks.heading: What it is
chunks.text: A systematic withdrawal plan (SWP) sells a fixed dollar amount from the client's account on a schedule and sends the money to their bank or by check. Retirees use it to create a regular "paycheck" from their savings.

chunks.heading: Plan details
chunks.text:
Setting: Amount; Options: Minimum $50 per withdrawal
Setting: Frequency; Options: Monthly, quarterly, or annually
Setting: Start date; Options: The first withdrawal date
Setting: Delivery; Options: Direct deposit (ACH) to a linked bank, or check by mail
Setting: Funds to sell; Options: Proportionally across holdings, or from specific funds the client chooses
Setting: Tax withholding (IRAs); Options: Federal (default 10% for Traditional and SEP IRAs) and state

chunks.heading: Taxes
chunks.text:
- Taxable accounts: each withdrawal sells shares and can produce capital gains or losses, reported on Form 1099-B.
- Traditional and SEP IRAs: each withdrawal is a taxable distribution, reported on Form 1099-R, with federal withholding unless the client elects 0%.
- Roth IRAs: withdrawals of contributions are tax-free; earnings depend on whether the distribution is qualified. See Roth IRA distribution rules.

chunks.heading: A note on sustainability
chunks.text: Withdrawals that exceed the account's returns will gradually use up the principal. You may describe this arithmetic neutrally if the client asks how long the money will last, but planning a sustainable withdrawal rate is advice; offer a callback.

chunks.heading: RMDs
chunks.text: A client who must take RMDs can use a SWP sized to meet their RMD, or the dedicated RMD settings, which calculate the amount automatically. See Procedure: Update RMD Settings (chat).
Step-by-step chat procedure for a systematic withdrawal plan, the fields collected, and the checks before approval.

chunks.heading: What the task collects
chunks.text:
Field: Account; Options or format: One of the client's accounts
Field: Amount per withdrawal; Options or format: Dollar amount, at least $50
Field: Frequency; Options or format: Monthly, Quarterly, Annually
Field: Start date; Options or format: The first withdrawal date
Field: Delivery method; Options or format: Direct deposit (ACH), Check by mail

chunks.heading: Procedure
chunks.text:
1. Confirm the account and that the client wants a recurring (not one-time) withdrawal. For one-time, use Procedure: Request a Distribution (chat).
2. For direct deposit, confirm a linked, verified bank account. Newly linked banks (within 10 days) require a verification call before the first payment.
3. Let the task expert collect the details.
4. Check the Proposed Action:
- Amount is at least $50 and not more than the account's value. - The start date is at least 3 business days away. - For Traditional and SEP IRAs: ask about federal withholding (default 10%) if the task did not capture it, and note the client's choice. - For clients under 59½ with a Traditional or SEP IRA: mention the 10% early-withdrawal penalty may apply unless an exception does. See The 10% early-withdrawal penalty. - Which funds to sell: proportionally by default; note any instruction otherwise.
1. Submit. Confirm the schedule in plain words.

chunks.heading: What to tell the client
chunks.text: "Starting November 1, $1,500 will be sold from your Traditional IRA each month and deposited to your bank, usually within 2–3 business days. We'll withhold 10% for federal taxes, so you'll receive $1,350 each month."
Special considerations for recurring IRA withdrawals: withholding, penalties, RMD interaction, and 72(t) plans.

chunks.heading: Withholding
chunks.text: Each withdrawal from a Traditional or SEP IRA is subject to 10% federal withholding by default. The client can elect any percentage from 0% to 100%. Some states require withholding when federal tax is withheld. See Federal tax withholding on IRA distributions and State tax withholding.

chunks.heading: Early withdrawals
chunks.text: For clients under 59½, withdrawals are subject to the 10% additional tax unless an exception applies. A specially structured series of withdrawals, called substantially equal periodic payments (72(t)), can avoid the penalty but has strict rules. Clients asking about 72(t) should be referred to a retirement specialist. See Substantially equal periodic payments (72(t)).

chunks.heading: Interaction with RMDs
chunks.text: Withdrawals during the year count toward the client's RMD for that year. If a client has a systematic withdrawal plan and also RMD settings, make sure they understand the total they will receive. If the withdrawals already satisfy the RMD, the RMD service will distribute only any shortfall in December. See RMDs: overview.

chunks.heading: Roth IRAs
chunks.text: Systematic withdrawals from a Roth IRA come first from contributions (tax- and penalty-free), then conversions, then earnings. Withholding is not required by default on Roth distributions.
How to help clients who have many automatic investment or withdrawal plans keep them straight.

chunks.heading: Seeing the plans
chunks.text: All plans are listed at My Account → Automatic Investments, showing account, fund, amount, frequency, day, bank, and status (active or paused). Each plan has an identifier.

chunks.heading: Common situations
chunks.text:
- Two plans into the same fund on different days (for example, payday on the 1st and 15th). Both are valid. When the client asks to change "my BF500 plan", ask which.
- A plan into a fund the client no longer holds. Plans continue even after a full redemption; ask whether to keep it.
- Plans across several accounts (Roth and taxable). Make sure the IRA plans fit within the limit.
- Investment and withdrawal plans in the same account. This is unusual and can be accidental; point it out neutrally.

chunks.heading: Consolidating
chunks.text: Clients who want to simplify can cancel several plans and set up one larger plan. Each change is a separate task in chat.

chunks.heading: Annual review
chunks.text: Encourage clients to review their plans at least once a year, and especially when the IRA contribution limit changes each January.

chunks.heading: Example
chunks.text: A client has: $300 monthly into BF500 (Roth, the 1st), $300 monthly into BF500 (Roth, the 15th), and $200 quarterly into BFBI (taxable). The two Roth plans total $7,200 a year, within the $7,500 limit if they make no other Roth contributions. When the client says "change my BF500 plan", ask which.
Why funds pay distributions, the two kinds, how often, and what happens to the money.

chunks.heading: Why funds distribute
chunks.text: A mutual fund collects dividends and interest from the securities it holds and realizes gains when it sells securities at a profit. Under tax law, a fund must pass substantially all of that income and those net gains to shareholders each year. These payments are called distributions.

chunks.heading: Two kinds
chunks.text:
Kind: Dividends (income distributions); Source: Dividends from stocks; interest from bonds; Typical timing: Monthly (bond funds), quarterly (most U.S. stock funds), semiannually (international funds)
Kind: Capital gain distributions; Source: Net gains the fund realized from selling securities; Typical timing: Usually once a year, in December; some years none
Index funds with low turnover usually distribute few capital gains. See Capital gain distributions.

chunks.heading: What happens to the money
chunks.text:
Each client chooses, per fund:
- Reinvest (DRIP, the default): the distribution buys more shares of the same fund at that day's NAV. See Dividend reinvestment (DRIP).
- Cash to the account: the distribution is added to the account's cash balance.
- Cash to the bank: the distribution is sent to the linked bank by ACH.

chunks.heading: Effect on price
chunks.text: On the ex-dividend date, the NAV drops by the distribution amount. The client's total value does not change because of the distribution itself. See Record, ex-dividend, reinvestment, and pay dates.

chunks.heading: Where clients see them
chunks.text: Distributions appear in the account's transaction history and on statements. Annual totals are reported on Form 1099-DIV for taxable accounts. See How fund distributions are taxed.
When each group of funds pays distributions, with recent example dates.

chunks.heading: Schedule by fund group
chunks.text:
Fund group: Fixed income (BFBI, BFST, BFITT, BFLTT, BFSTC, BFITC, BFLTC); Dividend frequency: Monthly; Typical pay dates: Around the 7th of each month
Fund group: U.S. equity and sector funds; Dividend frequency: Quarterly; Typical pay dates: Late March, late June, late September, late December
Fund group: International (BFIN, BFDEV, BFEMG, BFEUR, BFPAC); Dividend frequency: Semiannually; Typical pay dates: Mid-June and mid-December
Fund group: Capital gains (all funds, if any); Dividend frequency: Annually; Typical pay dates: Late December

chunks.heading: Recent examples
chunks.text:
Fund: BF500; Date: 2026-03-25; Type: Dividend; Per share: $1.636
Fund: BF500; Date: 2025-12-23; Type: Capital gain; Per share: $0.291
Fund: BFBI; Date: 2026-04-07; Type: Dividend; Per share: $0.176
Fund: BFIN; Date: 2025-12-15; Type: Dividend; Per share: $0.617
Fund: BFST; Date: 2026-04-07; Type: Dividend; Per share: $0.223
Each fund's profile page lists its recent distributions. See The BobsFunds lineup.

chunks.heading: Year-end estimates
chunks.text: In November, the funds publish estimated December capital gain distributions on the portal's Distributions page. Clients with taxable accounts sometimes ask about these when considering a purchase in late year. See "Buying the dividend".

chunks.heading: Amounts vary
chunks.text: Dividend amounts change from period to period with the income the fund earns. Past distributions do not guarantee future ones.
How automatic reinvestment works, the default setting, taxes on reinvested dividends, and how to change it.

chunks.heading: How it works
chunks.text: With dividend reinvestment on, each distribution is used to buy more shares of the same fund, at the NAV on the reinvestment date, with no fee. Example: a client holds 500 shares of BF500; the fund pays $0.45 per share ($225); at a NAV of $218.40, DRIP buys 1.030 additional shares.

chunks.heading: Default
chunks.text: Reinvestment is on by default for every fund in every new account. Clients can turn it off per fund.

chunks.heading: Changing the setting
chunks.text:
- Online: My Account → Dividend Preferences, per fund and account.
- Chat: the Change Dividend Reinvestment task. See Procedure: Change Dividend Reinvestment (chat).
A change applies to distributions with a record date after the change is processed. If a distribution's record date has already passed, that payment follows the old setting.

chunks.heading: Taxes
chunks.text: In a taxable account, reinvested distributions are taxable in the year paid, exactly like cash distributions. Each reinvestment adds to the client's cost basis, which we track and report. In IRAs, reinvested distributions are not taxed. See How fund distributions are taxed.

chunks.heading: Common questions
chunks.text:
"Why did I get a 1099-DIV if I never received cash?":
Because reinvested dividends are taxable in a taxable account. The reinvested amount increased their cost basis, so they will not be taxed on it again when they sell.
"Can I reinvest dividends from one fund into a different fund?":
Online, clients can direct distributions from one fund into another fund in the same account (cross-reinvestment) at My Account → Dividend Preferences. The chat task only turns same-fund reinvestment on or off.
Step-by-step chat procedure for turning dividend reinvestment on or off for a fund.

chunks.heading: What the task collects
chunks.text:
Field: Account; Options or format: One of the client's accounts
Field: Fund; Options or format: A fund held in that account
Field: Enable or disable; Options or format: Turn ON (reinvest), or Turn OFF (receive as cash)

chunks.heading: Procedure
chunks.text:
1. Confirm the account and fund. If the client wants to change all funds, each fund is a separate task; or direct them to Dividend Preferences online to change all at once.
2. If turning off, ask where the cash should go: to the account's cash balance (default) or to the linked bank. Note the answer.
3. Review the Proposed Action and submit.
4. Tell the client when it takes effect: "This applies to BFBI's next dividend. If a dividend's record date has already passed, that one will still be reinvested."

chunks.heading: Related questions
chunks.text:
- A client turning off DRIP in retirement to receive income may also want a systematic withdrawal plan. Mention it as an option, not a recommendation. See Systematic withdrawal plans.
- A client asking whether they should reinvest is asking for advice. Explain how each option works and offer a callback if they want guidance.
Why funds distribute capital gains, how index funds keep them low, and how they're taxed.

chunks.heading: What they are
chunks.text:
When a fund sells securities for more than it paid, it realizes a capital gain. After offsetting losses, net realized gains must be distributed to shareholders, usually in December. Distributions are classified as:
- Long-term capital gain distributions, from securities the fund held more than a year, taxed at long-term capital gain rates regardless of how long the client has owned the fund.
- Short-term capital gain distributions, from securities held a year or less, which are reported as ordinary dividends.

chunks.heading: Why index funds distribute little
chunks.text: Index funds trade only when their index changes, so they realize few gains. Many years they distribute none. Bond funds may distribute small gains when bonds are sold before maturity. Sector funds can distribute more when their index rebalances.

chunks.heading: Effect on the client
chunks.text:
- A capital gain distribution lowers the NAV by the amount paid. The client's value is unchanged, but in a taxable account they owe tax on the distribution.
- In an IRA, there is no tax effect.

chunks.heading: Questions
chunks.text:
"Why do I owe tax on gains when the fund lost value this year?":
A fund can realize gains on securities it sold even in a year its overall value fell. The distribution reflects realized gains, not the fund's return.
"Can I avoid the December distribution?":
Whether to time purchases around distributions is a tax planning decision. You can explain how distributions work and where the estimates are published. See "Buying the dividend".

chunks.page: Record, ex-dividend, reinvestment, and pay dates
chunks.text: The dates in a distribution, which one determines who gets paid, and why the NAV drops.

chunks.page: Record, ex-dividend, reinvestment, and pay dates
chunks.heading: The dates
chunks.text:
Date: Record date; Meaning: Shareholders on the fund's records at this date receive the distribution
Date: Ex-dividend date; Meaning: The date the NAV is reduced by the distribution amount. For mutual funds, usually the record date or the next business day
Date: Reinvestment date; Meaning: The date DRIP shares are purchased, usually the ex-date
Date: Payable date; Meaning: The date cash distributions are paid

chunks.page: Record, ex-dividend, reinvestment, and pay dates
chunks.heading: Who gets paid
chunks.text: A client who owns shares on the record date receives the distribution. A client who buys on or after the ex-dividend date does not receive that distribution. A client who sells on or after the ex-date still receives it.

chunks.page: Record, ex-dividend, reinvestment, and pay dates
chunks.heading: The NAV drop
chunks.text: On the ex-dividend date, the NAV falls by the amount distributed, in addition to any market movement. Example: BF500 NAV is $220.00; it distributes $1.636; on the ex-date, before market movement, the NAV is $218.364. The shareholder now has $218.364 per share plus $1.636 per share in cash or reinvested shares: still $220.00.

chunks.page: Record, ex-dividend, reinvestment, and pay dates
chunks.heading: Explaining it
chunks.text: Clients who see a drop on a distribution date may think they lost money. "The fund paid a dividend of $1.64 per share that day, so the share price dropped by that amount. You received the dividend, reinvested as additional shares, so your total value wasn't reduced by the payment." See "Why did my fund go down?".
Why some clients avoid buying shortly before a distribution in taxable accounts, and how to discuss it neutrally.

chunks.heading: The concept
chunks.text: If a client buys a fund in a taxable account just before the ex-dividend date, they receive the distribution right away and owe tax on it, even though the distribution simply returned part of what they paid (the NAV drops by the same amount). This is sometimes called "buying the dividend". It mostly matters for large December capital gain distributions.

chunks.heading: What it does not affect
chunks.text:
- It does not affect IRAs.
- It does not change the client's total value.
- It does not matter much for small quarterly dividends.

chunks.heading: How to discuss it
chunks.text:
If a client asks, explain the mechanics and point to the published distribution estimates and dates. Do not tell the client to delay or proceed with a purchase. Example:
"BF500 is expected to pay a capital gain distribution on December 22. If you buy before then in a taxable account, you'll receive that distribution and it will be taxable this year, though your total value is the same. Some investors time purchases around this. Whether that matters for you is a tax question."

chunks.heading: Example
chunks.text: A client invests $50,000 in BFMCG in a taxable account on December 18. On December 22 the fund distributes $2.00 per share as a capital gain (about 0.75% of the NAV). The client receives about $377 in distributions, taxable this year, and the NAV drops by the same amount. Their total value is unchanged; the difference is the tax timing.
How cash distributions are delivered, timing, and common questions from income-focused clients.

chunks.heading: Options
chunks.text:
When reinvestment is off, a distribution is either:
- Added to the account's cash balance on the payable date. It stays there until the client invests or withdraws it.
- Sent to the linked bank by ACH, arriving 2–3 business days after the payable date.
Distributions are not paid by check, except a final small distribution after an account is closed.

chunks.heading: Income-focused clients
chunks.text:
Retirees often turn off reinvestment on bond funds to receive monthly income. Point out, factually, that:
- Bond fund dividends vary month to month.
- Amounts are not guaranteed.
- A systematic withdrawal plan provides a fixed amount, if that's what they want. See Systematic withdrawal plans.

chunks.heading: Small amounts
chunks.text: Distributions under $10 sent to the bank are accumulated and sent once they reach $10, or at year end.

chunks.heading: IRAs
chunks.text: Cash distributions in an IRA stay in the IRA as cash. Sending them to the bank would be an IRA distribution, which has tax consequences; IRA distribution preferences are handled through the distribution tasks, not dividend preferences.

chunks.heading: Example
chunks.text: A retiree holds $200,000 in BFBI with reinvestment off and cash to bank. Each month around the 7th, about $600–$650 arrives in their bank two to three business days later. The amount varies.

chunks.heading: Switching back to reinvestment
chunks.text: Clients can turn reinvestment back on at any time; it takes effect for the next distribution whose record date is after the change.
The tax treatment of ordinary dividends, qualified dividends, capital gain distributions, and interest from Treasury funds.

chunks.heading: Taxable accounts
chunks.text:
Type: Qualified dividends; How it's taxed (federal): Long-term capital gain rates (0%, 15%, 20%); Where reported: 1099-DIV box 1b
Type: Ordinary (nonqualified) dividends, including bond fund income and short-term gains; How it's taxed (federal): Ordinary income rates; Where reported: 1099-DIV box 1a
Type: Long-term capital gain distributions; How it's taxed (federal): Long-term capital gain rates; Where reported: 1099-DIV box 2a
Type: Foreign tax paid by international funds; How it's taxed (federal): May be claimed as a credit or deduction; Where reported: 1099-DIV box 7
Distributions are taxable whether paid in cash or reinvested.

chunks.heading: Treasury fund interest
chunks.text: Interest from U.S. Treasury securities is exempt from state and local income tax in most states. Our Treasury funds (BFST, BFITT, BFLTT) and part of BFBI earn Treasury interest, and we publish the percentage each year so clients can claim the state exemption. See State tax on Treasury fund income.

chunks.heading: IRAs
chunks.text: Distributions inside an IRA are not taxed when paid. Traditional IRA withdrawals are taxed later as ordinary income regardless of the source of the money.

chunks.heading: What you can say
chunks.text: Explain the categories and where they appear on the 1099-DIV. Do not calculate the client's tax or advise how to report. See Form 1099-DIV and Tax information versus tax advice.
Every way money enters and leaves an account, with timing, costs, and limits on one page.

chunks.heading: Into an account
chunks.text:
Method: ACH from a linked bank; Timing: Invested on trade date; bank debited in 2–3 business days; Cost: Free; Limit: $100,000 per day
Method: Incoming wire; Timing: Same day if received before 4:00 PM ET; Cost: Free from us; Limit: None
Method: Check by mail; Timing: When received at the processing center; Cost: Free; Limit: None
Method: Transfer from another firm (ACAT); Timing: 5–7 business days; Cost: Free from us; Limit: None
Method: Rollover from an employer plan; Timing: 5–15 business days after release; Cost: Free from us; Limit: None
Method: Automatic investment; Timing: On schedule; Cost: Free; Limit: $50 minimum

chunks.heading: Out of an account
chunks.text:
Method: ACH to a linked bank; Timing: 2–3 business days after settlement; Cost: Free; Notes: 10-day rule for newly linked banks
Method: Outgoing wire; Timing: Same day if requested before 2:00 PM ET; Cost: $25; Notes: $1,000 minimum
Method: Check, standard mail; Timing: 5–7 business days; Cost: Free; Notes: To the address of record
Method: Check, overnight; Timing: 1–2 business days; Cost: $25; Notes: Street address required
Method: Transfer to another firm; Timing: Initiated by the receiving firm; Cost: Free; Notes: See Outgoing transfers to another firm
Method: Systematic withdrawal; Timing: On schedule; Cost: Free; Notes: $50 minimum

chunks.heading: Core rules
chunks.text:
- Money leaves only to the owner (their linked bank or address of record) unless a signature-guaranteed request directs otherwise. See Medallion signature guarantees.
- Proceeds from shares bought by ACH or check may be held up to 7 business days. See Holds on redemption proceeds.
- Money from an IRA to the client is a distribution with tax consequences. See IRA distributions overview.
- Recent contact or bank changes trigger extra verification. See Protective holds on money movement.
How electronic bank transfers work in each direction, timing, limits, and failures.

chunks.heading: What ACH is
chunks.text: ACH (Automated Clearing House) is the U.S. network for electronic bank transfers. It is free, reliable, and slower than a wire. We use it for purchases from a linked bank, automatic investments, redemptions to a bank, distributions by direct deposit, and cash dividends to the bank.

chunks.heading: Timing
chunks.text:
- Deposits (debits from the client's bank): the purchase is priced on the trade date; the bank is debited within 2–3 business days.
- Withdrawals (credits to the client's bank): sent the business day after the sale settles; arrives in 1–2 business days after that, typically 2–3 business days from the trade.
Some banks post incoming ACH credits early in the morning; others later in the day. We cannot control the bank's posting time.

chunks.heading: Limits
chunks.text:
- $100,000 per day per account for deposits.
- Withdrawals by ACH have no daily limit beyond the account's available cash, but very large withdrawals should go by wire.

chunks.heading: Failures
chunks.text: ACH debits can be returned by the client's bank (insufficient funds, account closed, debit blocked). See Returned payments and items. ACH credits can be returned if the bank account is closed; the money comes back to the client's Bob's account as cash.

chunks.heading: Business days
chunks.text: ACH does not move on weekends or bank holidays, including Columbus Day and Veterans Day when the stock market is open. See Holiday calendar 2026.

chunks.heading: ACH versus wire
chunks.text:
: Cost; ACH: Free; Wire: Incoming free; outgoing $25
: Speed; ACH: 2–3 business days; Wire: Same day
: Limit; ACH: $100,000 per day for deposits; Wire: None
: Best for; ACH: Routine deposits and withdrawals; Wire: Large or urgent amounts

chunks.heading: Explaining the timing to clients
chunks.text: "When you buy with your bank, you get today's price right away, and the money comes out of your bank in two to three business days. When you sell and send money to your bank, it usually arrives two to three business days after the sale."
Instant verification versus micro-deposits, what the client sees, and how to fix failed verifications.

chunks.heading: Instant verification
chunks.text:
The client selects their bank and signs in through a secure connection service. We receive confirmation that the account exists and the owner's name matches, then the bank is linked immediately. Their bank credentials are never shared with us.
Instant verification may not be available for small banks and credit unions, or when the bank requires extra security steps. In that case, use micro-deposits.

chunks.heading: Micro-deposits
chunks.text:
1. The client enters the routing number and account number (and chooses checking or savings).
2. Within 1–2 business days, two small deposits (each under $1) appear in their bank account, labeled from Bob's Mutual Funds.
3. The client enters the two amounts at My Account → Linked Bank Accounts.
4. The bank is linked, and the deposits are withdrawn.
The amounts must be entered within 14 days. Three wrong attempts lock the verification; the client must start again.

chunks.heading: Name matching
chunks.text: The bank account must belong to at least one owner of the Bob's account. If the names do not match (for example, a business account or a relative's account), verification fails. See Linking bank accounts.

chunks.heading: Troubleshooting
chunks.text: See "I can't link my bank".

chunks.heading: Which method to recommend
chunks.text: Instant verification is fastest. Micro-deposits work for any U.S. bank but take a couple of days. If the client needs to invest right away and instant verification isn't available, a wire or check is faster than waiting for micro-deposits.

chunks.heading: Security
chunks.text: Instant verification uses read-only access to confirm the account. We never see or store the client's bank password. Clients who are uncomfortable can always use micro-deposits.
Wire instructions for sending money to Bob's Mutual Funds, timing, and what to do when a wire hasn't arrived.

chunks.heading: Instructions
chunks.text:
Field: Receiving bank; Value: First National Bank of Funds (FNBF)
Field: ABA routing number; Value: 031000503
Field: For credit to; Value: Bob's Mutual Funds
Field: Beneficiary account; Value: The client's Bob's account number
Field: Beneficiary name; Value: The client's full name as registered
Field: Reference; Value: Fund ticker(s); for IRAs "contribution [year]", "rollover", or "transfer"
We never change wire instructions by email, text, or phone. A message claiming our instructions changed is fraud.

chunks.heading: Timing
chunks.text: Wires received and matched before 4:00 PM ET are credited (and invested if fund instructions are included) the same day. Later wires are credited the next business day.

chunks.heading: The wire hasn't arrived
chunks.text:
1. Ask the client for the amount, date sent, and the federal reference number (IMAD/OMAD) or confirmation from their bank.
2. Check the account's recent activity.
3. A wire with a mismatched account number or name is held while Money Movement Operations researches it; this can take 1–2 business days.
4. If the client's bank shows the wire as sent and it has not appeared after one business day, escalate to Money Movement Operations with the reference number.

chunks.heading: IRA wires
chunks.text: Wires into an IRA must be designated as a contribution (with year), a rollover, or a transfer. Undesignated IRA wires are held until the client confirms.

chunks.heading: Example
chunks.text: A client wires $250,000 from their bank on Tuesday morning for a purchase of BFTM in their taxable account. The wire arrives at 11:40 AM ET with the account number and name, matches, and is invested at Tuesday's NAV. If the wire had arrived at 4:20 PM ET, it would be invested at Wednesday's NAV.

chunks.heading: Advance notice for large wires
chunks.text: For wires over $250,000, a quick secure message or chat noting the amount and expected date helps Money Movement Operations match it promptly.
How clients send money out by wire, the fee, cutoff, minimum, and the verification required.

chunks.heading: Rules
chunks.text:
- Wires go only to a bank account in the owner's name that is linked and verified, unless a signature-guaranteed written request directs otherwise.
- Fee: $25 per wire, deducted from the proceeds.
- Minimum: $1,000.
- Cutoff: requests received before 2:00 PM ET on a business day are sent that day, if the cash is available (settled).
- No maximum beyond available cash.

chunks.heading: Steps
chunks.text:
1. If the money is invested, sell first. Sale proceeds settle T+1; the wire can go out on the settlement day.
2. Request the wire online (Transactions → Withdraw → Wire), by phone, or through chat as part of a sale or distribution.
3. The client's bank posts the wire the same day in most cases.

chunks.heading: Verification
chunks.text: For a wire over $50,000, or to a bank linked within the last 30 days, a representative confirms the request with the client by phone at a number on file. Explain this in advance so the client is not surprised.

chunks.heading: International wires
chunks.text: We do not send wires to foreign banks. See International money movement.

chunks.heading: Wire recall
chunks.text: Once sent, a wire is very difficult to recall. Confirm the destination carefully, and be alert for scams that pressure clients to wire money urgently. See Phishing and investment scams.

chunks.heading: Example timeline
chunks.text: Monday 11:00 AM ET: the client sells $20,000 of BF500. The sale prices at Monday's NAV and settles Tuesday. The client requests a wire; it is sent Tuesday before 2:00 PM ET and arrives at their bank Tuesday afternoon. $19,975 arrives after the $25 fee.

chunks.heading: Wires from IRAs
chunks.text: A wire from an IRA is a distribution. Withholding applies as usual, and the client must request it as a distribution. See Procedure: Request a Distribution (chat).
How deposits by check are handled: acceptable checks, endorsement, IRA designations, and timing.

chunks.heading: Acceptable and unacceptable
chunks.text: See Purchases by check for the full list. In short: personal, cashier's, and official checks payable to Bob's Mutual Funds are accepted; cash, money orders, traveler's checks, starter checks, third-party checks, and foreign checks are not.

chunks.heading: Rollover and transfer checks
chunks.text: Checks from another financial institution for a rollover or transfer should be payable to "Bob's Mutual Funds FBO [client name]" and include the client's Bob's account number. A rollover check payable to the client personally is an indirect rollover; the client may endorse it to us ("Pay to the order of Bob's Mutual Funds FBO [name], account [number]") and must deposit it within 60 days of receiving the distribution. See Handling rollover checks.

chunks.heading: Timing
chunks.text: Checks are credited at the NAV on the business day they are received in good order at the processing center before 4:00 PM ET. Mail takes several days to arrive, so the purchase date is usually several days after the client mails the check.

chunks.heading: Redemption hold
chunks.text: Proceeds from shares bought by check can't be withdrawn for up to 7 business days. See Holds on redemption proceeds.

chunks.heading: Mobile check deposit
chunks.text: Clients can deposit checks of up to $50,000 in the mobile app by photographing the front and back. Mobile deposits follow the same rules and holds. Write "For mobile deposit to Bob's Mutual Funds only" below the endorsement.

chunks.heading: Example deposit note
chunks.text: "Please deposit into account 2847-3311 (Roth IRA), 2026 contribution, invest $2,000 in BF500 and $1,000 in BFBI."

chunks.heading: Checks from relatives
chunks.text: A check written by a grandparent directly to Bob's Mutual Funds for a grandchild's custodial account is acceptable, because it is payable to us. A check written to the grandchild and endorsed over to us is a third-party check and is returned.
When we send money by check, delivery options, and who the check is payable to.

chunks.heading: When we issue checks
chunks.text:
- Redemptions or distributions where the client chose a check.
- Required minimum distributions by check.
- Final residual payments after an account closes.
- Refunds of excess contributions by check.

chunks.heading: Delivery
chunks.text:
Method: Standard mail; Timing: 5–7 business days; Cost: Free
Method: Overnight; Timing: 1–2 business days; Cost: $25
Checks are mailed to the address of record. If the address changed in the last 15 days, a check cannot be mailed there without a signature guarantee.

chunks.heading: Payee
chunks.text: The check is payable to the registered owner(s). For a joint account, to all owners. For a custodial account, to the custodian for the minor. For an IRA distribution, to the IRA owner. Checks payable to a third party (a charity for a QCD, a new custodian for a transfer) follow specific procedures.

chunks.heading: Check expiration
chunks.text: Checks are void after 180 days. See Lost, stolen, and uncashed checks.

chunks.heading: Checks for closed accounts
chunks.text: When an account closes, any final residual dividend is paid by check to the address of record, because there is no account left to hold it.

chunks.heading: Checks to the wrong address
chunks.text: If a check went to an outdated address, stop payment and reissue. See "I never got my check".
What to do when a client never received a check, lost it, or has an old uncashed check.

chunks.heading: Not received
chunks.text:
1. Confirm the date issued and the address it was mailed to.
2. Allow 10 business days for standard mail before taking action.
3. After 10 business days, the client can request a stop payment and reissue. See Stop payments.

chunks.heading: Lost or stolen
chunks.text: Request a stop payment immediately. Once the stop payment is confirmed, we reissue the check, by ACH if the client prefers (faster and safer). There is no fee for a stop payment and reissue on a check we mailed.

chunks.heading: Uncashed (stale) checks
chunks.text: Our checks are void after 180 days. If a client finds an old uncashed check, they should not deposit it. We cancel the old check and reissue the funds. Uncashed IRA distribution checks are still taxable distributions in the year issued; the 1099-R is not changed.

chunks.heading: Escheatment
chunks.text: Checks that remain uncashed for several years may be turned over to the state as unclaimed property. See Dormant accounts and unclaimed property.

chunks.heading: Example
chunks.text: A client finds a distribution check from 14 months ago in a drawer. It is void after 180 days. We cancel it and reissue the funds by ACH or a new check. The tax reporting for the original year doesn't change, because the distribution was made when the check was issued.
How to stop payment on a check we issued, timing, and limitations.

chunks.heading: Requesting
chunks.text: A stop payment on a check we issued can be requested by the payee (the client) in chat, by phone, or by secure message. Provide the check date, amount, and account. There is no fee.

chunks.heading: Processing
chunks.text: Money Movement Operations places the stop, usually the same business day. Once the stop is confirmed and the check is verified as not cashed, the funds are returned to the account and can be reissued.

chunks.heading: If the check was already cashed
