Usually not, though some plans allow "in-service" rollovers at 59½. The plan decides.
"My 401(k) has company stock.":
Employer stock can have special tax treatment (net unrealized appreciation) that is lost if rolled into an IRA. Refer the client to a tax advisor before they roll over company stock.
"I'm 55 and might need the money.":
The age-55 separation-from-service penalty exception applies to the 401(k), not to an IRA. See Exceptions to the early-withdrawal penalty.
Moving Roth 401(k) money into a Roth IRA, the five-year clock, and mixed accounts.

chunks.heading: Where it goes
chunks.text: Roth 401(k) (designated Roth) money must go to a Roth IRA to remain Roth. It can never go to a Traditional IRA.

chunks.heading: The five-year clock
chunks.text: The Roth 401(k)'s participation period does not carry over to the Roth IRA. Whether earnings are qualified in the Roth IRA depends on the Roth IRA five-year clock, which starts with the client's first Roth IRA contribution or conversion. A client who has never had a Roth IRA starts a new clock with the rollover. See Roth five-year rules.

chunks.heading: Mixed accounts
chunks.text: Most plans with Roth money also hold pre-tax money (including employer matches, which were historically pre-tax). The plan usually sends two checks: one for the Roth portion (to the Roth IRA) and one for the pre-tax portion (to the Traditional IRA). Make sure both receiving accounts exist and the client gives the plan both account numbers.

chunks.heading: RMDs
chunks.text: Roth 401(k)s no longer require RMDs for the owner (since 2024), and Roth IRAs never do.

chunks.heading: Example
chunks.text: A client's former employer plan holds $60,000 pre-tax and $25,000 Roth. The plan sends two checks: $60,000 to the client's Traditional IRA and $25,000 to their Roth IRA. If the client has no Roth IRA, open one first. See Procedure: Open a New Account (chat).

chunks.heading: Employer match
chunks.text: Employer matching contributions were traditionally pre-tax, even when the employee contributed to the Roth 401(k). Newer plans may allow Roth matching. The plan's statement shows which is which.
Rollovers from 403(b) and governmental 457(b) plans, and the special consideration for 457 money.

chunks.heading: 403(b)
chunks.text: 403(b) plans (offered by schools, hospitals, and nonprofits) roll over just like 401(k)s: pre-tax to a Traditional IRA, Roth to a Roth IRA, by direct rollover. Some 403(b)s are held in annuity contracts, which may have surrender charges; the client should check with the provider.

chunks.heading: Governmental 457(b)
chunks.text: Governmental 457(b) plans can be rolled into an IRA. One important difference: distributions from a governmental 457(b) are not subject to the 10% early-withdrawal penalty at any age after separation from service. Once rolled into an IRA, the money becomes subject to the IRA penalty rules. A client under 59½ who may need the money should know this before rolling over; mention it neutrally.

chunks.heading: Non-governmental 457(b)
chunks.text: Non-governmental 457(b) plans (offered by some nonprofits to executives) generally cannot be rolled into an IRA. The client should check with their plan.

chunks.heading: Process
chunks.text: The same as a 401(k): Rolling over a 401(k) and Procedure: Roll Over From Another Institution (chat).

chunks.heading: Example
chunks.text: A 54-year-old teacher who left their school district has a governmental 457(b) and a 403(b). They can take money from the 457(b) now without the 10% penalty. If they roll the 457(b) into an IRA, withdrawals before 59½ would face the penalty. This is a fact to share, not a recommendation.

chunks.heading: Annuity contracts
chunks.text: Some 403(b) accounts are annuities with surrender periods. The provider may charge a fee for leaving early. The client should check before requesting the rollover.
How after-tax (non-Roth) contributions in a 401(k) can be split between a Roth IRA and a Traditional IRA.

chunks.heading: What it is
chunks.text: Some 401(k) plans allow after-tax contributions, separate from pre-tax and Roth contributions. The contributions have already been taxed; the earnings on them have not.

chunks.heading: Splitting the rollover
chunks.text:
Under IRS rules, a client rolling over a distribution that includes after-tax contributions can direct:
- The after-tax contributions (basis) to a Roth IRA, tax-free, and
- The pre-tax amounts (including earnings on the after-tax money) to a Traditional IRA, tax-free.
This must be arranged with the plan, which issues separate checks, and the client must provide both account numbers.

chunks.heading: Why it matters
chunks.text: Getting after-tax money into a Roth IRA lets future earnings grow tax-free. Done incorrectly (for example, the whole amount to a Traditional IRA), the after-tax basis must be tracked on Form 8606 forever.

chunks.heading: In chat
chunks.text: Explain that the split is possible and that the plan administrator handles the allocation. Refer complex cases to Retirement Specialists. Do not advise whether to do it.

chunks.heading: Example
chunks.text: A client has a 401(k) with $300,000: $250,000 pre-tax, $40,000 of after-tax contributions, and $10,000 of earnings on the after-tax contributions. They can direct $40,000 to a Roth IRA and $260,000 (pre-tax plus the earnings) to a Traditional IRA, tax-free.

chunks.heading: Questions to send to the plan
chunks.text: Clients should ask their plan for a breakdown of pre-tax, Roth, and after-tax balances, and whether it will issue separate checks for each destination.
What to do with rollover checks made payable to Bob's, to the client, or to the old plan, and how to send them.

chunks.heading: Check payable to Bob's Mutual Funds FBO the client
chunks.text:
This is a direct rollover. The client mails the check to us with:
- Their Bob's IRA account number written on the check (or a note).
- A note saying "direct rollover" and which account and fund(s) to invest in.

chunks.heading: Check payable to the client personally
chunks.text:
This is an indirect rollover, with 20% likely withheld. The client can:
1. Deposit it in their bank and send us a check for the full original amount (making up the withholding) within 60 days, or
2. Endorse it to us: "Pay to the order of Bob's Mutual Funds FBO [name], account [number]", sign it, and mail it with a note marked "rollover". They should send any make-up amount separately.
See Indirect (60-day) rollovers.

chunks.heading: Check payable to the old plan or another firm
chunks.text: We cannot deposit it. The client must contact the issuer to reissue it.

chunks.heading: Deadlines
chunks.text: Indirect rollovers must be deposited with us within 60 days of the client receiving the distribution. Allow mail time.

chunks.heading: Tracking
chunks.text: Once we receive the check, it appears in the account as a pending rollover and is invested on the day it is processed. See Tracking rollovers and transfers.

chunks.heading: Example note to include with a check
chunks.text: "Direct rollover from Acme Corp 401(k). Deposit into Traditional IRA account 4419-8823 for Jane Smith. Invest 100% in BFTM."

chunks.heading: If the check is lost
chunks.text: The plan issued the check, so the plan must stop payment and reissue it. If it was an indirect rollover, the 60-day clock still runs from when the client received the original distribution; the IRS may grant relief for lost checks through self-certification.

chunks.page: Procedure: Roll Over From Another Institution (chat)
chunks.text: Step-by-step chat procedure to start an incoming rollover, the fields collected, and what to tell the client.

chunks.page: Procedure: Roll Over From Another Institution (chat)
chunks.heading: What the task collects
chunks.text:
Field: Source institution; Options or format: The plan or firm, e.g. "Fidelity 401(k) from my last employer"
Field: Source account type; Options or format: Traditional 401(k), Roth 401(k), 403(b), Traditional IRA, Other
Field: Estimated amount; Options or format: Approximate dollar amount
Field: Receiving account; Options or format: The client's Bob's IRA

chunks.page: Procedure: Roll Over From Another Institution (chat)
chunks.heading: Procedure
chunks.text:
1. Confirm the receiving account matches the money type: Traditional 401(k), 403(b), or Traditional IRA → Traditional IRA; Roth 401(k) → Roth IRA. If the client has no suitable IRA, open one first with Procedure: Open a New Account (chat).
2. Let the task expert collect the details.
3. Check the Proposed Action, especially the account-type match. A Roth 401(k) rolled into a Traditional IRA is not allowed; pre-tax money into a Roth IRA is a taxable conversion.
4. For a Traditional IRA from another firm, this is a transfer, which we request from the other firm. Explain that the client may need to complete a Transfer of Assets form or sign electronically. See IRA-to-IRA transfers.
5. Submit. The task records the expected rollover so the incoming money is matched and coded correctly.
6. Give the client our receiving details (see Direct rollovers) and explain the next step: they must request the rollover from their plan.

chunks.page: Procedure: Roll Over From Another Institution (chat)
chunks.heading: What to tell the client
chunks.text: "I've set up the rollover on our side. Next, contact your former employer's plan and ask for a direct rollover to Bob's Mutual Funds, payable to 'Bob's Mutual Funds FBO [your name]', with your Traditional IRA account number. Once they send it, it typically arrives within 5–15 business days, and you'll see it in your account."

chunks.page: Procedure: Roll Over From Another Institution (chat)
chunks.heading: Bonus opportunity
chunks.text: Rollover conversations may show a bonus opportunity badge. Focus on accuracy and clarity; never pressure a client to roll over.
Moving a brokerage account or IRA from another firm to Bob's, in kind or in cash, and what can go wrong.

chunks.heading: What ACAT is
chunks.text: ACAT (Automated Customer Account Transfer) is the industry system for moving brokerage accounts between firms. The receiving firm (us) starts it.

chunks.heading: Steps
chunks.text:
1. The client opens or identifies a Bob's account with the same registration as the account being moved (same owner names, same SSN, same account type: individual to individual, Roth IRA to Roth IRA).
2. The client completes the Transfer of Assets request at My Account → Transfer Assets, attaching a recent statement from the other firm.
3. We submit the ACAT request. The other firm validates it within about 1 business day.
4. Assets move, usually within 5–7 business days.

chunks.heading: In kind or cash
chunks.text:
- Cash: the other firm sells the holdings and sends cash. In a taxable account, the sale is taxable.
- In kind: holdings move as-is. We can hold only BobsFunds funds, so other firms' funds, stocks, and ETFs cannot be received in kind. The client must sell them at the other firm first (a taxable sale in a taxable account), or ask for a cash transfer.

chunks.heading: Common problems
chunks.text:
Problem: Name or SSN mismatch; Fix: Registrations must match exactly; open a matching account
Problem: Account type mismatch; Fix: IRA must go to the same IRA type
Problem: Non-transferable holdings; Fix: Sell at the other firm or transfer cash
Problem: Other firm charges a transfer fee; Fix: Their fee; we do not reimburse
Problem: Margin balance or pending trades; Fix: Must be resolved at the other firm
Problem: Partial transfer requested by ACAT; Fix: Some firms require a non-ACAT partial transfer form instead

chunks.heading: Tracking
chunks.text: The client can see status at My Account → Transfer Assets. See Tracking rollovers and transfers.
How clients move assets from Bob's to another firm, what we do, and retention guidance.

chunks.heading: How it works
chunks.text: The receiving firm starts the transfer. The client opens an account at the new firm and requests the transfer there. The new firm sends an ACAT request to us; we validate it and release the assets, usually within 5–7 business days.

chunks.heading: In kind or cash
chunks.text: BobsFunds funds can only be held at firms that offer them. If the new firm cannot hold them, the transfer will be in cash: we sell the shares (taxable in a taxable account) and send the proceeds.

chunks.heading: What we need
chunks.text: Nothing from the client in most cases. We validate that the registration and SSN match. If there is a mismatch, we reject the request and the new firm must correct it.

chunks.heading: Fees
chunks.text: We do not charge an outgoing transfer fee.

chunks.heading: IRAs
chunks.text: An IRA transfer to another custodian by ACAT or trustee-to-trustee transfer is not a distribution and is not taxable. A client who instead requests a distribution and redeposits it makes an indirect rollover (with withholding and the one-per-year limit). Encourage clients to use a direct transfer.

chunks.heading: Retention
chunks.text: Ask once, without pressure, whether there is anything we could do better, and handle any complaint properly. Do not delay or discourage a transfer. See Closing an account.

chunks.heading: Partial transfers
chunks.text: A client can transfer part of an account (for example, one fund) through a partial ACAT, started by the receiving firm with the specific assets listed.

chunks.heading: Automatic plans
chunks.text: Before an outgoing transfer, cancel automatic investments and systematic withdrawals on the account, so they don't fail or create activity after the transfer.

chunks.heading: Example
chunks.text: "Your new firm will send us the transfer request. Once we receive it, it usually completes within 5 to 7 business days. If they can't hold BobsFunds funds, the shares will be sold and sent as cash, which can be taxable in a taxable account."
Trustee-to-trustee transfers between IRAs at different firms, including non-ACAT transfers and same-firm moves.

chunks.heading: What it is
chunks.text: A trustee-to-trustee transfer moves IRA assets directly between custodians, without paying them to the client. It is not a distribution, not taxable, not reported as a rollover for the one-per-year rule, and has no withholding.

chunks.heading: Into Bob's
chunks.text: The client starts it with us at My Account → Transfer Assets, choosing their Bob's IRA of the same type. For firms on ACAT, it moves through ACAT (5–7 business days). For banks, credit unions, and insurance companies not on ACAT, we send a transfer request form to the other institution, which mails or wires the money (2–4 weeks). Some institutions require a medallion signature guarantee or their own form.

chunks.heading: Certificates of deposit
chunks.text: An IRA CD at a bank may not be transferable until maturity without penalty. The client should time the transfer with the CD's maturity.

chunks.heading: Between two of the client's IRAs at Bob's
chunks.text: Moving money from one of the client's Traditional IRAs to another of their Traditional IRAs at Bob's is an internal transfer (journal). It is not a distribution. Moving from a Traditional to a Roth IRA is a conversion. See Roth conversions: overview.

chunks.heading: Types must match
chunks.text: Traditional to Traditional, Roth to Roth, SEP to SEP or Traditional, inherited to inherited (same original owner and beneficiary).

chunks.heading: Example
chunks.text: A client has a Traditional IRA at a local bank holding CDs, maturing in March. They open a Traditional IRA at Bob's and start the transfer from My Account → Transfer Assets, choosing "at maturity". We send the bank our transfer request; the bank sends a check payable to Bob's FBO the client after the CD matures.

chunks.heading: Common delays
chunks.text: Banks often require their own transfer forms, signature guarantees, or a copy of the client's statement. Clients can speed things up by calling their bank to ask what's needed.
How clients and agents see the status of incoming money, and what to do when it's late.

chunks.heading: Where to look
chunks.text:
- Client: My Account → Transfer Assets shows each transfer's status. Rollovers appear as pending deposits once recorded.
- Agent: the client's recent transactions and pending activity.

chunks.heading: Statuses
chunks.text:
Status: Requested; Meaning: We have the request (rollover recorded or ACAT submitted)
Status: In review at other firm; Meaning: Waiting for the delivering firm to validate
Status: Rejected; Meaning: The other firm rejected it; the reason is shown (often a registration mismatch)
Status: In transit; Meaning: Assets or a check are on the way
Status: Received; Meaning: Funds arrived and were deposited
Status: Complete; Meaning: Funds invested or held as cash per instructions

chunks.heading: When it's late
chunks.text:
Situation: Employer plan rollover not received after 15 business days; Action: Client should confirm with the plan that it was sent, how (check or wire), and the date; ask for a check number or tracking
Situation: ACAT not complete after 7 business days; Action: Check for a rejection; Money Movement Operations can contact the other firm
Situation: Check sent to the client by mistake; Action: See Handling rollover checks
Situation: Rejected ACAT; Action: Explain the reason; usually the client needs a matching account or a statement

chunks.heading: Communicate realistic timelines
chunks.text: We control only what happens after the money arrives. Say "typically" and give the client the next checkpoint: "If it hasn't arrived by the 20th, contact the plan to confirm it was sent, and let us know."
What a Roth conversion is, who can do one, how it is taxed, and why it can't be undone.

chunks.heading: What it is
chunks.text: A Roth conversion moves money from a Traditional IRA or SEP-IRA (or from a pre-tax employer plan) into a Roth IRA. The pre-tax amount converted is added to the client's taxable income for the year. Afterward, the money grows in the Roth IRA, and qualified withdrawals are tax-free.

chunks.heading: Who can convert
chunks.text: Anyone with a Traditional, SEP, or SIMPLE IRA (after two years) can convert any amount. There is no income limit and no annual limit on conversions. Conversions do not count toward the contribution limit.

chunks.heading: Taxes
chunks.text:
- The converted amount is taxable as ordinary income, except for any nondeductible basis (pro-rata across all of the client's Traditional, SEP, and SIMPLE IRAs). See How conversions are taxed.
- The 10% early-withdrawal penalty does not apply to the conversion itself, as long as no tax is withheld from it. Withholding tax from a conversion makes the withheld amount a distribution, which can be penalized for clients under 59½.

chunks.heading: Irreversible
chunks.text: Since 2018, conversions cannot be recharacterized (undone). If the market falls after a conversion, or the client's income turns out higher than expected, the conversion stands. Make sure the client understands this before submitting.

chunks.heading: RMDs first
chunks.text: A client subject to RMDs must take the year's RMD before converting; RMD amounts cannot be converted.

chunks.heading: The advice boundary
chunks.text: Whether to convert, and how much, is a tax planning decision. You may explain how conversions work. You may not recommend one. Clients considering conversions are good candidates for a callback with a licensed professional.

chunks.heading: Procedure
chunks.text: See Procedure: Convert to Roth IRA (chat) and How a conversion is processed.
The taxable amount, the pro-rata rule, withholding, and reporting forms for conversions.

chunks.heading: Taxable amount
chunks.text: The amount converted is taxable as ordinary income in the year of the conversion, valued at the fair market value on the conversion date. If shares are converted in kind, the value on that date is used.

chunks.heading: The pro-rata rule
chunks.text: If the client has made nondeductible (after-tax) contributions to any Traditional IRA, they have basis. When converting, they cannot choose to convert only the basis: the taxable portion is the ratio of pre-tax money to total money across all of their Traditional, SEP, and SIMPLE IRAs (at every firm) as of December 31 of the conversion year. See The "backdoor Roth" strategy.

chunks.heading: Withholding
chunks.text: We do not withhold tax from conversions by default. A client may elect withholding, but the withheld amount is a distribution (not converted) and may be subject to the 10% penalty if they are under 59½. Most clients pay conversion tax from other funds or through estimated tax payments. Explain these facts; do not advise.

chunks.heading: Reporting
chunks.text:
- Form 1099-R from Bob's for the Traditional or SEP IRA, code 2 or 7 (depending on age), showing the conversion as a distribution.
- Form 5498 for the Roth IRA, showing the conversion amount.
- The client reports the conversion on IRS Form 8606.

chunks.heading: Effects beyond income tax
chunks.text: Additional income can affect other things: Medicare premiums (IRMAA, based on income two years earlier), taxation of Social Security benefits, eligibility for credits, and state taxes. Mention that conversions can have these effects and that a tax advisor can review them.
Converting in cash or in kind, partial and full conversions, timing, and where the money lands.

chunks.heading: Partial or full
chunks.text: The client can convert a specific dollar amount, a number of shares of a fund, or the entire balance. Many clients convert in pieces over several years.

chunks.heading: In kind or in cash
chunks.text:
- In kind: shares of a fund move from the Traditional IRA to the Roth IRA. The client remains invested in the same fund. This is our default.
- In cash: shares are sold in the Traditional IRA and the cash moves to the Roth IRA, where the client can buy something else.

chunks.heading: The receiving Roth IRA
chunks.text: If the client has a Roth IRA at Bob's, the conversion goes into it (or the client's choice, if they have more than one). If not, a Roth IRA is opened as part of the conversion. Beneficiaries are not copied from the Traditional IRA; the client should name beneficiaries for the Roth IRA.

chunks.heading: Timing
chunks.text: Conversions are processed the same business day if requested before 4:00 PM ET and are valued at that day's NAVs. The tax year of a conversion is the calendar year in which it is processed. A conversion requested in March 2026 is a 2026 conversion; conversions cannot be designated for the prior year (unlike contributions).

chunks.heading: Year-end
chunks.text: Conversions for a given year must be completed by December 31. Encourage clients to allow time before the holiday week.
Why each conversion has its own five-year clock for penalty purposes and how it affects clients under 59½.

chunks.heading: The rule
chunks.text: Each conversion starts its own five-year period, beginning January 1 of the year of the conversion. If the client withdraws converted money (under the Roth ordering rules) before that period ends and before age 59½, the 10% penalty applies to the portion of the conversion that was taxable, unless an exception applies.

chunks.heading: Examples
chunks.text:
- A 45-year-old converts $20,000 in 2026. If they withdraw it in 2028, the penalty may apply. In 2031 or later, no penalty.
- A 62-year-old converts in 2026 and withdraws in 2027: no penalty because they are over 59½. (Earnings withdrawn may still be taxable if the qualified-distribution test is not met.)

chunks.heading: Separate from the qualified-distribution clock
chunks.text: This conversion clock is different from the clock that determines whether earnings are tax-free. See Roth five-year rules.

chunks.heading: In chat
chunks.text: If a client under 59½ asks about converting and then using the money soon, explain the rule factually and suggest a tax advisor.

chunks.heading: Why the rule exists
chunks.text: Without it, someone under 59½ could avoid the early-withdrawal penalty by converting and immediately withdrawing. The five-year wait closes that loophole.

chunks.heading: Tracking
chunks.text: Each conversion's year appears on the client's Form 5498 for the Roth IRA. Clients should keep these to track their conversion clocks.
Step-by-step chat procedure for a Roth conversion, the fields collected, and the disclosures to make before approval.

chunks.heading: What the task collects
chunks.text:
Field: Convert from; Options or format: The client's Traditional IRA, SEP-IRA, or both
Field: Amount; Options or format: A dollar amount or the full balance
Field: Tax year; Options or format: The year the conversion is credited to; in practice, the current calendar year

chunks.heading: Before approving: required disclosures
chunks.text:
Confirm the client understands, in plain words:
1. "The amount you convert will be added to your taxable income for this year."
2. "A conversion can't be undone, even if the market falls afterward."
3. "We don't withhold tax from conversions unless you ask, and if we withhold, that part isn't converted and may be penalized if you're under 59½."
4. If the client is subject to RMDs: "This year's RMD must be taken first; it can't be converted."
If the client asks whether to convert or how much, do not answer; offer a callback. See Declining advice requests.

chunks.heading: Tax year
chunks.text: Conversions count for the calendar year in which they are processed. If the client asks to credit a conversion to the prior year (for example, "for 2025" in March 2026), explain that only contributions can be designated for the prior year; a conversion processed now is a 2026 conversion. Record 2026.

chunks.heading: Procedure
chunks.text:
1. Confirm the source account(s) and the amount.
2. Confirm the receiving Roth IRA, or that one will be opened.
3. Give the disclosures above and get clear confirmation.
4. Check the Proposed Action: source account, amount, tax year.
5. Submit. Confirm in plain words, and remind the client to name beneficiaries for a new Roth IRA.

chunks.heading: Script
chunks.text: "Your $15,000 conversion from your Traditional IRA to your Roth IRA is done. It's valued at today's closing prices and will be reported as 2026 income on the 1099-R we send in January. Because it's a conversion, it can't be reversed."
The errors clients make with conversions and how to help them avoid each, without giving advice.

chunks.heading: Common mistakes
chunks.text:
Mistake: Expecting to undo it later; What happens: Conversions can't be recharacterized; How to help: State it before submitting
Mistake: Converting the RMD; What happens: RMDs can't be converted; an excess contribution results; How to help: Confirm the RMD is taken first
Mistake: Withholding tax from the conversion under 59½; What happens: The withheld part is a distribution, possibly penalized; How to help: Explain withholding consequences
Mistake: Expecting to designate the prior year; What happens: Conversions count for the year processed; How to help: Explain the calendar-year rule
Mistake: Forgetting the pro-rata rule; What happens: More of the conversion is taxable than expected; How to help: Mention the rule exists; refer to a tax advisor
Mistake: Converting SEP money while contributing the same year; What happens: Allowed, but the year-end balance affects the pro-rata calculation; How to help: Refer to a tax advisor
Mistake: Forgetting beneficiaries on a new Roth IRA; What happens: The Roth IRA has no beneficiary; How to help: Remind them to name beneficiaries
Mistake: Converting from an inherited IRA; What happens: Not allowed for non-spouse beneficiaries; How to help: Explain; refer to Estate Services

chunks.heading: Tone
chunks.text: Present these as things to know, not reasons not to convert. The decision is the client's.
Why beneficiary designations matter, which accounts have them, how they interact with a will, and how clients manage them.

chunks.heading: Why they matter
chunks.text: A beneficiary designation tells us who receives an account when the owner dies. For IRAs and accounts with transfer-on-death (TOD) registration, the designation overrides the client's will: the assets go directly to the named beneficiaries without probate. An outdated designation can send money to an ex-spouse or a person who has died. Encourage clients to review beneficiaries after any major life event. See Reviewing beneficiaries after life events.

chunks.heading: Which accounts
chunks.text:
Account: Traditional, Roth, SEP IRAs; Beneficiaries: Yes, designated per account
Account: Inherited IRA; Beneficiaries: Yes (successor beneficiaries)
Account: Individual taxable; Beneficiaries: Optional, through TOD registration. See Transfer on death (TOD) for taxable accounts
Account: Joint taxable (JTWROS); Beneficiaries: Optional TOD, effective after the last owner dies
Account: Custodial (UTMA/UGMA); Beneficiaries: No; the account belongs to the minor and passes under state law
Account: Trust; Beneficiaries: No; the trust document governs

chunks.heading: Each account is separate
chunks.text: Beneficiaries are designated separately for each account. A client with a Roth IRA and a Traditional IRA must name beneficiaries on each. Ask which account(s) a change applies to.

chunks.heading: Where clients manage them
chunks.text: Online at My Account → Beneficiaries, or through chat with the Change Beneficiary Designations task (see Procedure: Change Beneficiary Designations (chat)). Some designations (trusts with complex terms, designations with conditions) require a paper form.

chunks.heading: If there is no beneficiary
chunks.text: If an IRA owner dies with no living beneficiary named, the IRA's governing agreement directs payment to the surviving spouse, or if none, the estate. Estate beneficiaries have less favorable distribution options. This is a good reason to name beneficiaries, which you may point out.

chunks.heading: What you may say
chunks.text: You can explain how designations work. You cannot advise whom to name or how to divide the account. For estate planning advice, suggest an estate planning attorney.
The difference between primary and contingent (secondary) beneficiaries and how shares pass when a beneficiary dies first.

chunks.heading: Primary beneficiaries
chunks.text: Primary beneficiaries inherit first. The client can name one or several, each with a percentage. Percentages for all primary beneficiaries must total 100%.

chunks.heading: Contingent beneficiaries
chunks.text: Contingent beneficiaries (also called secondary) inherit only if all primary beneficiaries have died before the owner, or disclaim. Their percentages must also total 100%. Naming contingents is strongly encouraged as a backstop.

chunks.heading: When one primary beneficiary dies first
chunks.text:
If one of several primary beneficiaries dies before the owner, their share is divided among the surviving primary beneficiaries in proportion to their percentages, unless the designation says "per stirpes". See Per stirpes designations.
Example: primary beneficiaries are three children at 33.33%, 33.33%, 33.34%. One dies before the owner. Without per stirpes, the two surviving children each receive 50%. With per stirpes, the deceased child's share goes to that child's descendants.

chunks.heading: Terminology
chunks.text: In the chat task, "primary" and "secondary" are used. Clients may say "backup", "alternate", or "contingent"; all mean the same as secondary.

chunks.heading: Example
chunks.text: Primary: spouse 100%. Contingent: two children at 50% each. If the spouse survives the owner, the spouse receives everything. If the spouse has already died, the children receive 50% each.

chunks.heading: Common mistakes
chunks.text:
- Naming children as primary alongside the spouse, when the client meant them as backups.
- Contingent percentages that don't add up to 100%.
- Forgetting to name contingents at all.
How percentages work, rounding, the 100% rule, and the information we need for each beneficiary.

chunks.heading: The 100% rule
chunks.text: At each level (primary and contingent), percentages must add up to exactly 100%. The system will not save a designation that doesn't. When a client adds a beneficiary, the existing beneficiaries' percentages usually need to change too. Ask: "With Maria added at 25%, how should the remaining 75% be divided?"

chunks.heading: Rounding
chunks.text: Percentages can have up to two decimal places. For three equal beneficiaries, use 33.33%, 33.33%, and 33.34%.

chunks.heading: Information for each beneficiary
chunks.text:
Field: Full legal name; Required?: Required
Field: Relationship (spouse, child, sibling, parent, friend, trust, charity, estate); Required?: Required
Field: Percentage; Required?: Required
Field: Primary or contingent; Required?: Required
Field: Date of birth; Required?: Requested; important for inherited IRA rules
Field: SSN or tax ID; Required?: Optional but recommended; speeds up payment
Field: Contact information; Required?: Optional
For a trust beneficiary, we need the trust's exact name, date, and tax ID. For a charity, its legal name and tax ID.

chunks.heading: Changes replace the previous designation
chunks.text: Each update replaces the entire designation for that account. Confirm the full resulting list with the client: "After this change, your Roth IRA's primary beneficiaries will be David at 50% and Maria at 50%, and there are no contingent beneficiaries. Is that right?"
What per stirpes means, how it differs from the default, and how clients elect it.

chunks.heading: Definition
chunks.text: Per stirpes ("by the branch") means that if a beneficiary dies before the owner, that beneficiary's share passes to their descendants (children, then grandchildren), rather than to the other named beneficiaries.

chunks.heading: Default versus per stirpes
chunks.text: Situation: Owner names children A and B at 50% each; A dies first, leaving two children; Default (per capita among survivors): B receives 100%; Per stirpes: B receives 50%; A's two children receive 25% each

chunks.heading: How to elect it
chunks.text: Per stirpes can be elected for a beneficiary online (a checkbox when adding the beneficiary) or on the paper beneficiary form. The chat task does not capture per stirpes; if the client wants it, guide them to the online page after the update, or note it for Account Services.

chunks.heading: Explaining it
chunks.text: "Per stirpes means that if one of your beneficiaries passes away before you, their share would go to their children instead of being split among your other beneficiaries." Whether to choose it is the client's decision; estate planning attorneys can advise.

chunks.heading: When clients ask about it
chunks.text: Clients with children often want each child's share to stay in that child's family line. Per stirpes does that. Clients who would rather the surviving beneficiaries share everything use the default.

chunks.heading: Example designation
chunks.text: "My three children, equally, per stirpes."
What happens when a minor inherits, the need for a guardian or custodian, and alternatives clients can consider.

chunks.heading: The problem
chunks.text: Minors cannot legally take control of inherited assets. If a minor is named directly, a court may need to appoint a guardian of the minor's property to manage the inheritance until adulthood, which takes time and cost.

chunks.heading: Alternatives clients use
chunks.text:
- Naming a custodian under the Uniform Transfers to Minors Act (UTMA) for the minor: "Jane Smith as custodian for Emma Smith under the [State] UTMA". The custodian manages the inheritance until the age of termination.
- Naming a trust for the minor's benefit. See Trusts, estates, and charities as beneficiaries.

chunks.heading: Inherited IRA rules for minors
chunks.text: A minor child of the IRA owner is an eligible designated beneficiary and can take life-expectancy RMDs until age 21, after which the 10-year rule applies. Grandchildren and other minors are not eligible designated beneficiaries on that basis; the 10-year rule applies. See Eligible designated beneficiaries.

chunks.heading: In chat
chunks.text: You can process a minor as beneficiary if the client wishes. Mention, neutrally, that minors can't take control of the assets directly and that clients often name a UTMA custodian or trust; suggest an estate planning attorney for guidance.

chunks.heading: Example
chunks.text: A grandmother names her 10-year-old grandson as 25% beneficiary of her Traditional IRA. If she dies while he is a minor, his parent typically needs to be appointed guardian of his property (or the grandmother can name "his mother, as UTMA custodian") before the inherited IRA can be set up. The grandson, not being the owner's own child, is subject to the 10-year rule.

chunks.page: Trusts, estates, and charities as beneficiaries
chunks.text: Naming a trust, the estate, or a charity as beneficiary, and the distribution consequences for IRAs.

chunks.page: Trusts, estates, and charities as beneficiaries
chunks.heading: Trusts
chunks.text: A client can name a trust as beneficiary. We need the trust's exact name, date, trustee name(s), and tax ID. For IRAs, how the trust is treated depends on whether it qualifies as a "see-through" trust, which depends on the trust's terms. Distribution rules can be complex. Refer the client to their estate planning attorney, and route any detailed questions to Retirement Specialists.

chunks.page: Trusts, estates, and charities as beneficiaries
chunks.heading: The estate
chunks.text: Naming "my estate" is allowed. For IRAs, an estate is not a designated beneficiary, so the distribution options are less favorable (generally the 5-year rule or the owner's remaining life expectancy). The assets also go through probate. Explain these facts if the client asks.

chunks.page: Trusts, estates, and charities as beneficiaries
chunks.heading: Charities
chunks.text: Charities can be named as full or partial beneficiaries. Because charities do not pay income tax, naming a charity as IRA beneficiary is common in charitable planning. We need the charity's legal name and tax ID. A charity named alongside individuals can complicate the individuals' options unless its share is paid out promptly after death; Estate Services handles this.

chunks.page: Trusts, estates, and charities as beneficiaries
chunks.heading: Processing
chunks.text: Trust and charity beneficiaries can be added online or through the chat task (relationship "trust" or "charity"). Complex trust provisions may require the paper form.

chunks.page: Trusts, estates, and charities as beneficiaries
chunks.heading: Example designation
chunks.text: "The Lee Family Trust dated March 14, 2019, Margaret Lee, Trustee — 100% primary."

chunks.page: Trusts, estates, and charities as beneficiaries
chunks.heading: Charities
chunks.text: "Philadelphia Children's Hospital Foundation, EIN 23-XXXXXXX — 10% primary."

chunks.page: Trusts, estates, and charities as beneficiaries
chunks.heading: Common question
chunks.text:
"Should I name my trust or my children?":
That's an estate planning decision. An estate planning attorney can help.
When a spouse must consent to a beneficiary designation that names someone else, especially in community property states.

chunks.heading: Community property states
chunks.text: In community property states (Arizona, California, Idaho, Louisiana, Nevada, New Mexico, Texas, Washington, Wisconsin), a married client's spouse may have a legal interest in an IRA funded with marital earnings. If a married client in these states names someone other than their spouse as primary beneficiary of more than 50% of an IRA, we require the spouse's written consent.

chunks.heading: How it works
chunks.text:
- The online beneficiary page asks about marital status and state.
- If consent is needed, the system generates a Spousal Consent form for the spouse to sign (notarized).
- Until consent is received, the designation is pending and the previous designation remains in effect.

chunks.heading: In chat
chunks.text: If a married client in a community property state names a non-spouse as primary, mention that spousal consent may be required and that they will receive instructions. Do not discuss whether the spouse would consent.

chunks.heading: Other states
chunks.text: Outside community property states, IRAs do not require spousal consent, although clients may wish to talk with their spouse. Employer plans such as 401(k)s have their own spousal consent rules, which do not apply to IRAs.

chunks.heading: Example
chunks.text: A married client in California wants to name their two adult children as 50% primary beneficiaries each on a Traditional IRA funded during the marriage. Because California is a community property state and the spouse is not the primary beneficiary of at least 50%, spousal consent is required. The client receives the consent form to have their spouse sign before a notary.

chunks.page: Transfer on death (TOD) for taxable accounts
chunks.text: How TOD registration lets individual and joint taxable accounts pass directly to beneficiaries without probate.

chunks.page: Transfer on death (TOD) for taxable accounts
chunks.heading: What it is
chunks.text: A transfer-on-death registration adds beneficiaries to an individual or joint (JTWROS) taxable account. When the owner (or last surviving joint owner) dies, the account passes directly to the TOD beneficiaries, avoiding probate, under the Uniform TOD Security Registration Act adopted in nearly every state.

chunks.page: Transfer on death (TOD) for taxable accounts
chunks.heading: How it differs from IRA beneficiaries
chunks.text:
- The account remains a taxable account; the beneficiaries' new accounts are regular taxable accounts.
- Beneficiaries receive a step-up in cost basis to the date-of-death value. See Inheriting taxable accounts.
- There are no distribution requirements.

chunks.page: Transfer on death (TOD) for taxable accounts
chunks.heading: Setting it up
chunks.text: The client adds TOD beneficiaries online at My Account → Beneficiaries by selecting the taxable account, or with the TOD Registration form. Primary and contingent beneficiaries with percentages, as for IRAs.

chunks.page: Transfer on death (TOD) for taxable accounts
chunks.heading: Chat limitation
chunks.text: The chat beneficiary task supports IRA accounts. For TOD on a taxable account, guide the client to the online Beneficiaries page (it supports taxable accounts) or send the TOD form. Do not tell the client that taxable accounts can't have beneficiaries; they can.

chunks.page: Transfer on death (TOD) for taxable accounts
chunks.heading: Not available for
chunks.text: Custodial accounts, trust accounts (the trust document governs), and tenants-in-common accounts (each owner's share passes through their estate).

chunks.page: Transfer on death (TOD) for taxable accounts
chunks.heading: Example
chunks.text: An individual taxable account with TOD to "Sam Park 50%, Jo Park 50%". When the owner dies, Sam and Jo each provide a death certificate copy and open accounts; each receives half the shares, with stepped-up basis.

chunks.page: Transfer on death (TOD) for taxable accounts
chunks.heading: TOD and wills
chunks.text: A TOD registration overrides the will for that account. Clients should coordinate TOD registrations with their estate plan.
The life events that should prompt a beneficiary review and how to raise the topic naturally.

chunks.heading: Events
chunks.text:
- Marriage or a new domestic partnership.
- Divorce or separation. In some states, divorce automatically revokes an ex-spouse designation for certain assets, but not always for IRAs; clients should not rely on it.
- Birth or adoption of a child or grandchild.
- Death of a named beneficiary.
- A beneficiary becoming disabled or needing special-needs planning.
- Creating a trust or a new estate plan.
- Opening a new IRA (beneficiaries do not carry over from other accounts).

chunks.heading: Raising it naturally
chunks.text: When a client mentions one of these events, it is appropriate (and helpful) to say: "Congratulations! Since you mentioned your new grandchild, some clients use moments like this to review their beneficiaries. Would you like me to show you who's currently listed?" This is a service reminder, not advice. See Proactive service and cross-sell.

chunks.heading: Showing current beneficiaries
chunks.text: Beneficiaries are visible to the client at My Account → Beneficiaries and in the client profile. You may tell the client who is listed on their own account after confirming identity.

chunks.heading: Example
chunks.text:
Client: "I just got divorced and I want to take my ex off everything."
Agent: "I can help. Let's start with your IRAs, where beneficiary designations override your will. Your Traditional IRA currently lists your former spouse as 100% primary. Who would you like to name instead?"

chunks.heading: After death of a beneficiary
chunks.text: If a named beneficiary has died, their share passes to other beneficiaries at that level (or their descendants, if per stirpes). The client should update the designation so their wishes are explicit.
Step-by-step chat procedure for adding, updating, or removing an IRA beneficiary, the fields collected, and the checks before approval.

chunks.heading: What the task collects
chunks.text:
Field: Account; Options or format: The IRA to update (asked if more than one)
Field: Action; Options or format: Add, Update, Remove
Field: Beneficiary name; Options or format: Full legal name
Field: Relationship; Options or format: Spouse, child, sibling, parent, etc. (not asked for Remove)
Field: Percentage; Options or format: Share of the account (not asked for Remove)
Field: Primary or secondary; Options or format: Primary or Secondary (not asked for Remove)

chunks.heading: Scope
chunks.text: The chat task changes beneficiaries on IRA accounts. For a taxable account, see Transfer on death (TOD) for taxable accounts: the client can do it online. Do not refer the client to "the support team" for a taxable-account TOD request; you are the support team. Guide them to My Account → Beneficiaries or the TOD form.

chunks.heading: Procedure
chunks.text:
1. Confirm the account. Each IRA has its own designations.
2. Show (or ask about) the current beneficiaries so the result is clear.
3. Let the task expert collect the details.
4. Check the percentages: after the change, primaries must total 100% and secondaries must total 100%. If adding a beneficiary, ask how existing percentages change. The final designation replaces the old one.
5. Check spousal consent for married clients in community property states naming a non-spouse. See Spousal consent.
6. Recap the complete resulting designation and get clear confirmation.
7. Review the Proposed Action: account, name spelling, relationship, percentage, level. Use the locate buttons.
8. Submit. The change takes effect immediately; the client receives a confirmation and a security alert.

chunks.heading: Sensitivity
chunks.text: Beneficiary conversations often follow a death, divorce, or diagnosis. Be warm and unhurried. Watch for exploitation: a new acquaintance replacing family as beneficiary, especially with someone else present in the conversation, warrants care. See Elder financial exploitation and vulnerable clients.

chunks.heading: Removing the last beneficiary
chunks.text: If the client removes all primary beneficiaries, contingent beneficiaries (if any) become primary in effect, or the account defaults to the spouse or estate. Point this out.
The first-contact procedure when a family member, executor, or beneficiary tells you an account holder has died.

chunks.heading: Your role
chunks.text: When someone reports that a client has died, your job is to respond with compassion, take the essential information, explain the next steps simply, and connect them with Estate Services. You do not settle the estate in chat.

chunks.heading: Steps
chunks.text:
1. Express condolences sincerely and briefly. See Communicating with grieving clients.
2. Identify the caller's role: spouse, child, executor, beneficiary, joint owner, attorney. Do not share any account information yet; they are not the account owner.
3. Collect basic information: the deceased's full name, and if known, their account number or the last four digits of their SSN, and the date of death. The caller's name, relationship, and contact details.
4. Explain what happens next:
- "We'll place a hold on the account to protect it while we review documentation." See Account holds after a death. - "Our Estate Services team will contact you within 2 business days to guide you through the process." - "You'll generally need a certified copy of the death certificate. Depending on the account, other documents may be needed; Estate Services will send a personalized checklist." See Documents needed after a death.
1. Route the notification to Estate Services (through the death-notification referral), or offer a callback, or give the Estate Services phone route (1-800-BOB-FUND, say "inherited account").
2. Document in ACW with the Estate Planning wrap-up code.

chunks.heading: What you can say about the accounts
chunks.text: Nothing specific until documentation establishes the caller's right to know. You may describe the general process for each account type ("For retirement accounts, the named beneficiaries will have options for how to receive their share") without confirming what accounts exist or who the beneficiaries are.

chunks.heading: Joint owners
chunks.text: If the person reporting the death is a joint owner of the account and is themselves a verified client, they may discuss the joint account. See Surviving joint owners.

chunks.heading: Never
chunks.text:
- Never ask for documents in chat by having the person paste them.
- Never pressure for a quick decision about inherited assets.
- Never suggest the family move money before documentation is complete.
How to write to someone who has lost a loved one: tone, pacing, words to use and avoid.

chunks.heading: Principles
chunks.text:
- Acknowledge first. Before anything procedural: "I'm so sorry for the loss of your mother."
- Slow down. Shorter messages, fewer questions at a time, and no autopilot.
- Use plain words. Say "died" or "passed away" (mirror the client's words). Avoid euphemisms that confuse and jargon like "decedent" or "beneficial owner".
- Explain the next step, not every step. A grieving person can absorb one or two actions. Put the rest in writing (a secure message or the checklist from Estate Services).
- Let them set the pace. If they need to stop, offer a callback.

chunks.heading: Words that help
chunks.text:
- "Take whatever time you need."
- "You don't need to decide anything today."
- "I'll make sure Estate Services has everything you've told me, so you won't have to repeat it."
- "Is there anything else I can help with right now?"

chunks.heading: Words to avoid
chunks.text:
- "I know how you feel."
- "At least they lived a long life."
- "Per our policy..."
- Anything about investment performance or "what to do with the money".

chunks.heading: When the caller is also a client
chunks.text: If a grieving client asks about their own accounts (for example, a surviving spouse), help them as usual, gently. They may have urgent needs (paying bills); answer clearly and connect them with Estate Services for the deceased's accounts.

chunks.heading: Look after yourself
chunks.text: These conversations can be hard. Take a moment after the chat if you need it, and talk with your team lead.
The documents Estate Services typically requires, by account type and claimant.

chunks.heading: Always
chunks.text:
- A certified copy of the death certificate (a photocopy is not enough; certified copies are available from the county or state vital records office or the funeral home).
- Government-issued photo ID for each person claiming assets.

chunks.heading: By situation
chunks.text:
Situation: Beneficiary of an IRA; Additional documents: Beneficiary claim form (provided by Estate Services); inherited IRA application or distribution election
Situation: TOD beneficiary of a taxable account; Additional documents: Beneficiary claim form; new account application
Situation: Surviving joint owner (JTWROS); Additional documents: Affidavit of domicile (some cases); re-registration form
Situation: Executor or administrator (estate account); Additional documents: Letters Testamentary or Letters of Administration, certified, generally dated within 60 days; estate EIN; estate account application
Situation: Small estate (no probate); Additional documents: Small-estate affidavit as permitted by state law. See Small estates and affidavits
Situation: Trust owned the account; Additional documents: Certification of trust showing the successor trustee
Situation: Medallion signature guarantee; Additional documents: For some transfers of assets to beneficiaries or between registrations

chunks.heading: How to submit
chunks.text: Upload through a secure message or the document upload page, or mail certified copies to the PO Box (or overnight to the street address). We do not need originals. Estate Services sends a personalized checklist within 1–2 business days of first contact.

chunks.heading: Timeline
chunks.text: Once documentation is complete, transfers typically finish in 5–10 business days. Complex estates or disputes take longer. See Estate settlement timelines.
What happens to an account when a death is reported: the hold, what stops, and what continues.

chunks.heading: The hold
chunks.text: When we learn of an account owner's death, we place an estate hold on the deceased's individually owned accounts. The hold protects the assets until we confirm who is entitled to them.

chunks.heading: What stops
chunks.text:
- Online access for the deceased's login.
- Withdrawals, transfers, and new transactions.
- Automatic investments and systematic withdrawals.
- Checks in process may be stopped if not yet cashed.

chunks.heading: What continues
chunks.text:
- The investments remain invested; the account value continues to move with the market.
- Dividends continue to be paid and reinvested (or held as cash).
- Statements continue to be produced.

chunks.heading: Social Security and pension deposits
chunks.text: If government benefits were deposited after the date of death into a bank account (not usually with us), the government may reclaim them; that is between the family and the bank.

chunks.heading: Joint accounts
chunks.text: JTWROS accounts are not frozen for the surviving owner beyond what is needed to process the re-registration, though large withdrawals may be reviewed. See Surviving joint owners.

chunks.heading: Releasing the hold
chunks.text: Estate Services lifts the hold for each account as assets are transferred to the rightful beneficiaries or estate.

chunks.heading: Example explanation
chunks.text: "We've placed a hold on your father's accounts, which is standard while we confirm who is entitled to them. His investments stay invested, and dividends continue to be paid into the account. Once Estate Services has the documents, they'll release the assets to the beneficiaries."

chunks.heading: Pending transactions at death
chunks.text: Automatic plans stop. Trades the deceased placed before death that already priced are completed. Withdrawals in process may be stopped; Estate Services decides.
The choices available to a spouse who inherits an IRA, and the considerations for each.

chunks.heading: The options
chunks.text:
Option: Treat as own (spousal transfer); What it means: The IRA becomes the spouse's own IRA; Key considerations: Own RMD rules; withdrawals before 59½ are subject to the 10% penalty
Option: Roll over to own IRA; What it means: Move the assets into the spouse's existing IRA; Key considerations: Same as treating as own
Option: Inherited (beneficiary) IRA; What it means: Keep as an inherited IRA; Key considerations: Withdrawals at any age without the 10% penalty; RMD rules for spouse beneficiaries, which may allow delaying until the deceased would have reached RMD age
Option: Disclaim; What it means: Refuse the inheritance within 9 months; Key considerations: Passes to contingent beneficiaries; must not have taken any of it
Option: Lump-sum distribution; What it means: Take everything; Key considerations: Taxable (except Roth); no penalty
A spouse can also start with an inherited IRA and later treat it as their own.

chunks.heading: Why the choice matters
chunks.text: A younger surviving spouse who may need the money before 59½ may prefer an inherited IRA to avoid the penalty, while a spouse who doesn't need it may prefer treating it as their own to delay RMDs. These are planning considerations. Explain the options; do not recommend.

chunks.heading: Roth IRAs
chunks.text: A spouse who treats an inherited Roth IRA as their own has no RMDs. As an inherited Roth, RMD rules apply.

chunks.heading: Process
chunks.text: Estate Services handles the election and paperwork. In chat, explain the options and connect the spouse with Estate Services or a Retirement Specialist callback.
The 10-year rule and other options for individuals who inherit an IRA and are not the owner's spouse.

chunks.heading: The 10-year rule
chunks.text: Most non-spouse individual beneficiaries of owners who died after 2019 are designated beneficiaries subject to the 10-year rule: the inherited IRA must be fully distributed by December 31 of the 10th year after the year of death. If the owner had started RMDs, the beneficiary also takes annual RMDs in years 1–9. See Inherited IRA RMDs.

chunks.heading: Options
chunks.text:
- Inherited IRA: transfer the beneficiary's share into an inherited IRA in their name; withdraw on their own schedule within the rules. Distributions are taxable (for Traditional) but never subject to the 10% penalty.
- Lump sum: take everything at once; fully taxable in that year (for Traditional).
- Disclaim: refuse within 9 months, so it passes to the next beneficiary.
A non-spouse beneficiary cannot roll an inherited IRA into their own IRA or make contributions to it, and cannot convert it to a Roth.

chunks.heading: Multiple beneficiaries
chunks.text: Each beneficiary's share can be split into a separate inherited IRA by December 31 of the year after death, so each beneficiary manages their own share.

chunks.heading: Eligible designated beneficiaries
chunks.text: Some beneficiaries qualify for life-expectancy payments instead. See Eligible designated beneficiaries.

chunks.heading: In chat
chunks.text: Explain the 10-year rule and options in general terms and route to Estate Services. Planning how to spread withdrawals over 10 years is advice; refer to a tax advisor or a licensed professional.
Who qualifies to stretch inherited IRA distributions over their life expectancy, and the special rule for minor children.

chunks.heading: Categories
chunks.text:
An eligible designated beneficiary (EDB) is:
1. The owner's surviving spouse.
2. The owner's minor child (under 21). When the child turns 21, the 10-year rule begins.
3. A disabled individual (as defined by the IRS).
4. A chronically ill individual.
5. An individual not more than 10 years younger than the owner (for example, a sibling close in age).
Certain trusts for disabled or chronically ill beneficiaries can also qualify.

chunks.heading: What EDBs can do
chunks.text: Take annual RMDs over their own single life expectancy, instead of emptying the account within 10 years. They can always take more than the minimum.

chunks.heading: Documentation
chunks.text: Disability or chronic illness status requires documentation. Estate Services collects it.

chunks.heading: Grandchildren
chunks.text: A grandchild is not an EDB on the basis of being a minor (only the owner's own minor children qualify). Grandchildren are subject to the 10-year rule.

chunks.heading: Examples
chunks.text:
- A 68-year-old sister inheriting from her 72-year-old brother: not more than 10 years younger, so an EDB.
- A 45-year-old son inheriting from his 75-year-old mother: not an EDB unless disabled or chronically ill; 10-year rule.
- A 12-year-old daughter of the owner: an EDB until 21, then the 10-year rule.

chunks.heading: Choosing life expectancy or 10 years
chunks.text: Some EDBs may elect the 10-year rule instead, which can be simpler. That choice is planning; refer to Estate Services and a tax advisor.
How individual taxable accounts pass at death, the step-up in cost basis, and what beneficiaries receive.

chunks.heading: How they pass
chunks.text:
Registration: Individual with TOD beneficiaries; Passes to: The TOD beneficiaries directly, no probate
Registration: Individual without TOD; Passes to: The estate, through probate (or small-estate process)
Registration: JTWROS; Passes to: The surviving joint owner
Registration: Tenants in common; Passes to: The deceased's share to their estate
Registration: Trust; Passes to: Successor trustee per the trust

chunks.heading: Step-up in basis
chunks.text: Shares in a taxable account generally receive a new cost basis equal to their fair market value on the date of death. Gains during the deceased's lifetime are never taxed as capital gains. Estate Services records date-of-death values for the beneficiaries' cost basis. For JTWROS accounts between spouses, typically half the account receives a step-up (rules differ in community property states). Refer tax specifics to a tax advisor.

chunks.heading: Receiving the assets
chunks.text: Beneficiaries open a taxable account at Bob's (or another firm) and receive the shares in kind. There is no requirement to sell and no distribution timeline.

chunks.heading: IRAs are different
chunks.text: Inherited IRAs do not receive a step-up; distributions are taxed as income (Traditional) or tax-free (qualified Roth).

chunks.heading: Example
chunks.text: A father bought BF500 shares for $40,000 years ago; they were worth $150,000 when he died. His daughter, the TOD beneficiary, receives them with a $150,000 basis. If she sells for $152,000, her gain is $2,000, not $112,000.

chunks.heading: Date-of-death valuation
chunks.text: Estate Services records the NAV on the date of death (or an alternate valuation date if the executor elects one for estate tax purposes).
What a surviving joint owner needs to do, and how JTWROS and tenants-in-common accounts differ at death.

chunks.heading: JTWROS
chunks.text:
When one owner of a Joint Tenants with Rights of Survivorship account dies, the account belongs to the surviving owner(s) automatically. To re-register:
1. The survivor provides a certified death certificate.
2. Estate Services re-registers the account in the survivor's name (or opens a new individual account and moves the assets).
3. The survivor should review TOD beneficiaries and automatic plans.
The surviving owner can usually continue to use the account during the process, though some transactions may be reviewed.

chunks.heading: Tenants in common
chunks.text: The deceased owner's share passes to their estate (or TOD beneficiaries if registered). The surviving owner keeps their own share. The account is split once the executor provides documentation.

chunks.heading: Surviving spouse who is also a beneficiary
chunks.text: Often the surviving joint owner is also the beneficiary of the deceased's IRAs. Help with both: the joint account re-registration and the IRA options. See Options for a surviving spouse.

chunks.heading: In chat
chunks.text: A surviving joint owner who is a verified client can discuss the joint account. Offer condolences and route the re-registration to Estate Services.

chunks.heading: Example
chunks.text: Spouses own a JTWROS account. One dies. The survivor sends a certified death certificate; the account is re-registered in the survivor's name within about a week of receiving the documents. Meanwhile, the survivor can continue to view the account and generally transact.

chunks.heading: Automatic plans
chunks.text: Automatic investments from a bank account in the deceased's name may need to be changed to the survivor's bank.
How assets of a small estate may be released without full probate, and when Estate Services can accept an affidavit.

chunks.heading: What it is
chunks.text: Most states allow assets of a small estate (below a dollar threshold set by the state, often $25,000 to $200,000) to be collected without formal probate, using a small-estate affidavit signed by the person entitled to the assets.

chunks.heading: When we accept one
chunks.text:
Estate Services may accept a small-estate affidavit for accounts that pass through the estate (no beneficiary, no TOD, no surviving joint owner), when:
- The total of the deceased's assets (as defined by state law) is under the state's threshold.
- The waiting period required by the state has passed (often 30–45 days after death).
- The affidavit is in the form the state requires, signed and notarized, with a medallion signature guarantee where required.

chunks.heading: IRAs
chunks.text: IRAs with named beneficiaries never need probate or an affidavit. IRAs payable to the estate may, depending on the amount.

chunks.heading: In chat
chunks.text: Explain that a simplified process may be available for small estates and that Estate Services will advise. Do not tell the family which process to use.

chunks.heading: Example
chunks.text: A man dies with a $12,000 individual taxable account and no TOD. His state allows small-estate affidavits under $50,000 after 30 days. His daughter completes the state's affidavit, has it notarized and medallion guaranteed, and submits it with a death certificate. Estate Services transfers the account.
How long each part of an estate settlement typically takes and how to set expectations.

chunks.heading: Typical timeline
chunks.text:
Step: Death reported, hold placed; Typical time: Same day
Step: Estate Services first contact; Typical time: Within 2 business days
Step: Personalized document checklist sent; Typical time: Within 1–2 business days of first contact
Step: Gathering documents (family side); Typical time: Days to weeks; death certificates can take 1–3 weeks
Step: Review of complete documents; Typical time: 3–5 business days
Step: Transfer of assets once approved; Typical time: 5–10 business days
Step: Probate (if needed); Typical time: Months, set by the court

chunks.heading: Factors that extend it
chunks.text:
- Missing or uncertified documents.
- Multiple beneficiaries who must each respond.
- Beneficiaries who are minors, incapacitated, or cannot be located.
- Disputes among beneficiaries or legal challenges.
- Trusts with complex terms.

chunks.heading: Setting expectations
chunks.text: Give the family the next step and a realistic range, and let them know Estate Services will keep them informed. Do not promise a completion date.

chunks.heading: Example
chunks.text:
Day: Day 1; Event: Daughter reports her mother's death in chat
Day: Day 2; Event: Estate Services calls and emails a checklist
Day: Day 12; Event: Daughter uploads certified death certificate and claim forms
Day: Day 16; Event: Review complete
Day: Day 22; Event: Inherited IRA established and funded

chunks.heading: Keeping families informed
chunks.text: Estate Services provides updates, but families sometimes contact chat for status. You can check whether documents have been received and the case status, and give the expected next step.
How assets are divided in a divorce: IRAs, taxable accounts, joint accounts, and what documents we need.

chunks.heading: IRAs: transfer incident to divorce
chunks.text:
An IRA can be divided between spouses without tax only under a divorce decree or separation agreement. The decree must direct the transfer. We then transfer the specified amount (or percentage) from one spouse's IRA directly into an IRA in the other spouse's name. Done this way, it is not a distribution and not taxable to either spouse. Afterward, the receiving spouse owns that IRA.
A client who withdraws money from their IRA and gives it to their ex-spouse has made a taxable distribution, not a divorce transfer.

chunks.heading: QDROs are for employer plans
chunks.text: A Qualified Domestic Relations Order (QDRO) divides an employer plan such as a 401(k). IRAs do not need a QDRO; a decree suffices. Clients often use the terms interchangeably. See QDRO versus divorce decree.

chunks.heading: Taxable accounts
chunks.text: Individual taxable accounts are transferred per the decree, in kind, to the receiving spouse's account. Transfers between spouses incident to divorce are not taxable; the cost basis carries over.

chunks.heading: Joint accounts
chunks.text: Removing a former spouse from a joint account requires both owners' signatures, or the decree directing the change. Usually the assets are moved into individual accounts for each.

chunks.heading: Documents
chunks.text:
- A certified copy of the divorce decree (or the relevant pages, plus the signature and judge's pages).
- Our Divorce Transfer form, signed by the account owner (or the decree must be specific enough to act on without it).
- An account at Bob's in the receiving spouse's name (we can help them open one).

chunks.heading: Beneficiaries
chunks.text: After a divorce, clients often need to update beneficiaries. In some states, divorce automatically revokes an ex-spouse designation for certain assets, but clients should not rely on that. Suggest a review. See Reviewing beneficiaries after life events.

chunks.heading: In chat
chunks.text: Explain the process, send the form, and route to Account Services. Be neutral and discreet; do not discuss one spouse's accounts with the other.
The difference between a QDRO and a divorce decree, and which one each account type needs.

chunks.heading: Comparison
chunks.text:
: Used for; QDRO: Employer plans: 401(k), 403(b), pensions; Divorce decree / separation agreement: IRAs and taxable accounts
: Issued by; QDRO: A court, approved by the plan administrator; Divorce decree / separation agreement: A court
: What it does; QDRO: Assigns part of the plan to an "alternate payee"; Divorce decree / separation agreement: Divides marital property
: Tax effect; QDRO: Alternate payee can roll to their IRA tax-free; Divorce decree / separation agreement: IRA transfer incident to divorce is tax-free

chunks.heading: Special QDRO rule
chunks.text: An alternate payee spouse receiving a distribution from an employer plan under a QDRO can take it in cash without the 10% early-withdrawal penalty (it is still taxable). Once rolled into an IRA, the IRA penalty rules apply. Mention this neutrally to a client receiving QDRO money who may need cash.

chunks.heading: At Bob's
chunks.text: We do not administer employer plans, so we do not process QDROs. We receive rollovers of QDRO distributions into IRAs. We process IRA divisions under divorce decrees.

chunks.heading: Example
chunks.text: A client's divorce decree awards her half of her ex-husband's 401(k) and $50,000 from his IRA at Bob's. The 401(k) portion needs a QDRO approved by the plan; once paid, she can roll it into her own IRA at Bob's. The IRA portion is transferred directly under the decree into her IRA at Bob's. Neither is taxable to her at the time.
How clients give fund shares to someone else, tax considerations, and the paperwork.

chunks.heading: How it works
chunks.text: A client can transfer shares from their taxable account to another person's taxable account (at Bob's) in kind. The recipient receives the shares with the giver's cost basis (carryover basis), with special rules if the value has fallen below basis.

chunks.heading: Requirements
chunks.text:
- The recipient must have, or open, an account at Bob's.
- The giver completes the Gift/Transfer of Shares form, with a medallion signature guarantee.
- For gifts to a minor, the recipient account is a custodial account. See Custodial accounts (UTMA/UGMA).

chunks.heading: Taxes
chunks.text: Gifts are not taxable to the recipient. The giver may need to file a gift tax return if gifts to one person exceed the annual exclusion ($19,000 per recipient for 2025 and 2026), though tax is rarely owed. Refer details to a tax advisor.

chunks.heading: IRAs
chunks.text: IRA assets cannot be gifted. A client would have to take a taxable distribution first.

chunks.heading: Gifts to charity
chunks.text: Clients can donate shares from a taxable account to a charity's brokerage account, typically to avoid capital gains on appreciated shares. The charity provides its account details; the client completes the transfer form. For IRA giving, see Qualified charitable distributions (QCDs).

chunks.heading: Example
chunks.text: A grandfather gives 50 shares of BF500 from his taxable account to his granddaughter's custodial account. The shares move in kind with his cost basis. He completes the gift form with a medallion signature guarantee.
Moving taxable accounts into a revocable living trust, changing trustees, and what can't go into a trust.

chunks.heading: Moving an account into a trust
chunks.text:
When a client creates a revocable living trust, their estate attorney may advise retitling taxable accounts in the trust's name. The process:
1. Open a trust account at Bob's (see Opening trust accounts).
2. Complete the transfer form to move shares in kind from the individual (or joint) account to the trust account.
3. Account Services reviews the trust certification.
For a revocable trust using the grantor's SSN, this is not a taxable event, and the cost basis carries over.

chunks.heading: IRAs can't be retitled
chunks.text: An IRA must be owned by an individual. To coordinate an IRA with a trust, the client names the trust as beneficiary. See Trusts, estates, and charities as beneficiaries.

chunks.heading: Changing trustees
chunks.text:
When a trustee dies, resigns, or is added, Account Services needs:
- An updated Certification of Trust or the trust amendment naming the current trustees.
- A death certificate (if a trustee died).
- ID for any new trustee.

chunks.heading: In chat
chunks.text: Explain the steps and route to Account Services. Questions about whether to use a trust go to an estate planning attorney.

chunks.heading: Example
chunks.text: A couple creates the "Patel Family Revocable Trust" and wants their joint account in it. They open a trust account at Bob's, provide the Certification of Trust, and transfer the shares in kind. Their SSN remains the tax ID, so nothing is taxable.

chunks.page: When a custodial account's minor comes of age
chunks.text: What happens when a UTMA/UGMA beneficiary reaches the age of termination, and the custodian's obligations.

chunks.page: When a custodial account's minor comes of age
chunks.heading: The rule
chunks.text: A custodial account must be turned over to the beneficiary when they reach the age of termination set by the account's state law (commonly 18 or 21; some states allow the custodian to elect up to 25 when the account is created).

chunks.page: When a custodial account's minor comes of age
chunks.heading: Process
chunks.text:
1. About 60 days before the termination age, we notify the custodian and the beneficiary.
2. The beneficiary opens an individual account in their own name (or we convert the account), verifying their identity.
3. The assets move to the beneficiary's account in kind.
4. The custodian's access ends.

chunks.page: When a custodial account's minor comes of age
chunks.heading: If the custodian does nothing
chunks.text: The obligation exists regardless. Once the beneficiary reaches the termination age, the beneficiary can provide proof of age and identity and request the transfer.

chunks.page: When a custodial account's minor comes of age
chunks.heading: Custodian concerns
chunks.text: Custodians sometimes worry about a young adult receiving the money. The gift is irrevocable; the account legally belongs to the beneficiary. Custodians cannot extend control beyond the termination age. Explain kindly and factually.

chunks.page: When a custodial account's minor comes of age
chunks.heading: Custodial Roth IRAs
chunks.text: When the owner of a custodial Roth IRA reaches the age of majority, the custodian's role ends and the owner takes control of their own Roth IRA.

chunks.page: When a custodial account's minor comes of age
chunks.heading: Example
chunks.text: A UTMA account under Pennsylvania law terminates at 21. When the beneficiary turns 21, we notify the custodian and the young adult, who opens an individual account and receives the shares.
The general steps for any change of ownership: death, divorce, trust, or gift, and who handles each.

chunks.heading: When it applies
chunks.text:
Any time assets move from one owner or registration to another:
- Death of an account holder (Estate Services). See When someone reports a death.
- Divorce (Account Services). See Divorce and account transfers.
- Transfer to or between trusts (Account Services). See Retitling accounts to a trust.
- Gifts of shares (Account Services). See Gifting shares to another person.
- Custodial termination (Account Services). See When a custodial account's minor comes of age.
- Legal name change, which is not a change of ownership but uses similar paperwork. See Legal name changes.

chunks.heading: General steps
chunks.text:
1. The client or claimant contacts us.
2. We identify the type of change and send a personalized document checklist.
3. The client submits documents (secure upload, mail).
4. The responsible team reviews; we may ask for missing items.
5. Assets are transferred, usually 5–10 business days after documents are complete.
6. Written confirmation is sent.

chunks.heading: In chat
chunks.text: Your job is to identify the type of change, explain the general process, send the right form, and route to the responsible team, with a clear next step for the client.

chunks.heading: Example
chunks.text: A client says, "My mother died, and my brother and I are her beneficiaries." That is a death-related change handled by Estate Services. A client who says, "I want to put my account in my trust" is handled by Account Services. Identifying the type early sends the client to the right team the first time.

chunks.page: Marriage and other happy life events
chunks.text: Account housekeeping clients often want after marriage, a new child, a new job, or retirement.

chunks.page: Marriage and other happy life events
chunks.heading: Marriage
chunks.text:
- Name change, if any. See Legal name changes.
- Review beneficiaries. See Reviewing beneficiaries after life events.
- Consider adding a spouse as joint owner or authorized user. See Registration changes and Authorized users and access levels.
- Spousal IRA contributions become possible if one spouse has little income. See Spousal IRA contributions.

chunks.page: Marriage and other happy life events
chunks.heading: New child or grandchild
chunks.text:
- Review beneficiaries.
- Custodial accounts for the child. See Custodial accounts (UTMA/UGMA).

chunks.page: Marriage and other happy life events
chunks.heading: New job
chunks.text:
- Rolling over the old employer's 401(k) is an option. See Rolling over a 401(k).
- A workplace plan may affect Traditional IRA deductibility. See Traditional IRA deductibility.

chunks.page: Marriage and other happy life events
chunks.heading: Retirement
chunks.text:
- Systematic withdrawals for income. See Systematic withdrawal plans.
- RMDs approaching. See RMDs: overview.
- Rollover of workplace plans.
