chunks.page: Marriage and other happy life events
chunks.heading: How to raise these
chunks.text: Mention one relevant service, naturally, as a helpful reminder: "Congratulations on the wedding! If you'd like, I can show you how to update your beneficiaries." Never pressure, never advise. See Proactive service and cross-sell.

chunks.page: Marriage and other happy life events
chunks.heading: Example conversation
chunks.text:
Client: "I got married last month and changed my last name."
Agent: "Congratulations! For the name change, you'll upload our name change form and a copy of your marriage certificate. And since your Roth IRA lists your sister as beneficiary, would you like to review that too?"
Which tax forms each account type produces, where clients find them, and how to handle tax-season questions.

chunks.heading: Forms by account type
chunks.text:
Account: Taxable (individual, joint, trust, custodial); Forms: Consolidated Form 1099 (1099-DIV, 1099-B, 1099-INT if any); What they report: Dividends, capital gain distributions, sales and exchanges, foreign tax paid
Account: Traditional, Roth, SEP, inherited IRA; Forms: Form 1099-R (if there was a distribution); What they report: Distributions, conversions, excess removals
Account: Traditional, Roth, SEP, inherited IRA; Forms: Form 5498; What they report: Contributions, rollovers, conversions, year-end value, RMD for next year
IRA dividends and trades are not reported each year; nothing is taxable until a distribution.

chunks.heading: Where to find forms
chunks.text: My Account → Tax Documents. Forms stay online for 7 years. Paperless clients receive an email when forms are ready; others receive paper by mail by the deadlines. See Tax form calendar.

chunks.heading: Not every client gets every form
chunks.text:
- No 1099-DIV if the account received less than $10 of dividends (but the income is still taxable).
- No 1099-B if there were no sales or exchanges in a taxable account.
- No 1099-R if there were no IRA distributions.
- Form 5498 is produced for every IRA with a year-end balance.

chunks.heading: Tax season tips
chunks.text:
- Forms can't be produced earlier than their availability date. Clients who file very early may need a corrected return if a form changes. See Corrected tax forms.
- Clients who say a form is "missing" usually had no reportable activity on that account or are looking at the wrong year.

chunks.heading: The advice boundary
chunks.text: Explain what each form shows and where the numbers come from. Do not tell clients how to file, what is deductible, or how much they will owe. See Tax information versus tax advice.
When each tax form is available, mailing deadlines, and the dates clients ask about most.

chunks.heading: Calendar for tax year 2025 (forms issued in 2026)
chunks.text:
Form: 1099-R (IRA distributions); Available online: Mid-January; Mailed by: January 31, 2026
Form: 1099-DIV (if not consolidated); Available online: Mid-January; Mailed by: January 31, 2026
Form: Consolidated 1099 (DIV, B, INT); Available online: Early February; Mailed by: February 15, 2026
Form: Corrected consolidated 1099s; Available online: As needed; Mailed by: Up to March 15, 2026
Form: Form 5498 (IRA contributions and values); Available online: May; Mailed by: May 31, 2026
Form: RMD notice for 2026; Available online: January; Mailed by: January 31, 2026
Forms for tax year 2026 follow the same pattern in 2027.

chunks.heading: Why 5498 comes in May
chunks.text: Clients can make prior-year IRA contributions until April 15, so the 5498 is produced after the deadline to include them. Clients do not need the 5498 to file; their own records of contributions are enough.

chunks.heading: Why the consolidated 1099 comes later
chunks.text: Funds finalize the character of distributions (for example, how much was qualified dividend or return of capital) in January, so consolidated forms are produced after that information is final.

chunks.heading: Questions in January
chunks.text:
"Where's my 1099?":
1099-R and 1099-DIV forms (when not consolidated) are mailed by January 31; consolidated forms by February 15. Online availability is often a little earlier.
"Can I file without the 5498?":
Yes. It is informational and arrives in May.
"I need my RMD amount for this year.":
The RMD notice is mailed in January and the amount is shown on the retirement account page. See RMDs: overview.
What each box on the 1099-DIV means for our funds, and common client questions.

chunks.heading: What it reports
chunks.text: Dividends and capital gain distributions paid in a taxable account during the year, whether paid in cash or reinvested.

chunks.heading: Key boxes
chunks.text:
Box: 1a Total ordinary dividends; Meaning: All dividends, including qualified dividends and short-term capital gain distributions
Box: 1b Qualified dividends; Meaning: The portion of 1a eligible for lower long-term capital gain rates. See Qualified dividends
Box: 2a Total capital gain distributions; Meaning: Long-term capital gain distributions
Box: 3 Nondividend distributions; Meaning: Return of capital (reduces cost basis; not currently taxable)
Box: 4 Federal income tax withheld; Meaning: Backup withholding, if any. See Form W-9 and backup withholding
Box: 5 Section 199A dividends; Meaning: REIT dividends from BFREI that may qualify for a deduction
Box: 7 Foreign tax paid; Meaning: For international funds. See Foreign tax credit
Box: 12 Exempt-interest dividends; Meaning: Not applicable to our funds

chunks.heading: Common questions
chunks.text:
"I reinvested everything. Why is this taxable?":
Reinvested distributions are taxable in a taxable account. They also increase cost basis. See Dividend reinvestment (DRIP).
"Why is the bond fund income not qualified?":
Bond interest is never a qualified dividend; it is ordinary income.
"My fund lost value. Why do I have dividends?":
Dividends and the fund's price change are separate. The fund paid out income it earned.
"What about my IRA?":
No 1099-DIV for IRAs. Nothing is taxed until distributions.
How sales and exchanges in taxable accounts are reported, including cost basis, holding period, and covered status.

chunks.heading: What it reports
chunks.text: Every sale and exchange in a taxable account during the year: the date sold, proceeds, cost basis (for covered shares), date acquired, whether the gain or loss is short-term or long-term, and any wash-sale adjustments.

chunks.heading: Covered and noncovered
chunks.text:
- Covered shares (fund shares acquired since January 1, 2012): we report cost basis to the IRS.
- Noncovered shares (acquired before 2012, or transferred in without basis): we may show basis if we have it, but do not report it to the IRS; the client is responsible.
See Covered and noncovered shares.

chunks.heading: Sections of the form
chunks.text: The 1099-B is organized by short-term and long-term, and covered and noncovered, matching the categories the client reports on IRS Form 8949.

chunks.heading: Cost basis method
chunks.text: The basis shown depends on the method in effect when the shares were sold: average cost (default), FIFO, or specific identification. See Cost basis methods.

chunks.heading: Exchanges
chunks.text: An exchange appears as a sale of the "from" fund. Clients often forget this.

chunks.heading: Common questions
chunks.text:
"The basis is missing.":
The shares may be noncovered. The client can use their own records, or contact us for any historical information we have (Tax Reporting).
"The gain looks too high.":
Check whether reinvested dividends are included in the basis (they are, for covered shares) and whether the method is what the client expected. Refer suspected errors to Tax Reporting.
How IRA distributions, conversions, and corrections are reported on the 1099-R, and what the distribution codes mean.

chunks.heading: What it reports
chunks.text: Any distribution from an IRA during the year: withdrawals, RMDs, conversions to Roth, removals of excess contributions, QCDs (shown as normal distributions), and inherited IRA distributions.

chunks.heading: Key boxes
chunks.text:
Box: 1 Gross distribution; Meaning: The total amount distributed, before withholding
Box: 2a Taxable amount; Meaning: Often the same as box 1 for Traditional IRAs; may be blank or "not determined" (box 2b) when we can't know the client's basis
Box: 4 Federal income tax withheld; Meaning: Withholding we sent to the IRS
Box: 7 Distribution code; Meaning: Why the distribution was made
Box: 7 IRA/SEP/SIMPLE checkbox; Meaning: Checked for Traditional, SEP, SIMPLE IRAs
Box: 14 State tax withheld; Meaning: If any

chunks.heading: Common codes in box 7
chunks.text:
Code: 1; Meaning: Early distribution, no known exception
Code: 2; Meaning: Early distribution, exception applies (includes Roth conversions under 59½)
Code: 3; Meaning: Disability
Code: 4; Meaning: Death (beneficiary)
Code: 7; Meaning: Normal distribution
Code: G; Meaning: Direct rollover from a plan
Code: J; Meaning: Early distribution from a Roth IRA
Code: Q; Meaning: Qualified distribution from a Roth IRA
Code: T; Meaning: Roth distribution, exception applies
Code: 8 or P; Meaning: Excess contribution removal (year of the contribution)

chunks.heading: Common questions
chunks.text:
"I rolled it over. Why did I get a 1099-R?":
An indirect rollover is reported as a distribution; the client reports the rollover on their return, and our 5498 shows the rollover deposit.
"I gave to charity (QCD). Why does the 1099-R show it as taxable?":
QCDs are reported as normal distributions. The client excludes it on their return. See Qualified charitable distributions (QCDs).
"Is my Roth withdrawal taxable?":
Often box 2a is blank because we don't know their basis. They determine it on Form 8606.
What the 5498 reports, why it arrives in May, and why clients usually don't need it to file.

chunks.heading: What it reports
chunks.text:
For each IRA, for the tax year:
Box: 1 IRA contributions; Meaning: Traditional IRA contributions for the year, including those made January–April of the next year
Box: 2 Rollover contributions; Meaning: Rollovers received
Box: 3 Roth conversion amount; Meaning: Amounts converted into a Roth IRA
Box: 4 Recharacterized contributions; Meaning: Recharacterizations
Box: 5 Fair market value; Meaning: Account value on December 31
Box: 8 SEP contributions; Meaning: SEP employer contributions
Box: 10 Roth IRA contributions; Meaning: Roth contributions for the year
Box: 11–12 RMD; Meaning: Whether an RMD is required for the next year, and the amount

chunks.heading: Timing
chunks.text: Mailed by May 31, after the prior-year contribution deadline. Clients can file their tax returns without it; their contribution records are enough. It is informational: the client doesn't file it.

chunks.heading: Common questions
chunks.text:
"My 5498 shows the wrong year for my contribution.":
Contributions are reported for the tax year designated. If the designation was wrong, see Prior-year contributions (January to April).
"Why didn't I get one?":
Every IRA with a balance gets one. If the account was opened and closed in the same year with no contributions, there may be none.

chunks.heading: Example
chunks.text: A client made a $7,000 Roth contribution for 2025 on March 15, 2026. It appears in box 10 of the 2025 Form 5498, mailed by May 31, 2026.

chunks.heading: RMD boxes
chunks.text: For clients subject to RMDs, boxes 11 and 12 show that an RMD is due for the next year and its amount (or that one is required). This is also how the IRS knows an RMD is due.
How the combined 1099 package for taxable accounts is organized and how to help clients read it.

chunks.heading: What it is
chunks.text: For each taxable account, we combine the 1099-DIV, 1099-B, and 1099-INT (if any) into one document, the consolidated Form 1099, with a summary page and detail pages.

chunks.heading: Structure
chunks.text:
1. Summary: totals from each form.
2. 1099-DIV detail: dividends and capital gains by fund.
3. 1099-B detail: each sale and exchange, grouped by short-term/long-term and covered/noncovered.
4. Supplemental information (not reported to the IRS): Treasury interest percentages for state tax, foreign source income, and other details that help with filing.

chunks.heading: Delivery
chunks.text: Available online in early February; mailed by February 15. Corrections may be issued until March 15.

chunks.heading: Tax software
chunks.text: Most tax software can import the consolidated 1099 directly using the client's online credentials or a downloaded file (My Account → Tax Documents → Download for tax software).

chunks.heading: Questions
chunks.text: Help clients find numbers on the form; do not tell them where to enter numbers on their return.

chunks.heading: Common questions
chunks.text:
"I have two accounts. Do I get two forms?":
Each taxable account has its own consolidated 1099. IRAs produce their own 1099-R and 5498.
"The summary and detail pages don't match.":
The summary totals each category; the detail lists each transaction. Short-term and long-term, covered and noncovered sales are totaled separately.
"Why does it say 'supplemental information, not reported to the IRS'?":
Those pages help with filing (for example, Treasury percentages) but are not part of what we report to the IRS.
Why tax forms are sometimes corrected, how clients are notified, and what they should do.

chunks.heading: Why corrections happen
chunks.text:
- Funds reclassify distributions after year end (for example, part of a dividend turns out to be return of capital).
- A cost basis adjustment (a transfer-in with late basis information, a wash-sale correction).
- A transaction correction (an as-of trade, a contribution recoded to another year).
- A client's tax ID or name was wrong.

chunks.heading: Notification
chunks.text: Corrected forms are marked "CORRECTED" and posted online, with an email to paperless clients, and mailed to others. Most corrections occur by March 15.

chunks.heading: What the client should do
chunks.text: If they have not filed, use the corrected form. If they already filed, they may need to amend their return; whether the change matters is a question for their tax advisor.

chunks.heading: Requesting a correction
chunks.text: If a client believes a form is wrong, collect the account, the form, the box, and why they think it is wrong, and refer to Tax Reporting. Do not promise a correction. See "My tax form is wrong".

chunks.heading: Example
chunks.text: In February a client files using their consolidated 1099. In March, a fund reclassifies part of a December distribution as return of capital, and we issue a corrected 1099-DIV with a slightly lower box 1a. The client should ask their tax preparer whether an amended return is needed; small changes often don't warrant one, but that is their decision.

chunks.heading: Delaying filing
chunks.text: Some clients with taxable accounts wait until mid-March to file, to reduce the chance of corrections. That's a common practice you can mention as information.
The three methods available (average cost, FIFO, specific identification), how to change, and how each works.

chunks.heading: What cost basis is
chunks.text: Cost basis is what the client paid for their shares, including reinvested dividends and capital gains. When they sell, the gain or loss is proceeds minus basis.

chunks.heading: Methods
chunks.text:
Method: Average cost (default); How it works: The basis per share is the average of all shares owned; Notes: Simple; most common for mutual funds
Method: FIFO (first in, first out); How it works: The oldest shares are sold first; Notes: Oldest shares often have the lowest basis (larger gains) but are long-term
Method: Specific identification; How it works: The client chooses which lots to sell; Notes: Requires choosing lots at the time of each sale

chunks.heading: Changing the method
chunks.text: Clients change the method at My Account → Tax Settings, per fund or for the account. The method must be in place before a sale; it cannot be changed retroactively for shares already sold. Changing away from average cost applies to future sales; the basis of shares already averaged may remain averaged.

chunks.heading: Example
chunks.text:
A client bought 10 shares at $100 and 10 at $150 and sells 10 at $160.
- Average cost: basis $125/share; gain $350.
- FIFO: basis $100/share; gain $600.
- Specific ID (choosing the $150 shares): gain $100.

chunks.heading: What you can say
chunks.text: Explain the methods and how to change them. Which method to use is a tax decision.
Which shares have cost basis reported to the IRS, why, and what clients need for older shares.

chunks.heading: Definitions
chunks.text:
- Covered: mutual fund shares acquired on or after January 1, 2012. We track and report their basis to the IRS on Form 1099-B.
- Noncovered: shares acquired before 2012, or transferred from another firm without basis information. Basis is the client's responsibility.

chunks.heading: Transfers in
chunks.text: When shares transfer to us from another firm (where the shares are BobsFunds shares), the delivering firm should send basis information for covered shares within 15 days. If it doesn't arrive, the shares are treated as noncovered until updated.

chunks.heading: Inherited and gifted shares
chunks.text: Inherited shares receive date-of-death basis, which we record when Estate Services processes the transfer. Gifted shares carry the giver's basis, which the giver should provide.

chunks.heading: Finding old basis
chunks.text: For noncovered shares, clients can use old statements and confirmations. We may have historical records; requests go to Tax Reporting.

chunks.heading: Example
chunks.text: A client has owned BF500 since 2008 and kept buying through 2026. Shares bought before 2012 are noncovered; shares bought since are covered. When they sell, the 1099-B shows covered and noncovered sales in separate sections. For noncovered shares, we may show basis "for information only", which the client should verify.

chunks.heading: Average cost and the 2012 split
chunks.text: Under average cost, covered and noncovered shares are averaged separately. Clients who switch methods should ask their tax advisor about the effect.
What a wash sale is, how it can affect clients who sell at a loss, and what we report.

chunks.heading: The rule
chunks.text: If a client sells shares at a loss and buys the same or a "substantially identical" security within 30 days before or after the sale, the loss is disallowed (deferred). The disallowed loss is added to the basis of the replacement shares.

chunks.heading: Common triggers
chunks.text:
- Selling a fund at a loss while an automatic investment buys more of the same fund within 30 days.
- Dividend reinvestments within 30 days of the loss sale.
- Buying the same fund in an IRA within 30 days (the loss is permanently disallowed in that case).

chunks.heading: What we report
chunks.text: On Form 1099-B, we report wash sales we can identify within the same account for the same fund. We do not track purchases at other firms or in other accounts; the client is responsible for those.

chunks.heading: "Substantially identical"
chunks.text: Whether two different funds (for example, two different S&P 500 index funds) are substantially identical is not clearly defined. It is a question for the client's tax advisor.

chunks.heading: In chat
chunks.text: Explain the rule if asked, and note that automatic investments and dividend reinvestment can trigger it. Do not advise how to structure sales.

chunks.heading: Example
chunks.text: A client sells 100 shares of BF500 at a $1,000 loss on November 10. Their automatic investment buys 2 shares of BF500 on November 15. The loss on 2 of the 100 shares (about $20) is disallowed and added to the basis of the 2 new shares; the remaining $980 loss is allowed.

chunks.heading: Reinvested dividends
chunks.text: A December dividend reinvestment within 30 days of a loss sale can create a small wash sale. Clients who want to avoid this sometimes turn off reinvestment temporarily; that is the client's choice.

chunks.heading: Reporting
chunks.text: Form 1099-B shows "wash sale loss disallowed" amounts for wash sales we identify. The adjusted basis carries to the replacement shares.
What makes a dividend qualified, which of our funds pay them, and the holding period requirement.

chunks.heading: Definition
chunks.text: Qualified dividends are taxed at long-term capital gain rates (0%, 15%, or 20%) instead of ordinary income rates. Most dividends from U.S. companies and many foreign companies qualify.

chunks.heading: Which funds
chunks.text:
- U.S. stock funds (BF500, BFTM, BFGR, and others): mostly qualified.
- International funds: largely qualified (dividends from companies in treaty countries).
- REIT fund (BFREI): REIT dividends are mostly not qualified (but may qualify for the Section 199A deduction).
- Bond funds: interest is not qualified.
The fund reports the qualified portion in box 1b of Form 1099-DIV.

chunks.heading: Holding period
chunks.text: The client must hold the fund shares for more than 60 days during the 121-day period around the ex-dividend date for dividends to be treated as qualified. Most long-term holders meet this; very short-term holders might not.

chunks.heading: Examples
chunks.text:
Fund: BF500, BFTM, BFDGA, BFHDY; Typical treatment of its dividends: Mostly qualified
Fund: BFIN, BFDEV, BFEUR, BFPAC; Typical treatment of its dividends: Largely qualified
Fund: BFEMG; Typical treatment of its dividends: Partly qualified (depends on countries)
Fund: BFREI; Typical treatment of its dividends: Mostly not qualified; may be Section 199A dividends
Fund: BFBI, BFST, and other bond funds; Typical treatment of its dividends: Not qualified (interest income)

chunks.heading: Where the client sees it
chunks.text: Box 1a of Form 1099-DIV shows total ordinary dividends; box 1b shows the qualified portion included in 1a.
Federal long-term and short-term capital gains rates, the net investment income tax, and how to discuss them.

chunks.heading: Long-term rates (2025 tax year)
chunks.text:
Rate: 0%; Single: Taxable income up to $48,350; Married filing jointly: Up to $96,700
Rate: 15%; Single: $48,351–$533,400; Married filing jointly: $96,701–$600,050
Rate: 20%; Single: Above $533,400; Married filing jointly: Above $600,050
Thresholds are adjusted for inflation each year; 2026 thresholds are slightly higher.

chunks.heading: Short-term gains
chunks.text: Gains on shares held one year or less are taxed as ordinary income, at rates up to 37%.

chunks.heading: Net investment income tax
chunks.text: An additional 3.8% applies to investment income for clients with modified AGI above $200,000 (single) or $250,000 (married filing jointly).

chunks.heading: State taxes
chunks.text: Most states tax capital gains as ordinary income. A few have no income tax.

chunks.heading: How to discuss
chunks.text: These are published facts you may share. Do not estimate a client's tax or suggest timing sales for tax purposes.

chunks.heading: Holding period examples
chunks.text:
- Shares bought March 3, 2025 and sold March 3, 2026: held exactly one year, which is short-term. Long-term requires more than one year (sold March 4, 2026 or later).
- Under average cost, the holding period uses the first-in shares for the shares sold, so a mix of long- and short-term may be reported.

chunks.heading: Capital gain distributions
chunks.text: Long-term capital gain distributions from a fund are long-term regardless of how long the client has owned the fund.
Why international funds report foreign taxes paid, and how clients may use the credit.

chunks.heading: Why it exists
chunks.text: Foreign countries often withhold tax on dividends paid by their companies. When our international funds (BFIN, BFDEV, BFEMG, BFEUR, BFPAC) pay foreign taxes, they can pass the taxes through to shareholders, who may claim a foreign tax credit or deduction on their U.S. return.

chunks.heading: What we report
chunks.text: Box 7 of Form 1099-DIV shows the client's share of foreign tax paid. The supplemental information shows foreign-source income by country, which some clients need for IRS Form 1116.

chunks.heading: Simplified election
chunks.text: Clients with $300 or less of creditable foreign taxes ($600 married filing jointly) can often claim the credit directly without Form 1116.

chunks.heading: IRAs
chunks.text: Foreign taxes paid inside an IRA cannot be claimed. That's a fact clients sometimes ask about; whether to hold international funds in taxable or IRA accounts is a planning question.

chunks.heading: Example
chunks.text: A client receives $1,200 in dividends from BFIN in a taxable account. The 1099-DIV shows $85 of foreign tax paid in box 7. The client may be able to claim an $85 credit on their federal return, or deduct it if they itemize. Which to choose is a tax question.

chunks.heading: Where the numbers come from
chunks.text: The international funds report each country's share of income and foreign tax in the annual supplemental information. Clients filing Form 1116 need these figures.

chunks.page: State tax on Treasury fund income
chunks.text: How interest from U.S. Treasury obligations is exempt from state tax and how clients find the percentage for each fund.

chunks.page: State tax on Treasury fund income
chunks.heading: The exemption
chunks.text: Interest from U.S. Treasury securities is exempt from state and local income taxes in all states, though a few states require a minimum percentage of a fund's assets in Treasuries for the fund's dividends to qualify.

chunks.page: State tax on Treasury fund income
chunks.heading: Which funds
chunks.text:
- BFST (Short-Term Treasury), BFITT (Intermediate Treasury), BFLTT (Long-Term Treasury): nearly all income is from Treasuries.
- BFBI (Bond Income): a portion comes from Treasuries (about 45% of holdings).
- Corporate bond funds and stock funds: no Treasury interest.

chunks.page: State tax on Treasury fund income
chunks.heading: The percentage
chunks.text: Each January we publish the percentage of each fund's income from U.S. government obligations in the supplemental information of the consolidated 1099 and on the Tax Center page. The client applies it to their dividends from that fund on their state return. Specific state requirements (for example, minimum thresholds in California, Connecticut, and New York) are a question for the client's tax preparer.

chunks.page: State tax on Treasury fund income
chunks.heading: IRAs
chunks.text: Not applicable; IRA distributions are taxed by states as ordinary income regardless of the source.

chunks.page: State tax on Treasury fund income
chunks.heading: Example
chunks.text: A client received $1,000 in dividends from BFITT. If 98% of BFITT's income came from U.S. Treasury obligations, $980 may be excluded from the client's state taxable income, subject to state rules.

chunks.page: State tax on Treasury fund income
chunks.heading: Where to find the percentage
chunks.text: The consolidated 1099 supplemental information and the Tax Center page list the percentage for each fund each year.
Taxpayer ID certification, TIN mismatches, and why backup withholding happens.

chunks.heading: Form W-9
chunks.text: Every U.S. client certifies their name and taxpayer identification number (SSN or EIN) on a Form W-9 at account opening. This certification also states they are not subject to backup withholding.

chunks.heading: Backup withholding
chunks.text:
We must withhold 24% of dividends and sale proceeds in a taxable account (backup withholding) if:
- The client has not provided a certified TIN.
- The IRS notifies us that the name and TIN don't match (a "B notice").
- The IRS notifies us that the client is subject to backup withholding for under-reporting.
Backup withholding is reported on Form 1099 and is credited against the client's tax.

chunks.heading: Fixing a TIN mismatch
chunks.text: The client must confirm their name and SSN match Social Security records (often a name change not reported to SSA) and submit a new Form W-9, or in some cases a copy of their Social Security card. Account Services processes it. See Legal name changes.

chunks.heading: Non-U.S. persons
chunks.text: Non-resident clients provide Form W-8BEN instead. See Non-U.S. persons and clients living abroad.

chunks.heading: B notices
chunks.text: When the IRS tells us a client's name and TIN don't match, we send the client a "B notice" letter with instructions. If the client doesn't fix it in time, backup withholding begins. A second B notice within three years requires the client to validate their TIN with the IRS or SSA.

chunks.heading: Stopping backup withholding
chunks.text: Once the client provides a corrected, certified TIN (and any required validation), backup withholding stops for future payments. Amounts already withheld are credited on the client's tax return.
Step-by-step chat procedure for sending a client a copy of a tax form, and what to check first.

chunks.heading: What the task collects
chunks.text:
Field: Form type; Options or format: 1099-R, 1099-B, 1099-DIV, 5498
Field: Tax year; Options or format: The year the client needs

chunks.heading: Before you start
chunks.text:
- Check availability: forms are not available before their dates. A 2026 Form 5498 requested in March 2027 does not exist yet. See Tax form calendar.
- Check the account type: IRAs produce 1099-R and 5498; taxable accounts produce the consolidated 1099 (DIV and B). A client asking for a "1099" for their Roth IRA with no distributions will not have one.
- Self-service first: the client can download any form from the last 7 years at My Account → Tax Documents in seconds. Offer the link; if they prefer, proceed with the task.

chunks.heading: Procedure
chunks.text:
1. Confirm the form and year.
2. Let the task expert collect them, or choose the task from the menu.
3. Review the Proposed Action and submit.
4. Tell the client how they will receive it: posted to Tax Documents and emailed (paperless) or mailed within 5 business days.

chunks.heading: Older years
chunks.text: The task offers recent years. For forms older than 7 years, route to Client Records.

chunks.heading: Questions about the contents
chunks.text: If the client asks what a number means, see the form pages in this section. If they believe it is wrong, see Corrected tax forms.
Exactly where the line is between explaining tax rules and giving tax advice, with examples.

chunks.heading: The rule
chunks.text: Chat agents may explain tax rules, forms, deadlines, and how our accounts are taxed. Chat agents may not tell a client how to handle their own taxes, what they will owe, or what to do to reduce taxes.

chunks.heading: Examples
chunks.text:
Information (allowed): "Traditional IRA withdrawals are taxed as ordinary income."; Advice (not allowed): "You'll owe about $1,200 on this withdrawal."
Information (allowed): "The 2026 contribution limit is $7,500."; Advice (not allowed): "You should max out your Roth this year."
Information (allowed): "Box 1b shows qualified dividends."; Advice (not allowed): "Enter this on line 3a of your 1040."
Information (allowed): "Conversions are added to taxable income."; Advice (not allowed): "Convert $20,000 to stay in the 22% bracket."
Information (allowed): "The wash-sale rule disallows losses if you rebuy within 30 days."; Advice (not allowed): "Sell now and buy BFTM instead to harvest the loss."
Information (allowed): "You can choose 0% to 100% withholding."; Advice (not allowed): "Withhold 15%; that should cover it."
Information (allowed): "QCDs are excluded from income."; Advice (not allowed): "A QCD would be better than taking your RMD."

chunks.heading: How to respond
chunks.text: "I can explain how this works, but for how it applies to your taxes, a tax professional is the right person to ask." Offer the relevant client-facing article.

chunks.heading: Tax Information wrap-up
chunks.text: Use the Tax Information wrap-up code for chats mainly about taxes.

chunks.heading: Talking about the lineup
chunks.text: You may describe any fund factually and compare funds on published characteristics. You may not recommend a fund or a mix of funds. See Comparing funds with a client and The investment advice boundary.
What distinguishes the four fund groups and the style categories within U.S. equity.

chunks.heading: The four groups
chunks.text:
- U.S. Equity: funds holding stocks of U.S. companies. They differ by company size (large, mid, small), by style (growth, value, blend), and by special focus (dividends, ESG screening).
- Sector Equity: funds concentrated in one of the eleven sectors of the U.S. economy, such as technology or utilities. Narrower and usually more volatile than broad funds.
- International: funds holding stocks of companies outside the United States, broadly (BFIN, BFDEV) or by region (BFEUR, BFPAC) or in emerging markets (BFEMG).
- Fixed Income: bond funds, differing by issuer (U.S. Treasury, corporate, or a broad mix) and by maturity (short, intermediate, long).

chunks.heading: Size and style
chunks.text:
U.S. stock funds are described with a "style box": size (Large, Mid, Small) and style (Value, Blend, Growth).
- Growth funds hold companies whose earnings and sales are expected to grow faster than average; they tend to have higher prices relative to earnings and lower dividends.
- Value funds hold companies that look inexpensive relative to earnings, book value, or dividends; they tend to pay higher dividends.
- Blend funds hold both.
Large companies are generally more established and less volatile; small companies offer more growth potential with more volatility. These are general characteristics, not predictions.

chunks.heading: Total market versus 500
chunks.text: BF500 holds the 500 largest U.S. companies. BFTM holds the whole U.S. market, about 3,650 companies, including mid and small caps. Because the largest companies dominate both by weight, their returns are usually similar. See BobsFunds 500 Index (BF500) and BobsFunds Total Market Index (BFTM).

chunks.heading: Bond funds by maturity
chunks.text: Shorter-maturity bond funds (BFST, BFSTC) are less sensitive to interest rates and usually yield less; longer funds (BFLTT, BFLTC) are more sensitive and usually yield more. Treasury funds carry no credit risk; corporate funds carry credit risk and usually yield more. See Bonds and interest rates.
How a mutual fund's net asset value is calculated, when it is set, and why it differs from stock and ETF pricing.

chunks.heading: What NAV is
chunks.text: A mutual fund's price is its net asset value (NAV) per share: the total value of everything the fund owns, minus its liabilities, divided by the number of shares outstanding. Every buyer and seller on a given day transacts at that day's NAV.

chunks.heading: When it is set
chunks.text: NAV is calculated once each business day after the New York Stock Exchange closes at 4:00 PM ET, usually published by 6:00 PM ET. Orders received in good order before 4:00 PM ET receive that day's NAV; orders received later receive the next business day's NAV. See Trade cutoff and NAV pricing.

chunks.heading: Differences from stocks and ETFs
chunks.text: Stocks and ETFs trade continuously during the day at changing prices. Mutual funds do not: there is no intraday price, no bid-ask spread, and no limit order. A client who asks "what price will I get?" should hear that it will be the NAV calculated at today's close (if before the cutoff), which is not known in advance.

chunks.heading: Why NAV drops on distribution dates
chunks.text: When a fund pays a dividend or capital gain distribution, the NAV falls by the amount paid out on the ex-dividend date. The client's total value is unchanged: they have fewer dollars in the share price and the same dollars in cash or reinvested shares. See Record, ex-dividend, reinvestment, and pay dates.

chunks.heading: Dollar-based orders
chunks.text: Because the NAV is not known in advance, most clients buy and sell in dollars. The number of shares is calculated at the NAV, to three decimal places. A $1,000 purchase at a $218.40 NAV buys 4.579 shares.

chunks.heading: Where to find NAV
chunks.text: The fund's Research page shows the latest NAV and the daily change. Historical NAVs appear on the price history chart. Clients' trade confirmations show the NAV of each transaction.
What an expense ratio is, how it is charged, the range across our lineup, and how to explain cost to clients.

chunks.heading: Definition
chunks.text: The expense ratio is the annual cost of operating a fund, expressed as a percentage of the fund's assets. It covers management, administration, custody, and other fund costs. A 0.03% expense ratio means $3 per year for every $10,000 invested.

chunks.heading: How it is charged
chunks.text: The expense ratio is not billed to the client's account. It is accrued daily inside the fund and reflected in the NAV. The returns we publish are already net of expenses. This is why a client never sees a line item for it on a statement.

chunks.heading: Our range
chunks.text: BobsFunds expense ratios range from 0.03% (BF500, BFTM, BFBI) to 0.13% (BFREI). Sector funds are 0.09%. See The BobsFunds lineup for every fund.

chunks.heading: Common questions
chunks.text:
"How much am I paying in fees?":
Multiply each holding's value by its expense ratio. A client with $40,000 in BF500 pays about $12 a year. There are no other account fees unless they use a paid service such as an outgoing wire. See Fee schedule.
"Why did the expense ratio change?":
Expense ratios are updated in each annual prospectus and can go up or down slightly as fund assets and costs change. The current prospectus figure applies.
"An old page says BFGR costs 0.25%.":
Some older client materials listed higher expense ratios for the original funds. The current prospectus figure (shown on the fund's profile and Research pages) is authoritative. Apologize for any confusion and report the outdated page.
The five risk levels shown on fund pages, what they are based on, and how to discuss them without advising.

chunks.heading: The scale
chunks.text:
Every fund page shows one of five risk levels: Low, Low–Medium, Medium, Medium–High, High. The level reflects the fund's historical volatility and the nature of its holdings.
Level: Low; Typical funds: BFST; General characteristics: Short-term government bonds; small price movements
Level: Low–Medium; Typical funds: BFBI, BFITT, BFSTC, BFSTP, BFUTL; General characteristics: Intermediate bonds or defensive stock sectors
Level: Medium; Typical funds: BF500, BFTM, BFIN, BFDEV, BFLTT; General characteristics: Broad diversified stock funds; long Treasuries
Level: Medium–High; Typical funds: BFGR, BFMC, sector funds such as BFFIN, BFLTC; General characteristics: More concentrated or more rate-sensitive
Level: High; Typical funds: BFSC, BFSCV, BFSCG, BFMCG, BFTEC, BFENE, BFEMG, BFDIS; General characteristics: Small companies, single sectors, emerging markets

chunks.heading: What it is not
chunks.text: The risk level describes the fund, not whether it suits the client. Every fund, including the Low-risk fund, can lose value. A risk level is not a prediction.

chunks.heading: How to discuss it
chunks.text: Quote the risk level and explain what it means in general terms. If the client asks "is this too risky for me?", that is a suitability question. Say: "I can tell you how this fund is rated and how it has behaved historically; whether it fits your situation is something a licensed professional can help you decide." See Declining advice requests.

chunks.heading: Standard deviation and beta
chunks.text: Fund profiles also show standard deviation (how much returns have varied, annualized over three years) and beta (how much the fund has moved relative to the S&P 500; 1.0 means in line, above 1 means more, below 1 means less). These are historical statistics.
What a benchmark index is, why index funds track one, and why fund returns differ slightly from their benchmark.

chunks.heading: Benchmarks
chunks.text: A benchmark is an index that represents the market segment a fund invests in, such as the S&P 500 Index for BF500 or the Bloomberg U.S. Aggregate Float Adjusted Index for BFBI. Index funds aim to match their benchmark's return; the benchmark is also the yardstick for judging the fund.

chunks.heading: Why a fund's return differs from its benchmark
chunks.text:
- Expenses: the index has no costs; the fund does. A fund with a 0.03% expense ratio will typically trail its index by about that much.
- Cash and trading: funds hold small amounts of cash for redemptions and incur trading costs.
- Sampling: bond index funds and very broad stock funds often hold a representative sample rather than every security.
- Timing: distributions and the treatment of dividends can cause small differences over short periods.
The gap is called tracking difference. For our index funds it is usually very small.

chunks.heading: Benchmarks for each fund
chunks.text: Each fund's profile page lists its benchmark. Older documents for the original six funds listed different benchmarks (for example, Russell 1000 Growth for BFGR); the current prospectus benchmark is authoritative.

chunks.heading: Example
chunks.text: In 2025 BF500 returned 12.6%, while the S&P 500 Index returned slightly more, the difference being mostly the fund's 0.03% expense ratio and small trading costs.

chunks.heading: Benchmarks for sector funds
chunks.text: Sector funds track "25/50" indexes, which cap individual company weights to meet diversification rules for registered funds. That's why a sector fund's largest holdings may be slightly smaller than in an uncapped sector index.

chunks.heading: How to present a comparison
chunks.text:
Present the facts in parallel and let the client draw conclusions:

BFGR holds about 235 large growth companies, costs 0.04%, and is rated Medium–High; it has had bigger swings in both directions, for example +46.8% in 2023 and −33.2% in 2022, versus +26.3% and −18.2% for BF500."

chunks.heading: What not to say
chunks.text:
- "This one is better."
- "I'd go with..." or "Most people pick..."
- "Growth funds always beat the market over time."
- Any forecast of future returns.

chunks.heading: Servicing notes
chunks.text:
This is a U.S. stock fund. Its value moves with the U.S. stock market and can fall significantly over short periods; the 2022 row in the return table shows what a difficult year looks like. Clients who ask "is it safe" should hear, factually, that stock funds carry market risk and that the fund's risk level is published as part of its profile. Do not characterize the fund as appropriate or inappropriate for the client.

What a fund prospectus contains, when clients must receive it, and how to send or explain one.

chunks.heading: What it is
chunks.text: The prospectus is the fund's primary legal disclosure document, filed with the SEC. Every fund has one, updated at least annually. Clients should read it before investing; we deliver it (or a summary prospectus) at the time of a client's first purchase of a fund.

chunks.heading: What's in it
chunks.text:
- Investment objective and principal strategies: what the fund is trying to do and how.
- Principal risks: market, interest-rate, credit, foreign, sector concentration, and others.
- Fees and expenses: the expense ratio and any other costs (our funds have no loads or redemption fees).
- Performance: a bar chart of calendar-year returns and a table comparing returns to the benchmark.
- Management: the adviser and portfolio managers.
- Purchase and sale of shares, including the frequent-trading policy.
- Distributions and taxes.

chunks.heading: Summary prospectus
chunks.text: A short version (a few pages) covering the key facts, with the full prospectus available online. Clients usually receive the summary.

chunks.heading: Where clients find it
chunks.text: Each fund's Research page has links to the prospectus, SAI, and shareholder reports. Printed copies can be mailed free on request. See Requests for fund documents.

chunks.heading: How to use it in chat
chunks.text: When a client asks about a fund's risks or strategy in detail, quote the fund profile in this library and send the prospectus link. Never paraphrase risk in a way that minimizes it.
What the SAI contains and when clients need it.

chunks.heading: What it is
chunks.text: The Statement of Additional Information is a supplement to the prospectus with more detailed information: the fund's investment policies and restrictions, trustees and officers, portfolio manager compensation and fund ownership, the custodian and auditor, tax matters, and how the NAV is calculated.

chunks.heading: Who asks for it
chunks.text: Usually professionals: financial advisors, attorneys, or academically minded clients. It is available on each fund's Research page and by mail on request.

chunks.heading: In chat
chunks.text: Send the link. You don't need to explain its contents in detail; refer specific questions about governance or policies to the document.

chunks.heading: Typical contents
chunks.text:
- Fund history and organization.
- Investment policies, permitted investments, and fundamental restrictions (for example, limits on borrowing and concentration).
- Board of trustees and officers, with their backgrounds and compensation.
- Portfolio managers' other accounts, compensation structure, and fund ownership ranges.
- Control persons and principal holders.
- The investment adviser, distributor, custodian, transfer agent, and independent auditor.
- Brokerage allocation and soft dollars.
- Net asset value calculation methodology.
- Tax status of the fund.
- Proxy voting policies.

chunks.heading: When it's useful
chunks.text: Advisors doing due diligence, clients interested in governance, and questions about specific restrictions ("Can the fund use derivatives?") are answered in the SAI.
What shareholder reports show, when they're published, and how clients receive them.

chunks.heading: What they are
chunks.text:
Each fund publishes:
- An annual report for its fiscal year, with audited financial statements, a complete list of holdings, a management discussion of performance, and expense information.
- A semiannual report for the first six months of the fiscal year, with unaudited financial statements and holdings.
Shorter "tailored shareholder reports" summarize performance, expenses, and holdings in a few pages; the full financial statements are available online.

chunks.heading: Delivery
chunks.text: Clients who own a fund receive the tailored shareholder report by email (paperless) or mail. Households with several members owning the same fund may receive one copy (householding) unless they ask for separate copies.

chunks.heading: In chat
chunks.text: Send the link from the fund's Research page. Questions about holdings: the fund profile and Research page list the top holdings; the reports list everything.

chunks.heading: Fiscal years
chunks.text: Our funds' fiscal years end on various dates (for example, December 31 for the U.S. equity funds). The annual report covers the fiscal year; the semiannual report covers its first half.

chunks.heading: What clients look for
chunks.text:
- Holdings: the full list as of the report date.
- Expense example: what a $1,000 investment would have cost during the period.
- Management discussion: why the fund performed as it did.
- Financial highlights: per-share data over five years, including total return and expense ratio.

chunks.heading: Householding
chunks.text: To reduce mail, households receive one copy of a report per address. A client who wants their own copy can ask; we resume individual delivery within 30 days.
Total return, standard periods, annualized versus cumulative returns, and the rules for quoting performance.

chunks.heading: Total return
chunks.text: Fund performance is reported as total return: the change in NAV plus distributions, assuming they were reinvested. It is net of the expense ratio.

chunks.heading: Standard periods
chunks.text:
Period: Year to date (YTD); Notes: From January 1
Period: 1 year; Notes: Trailing 12 months
Period: 3, 5, 10 years; Notes: Annualized (average annual return)
Period: Since inception; Notes: Annualized
Period: Calendar years; Notes: Each full year

chunks.heading: Annualized versus cumulative
chunks.text: A 3-year annualized return of 8% means the fund grew at an average of 8% per year, about 26% cumulatively. Clients sometimes confuse the two; clarify which you are quoting.

chunks.heading: Where to find current figures
chunks.text: The fund's Research page shows YTD and trailing returns, refreshed nightly. Calendar-year returns are on each fund profile page in this library.

chunks.heading: Rules for quoting performance
chunks.text:
- Always include the time period and the date: "As of September 30, 2026, BF500's one-year return was..."
- Always add: "Past performance doesn't guarantee future results."
- Quote standard periods, not cherry-picked ones.
- Never project future returns.
- Never compare our fund's performance to a competitor's fund in a promotional way.
See Communications standards.

chunks.heading: Personal performance
chunks.text: A client's own account performance (their personal rate of return) depends on when they invested. The portal's Performance tab shows the client's personal return. It can differ from the fund's return; that is normal.
Why a fund's price change understates its return, especially for funds that distribute a lot.

chunks.heading: The difference
chunks.text:
A fund's NAV change ignores distributions. When a fund pays a distribution, its NAV drops by that amount. So:
- Price return = change in NAV only.
- Total return = change in NAV plus distributions reinvested.
For bond funds, which pay out most of their return as income, price return can be near zero or negative while total return is positive.

chunks.heading: Example
chunks.text: BFBI's NAV starts the year at $98.30 and ends at $98.10 (price return about −0.2%). It paid about $2.10 per share in monthly dividends during the year. Its total return is about +1.9%.

chunks.heading: Client questions
chunks.text:
"My bond fund price hasn't moved in years.":
Explain that bond funds pay their return mostly as monthly dividends; with reinvestment on, the client owns more shares over time.
"The chart shows a drop but the return is positive.":
The chart may show NAV only. Check the total-return figures.

chunks.heading: Stock funds too
chunks.text: Stock funds that pay larger dividends (BFHDY, BFUTL) also show a noticeable gap between price return and total return. Growth funds (BFGR) pay small dividends, so the gap is small.

chunks.heading: Where to see total return
chunks.text: Fund profile return tables and the Research page's performance tab show total returns. Price charts show NAV only unless the "include distributions" option is selected.
The kinds of yield quoted for funds, what each means, and how to explain that yields are not guaranteed.

chunks.heading: Types of yield
chunks.text:
Yield: Distribution yield (trailing 12-month); What it measures: The fund's distributions over the past 12 months divided by the current NAV. Shown on fund profiles in this library
Yield: SEC 30-day yield; What it measures: A standardized calculation of the fund's net investment income over the last 30 days, annualized. Useful for comparing bond funds
Yield: Dividend yield (for stock funds); What it measures: The income from the stocks the fund holds

chunks.heading: Yields vary
chunks.text: Yields are not guaranteed and change with market rates and the fund's holdings. A bond fund's yield is not like a CD's fixed rate: the fund has no maturity, and its price changes.

chunks.heading: Yield versus return
chunks.text: Yield is income only. Total return includes price changes. A fund can have a 4% yield and a negative total return in a year when rates rise.

chunks.heading: In chat
chunks.text: Quote the yield shown with its type and date. "BFST's trailing 12-month distribution yield is 4.58%; that's what it paid over the past year relative to today's price. It isn't a guaranteed rate."

chunks.heading: Example
chunks.text: BFBI shows a trailing 12-month distribution yield of 3.82%. A client with $10,000 in BFBI received about $382 in dividends over the past year. This year's dividends could be higher or lower.

chunks.heading: Why yields change
chunks.text: As bonds in the fund mature and are replaced at current market rates, the fund's yield moves toward those rates. When rates fall, yields drift lower; when rates rise, they drift higher.
Which fund figures are static catalog data and which are refreshed nightly, so you know what's current.

chunks.heading: Two kinds of data
chunks.text:
Data: Name, ticker, category, expense ratio, benchmark, minimum, risk level, description; Source: Fund catalog; Updated: When the prospectus changes
Data: Holdings count, allocations, calendar-year returns, recent distributions, yield, beta, standard deviation; Source: Fund catalog; Updated: Periodically

The fund profile pages in this library are generated from the same catalog the client portal uses. For anything time-sensitive (today's price, YTD return), use the fund's Research page in the portal.

chunks.heading: If numbers disagree
chunks.text: If the Research page and a library page disagree on a time-sensitive figure, the Research page is more current. If they disagree on a catalog figure (expense ratio, benchmark), report it as a content issue. Older client-facing help pages may show outdated figures for the original six funds.

chunks.heading: Nightly refresh
chunks.text: Market data (NAV, returns, price history) refreshes every night after the markets close. If the nightly refresh is delayed, the Research page continues to show the last good data; it never shows partial or broken data.

chunks.heading: Questions
chunks.text:
"Why does the Research page show yesterday's price?":
Before about 6:00 PM ET, the latest NAV is the previous business day's. Today's NAV appears after the close.
"The return on the website doesn't match my statement.":
Fund returns and the client's personal return differ. See How performance is reported.
How to send prospectuses, reports, and other fund documents by link or mail.

chunks.heading: By link
chunks.text: Every fund's Research page has links to the summary prospectus, full prospectus, SAI, and shareholder reports. Send the link in chat.

chunks.heading: By mail
chunks.text: Clients can request printed copies free of charge. Note the request (fund, document, mailing address on file) and route it to Client Services fulfillment; documents are mailed within 3 business days.
