chunks.heading: Prospectus delivery rules
chunks.text: Clients receive a summary prospectus when they first buy a fund, and updated prospectuses annually. Electronic delivery is used for paperless clients. A client can always request a free printed copy.

chunks.heading: Proxy materials
chunks.text: When a fund holds a shareholder vote (for example, to elect trustees or change a fundamental policy), shareholders of record receive proxy materials and can vote online, by phone, or by mail. Questions about a specific proxy can be answered from the proxy statement.

chunks.heading: Historical documents
chunks.text: Prospectuses and reports for prior years are available from Client Services fulfillment on request.
What a mutual fund is, how it works, and how to explain it to a new investor.

chunks.heading: The idea
chunks.text: A mutual fund pools money from many investors to buy a portfolio of stocks, bonds, or both. Each investor owns shares of the fund, and the value of their shares rises and falls with the value of everything the fund owns.

chunks.heading: Benefits clients often ask about
chunks.text:
- Diversification: one fund can hold hundreds or thousands of securities, so no single company's troubles dominate. See Diversification.
- Professional management: for index funds, management means tracking an index precisely and cheaply.
- Low minimums: our funds start at $1.
- Daily liquidity: shares can be sold any business day at that day's NAV.
- Automatic features: reinvested dividends and automatic investing.

chunks.heading: How it differs from an ETF
chunks.text: ETFs are also pooled funds, but they trade on an exchange throughout the day like stocks. Mutual funds trade once a day at NAV. Many index mutual funds and ETFs track the same indexes. See NAV: how fund prices work.

chunks.heading: Explaining it simply
chunks.text: "A mutual fund is like a basket that holds many investments. When you buy a share, you own a small piece of the whole basket. Our 500 Index fund, for example, holds about 500 of the largest U.S. companies."

chunks.heading: What not to say
chunks.text: Avoid implying a fund can't lose money. Every fund can lose value.
How index funds differ from actively managed funds, and why our lineup is mostly index funds.

chunks.heading: Definitions
chunks.text:
- Index fund: tracks a published index (for example, the S&P 500) by holding the same securities in the same proportions. Low turnover, low cost.
- Actively managed fund: a manager picks securities trying to beat a benchmark. Higher costs and turnover.

chunks.heading: The evidence clients may have heard about
chunks.text: Research over many decades (for example, the S&P SPIVA reports) has found that most actively managed funds trail their benchmarks over long periods, after costs. This is a general finding, not a guarantee about any fund.

chunks.heading: Our lineup
chunks.text: Nearly all BobsFunds funds are index funds, reflecting our founder's philosophy that low costs and broad diversification are the most reliable drivers of long-term results. The client Library has a guide, "Index Funds vs. Active Funds".

chunks.heading: How to discuss
chunks.text: Explain the difference. You may describe our philosophy as the firm's view. Do not say index funds are right for the client.

chunks.heading: Characteristics compared
chunks.text:
: Goal; Index funds: Match an index; Active funds: Beat a benchmark
: Costs; Index funds: Usually low; Active funds: Usually higher
: Turnover; Index funds: Low; Active funds: Often higher
: Tax efficiency (taxable accounts); Index funds: Usually higher; Active funds: Often lower
: Predictability relative to the market; Index funds: High; Active funds: Varies

chunks.heading: Our expense ratios as context
chunks.text: Our index funds cost 0.03%–0.13% a year. See Expense ratios.

chunks.heading: Common client question
chunks.text:
"Can an index fund beat the market?":
By design an index fund aims to match its index, minus small costs. It will not beat its index by much, and it won't trail by much either.
The idea of dividing investments among stocks, bonds, and cash, explained neutrally.

chunks.heading: What it is
chunks.text: Asset allocation is how an investor divides their money among asset classes: stocks (growth potential, more volatility), bonds (income, usually less volatility), and cash. It is often described as a percentage mix, such as 60% stocks and 40% bonds.

chunks.heading: Why it matters
chunks.text: Studies have found that the allocation explains a large share of the variation in a portfolio's returns and volatility over time, more than individual fund selection.

chunks.heading: Factors investors consider
chunks.text:
- Time horizon: when they need the money.
- Risk tolerance: how they would react to a large drop.
- Goals and other resources.

chunks.heading: Rules of thumb
chunks.text: Clients may mention rules of thumb such as "110 minus your age in stocks". You may acknowledge such rules exist; do not endorse one for the client.

chunks.heading: The advice boundary
chunks.text: Choosing an allocation for a client is advice. You may explain the concept, show their current allocation, and process changes they choose. For help choosing, offer a callback. See The investment advice boundary.

chunks.heading: Seeing a client's current allocation
chunks.text: The portal's Portfolio page shows the client's mix by asset class (U.S. stocks, international stocks, bonds, cash) across all accounts. You can read it to the client as a fact: "Right now you're about 72% stock funds, 23% bond funds, and 5% cash."

chunks.heading: Funds by asset class
chunks.text:
Asset class: U.S. stocks; Our funds: BF500, BFTM, style and size funds, dividend funds, sector funds
Asset class: International stocks; Our funds: BFIN, BFDEV, BFEMG, BFEUR, BFPAC
Asset class: Bonds; Our funds: BFST, BFSTC, BFITT, BFBI, BFITC, BFLTC, BFLTT

chunks.heading: Processing a client's chosen allocation
chunks.text: If the client tells you their target, you can calculate and process the exchanges. See Rebalancing requests.
Why spreading investments across many securities and asset classes reduces risk, and its limits.

chunks.heading: The idea
chunks.text: Diversification means not putting all your eggs in one basket. Holding many securities across companies, industries, countries, and asset classes reduces the impact of any one investment performing badly.

chunks.heading: What it does and doesn't do
chunks.text:
- It reduces the risk specific to individual companies or sectors.
- It does not eliminate market risk: in a broad decline, most stocks fall together.
- It does not guarantee a profit or protect against loss.

chunks.heading: Concentration
chunks.text: Clients sometimes hold a single sector fund or a large position in an employer's stock. Concentration increases risk. You may explain this generally; whether to reduce it is advice.

chunks.heading: Our funds
chunks.text:
Broad funds (BFTM with about 3,650 holdings, BFIN with about 8,500) are highly diversified within their asset class. Sector funds (BFTEC, BFENE) are concentrated by design.
The client Library's "Bob's View: Diversification, The Free Lunch" column discusses the idea.

chunks.heading: Example
chunks.text: A client holds only BFTEC (technology). In 2022 the fund returned −29.7%. A client holding BFTM (total market) that year had technology exposure too, but diluted by every other sector, and lost −19.5%. Neither was a gain; diversification reduced, not eliminated, the decline.

chunks.heading: Across asset classes
chunks.text: Stocks and bonds sometimes move in opposite directions, which helps a mixed portfolio. In some years (2022 was one) both fall together. Diversification works on average over time, not every year.
How to explain investment risk, volatility measures, and the relationship between risk and return.

chunks.heading: Kinds of risk
chunks.text:
- Market risk: the whole market falls.
- Interest-rate risk: bond prices fall when rates rise.
- Credit risk: a bond issuer can't pay.
- Currency risk: for international investments.
- Concentration risk: too much in one area.
- Inflation risk: returns don't keep up with rising prices.
- Longevity risk: outliving savings.

chunks.heading: Measuring volatility
chunks.text:
- Standard deviation: how widely returns have varied around their average. Higher means bumpier.
- Beta: how much a fund has moved relative to the market (S&P 500 = 1.0).
- Worst calendar year: an intuitive measure. Fund profiles show calendar-year returns, including 2022, a difficult year for both stocks and bonds.

chunks.heading: Risk and return
chunks.text: Historically, investments with higher expected returns have come with higher volatility. That relationship is general, not a promise.

chunks.heading: How to discuss
chunks.text: Use published measures and history. Avoid "safe", "risky for you", or predictions. See Published risk levels.

chunks.heading: Example: comparing volatility
chunks.text:
Fund: BFST; Standard deviation: 1.4%; Worst recent year: −4.2% (2022)
Fund: BFBI; Standard deviation: 5.2%; Worst recent year: −13.1% (2022)
Fund: BF500; Standard deviation: 14.8%; Worst recent year: −18.2% (2022)
Fund: BFSCG; Standard deviation: 22.0%; Worst recent year: −28.4% (2022)
Fund: BFENE; Standard deviation: 26.0%; Worst recent year: −33.5% (2020)
Higher standard deviation has meant bigger swings in both directions.

chunks.heading: Talking about risk tolerance
chunks.text: Clients sometimes ask "how much risk should I take?" That is advice. You can ask how they would feel about a large decline as a way to help them think about it, but you should not translate the answer into a recommendation. Offer a callback.
How bonds work, why bond fund prices move inversely with interest rates, and how to explain bond fund behavior.

chunks.heading: How bonds work
chunks.text: A bond is a loan to a government or company. The issuer pays interest and returns the principal at maturity. Bond funds hold many bonds and constantly replace those that mature.

chunks.heading: Prices and rates move in opposite directions
chunks.text: When interest rates rise, newly issued bonds pay more, so existing bonds with lower rates become less valuable and their prices fall. When rates fall, existing bonds become more valuable. The longer a bond's maturity, the bigger the effect. See Duration.

chunks.heading: 2022 as an example
chunks.text: Rates rose sharply in 2022. BFBI returned −13.1% and BFLTT −29.3%, while short-term BFST returned −4.2%. Over the following years, higher rates meant higher income for the funds.

chunks.heading: The upside of higher rates
chunks.text: After rates rise, bond funds earn more income from new bonds, which over time can offset the price decline. This is a general mechanism, not a prediction.

chunks.heading: Credit
chunks.text: Treasury bonds have essentially no credit risk. Corporate bonds pay more interest to compensate for the risk that the company can't pay. BBB-rated bonds are the lowest investment-grade rating.

chunks.heading: Explaining it
chunks.text: "When interest rates go up, the prices of existing bonds go down, because new bonds pay more. Longer-term bond funds feel that more. Over time, the fund also earns more income as it buys new, higher-yielding bonds."
What duration measures, how to use it to explain a bond fund's rate sensitivity, and our funds' durations.

chunks.heading: Definition
chunks.text: Duration, in years, measures a bond fund's sensitivity to interest-rate changes. As a rule of thumb, a fund's price changes by about its duration in percent for each 1 percentage-point change in rates, in the opposite direction.

chunks.heading: Our funds
chunks.text:
Fund: BFST; Average duration: 1.8 years; Approximate price change if rates rise 1 point: −1.8%
Fund: BFSTC; Average duration: 2.6 years; Approximate price change if rates rise 1 point: −2.6%
Fund: BFITT; Average duration: 5.2 years; Approximate price change if rates rise 1 point: −5.2%
Fund: BFBI; Average duration: 6.0 years; Approximate price change if rates rise 1 point: −6.0%
Fund: BFITC; Average duration: 6.3 years; Approximate price change if rates rise 1 point: −6.3%
Fund: BFLTC; Average duration: 12.5 years; Approximate price change if rates rise 1 point: −12.5%
Fund: BFLTT; Average duration: 15.5 years; Approximate price change if rates rise 1 point: −15.5%

chunks.heading: Caveats
chunks.text: The rule of thumb is an approximation; actual changes depend on how rates move across maturities, credit spreads, and other factors.

chunks.heading: How to discuss
chunks.text: Use duration to explain past behavior or sensitivity. Do not predict rate moves or recommend durations.
How investing a fixed amount regularly works, its effect on average cost, and how to describe it accurately.

chunks.heading: What it is
chunks.text: Dollar-cost averaging (DCA) means investing a fixed dollar amount at regular intervals regardless of the price. Automatic investment plans do this automatically.

chunks.heading: The effect
chunks.text:
A fixed amount buys more shares when prices are low and fewer when prices are high, so the average cost per share is lower than the average price over the period.
Month: 1; Investment: $300; NAV: $30; Shares bought: 10.000
Month: 2; Investment: $300; NAV: $25; Shares bought: 12.000
Month: 3; Investment: $300; NAV: $20; Shares bought: 15.000
Month: 4; Investment: $300; NAV: $25; Shares bought: 12.000
$1,200 bought 49 shares: average cost $24.49, versus an average price of $25.00.

chunks.heading: What it doesn't do
chunks.text: DCA does not guarantee a profit or protect against loss in a declining market. Studies show that investing a lump sum at once has historically produced higher returns more often than not, because markets have risen more often than fallen; DCA reduces the regret of investing just before a decline. That is a general observation, not advice.

chunks.heading: How to discuss
chunks.text: Explain the mechanics. Whether to invest a lump sum or spread it out is the client's decision.
What rebalancing is, why investors do it, common approaches, and the tax consideration.

chunks.heading: What it is
chunks.text: Over time, investments that grow faster become a bigger share of a portfolio. Rebalancing means selling some of what grew and buying what lagged, to restore the original mix.

chunks.heading: Why investors do it
chunks.text: To keep the portfolio's risk level consistent with their chosen allocation. Without rebalancing, a 60/40 portfolio can drift to 75/25 after a strong stock market.

chunks.heading: Common approaches
chunks.text:
- Calendar: rebalance once a year.
- Threshold: rebalance when an asset class drifts more than a set amount (for example, 5 percentage points).
- With cash flows: direct new contributions to whatever is underweight, which avoids selling.

chunks.heading: Taxes
chunks.text: Rebalancing by exchange in a taxable account can create capital gains. In IRAs, there is no tax effect.

chunks.heading: In chat
chunks.text: See Rebalancing requests for the procedure. Calculating the trades for a client's own target is arithmetic; choosing the target is advice.

chunks.heading: Example
chunks.text: A client started the year at 60% stock funds ($60,000) and 40% bond funds ($40,000). Stocks rose 20% and bonds rose 2%, so they now have $72,000 in stocks (63.8%) and $40,800 in bonds (36.2%). To return to 60/40 of $112,800, they would move about $4,320 from stock funds to bond funds.

chunks.heading: Rebalancing with new money
chunks.text: Directing new contributions to the underweight asset avoids selling (and, in taxable accounts, avoids realizing gains). Clients can adjust automatic investment plans for this.

chunks.heading: The advice boundary
chunks.text: Explaining the mechanics and doing the arithmetic for a client's own target is fine; recommending a target or a schedule is advice.
How growth on growth works, the rule of 72, and why reinvesting distributions matters.

chunks.heading: The idea
chunks.text: Compounding means earning returns on previous returns. Reinvested dividends buy more shares, which earn their own dividends and growth.

chunks.heading: Rule of 72
chunks.text: Divide 72 by an annual growth rate to estimate how many years money takes to double: at 6%, about 12 years; at 8%, about 9 years. This is an arithmetic illustration, not a projection.

chunks.heading: Time matters
chunks.text: Because compounding builds on itself, time in the market has a large effect. The client Library guide "Compound Interest" illustrates this.

chunks.heading: How to discuss
chunks.text: Use hypothetical illustrations clearly labeled as such: "As a hypothetical example, $10,000 growing at 6% a year would be about $32,000 after 20 years. That's arithmetic, not a forecast for any fund."

chunks.heading: Reinvested distributions and compounding
chunks.text: For mutual funds, compounding happens mainly through reinvested distributions and growth in the value of the shares those distributions bought. With DRIP on, each dividend buys more shares, and those shares earn the next dividend. See Dividend reinvestment (DRIP).

chunks.heading: Hypothetical illustration
chunks.text:
Years: 10; $10,000 at 4%: $14,802; $10,000 at 6%: $17,908; $10,000 at 8%: $21,589
Years: 20; $10,000 at 4%: $21,911; $10,000 at 6%: $32,071; $10,000 at 8%: $46,610
Years: 30; $10,000 at 4%: $32,434; $10,000 at 6%: $57,435; $10,000 at 8%: $100,627
These figures are arithmetic, assume a constant rate, and ignore taxes and costs. Real investments do not grow at a constant rate and can lose value.

chunks.heading: Questions clients ask
chunks.text:
"Is it too late for me to start?":
You can explain that compounding works over any period, with longer periods producing larger effects. Whether and how much to invest is the client's decision.
"Does my money compound in a bond fund?":
Yes, if distributions are reinvested; bond funds pay most of their return as income, so reinvestment matters even more.
Why expense ratios matter over time, with an illustration, and how to discuss costs factually.

chunks.heading: The effect
chunks.text: Costs are deducted every year regardless of returns, so they compound against the investor. A difference of 0.5% a year sounds small but adds up over decades.

chunks.heading: Illustration (hypothetical)
chunks.text:
$100,000 growing at 6% before costs for 30 years:
Annual cost: 0.03%; Ending value: about $568,000
Annual cost: 0.50%; Ending value: about $497,000
Annual cost: 1.00%; Ending value: about $432,000

chunks.heading: Our costs
chunks.text: Our expense ratios range from 0.03% to 0.13%, and there are no account fees or transaction fees. See Expense ratios.

chunks.heading: How to discuss
chunks.text: You may present our costs and the arithmetic. Avoid disparaging competitors by name.

chunks.heading: Why low costs matter more over time
chunks.text: An expense ratio is charged every year on the whole balance, including past growth. The difference between two costs is therefore not just the fee itself but the growth those fees would have earned.

chunks.heading: Explaining expense ratios in dollars
chunks.text:
Clients relate better to dollars than percentages:
Balance: $10,000; At 0.03%: $3 a year; At 0.13%: $13 a year; At 0.50%: $50 a year
Balance: $100,000; At 0.03%: $30 a year; At 0.13%: $130 a year; At 0.50%: $500 a year
Balance: $500,000; At 0.03%: $150 a year; At 0.13%: $650 a year; At 0.50%: $2,500 a year

chunks.heading: Talking about competitors
chunks.text: Do not name or disparage other firms. You may say our expense ratios range from 0.03% to 0.13% and that we charge no account or transaction fees, and let the client compare.
How inflation erodes money's value, how different investments have related to inflation, and how to discuss it.

chunks.heading: The idea
chunks.text: Inflation is the general rise in prices. Money that earns less than inflation loses purchasing power: at 3% inflation, $100 buys about $74 worth of today's goods in 10 years.

chunks.heading: Real return
chunks.text: A real return is the return after inflation. A 4% return with 3% inflation is about a 1% real return.

chunks.heading: Different investments
chunks.text:
Historically, stocks have tended to outpace inflation over long periods, with volatility along the way; cash and short-term bonds have often roughly kept pace; long-term bonds have struggled when inflation rose unexpectedly. Some sectors (energy, real estate, materials) are often described as inflation-sensitive. These are general historical patterns.
The client Library's "Bob's View: The Hidden Tax of Inflation" column discusses it.

chunks.heading: How to discuss
chunks.text: Explain the concept. Don't recommend investments as inflation protection for the client.

chunks.heading: Examples clients relate to
chunks.text:
- At 3% inflation, prices double in about 24 years (rule of 72).
- A retiree spending $50,000 a year today would need about $67,000 in 10 years at 3% inflation for the same lifestyle.
- Cash earning 0% loses about 3% of its purchasing power each year at 3% inflation.

chunks.heading: Uninvested cash
chunks.text: Cash held uninvested in a Bob's account earns no return, so it loses purchasing power to inflation. Pointing that out neutrally is helpful; recommending what to buy is not.

chunks.heading: Questions
chunks.text:
"What's the best inflation hedge?":
Explain the general patterns above and that no investment reliably protects against inflation in every period. Offer a callback for planning.

chunks.page: Talking with clients during market downturns
chunks.text: How to support anxious clients when markets fall, what you can say, and what you must not say.

chunks.page: Talking with clients during market downturns
chunks.heading: What clients feel
chunks.text: Falling markets frighten people, especially those near or in retirement. Clients may want reassurance, an explanation, or to sell everything.

chunks.page: Talking with clients during market downturns
chunks.heading: What you can do
chunks.text:
- Acknowledge the feeling: "It's completely understandable to be concerned when you see your balance drop."
- Explain what happened, factually: "Stock funds across the market declined this week" or "Bond prices fell as interest rates rose."
- Provide context from published history: markets have experienced many declines, including −18.2% for BF500 in 2022, and past declines have been followed by recoveries, though past performance does not guarantee future results.
- Point to educational resources: the client Library's "Investing Through Market Volatility" guide and "Bob's View: The Illusion of Market Timing" column.
- Process what the client decides, accurately and without commentary.
- Offer a callback with a licensed professional for guidance.

chunks.page: Talking with clients during market downturns
chunks.heading: What you must not do
chunks.text:
- Predict where markets are going ("It'll bounce back soon").
- Tell the client to stay invested or to sell.
- Minimize the loss ("It's only a paper loss").
- Express your own fear or opinions.

chunks.page: Talking with clients during market downturns
chunks.heading: If the client wants to sell everything
chunks.text: Confirm what they want, once, clearly: "Just to confirm, you'd like to sell all of your BF500 and BFGR in your Traditional IRA and hold the proceeds as cash in the account?" Then process it. You may mention, factually, that selling locks in the current value and that in a taxable account sales can have tax consequences. Do not try to talk them out of it.

chunks.page: Talking with clients during market downturns
chunks.heading: Wrap-up
chunks.text: Use Market Question, or Investment Advice if the client was referred.
What sector investing is, how sector funds behave, and how to describe them neutrally.

chunks.heading: What they are
chunks.text: Sector funds invest in one of the 11 sectors of the economy (technology, health care, financials, consumer discretionary, consumer staples, industrials, energy, materials, communication services, utilities, real estate). Our lineup has a sector fund for each.

chunks.heading: Behavior
chunks.text:
- Sectors respond differently to economic conditions: utilities and consumer staples are often called defensive; technology and consumer discretionary are more cyclical.
- Sector funds can be much more volatile than the broad market. BFENE returned +61% in 2022 and −33.5% in 2020.
- A broad market fund already holds every sector in proportion to its size.

chunks.heading: How investors use them
chunks.text: Typically as a smaller "tilt" alongside a diversified core, not as a whole portfolio. That is a description of common practice, not a recommendation.

chunks.heading: In chat
chunks.text: Describe the sector and its characteristics from the fund profile. Do not comment on which sector will do well.

Why investors hold international stocks, the added risks, and how our international funds differ.

chunks.heading: Why international
chunks.text: Companies outside the U.S. make up roughly 40% of the world's stock market value. International funds provide exposure to economies and companies not available in U.S. funds, and their returns don't move in lockstep with U.S. stocks.

chunks.heading: Added risks
chunks.text:
- Currency: returns in dollars depend on exchange rates.
- Political and economic risk, especially in emerging markets.
- Different accounting and market practices.
- Foreign taxes on dividends. See Foreign tax credit.

chunks.heading: Our funds
chunks.text:
Fund: BFIN; Coverage: Developed and emerging markets, 40+ countries
Fund: BFDEV; Coverage: Developed markets: Europe, Pacific, Canada
Fund: BFEMG; Coverage: Emerging markets: China, India, Taiwan, Brazil, and others
Fund: BFEUR; Coverage: Developed Europe
Fund: BFPAC; Coverage: Developed Asia-Pacific, led by Japan

chunks.heading: In chat
chunks.text: Describe the differences. How much to hold internationally is a planning decision.

chunks.heading: Currency example
chunks.text: If European stocks rise 5% in euros and the euro falls 5% against the dollar, a U.S. investor in BFEUR earns roughly 0%. If both rise 5%, the investor earns roughly 10%.

chunks.heading: Distribution timing
chunks.text: Our international funds distribute semiannually, in June and December, so clients expecting quarterly dividends should be told this is normal.

chunks.heading: Emerging versus developed
chunks.text: Emerging markets (BFEMG) have historically been more volatile than developed markets (BFDEV), with a higher risk level on our scale.
The single most important compliance rule for chat agents: what counts as advice, why we can't give it, and what to do instead.

chunks.heading: The rule
chunks.text: Chat agents are not licensed to provide individualized investment recommendations. You may give information and education; you may not give advice, meaning a recommendation about what a specific client should do with their money.

chunks.heading: What counts as advice
chunks.text:
Any statement that tells or suggests to a client what to buy, sell, hold, or how to allocate, given their situation:
- "You should buy BF500."
- "That fund is a good fit for you."
- "I'd move to bonds if I were you."
- "At your age, you should be more conservative."
- "Now's a good time to buy."
- "Don't sell now; it'll come back."
- "Most people in your situation choose the Roth."

chunks.heading: What is allowed
chunks.text:
- Explaining how funds, accounts, and rules work.
- Describing a fund's published characteristics, including risk and history.
- Comparing funds factually on published data.
- Doing arithmetic on the client's own stated targets.
- Sharing the firm's general philosophy and educational materials (Library guides, Bob's View columns), clearly as general education.
- Processing the transactions the client decides on.

chunks.heading: What to do instead
chunks.text:
1. Acknowledge the question: "That's an important decision."
2. State the boundary simply: "I'm not able to recommend investments, but I can explain how these options work."
3. Offer education and facts.
4. Offer a callback with a licensed professional who can give personalized guidance. See Scheduling callbacks.
Scripts: Declining advice requests.

chunks.heading: Why it matters
chunks.text: Advice must be based on the client's full financial picture, and must meet suitability and best-interest obligations that only licensed, supervised professionals can fulfill. Giving advice without that basis can harm clients and expose the firm to regulatory action.

chunks.heading: The AI tools follow the same rule
chunks.text: The virtual assistant and task experts are designed to route advice requests to a callback. If a suggested reply ever crosses the line, edit it before sending.

chunks.heading: Wrap-up
chunks.text: Use the Investment Advice wrap-up code when a client sought advice and was referred.
Twenty realistic client questions, with compliant answers and the lines to avoid.

chunks.heading: Examples
chunks.text:
Client asks: "Which fund should I buy?"; Compliant response: Explain the lineup groups; offer a callback; Avoid: Naming a fund
Client asks: "Is BFGR riskier than BF500?"; Compliant response: Compare risk levels, standard deviation, worst years; Avoid: "Yes, too risky for you"
Client asks: "Should I sell before it drops more?"; Compliant response: Acknowledge concern; explain options; callback; Avoid: "Hold on" or "Sell now"
Client asks: "Is a Roth better for me?"; Compliant response: Explain differences; callback; Avoid: "Yes, go Roth"
Client asks: "What's the best bond fund?"; Compliant response: Explain differences by duration and credit; Avoid: "BFST is safest"
Client asks: "How much should I keep in cash?"; Compliant response: Explain cash isn't invested; callback; Avoid: Any amount
Client asks: "What did BF500 return last year?"; Compliant response: Quote with date and disclaimer; Avoid: Projecting next year
Client asks: "Should I max out my IRA?"; Compliant response: State the limit and remaining room; Avoid: "Yes, always max out"
Client asks: "Is now a good time to invest?"; Compliant response: Explain DCA and lump-sum concepts neutrally; Avoid: Market timing views
Client asks: "What do most people pick?"; Compliant response: Describe what the options are for; Avoid: Popularity as endorsement
Client asks: "Can you look at my portfolio?"; Compliant response: Show holdings and allocation facts; callback for review; Avoid: Judging the allocation

chunks.heading: Examples
chunks.text:
Client asks: "Should I convert to Roth this year?"; Compliant response: Explain conversion mechanics and tax effects generally; Avoid: Recommending
Client asks: "Is ESG a good investment?"; Compliant response: Describe BFESG's screens and history; Avoid: Value judgments
Client asks: "Will the market crash?"; Compliant response: "No one can predict markets"; share history; Avoid: Any forecast
Client asks: "Should I rebalance?"; Compliant response: Explain rebalancing; calculate to the client's own target; Avoid: Setting a target
Client asks: "Is my withdrawal rate too high?"; Compliant response: Explain the arithmetic of withdrawals versus returns; Avoid: "Yes, lower it"
Client asks: "Should I take my RMD now or in December?"; Compliant response: Explain both are allowed; Avoid: Recommending timing
Client asks: "Should I roll over my 401(k)?"; Compliant response: Explain options and considerations; Avoid: Recommending
Client asks: "Is BFTEC overvalued?"; Compliant response: Quote P/E from the profile without judgment; Avoid: Valuation opinions
Client asks: "What would you do?"; Compliant response: "I'm not able to say, but a licensed professional can help."; Avoid: Personal opinions

chunks.heading: The test
chunks.text: Before sending, ask: does my message tell this client, directly or by implication, what they should do with their investments? If yes, rewrite it.
How to refer clients who want advice, what the licensed professional will do, and how to set expectations.

chunks.heading: When to refer
chunks.text:
- The client asks for a recommendation.
- The client wants a portfolio review or retirement plan.
- The client wants help with complex tax-sensitive decisions (conversions, withdrawal strategies).
- The client is making a major decision and wants a second opinion.

chunks.heading: How to refer
chunks.text: Schedule a callback with a licensed professional through the callback scope (see Scheduling callbacks). Make sure the chat captures the client's goal and key facts so the callback dossier is accurate.

chunks.heading: Setting expectations
chunks.text: "I've scheduled a call with one of our licensed professionals for Thursday at 2:00 PM Eastern. They'll be able to talk through your options and give you personalized guidance. They'll have a summary of our conversation, so you won't need to start from scratch."

chunks.heading: What not to promise
chunks.text: Don't promise a specific recommendation, an outcome, or that the call will be free of any cost if advisory services have fees (our service callbacks are free).

chunks.heading: Wrap-up
chunks.text: Use Referral or Investment Advice.

chunks.heading: What makes a good callback request
chunks.text:
The phone dossier is built from the chat. Before scheduling, capture in the chat:
- The client's goal in their words ("I'm 61 and want to know whether to convert some of my IRA to Roth before I retire").
- Relevant facts the client shared (timeline, other accounts, concerns).
- What you've already explained.

chunks.heading: Example
chunks.text: "I've set up a call for Thursday at 2:00 PM Eastern with a licensed professional. They'll see that you're thinking about converting part of your Traditional IRA this year and want to understand the tax impact. Is there anything else you'd like them to know?"
The regulatory rules that govern what we say to clients: fair and balanced, no promises, no misleading statements.

chunks.heading: The principles
chunks.text:
Communications with clients must be:
- Fair and balanced: benefits are never presented without the corresponding risks.
- Not misleading: no exaggerated, promissory, or unwarranted claims.
- Clear: in plain language the client can understand.
These standards come from FINRA rules on communications with the public and apply to chat.

chunks.heading: Specific rules
chunks.text:
- No predictions or projections of performance.
- No guarantees ("guaranteed", "can't lose", "safe").
- Performance must include the period, date, and a past-performance disclaimer. See How performance is reported.
- Comparisons must be fair and use comparable data.
- No testimonials about our funds.
- No promissory language about timing we don't control.

chunks.heading: Approved materials
chunks.text: Client-facing articles in the Help pages and the Library have been reviewed. Prefer sending them over composing long explanations.

chunks.heading: Templates
chunks.text: Scripts in this library comply with these standards. See Greetings and related pages.

chunks.heading: Examples
chunks.text:
Not compliant: "BFGR is a great performer."; Compliant: "BFGR returned 46.8% in 2023 and −33.2% in 2022. Past performance doesn't guarantee future results."
Not compliant: "Bond funds are safe."; Compliant: "BFST is rated Low risk, but all funds can lose value."
Not compliant: "You'll get your money in two days."; Compliant: "ACH typically arrives within 2–3 business days."
Not compliant: "Our funds beat [competitor]."; Compliant: "Our expense ratios range from 0.03% to 0.13%."
Not compliant: "This is guaranteed to be tax-free."; Compliant: "Qualified Roth distributions are tax-free; your tax advisor can confirm your situation."

chunks.heading: AI-drafted messages
chunks.text: Suggested replies are designed to meet these standards, but you are responsible for what you send. Edit any message that overstates, predicts, or promises.
What counts as a complaint, how to respond, how to log it, and the regulatory obligations.

chunks.heading: What counts as a complaint
chunks.text:
A complaint is any statement by a client (or someone acting for them) expressing a grievance about our service, products, or people, especially involving an allegation of harm, error, or wrongdoing. Signals: "I want to complain", "this is unacceptable", "I lost money because of you", "I'm going to report you", or a request for compensation.
When unsure, treat it as a complaint. Under-recording complaints is a compliance failure.

chunks.heading: How to respond
chunks.text:
1. Listen and acknowledge: "I'm sorry this happened. I want to make sure I understand everything."
2. Get the facts: what happened, when, which account, what outcome the client wants.
3. Fix what you can, if within your authority (a clear error, a misunderstanding).
4. Do not admit legal liability or speculate about fault. "Let me look into what happened" is appropriate; "That's our fault and we'll pay you back" is not, unless your team lead has authorized it.
5. Log the complaint using the complaint form in the workspace, with the client's words.
6. Explain next steps: "I've recorded your complaint. Our team will review it and respond within 5 business days."

chunks.heading: Written complaints
chunks.text: Written complaints (secure messages, letters, emails) must be forwarded to Compliance the same day. Compliance reports written complaints to regulators as required.

chunks.heading: Escalation
chunks.text: If the client asks for a supervisor, or the complaint involves alleged misconduct, fraud, or a large financial loss, escalate immediately. See Escalating complaints.

chunks.heading: Wrap-up
chunks.text: Complaint Filed if logged; Grievance if the client expressed dissatisfaction without a complaint.

chunks.heading: Scripts
chunks.text: See Complaints and de-escalation.
When and how to escalate a complaint to a supervisor or Compliance, and the response timelines.

chunks.heading: Escalate immediately when
chunks.text:
- The client asks for a supervisor or manager.
- The complaint alleges misconduct by an employee.
- The complaint involves alleged fraud or unauthorized activity.
- The client mentions an attorney, regulator (FINRA, SEC, state), or the media.
- The client claims a financial loss and asks for compensation.
- The client is a senior or vulnerable adult and the complaint involves a third party.

chunks.heading: How
chunks.text:
1. Tell the client you are escalating and what to expect.
2. Notify your team lead in the workspace (or by the escalation channel).
3. If the supervisor joins, brief them in a sentence or two.
4. If no supervisor is immediately available, schedule a supervisor callback within 1 business day.

chunks.heading: Timelines
chunks.text:
- Acknowledgment: same day.
- Supervisor contact: within 1 business day.
- Resolution or written response: typically within 5 business days for routine complaints; Compliance handles complex cases.

chunks.heading: Regulator references
chunks.text: If a client says they will complain to FINRA or the SEC, do not discourage them. They have the right to. Log it and escalate.

chunks.heading: Example
chunks.text:
Client: "If this isn't fixed, I'm reporting you to FINRA."
Agent: "I understand, and you have every right to contact FINRA. I want to help resolve this too. I've logged your complaint and asked a supervisor to contact you by tomorrow."

chunks.heading: After escalation
chunks.text: Note the complaint and the escalation in ACW, with the complaint reference.
Signs of possible money laundering or terrorist financing that agents must report, and how to report without tipping off.

chunks.heading: Our obligation
chunks.text: Federal law requires financial firms to have an anti-money-laundering (AML) program, including identifying and reporting suspicious activity. Every employee must escalate red flags.

chunks.heading: Red flags
chunks.text:
- Large deposits immediately followed by withdrawals, with little investment activity.
- Deposits from or withdrawals to unrelated third parties.
- Deposits structured just under reporting thresholds.
- Reluctance to provide identity information, or inconsistent information.
- Requests to move money to or from high-risk jurisdictions.
- A client asking how to avoid reporting requirements.
- Activity inconsistent with the client's stated occupation or profile.
- Multiple accounts with shared addresses or bank accounts and no apparent relationship.

chunks.heading: How to report
chunks.text: Report to the AML team through the internal referral (via your team lead). Include what you observed and why it seemed unusual.

chunks.heading: Do not tip off
chunks.text: It is illegal to tell a client that a suspicious activity report is being or may be filed. Do not mention AML reviews or reports. If a transaction is delayed for review, use neutral language: "This request needs an additional review."

chunks.heading: Example
chunks.text: A new client funds a taxable account with three $9,500 checks from different people, then asks two weeks later to wire the money to an unrelated person. Several red flags: structured amounts, third-party sources, and a third-party destination. Report to AML through your team lead; tell the client only that the request is under review.

chunks.heading: Your protection
chunks.text: Reporting suspicious activity in good faith is protected. When in doubt, report.
Why we screen clients and transactions against sanctions lists, and what agents should know.

chunks.heading: What it is
chunks.text: The U.S. Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) maintains lists of individuals, entities, and countries subject to sanctions. We screen all clients, beneficiaries, and money movements against these lists.

chunks.heading: What agents see
chunks.text: Occasionally, an application or transaction is held because of a potential match (often a common name). Compliance reviews and clears false matches.

chunks.heading: What to say
chunks.text: Do not mention sanctions screening to the client. "Your request needs an additional review; we'll contact you if we need anything." Never speculate about why.

chunks.heading: Prohibited activity
chunks.text: We cannot process transactions involving sanctioned countries or persons. If a client asks about sending money to a sanctioned country, decline and escalate to Compliance.

chunks.heading: Common situations
chunks.text:
- An application pends because the applicant's name resembles a listed name. Compliance clears false matches, usually within 1–2 business days.
- A beneficiary claim pends for the same reason.
- A client asks to send a wire abroad; we don't send foreign wires in any case. See International money movement.

chunks.heading: What not to do
chunks.text: Never suggest a client change details (for example, a middle name) to avoid a screening match, and never describe screening criteria.
What records we keep, for how long, and the rules about records requests.

chunks.heading: What we keep
chunks.text:
- Chat transcripts with live agents (all messages, including AI-drafted messages sent).
- After-chat work (wrap-up code, summary).
- Account records, transactions, statements, confirmations, and tax forms.
- Complaints and their resolution.
Regulations require most records to be kept for at least 3 to 6 years; we retain client statements and documents online for 7 years and archive longer.

chunks.heading: Your responsibility
chunks.text:
- Use only approved channels to communicate with clients (the chat workspace, phone, secure messages). Never use personal email, text messages, or social media to communicate with clients.
- Do not delete or alter records.
- Write as though every message will be reviewed.

chunks.heading: Records requests
chunks.text:
- Clients: statements and tax forms for 7 years online; chat history for 3 months in the chat menu. Older records via Client Records.
- Third parties (attorneys, courts, government agencies): Legal department only.

chunks.heading: Off-channel communication
chunks.text: Communicating with clients through personal phones, personal email, or messaging apps is prohibited, because those messages can't be retained and supervised as the rules require. If a client asks for your direct number or email, refer them to our official channels.

chunks.heading: Corrections in chat
chunks.text: If you send a message with an error, correct it in a new message rather than asking the client to ignore it. The full record, including the correction, is retained.
How errors in transactions are corrected, who pays, and how to handle a client who reports a mistake.

chunks.heading: Kinds of errors
chunks.text:
- Our error: we processed something differently from what the client authorized (wrong fund, wrong amount, wrong account, missed deadline).
- Client error: the client entered or authorized the wrong instruction.

chunks.heading: Our errors
chunks.text: When we make an error, we correct it so the client is in the position they would have been in had the error not occurred. This often means an as-of trade: processing the correct transaction at the NAV of the original date and reversing the wrong one. Any market loss from the correction is absorbed by the firm. Corrections require supervisor approval.

chunks.heading: Client errors
chunks.text: If a client made the mistake, we can help them correct it going forward (for example, exchanging back), but the transaction is processed at the current NAV, and market movements are the client's. For IRA contributions designated for the wrong year or type, see Prior-year contributions (January to April) and Recharacterizations.

chunks.heading: Procedure
chunks.text:
1. Gather facts: what was requested, what happened, the reference numbers and dates.
2. Check the transcript or records to determine what the client authorized.
3. Escalate to your team lead with the details. Do not promise a correction until it is approved.
4. Tell the client: "I've sent this to our team to review. If we made an error, we'll correct it so you're not harmed by it."

chunks.heading: Chat-originated errors
chunks.text: For actions submitted in chat, the transcript and evidence highlighting show what the client confirmed. That is why accurate confirmation recaps matter. See Confirmation recaps.
The firm's policy against market timing, how it is enforced, and how to explain it.

chunks.heading: Policy
chunks.text: The BobsFunds funds are intended for long-term investors. Frequent trading to profit from short-term price movements harms other shareholders through higher costs and dilution. The funds' prospectuses describe the restrictions.

chunks.heading: Enforcement
chunks.text:
- Automated round-trip restrictions: see Frequent trading (market timing) policy.
- Monitoring for patterns across accounts and households.
- Clients who repeatedly attempt to time the market may have purchase or exchange privileges restricted or be limited to purchases by mail.

chunks.heading: Explaining it
chunks.text: "Our funds are designed for long-term investing, and they limit short-term trading to protect all shareholders from extra costs."

chunks.heading: What counts as a pattern
chunks.text: Compliance looks for repeated round trips, large exchanges timed around market events, and coordinated trading across accounts in a household. Isolated trades do not trigger review.

chunks.heading: Exempt activity
chunks.text: Automatic investments, systematic withdrawals, dividend reinvestments, RMDs, and transactions in BFST are exempt from round-trip restrictions. See Frequent trading (market timing) policy.

chunks.heading: If a client is restricted
chunks.text: Explain the restriction neutrally and the date it ends. Do not discuss surveillance methods. If the client disputes the restriction, take the details and route to Compliance.
How we serve clients with disabilities, including vision, hearing, cognitive, and mobility needs.

chunks.heading: Commitments
chunks.text: We provide equal access to our services. Clients may request accommodations at any time.

chunks.heading: Available accommodations
chunks.text:
Need: Vision; What we offer: Screen-reader-compatible portal; large-print and Braille statements on request; documents in accessible formats
Need: Hearing; What we offer: Chat and secure messaging; relay service calls to 1-800-BOB-FUND
Need: Cognitive; What we offer: Patient, plain-language communication; written follow-ups; extra time
Need: Mobility; What we offer: All services available remotely; forms can be signed electronically

chunks.heading: Requesting
chunks.text: Clients can request large-print or Braille documents and accessible formats at My Account → Preferences or by asking any agent. Note the request and route it to Client Services fulfillment.

chunks.heading: In chat
chunks.text: Adapt to the client: shorter sentences, one step at a time, confirm understanding. Don't make assumptions; ask what works best.

chunks.heading: Example requests
chunks.text:
- "Can I get my statements in large print?" Yes; note the request for fulfillment.
- "I'm deaf; can I call?" Yes, through any relay service, or keep using chat and secure messages.
- "Your website doesn't work with my screen reader." Help with the task in chat and log a Technical Issue with details.

chunks.heading: Paper fees
chunks.text: Clients with an accessibility accommodation for printed documents are not charged the paper statement fee. See Paper statement fee.

chunks.heading: Communication approach
chunks.text: Ask what works best rather than assuming. Some clients with cognitive or memory challenges appreciate a written recap at the end of the chat; offer to send one by secure message.
How we serve clients who prefer a language other than English.

chunks.heading: Available
chunks.text:
- Phone service in Spanish (select Spanish at the start of the call).
- Telephone interpretation in over 100 languages through an interpreter service, arranged by phone agents.
- Some key forms and documents in Spanish.

chunks.heading: In chat
chunks.text:
Chat is in English. If a client writes in another language:
1. Respond briefly in English (and in their language if you are certified to communicate in it).
2. Offer a phone call with Spanish service or an interpreter.
3. Do not use machine translation for account actions or disclosures.
Agents who are bilingual may support clients in that language only if certified through our language proficiency program.

chunks.heading: Example
chunks.text:
Client writes in Spanish: "Hola, necesito ayuda con mi cuenta."
Agent (not Spanish-certified): "Hello! I'm happy to help in English here in chat. If you'd prefer Spanish, our phone team can help at 1-800-BOB-FUND (choose Spanish), or I can schedule a callback with a Spanish-speaking representative."

chunks.heading: Documents
chunks.text: Some forms (account application, beneficiary designation) are available in Spanish from the Forms page. Statements are in English.

chunks.heading: Interpreters for other languages
chunks.text: Phone representatives can add a professional interpreter to a call. Clients should not rely on family members to interpret for account changes when an interpreter is available.

chunks.page: Gifts, entertainment, and conflicts of interest
chunks.text: Rules for accepting gifts from clients and avoiding conflicts.

chunks.page: Gifts, entertainment, and conflicts of interest
chunks.heading: Gifts from clients
chunks.text: Clients sometimes offer thanks in the form of gifts. Agents may not accept cash or cash equivalents (gift cards) in any amount. Non-cash gifts must be reported to your team lead and may be accepted only within firm limits (currently $100 per person per year). Politely decline anything beyond: "That's so kind, but we're not able to accept gifts. Your thanks means a lot."

chunks.page: Gifts, entertainment, and conflicts of interest
chunks.heading: Bequests and beneficiary designations
chunks.text: An agent may never be named as a client's beneficiary, executor, trustee, or power of attorney (unless a family member, with Compliance approval). If a client suggests this, decline and inform your team lead.

chunks.page: Gifts, entertainment, and conflicts of interest
chunks.heading: Personal dealings
chunks.text: Do not lend money to or borrow from clients, share in their accounts, or do business with them outside the firm.

chunks.page: Gifts, entertainment, and conflicts of interest
chunks.heading: Conflicts
chunks.text: Disclose any personal relationship with a client (a relative, a friend) to your team lead and do not service their accounts.

chunks.page: Gifts, entertainment, and conflicts of interest
chunks.heading: Example
chunks.text:
Client: "You've been so helpful. Can I send you a gift card?"
Agent: "That's very kind of you, but we're not able to accept gifts. Your thanks really does mean a lot."

chunks.page: Gifts, entertainment, and conflicts of interest
chunks.heading: Holiday cards and small tokens
chunks.text: Cards and notes of thanks are welcome. Non-cash items must be reported to your team lead.
Why helping clients discover relevant services is good service, how to do it naturally, and where the line is.

chunks.heading: The principle
chunks.text: Good service anticipates needs. When a client's situation makes a feature or service relevant, mentioning it is helpful, not pushy. The AI tools often surface these moments (for example, the predicted questions or a suggested reply that mentions automatic investing after a purchase). Use them.

chunks.heading: Natural moments
chunks.text:
Client situation: Just made a one-time purchase; Helpful mention: Automatic investing, if they plan to invest regularly
Client situation: Opened an IRA; Helpful mention: Naming beneficiaries; automatic contributions
Client situation: Mentioned a new job; Helpful mention: Rolling over the old 401(k)
Client situation: Mentioned a new child or grandchild; Helpful mention: Reviewing beneficiaries; custodial accounts
Client situation: Receives paper statements; Helpful mention: Paperless delivery (and the waived fee)
Client situation: Approaching 73; Helpful mention: RMD settings
Client situation: Has uninvested cash; Helpful mention: That cash isn't invested (neutrally)
Client situation: Multiple tasks in one chat; Helpful mention: Handle them all; offer anything related

chunks.heading: How to do it
chunks.text:
- One relevant mention, at a natural pause, after the client's main request is done.
- Frame it as information: "Since you're investing each month anyway, some clients set up an automatic investment so it happens on its own. Want me to show you how?"
- Respect a "no" immediately.

chunks.heading: The line
chunks.text: Proactive service describes our services; it never recommends investments. "You might find automatic investing convenient" is fine; "You should put more into growth funds" is advice.

chunks.heading: Bonus opportunities
chunks.text: Some conversations show a bonus opportunity badge (for example, rollovers or new accounts). Bonuses reward service, never pressure. A client who declines must receive the same quality of service.
What a statement shows, how to read each section, and common client questions.

chunks.heading: Sections of a statement
chunks.text:
1. Account summary: beginning value, deposits, withdrawals, change in value, ending value for the period.
2. Holdings: each fund, shares, NAV, value, and the cash balance.
3. Activity: every transaction in the period (purchases, sales, exchanges, distributions, fees).
4. Income summary: dividends and capital gains year to date.
5. IRA information (for IRAs): contributions by tax year, distributions, withholding, the year's RMD if applicable.
6. Cost basis summary (taxable accounts): unrealized gains and losses.
7. Messages: notices about policy changes and upcoming deadlines.

chunks.heading: Common questions
chunks.text:
"Why is the change in value negative when I added money?":
Market changes can exceed deposits. The summary separates deposits from the market change.
"My statement balance differs from the website.":
The statement shows the value at the statement date; the website shows the latest value. See "My balance looks wrong".
"Where's my cash?":
Cash appears as its own line in Holdings.

chunks.heading: Example: reading the summary
chunks.text:
Line: Beginning value (July 1); Amount: $42,180.55
Line: Deposits; Amount: $600.00
Line: Withdrawals; Amount: $0.00
Line: Dividends and distributions; Amount: $118.42
Line: Change in market value; Amount: −$912.10
Line: Ending value (September 30); Amount: $41,986.87
Dividends that were reinvested appear both as income and as purchases; they do not change the total value by themselves.

chunks.heading: IRA section
chunks.text: For IRAs, the statement shows contributions by tax year so clients can track their limits, and any RMD due for the year with the amount already distributed.

chunks.heading: Personal performance
chunks.text: Quarterly statements show the client's personal rate of return for the quarter, year to date, and since the account opened, which can differ from the funds' published returns because of timing of deposits and withdrawals.
When confirmations are sent, what they contain, and when automatic transactions are confirmed on statements instead.

chunks.heading: When
chunks.text: A confirmation is produced for every purchase, sale, and exchange, available the business day after the trade. Automatic investments, systematic withdrawals, and dividend reinvestments are confirmed on the statement instead (unless the client opts for individual confirmations).

chunks.heading: Contents
chunks.text: Trade date, settlement date, account, fund, transaction type, dollar amount, NAV, shares, funding source or proceeds destination, IRA contribution year or distribution details, and a reference number.

chunks.heading: Review
chunks.text: Clients should review confirmations promptly and report errors right away; prompt reporting makes corrections simpler. See Correcting errors (as-of trades).

chunks.heading: Reading a confirmation
chunks.text: A client looking at a confirmation for a $1,000 purchase of BF500 sees: trade date (the pricing date), settlement date (one business day later), amount $1,000.00, NAV $218.40, shares 4.579, funding "Linked bank ••4421", and for an IRA "2026 contribution".

chunks.heading: Confirmations versus chat confirmation cards
chunks.text: The green card the client receives in chat confirms the order was placed and gives the reference number. The trade confirmation, available the next business day, shows the price and shares. Both are records; the trade confirmation is the official one.

chunks.heading: Paper or paperless
chunks.text: Confirmations follow the client's document delivery preference. Clients who want text alerts for each trade can enable them at My Account → Preferences.
When each type of statement and report is produced.

chunks.heading: Schedule
chunks.text:
Document: Account statement; Frequency: Quarterly; monthly for any month with activity; Available: Within 5 business days after period end
Document: Annual statement; Frequency: Yearly; Available: January
Document: Trade confirmations; Frequency: Per trade; Available: Next business day
Document: Performance report; Frequency: Quarterly; Available: Online only
Document: Tax forms; Frequency: Annually; Available: See Tax form calendar
Document: RMD notice; Frequency: Annually; Available: January
Document: Fund shareholder reports; Frequency: Semiannual and annual; Available: As published

chunks.heading: Activity triggering monthly statements
chunks.text: Purchases, sales, exchanges, deposits, withdrawals. Dividend reinvestments alone do not trigger a monthly statement.

chunks.heading: Common questions
chunks.text:
"When will my September statement be ready?":
Quarterly statements are available within 5 business days after the quarter ends, so early October for the September quarter.
"I didn't get a monthly statement.":
Monthly statements are produced only for months with activity other than dividend reinvestment. A quiet month rolls into the quarterly statement.
"Can I get statements more often?":
Clients can view current balances and activity online any time. Statement frequency itself is not adjustable.
"Do I get a separate statement for each account?":
Clients with several accounts receive a consolidated statement covering all accounts registered to them under the same profile, with a section for each account.
Where clients find documents online, how long they stay, and how to get older copies.

chunks.heading: Online
chunks.text: My Account → Statements & Documents, with filters for account, year, and document type. Tax forms also appear under My Account → Tax Documents. Everything is downloadable as PDF.

chunks.heading: Retention
chunks.text: Statements, confirmations, and tax forms remain online for 7 years. Older documents can be requested from Client Records (typically within 10 business days).

chunks.heading: Closed accounts
chunks.text: Documents for closed accounts remain accessible online for 7 years, as long as the client has an active login (or can enroll).

chunks.heading: Clients' own records
chunks.text: Encourage clients to keep year-end statements and tax forms and records of IRA contributions and nondeductible basis indefinitely. This is general good practice, not tax advice.

chunks.heading: Downloading in bulk
chunks.text: Clients can download a year's statements together as a ZIP file from My Account → Statements & Documents → Download all for year.

chunks.heading: Sharing with an accountant
chunks.text: Rather than forwarding documents, clients can add their accountant as a view-only authorized user or an interested party for duplicate statements. See Duplicate statements and interested parties.

chunks.heading: Documents for an estate
chunks.text: Executors may need statements for the deceased's accounts, including date-of-death values. Estate Services provides these once the executor's authority is documented.
Every fee Bob's Mutual Funds charges, and the fees we don't charge.

chunks.heading: Fees we don't charge
chunks.text:
Item: Account opening, maintenance, or closing; Fee: None
Item: IRA annual custodial fee; Fee: None
Item: Buying, selling, or exchanging BobsFunds funds; Fee: $0
Item: Sales loads (front-end, back-end) and 12b-1 fees; Fee: None
Item: Redemption fees; Fee: None
Item: Incoming wires; Fee: None (the sending bank may charge)
Item: ACH transfers; Fee: None
Item: Outgoing ACAT transfers; Fee: None
Item: Stop payment on a check we issued; Fee: None

chunks.heading: Fees we charge
chunks.text:
Service: Outgoing wire; Fee: $25
Service: Overnight check delivery; Fee: $25
Service: Paper statement fee; Fee: $2 per month per account (waived; see below)
Service: Returned payment (ACH or check); Fee: $20

chunks.heading: Fund expenses
chunks.text: Each fund has an expense ratio (0.03% to 0.13%), deducted inside the fund, not charged to the account. See Expense ratios.

chunks.heading: Paper statement fee waivers
chunks.text: Waived for paperless delivery, clients aged 75 or older, and accounts with balances over $250,000. See Paper statement fee.

chunks.heading: Explaining "no fees"
chunks.text: When clients ask what they pay, a complete answer is: "There are no account fees and no transaction fees for our funds. The only ongoing cost is each fund's expense ratio, which is built into the fund's price. A few optional services have fees, like $25 for an outgoing wire."

chunks.heading: Fees at other institutions
chunks.text: The client's bank may charge for wires it sends or receives, and other firms may charge transfer-out fees when a client moves assets to us. We do not reimburse other firms' fees.

chunks.heading: Changes to fees
chunks.text: Any change to our fee schedule is announced at least 30 days in advance on statements and by notice. If a client says they were charged a fee they didn't expect, check the schedule and see Fee disputes and adjustments.
The $2 monthly paper statement fee, who pays it, the waivers, and how to help clients avoid it.

chunks.heading: The fee
chunks.text: $2 per month per account for clients who receive statements by mail. It is charged quarterly ($6) from the account's cash or, if there is no cash, by selling a small amount of the largest holding.

chunks.heading: Waivers
chunks.text:
- Paperless delivery of statements.
- Clients aged 75 or older.
- Accounts with a balance over $250,000.
- Accounts with an accessibility accommodation for printed documents.

chunks.heading: Avoiding it
chunks.text: Switching to paperless at My Account → Preferences stops the fee from the next quarter. See Paperless delivery.

chunks.heading: Refunds
chunks.text: If a client qualified for a waiver that was not applied (for example, they turned 75), refund the fees through a fee adjustment request (team lead approval). See Fee disputes and adjustments.

chunks.heading: Example
chunks.text: A client with two accounts, both receiving paper statements, pays $2 × 2 accounts × 3 months = $12 per quarter. Switching to paperless stops it from the next quarter.

chunks.heading: How the fee appears
chunks.text: It appears in the account activity as "Paper statement fee" each quarter, and on the statement.

chunks.heading: Clients who prefer paper
chunks.text: Some clients prefer paper and are willing to pay; that is their choice. Don't pressure them. Mention the waivers in case they qualify (age 75+, balances over $250,000).
The outgoing wire fee, when it is charged, and when it may be waived.

chunks.heading: The fee
chunks.text: $25 per outgoing wire, deducted from the wired amount (a $10,000 wire delivers $9,975) unless the client asks for it to be charged separately to cash in the account.

chunks.heading: Incoming wires
chunks.text: We do not charge for incoming wires. The client's bank (and any intermediary bank for international wires) may charge.

chunks.heading: Waivers
chunks.text:
The fee may be waived when:
- The wire is needed to correct our error.
- A returned wire was caused by our error.
Waivers require team lead approval. Repeated requests to waive for convenience are not granted; suggest ACH (free) when timing allows.

chunks.heading: Example
chunks.text: A client sells $10,000 and requests a wire. The wire delivers $9,975 to their bank. If they want $10,000 to arrive, they can wire $10,025 or ask for the fee to be taken from cash in the account.

chunks.heading: Free alternatives
chunks.text: ACH is free and arrives in 2–3 business days. When a client's need isn't urgent, mention it.
How to handle a client who disputes a fee, when fees can be refunded, and the approval process.

chunks.heading: Steps
chunks.text:
1. Identify the fee: type, amount, date, account.
2. Determine whether it was charged correctly under the fee schedule. See Fee schedule.
3. If charged in error (a waiver not applied, a fee caused by our mistake), request a refund through a fee adjustment (team lead approval) and tell the client the expected timeline (credited within 3 business days).
4. If charged correctly, explain the fee and how to avoid it in the future. Your team lead may approve a one-time courtesy refund in some circumstances; do not promise one.

chunks.heading: Wrap-up
chunks.text: Use Fee Dispute.

chunks.heading: Fund expenses
chunks.text: Expense ratios are not refundable fees; they are fund operating costs disclosed in the prospectus.

chunks.heading: Example
chunks.text:
Client: "Why was I charged $20?"
Agent: "That's a returned-payment fee. On March 3, your bank returned the $500 automatic investment into BF500 for insufficient funds, so the purchase was reversed and the fee applied."
If the client says the bank account had money, ask them to check with their bank for the return reason. If the return was our error (for example, we debited the wrong bank account), request a refund.

chunks.heading: Courtesy refunds
chunks.text: Team leads may approve a one-time courtesy refund of a returned-payment fee or paper fee for a long-standing client with no prior refunds. Never promise one before approval.
The five transaction statuses clients see, what each means, and how long each lasts.

chunks.heading: The lifecycle
chunks.text:
Mutual funds price once a day and settle the next business day, so every order moves through the same stages:
Status: Scheduled; Meaning: A future-dated transaction (an automatic investment or withdrawal, or an order placed on a weekend or holiday); Typical duration: Until its date
Status: Pending; Meaning: Placed and waiting for tonight's NAV; Typical duration: Until about 6:00 PM ET on the trade date
Status: Settling; Meaning: Executed at the NAV, in T+1 settlement; Typical duration: One business day
Status: Completed; Meaning: Settled and posted to the account; Typical duration: Final
Status: Canceled; Meaning: Cancelled by the client before the cutoff, or reversed (for example, a returned payment); Typical duration: Final

chunks.heading: Common questions
chunks.text:
"My purchase says pending. Did it go through?":
Yes, it was received. It will be priced at today's closing NAV (if placed before 4:00 PM ET) and show the number of shares tonight.
"Why is it 'settling' if I already have the shares?":
The shares are credited when the trade is priced; settlement is the back-office completion the next business day.
"My order was canceled. I didn't cancel it.":
Check the reason: a returned payment, an IRA contribution over the limit, a frequent-trading block, or an incomplete order. See Returned and failed purchases.

chunks.heading: Reference numbers
chunks.text: Orders placed in chat have a reference number (REF-XXXXXX) shown on the confirmation card. See Reference numbers.
What reference numbers are, where clients find them, and how to use them to trace an action.

chunks.heading: Format
chunks.text: Every action submitted through the chat Proposed Action flow returns a reference number in the format REF-XXXXXX. It appears on the green confirmation card in the client's chat, in the transcript, and in the after-chat summary.

chunks.heading: Using them
chunks.text:
- A client referring back to a chat action can quote the reference number; search the client's transcripts or recent activity for it.
- Include reference numbers in escalations and complaint records.
- Trade confirmations carry their own confirmation numbers, which may differ from the chat reference number.

chunks.heading: If the client lost it
chunks.text: Find the chat in the client's transcript history (the client can see their last 3 months of live-agent chats in the chat menu) or locate the transaction by date and amount.

chunks.heading: Where the number appears
chunks.text:
Place: Client's chat; What it shows: The green confirmation card
Place: Client's chat history; What it shows: The transcript, for 3 months
Place: Agent workspace; What it shows: The Proposed Action result and transcript
Place: After-chat summary; What it shows: Included by the ACW generator

chunks.heading: Quoting them
chunks.text: Read the full reference number to the client in your closing message for any completed action, so they have it even if they don't save the transcript. See Closing a chat.

chunks.heading: When a client calls about an action
chunks.text: Ask for the reference number first; it is the fastest way to find the exact action. If they don't have it, the date, account, and amount are usually enough.
A diagnostic path for deposits that a client expected but doesn't see, by method.

chunks.heading: Ask
chunks.text:
- How was the money sent (ACH from a linked bank, wire, check, transfer from another firm, rollover)?
- When, and how much?
- Into which account?

chunks.heading: By method
chunks.text:
Method: ACH purchase; What to check: Recent transactions for the purchase; the client's bank shows the debit 2–3 business days later; Typical cause: The shares are credited before the bank is debited, so a client watching their bank may be confused; or the order was placed after 4:00 PM
Method: Automatic investment; What to check: Plan status, the scheduled day, bank link; Typical cause: Paused plan, weekend/holiday, returned payment
Method: Wire; What to check: Wire received but unmatched; Typical cause: Missing account number or name mismatch; ask for the federal reference number. See Incoming wires
Method: Check; What to check: Mail time; whether the check was acceptable; Typical cause: Still in the mail; a third-party or starter check returned
Method: Mobile check deposit; What to check: Deposit status in the app; Typical cause: Under review; image quality
Method: ACAT transfer; What to check: Transfer status; Typical cause: Rejected for mismatch; still in progress. See Tracking rollovers and transfers
Method: Rollover; What to check: Whether the plan sent it, how, when; Typical cause: Plan still processing; check mailed to the client

chunks.heading: Next steps
chunks.text: If the money left the client's bank or the other institution more than 2 business days ago and nothing appears, escalate to Money Movement Operations with the details (amount, date, method, reference or trace numbers). Tell the client what you've done and when they'll hear back.
Common reasons a balance differs from what the client expects and how to explain each.

chunks.heading: Common reasons
chunks.text:
Reason: Market movement; Explanation: Values change daily with NAVs
Reason: A distribution date; Explanation: The NAV dropped by the distribution; the value moved to cash or new shares. See Record, ex-dividend, reinvestment, and pay dates
Reason: Pending transactions; Explanation: A purchase or sale placed today isn't priced until tonight
Reason: Cash versus invested; Explanation: The total includes uninvested cash; the client may be looking at holdings only
Reason: Statement date; Explanation: Statements show period-end values
Reason: Withholding; Explanation: An IRA distribution was reduced by tax withholding
Reason: A fee; Explanation: Paper statement fee, wire fee
Reason: A returned payment; Explanation: A purchase was reversed
Reason: Looking at the wrong account; Explanation: Clients with several accounts

chunks.heading: How to explain
chunks.text: Walk through the activity since the date the client remembers: "On the 1st your account was $41,200. Since then, BF500 paid a dividend that was reinvested, and the market fell about 2%, which brings it to today's $40,600."

chunks.heading: If something is truly wrong
chunks.text: If after review the numbers don't reconcile (a missing transaction, a duplicate), escalate with specifics. See Duplicate or unexpected transactions.

chunks.heading: Example
chunks.text:
Client: "My statement said $41,986 but now the website says $41,650. Where did $336 go?"
Agent: "Your statement shows September 30. Since then, the market has moved: BF500, your largest holding, is down a little over 1% this month, which accounts for about $330. There have been no withdrawals or fees."
How to answer questions about orders that haven't completed, including cancellations.

chunks.heading: What's in process
chunks.text: The client's activity shows Scheduled, Pending, and Settling items at the top. See Transaction statuses.

chunks.heading: Can it be canceled?
chunks.text:
Item: Scheduled automatic investment or withdrawal; Cancel?: Yes, at least 3 business days before the date (pause or skip the plan)
Item: Pending order placed online; Cancel?: Yes, from Pending Orders, before 4:00 PM ET on the trade date
Item: Pending order placed in chat or by phone; Cancel?: Contact us before 4:00 PM ET; we can cancel
Item: Settling or Completed; Cancel?: No; place an offsetting transaction if needed
Item: Outgoing wire already sent; Cancel?: Generally no; recalls are rarely successful

chunks.heading: Duplicate orders
chunks.text: If a client placed the same order twice by mistake, cancel the duplicate if still pending. If already priced, the client can sell the extra shares (which may create a round trip under the frequent-trading policy; corrections of our errors are exempt).

chunks.heading: Explaining pending orders
chunks.text: "Your order to buy $1,000 of BF500 is pending, which means we've received it and it will be priced at today's closing NAV after 4:00 PM Eastern. Tonight you'll see the number of shares, and tomorrow it will settle."

chunks.heading: Weekend and holiday orders
chunks.text: Orders placed on a weekend or holiday show as Scheduled or Pending until the next business day's close. Clients sometimes worry the order is stuck; explain the next pricing date.

chunks.heading: Large pending withdrawals
chunks.text: A withdrawal can show pending longer if it is under a protective review. Do not speculate; see Protective holds on money movement.
Handling transactions that appear twice or that the client doesn't recognize.

chunks.heading: Duplicates
chunks.text:
1. Confirm whether there are truly two transactions (same amount, fund, date) or one transaction shown in two places (for example, a purchase and its matching bank debit).
2. If two orders were placed (for example, a client clicked twice online, or both an online and a chat order), see Pending and in-process activity.
3. If a system error created a duplicate, escalate as an error. See Correcting errors (as-of trades).

chunks.heading: Unrecognized transactions
chunks.text:
Common legitimate causes: dividend reinvestments, automatic investments, RMD payments, fees, a joint owner's or authorized user's action. Check the transaction type and who initiated it.
If the client still doesn't recognize it, treat it as possible unauthorized activity. See Suspected account takeover or unauthorized activity.

chunks.heading: Things that look like duplicates but aren't
chunks.text:
Looks like: Two purchases of the same amount on the same day; Actually: One online, one from an automatic plan
Looks like: A purchase and a matching "deposit" line; Actually: The ACH deposit and the purchase it funded
Looks like: Two dividend lines; Actually: A dividend and its reinvestment
Looks like: Two withdrawals; Actually: A gross distribution and its tax withholding line
Looks like: The same transaction on two statements; Actually: A transaction near the statement cutoff, shown as pending then completed

chunks.heading: When it is a real duplicate
chunks.text: If the client placed the same order twice (for example, once online and once in chat), and both have priced, the client can sell the extra shares at the current NAV. If the duplicate was caused by our system or by an agent submitting twice, escalate for an as-of correction so the client bears no market loss. See Correcting errors (as-of trades).
Steps when a client hasn't received a redemption, distribution, or other check.

chunks.heading: Steps
chunks.text:
1. Confirm the check was issued: date, amount, and the address it was mailed to.
2. Confirm the address is correct. If not, the check may have gone to an old address; a stop payment and reissue are needed.
3. Allow 10 business days from the issue date for standard mail.
4. After 10 business days, request a stop payment and reissue. See Stop payments.
5. Offer to reissue by ACH (faster) if the client has a linked bank.

chunks.heading: If it was cashed
chunks.text: If the check shows as cashed and the client didn't cash it, start a forgery claim through Money Movement Operations. See Lost, stolen, and uncashed checks.

chunks.heading: Questions to ask
chunks.text:
