- What was the check for: a sale, an IRA distribution, an RMD, a closed-account residual?
- What date did they expect it, and which address?
- Did they recently move or change their address with us?

chunks.heading: What to look up
chunks.text: The transaction shows the issue date, amount, payee, and mailing address. If the check was sent overnight ($25), there is a tracking number you can share.

chunks.heading: IRA distribution checks
chunks.text: Remember that an IRA distribution check is still a taxable distribution in the year it was issued, even if it is lost and reissued later. The reissued check does not create a second distribution. Withholding already sent to the IRS stays sent.

chunks.heading: Faster alternatives
chunks.text: Clients who need money quickly may prefer to cancel the check and receive the funds by ACH (2–3 business days) or wire ($25, same day if before 2:00 PM ET). See Where sale proceeds go.

chunks.heading: Address problems
chunks.text: If the check went to an old address, update the address first. Remember the 15-day rule: a reissued check cannot be mailed to a newly changed address within 15 days without a medallion signature guarantee, so ACH is often the better route. See Address changes: special situations.
Why a client might not see an expected dividend, and how to check.

chunks.heading: Common reasons
chunks.text:
- Timing: the fund pays monthly, quarterly, or semiannually; check the schedule. See Distribution calendar.
- Reinvested: with DRIP on, the dividend bought more shares rather than appearing as cash.
- Bought after the record date: the client wasn't a shareholder on the record date.
- Sold before the record date: no longer a shareholder.
- Cash to bank: the dividend went to the linked bank; amounts under $10 accumulate.
- IRA: the dividend stayed in the IRA.
- The fund paid none: capital gain distributions don't occur every year.

chunks.heading: How to check
chunks.text: Look for a "Dividend" or "Reinvestment" transaction in the account activity around the fund's pay date.

chunks.heading: A worked check
chunks.text:
Client: "BFBI usually pays me around $180 a month. I didn't see anything this month."
1. BFBI is a bond fund that pays monthly, around the 7th. Today is the 9th.
2. The client's dividend preference for BFBI is "reinvest", so the payment would appear as a reinvestment purchase, not cash.
3. The activity shows a reinvestment on the 7th of 1.832 shares. That is the dividend.

chunks.heading: Amounts change
chunks.text: Dividend amounts vary with the income the fund earns and the number of shares the client owns. Bond fund dividends move with interest rates; stock fund dividends move with company payouts. A smaller dividend is not an error.

chunks.heading: Year-end capital gains
chunks.text: Capital gain distributions are not paid every year. A client who received one last December may not receive one this year. That is normal for index funds.

chunks.heading: Changing what happens to dividends
chunks.text: If the client wants dividends paid as cash instead of reinvested, see Procedure: Change Dividend Reinvestment (chat).
A quick diagnostic for an automatic investment that didn't occur as expected.

chunks.heading: Checks
chunks.text:
1. Is the plan active or paused?
2. What was the scheduled day, and was it a weekend or holiday (then the next business day)?
3. Was the plan changed fewer than 3 business days before the date?
4. Was the purchase made and then reversed by the bank?
5. For IRAs, has the client reached their contribution limit?
6. Is the bank account still open and linked?
Full diagnostic: When an automatic investment doesn't run.

chunks.heading: Walking the client through it
chunks.text:
Most clients notice a missed investment when they look at their bank statement or their holdings. Start by finding out which plan they mean (account, fund, amount, day), then work down the checklist above in order. The first check that fails is almost always the answer.
Example conversation:
Client: "My $200 didn't go into BF500 this month."
Agent: "Let me look. Your plan for $200 into BF500 in your Roth IRA runs on the 15th. This month the 15th was a Saturday, so it ran Monday the 17th; I can see it here, priced at Monday's NAV. Your bank should show the debit by Wednesday."

chunks.heading: If we caused it
chunks.text: If the plan should have run and didn't because of an error on our side (for example, a pause the client never requested), escalate to your team lead. We can process the missed investment as of the original date so the client isn't disadvantaged. See Correcting errors (as-of trades).

chunks.heading: If the client wants to make it up
chunks.text: The client can place a one-time purchase now for the missed amount. For an IRA, it counts as a contribution for the current year. See Procedure: Buy / Make a Contribution (chat).

chunks.heading: Preventing repeats
chunks.text:
- Remind the client that changes need 3 business days' notice.
- If the cause was a returned payment, suggest they check their bank balance before the investment date, or move the date to just after payday.
- If the bank account changed, update the plan to the new bank.

chunks.page: "I can't see one of my accounts"
chunks.text: Why an account might not appear in a client's portal view, and how to fix it.

chunks.page: "I can't see one of my accounts"
chunks.heading: Common reasons
chunks.text:
- The account is under a different login: a joint account opened by the other owner, a custodial account under the custodian, a trust account under the trustee login, or a second profile created with a different email.
- The account was closed (zero balance for 12 months closes automatically).
- New account still pending: application not yet approved.
- Estate or protective hold restricting access.
- Authorized-user access removed by the owner.

chunks.page: "I can't see one of my accounts"
chunks.heading: Fixing it
chunks.text: Linking profiles (for example, a client with two logins) is done by Account Services after verification. Joint owners each have their own login; they can link the joint account to their profile through My Account → Add Existing Account.

chunks.page: "I can't see one of my accounts"
chunks.heading: Before you change anything
chunks.text: Verify the client's identity carefully. A request to "add an account to my login" is a request to give someone access to assets, so it must come from an owner of that account.

chunks.page: "I can't see one of my accounts"
chunks.heading: Joint owners
chunks.text: Each joint owner has their own login. If the second owner can't see a joint account, they can add it from My Account → Add Existing Account by entering the account number and verifying with their own SSN; the system confirms they are an owner.

chunks.page: "I can't see one of my accounts"
chunks.heading: Custodial and trust accounts
chunks.text: The custodian or trustee sees these accounts under their own login. The minor or trust beneficiary does not.

chunks.page: "I can't see one of my accounts"
chunks.heading: Closed accounts
chunks.text: Closed accounts disappear from the portfolio view, but their documents remain at My Account → Statements & Documents for 7 years.

chunks.page: "I can't see one of my accounts"
chunks.heading: Duplicate profiles
chunks.text: Clients who opened accounts years apart with different email addresses may have two profiles. Account Services can merge them after verification, so all accounts appear under one login.
Troubleshooting failed bank linking by instant verification and micro-deposits.

chunks.heading: Instant verification fails
chunks.text:
- The bank may not support it or may require additional security steps. Use micro-deposits instead.
- The client's online banking credentials or multi-factor prompt failed; try again on the bank's own site first.

chunks.heading: Micro-deposits issues
chunks.text:
Issue: Deposits haven't appeared; Fix: Allow 2 business days; check the correct bank account; savings accounts may show them differently
Issue: Wrong amounts entered three times; Fix: Verification locked; remove and start again
Issue: More than 14 days passed; Fix: Start again

chunks.heading: Name or ownership mismatch
chunks.text: The bank account must belong to an owner of the Bob's account. Business accounts and relatives' accounts cannot be linked. See Linking bank accounts.

chunks.heading: Bank account types
chunks.text: Checking and savings accounts at U.S. banks and credit unions are supported. Prepaid cards, some online-only "neobank" accounts, and brokerage cash accounts may not support ACH debits.

chunks.heading: Business and joint bank accounts
chunks.text:
- A business bank account can be linked only to a business-related registration (for example, a sole proprietor's SEP-IRA contributions from their business account are allowed if the client is the account holder of record).
- A joint bank account can be linked if at least one owner of the bank account is an owner of the Bob's account.

chunks.heading: After linking
chunks.text: Remind the client about the 10-day rule: a newly linked bank can fund purchases right away, but electronic withdrawals to it need a verification call in the first 10 days. See Linking bank accounts.

chunks.heading: Alternatives while linking is pending
chunks.text: If the client needs to invest today, a wire is the fastest alternative; for slower needs, a check by mail works. See Funding a new account.
How to explain a decline in a fund's value factually, including distribution-date drops.

chunks.heading: Steps
chunks.text:
1. Check the date and size of the drop.
2. Distribution date? If the fund paid a distribution that day, the NAV dropped by the amount paid. The client didn't lose that value. See Record, ex-dividend, reinvestment, and pay dates.
3. Market movement? Explain what the fund holds and that its value follows those markets. Use the fund profile for context (group, risk level, past calendar-year ranges).
4. Bond fund? Rising interest rates lower bond prices. See Bonds and interest rates.
5. International fund? A stronger dollar lowers the value of foreign holdings.

chunks.heading: What to avoid
chunks.text: Explanations based on news events you can't verify, predictions, and advice. If the client is anxious, see Talking with clients during market downturns.

chunks.heading: Example explanations
chunks.text:
Distribution day: "BF500's price dropped $1.64 on March 25 because the fund paid a dividend of $1.64 per share that day. Your dividend was reinvested, so you now own a few more shares. Your total value wasn't reduced by the payment."
Market day: "BF500 holds the 500 largest U.S. companies, so it moves with the U.S. stock market. Yesterday the broad market fell about 2%, and the fund fell by a similar amount."
Bond fund: "BFLTT holds long-term Treasury bonds, which are sensitive to interest rates. When rates rise, their prices fall. The fund's average duration is about 15.5 years, so a 1 percentage-point rise in rates would lower its price roughly 15%."
International fund: "BFEUR holds European stocks. Its value in dollars depends on both European stock prices and the euro's exchange rate."

chunks.heading: Point to history
chunks.text: Each fund profile shows calendar-year returns, which helps clients see that declines have happened before. Pair any history with "past performance doesn't guarantee future results".
How to triage a client's report that a tax form is wrong before routing it to Tax Reporting.

chunks.heading: Common misunderstandings (check first)
chunks.text:
Concern: "I reinvested, so I shouldn't have dividends"; Usually: Reinvested dividends are taxable. See Form 1099-DIV
Concern: "My exchange shows as a sale"; Usually: Exchanges are sales in taxable accounts
Concern: "My rollover shows as a distribution"; Usually: Indirect rollovers are reported as distributions; the 5498 shows the rollover
Concern: "My QCD is shown as taxable"; Usually: QCDs are reported as normal distributions
Concern: "Cost basis is missing"; Usually: Noncovered shares. See Covered and noncovered shares
Concern: "The contribution is in the wrong year"; Usually: Check the designation. See Prior-year contributions (January to April)
Concern: "I didn't get a 5498 yet"; Usually: It's mailed by May 31

chunks.heading: Real errors
chunks.text: If the form appears genuinely wrong (a transaction missing or duplicated, wrong withholding, wrong name or TIN), collect the account, form, box, and the client's explanation, and refer to Tax Reporting. Tell the client that if a correction is needed, a corrected form will be issued and posted. See Corrected tax forms.

chunks.heading: Example
chunks.text:
Client: "My 1099-R says $10,000 but I only got $9,000."
Agent: "The 1099-R shows the gross distribution of $10,000 in box 1. We withheld $1,000 for federal taxes, which appears in box 4, so you received $9,000. You'll get credit for the $1,000 withheld when you file."

chunks.heading: Example: a genuine error
chunks.text:
Client: "My 5498 shows my contribution for 2026, but I made it for 2025."
Check the transaction's designation. If the designation is 2026 but the client says they requested 2025, review the transcript or request. If our error, route to Retirement Specialists for recoding and a corrected form.
First-line troubleshooting for portal and mobile app problems.

chunks.heading: Quick fixes
chunks.text:
1. Refresh the page or restart the app.
2. Sign out and back in.
3. Clear the browser cache and cookies, or try a private/incognito window.
4. Try a different supported browser (current versions of Chrome, Edge, Safari, Firefox).
5. Update the mobile app.
6. Check the internet connection; turn off VPNs or ad blockers that may interfere.

chunks.heading: Known maintenance
chunks.text: The portal has a maintenance window Sundays 1:00–3:00 AM ET. Status messages appear on the sign-in page during outages.

chunks.heading: When to escalate
chunks.text: If the problem persists, collect: the page or feature, the exact error message, device and browser, time it occurred, and steps to reproduce. Log it as a Technical Issue. Help the client complete their task another way in the meantime (often you can do it in chat).

chunks.heading: Common error messages
chunks.text:
Message: "Session expired"; Meaning: Signed out after inactivity (15 minutes); What to do: Sign in again
Message: "We couldn't complete your request"; Meaning: A temporary error; What to do: Wait a minute and try again; use chat if urgent
Message: "This transaction isn't available for this account"; Meaning: A restriction (foreign address, frequent-trading block, estate hold); What to do: Check account restrictions
Message: "Verification required"; Meaning: A security check; What to do: Complete the code verification
Message: "Page not found"; Meaning: An old bookmark; What to do: Navigate from the home page

chunks.heading: Accessibility tools
chunks.text: Clients using screen readers or magnification can use the portal fully; if a page doesn't work with their assistive technology, log it as a Technical Issue and help them complete the task in chat. See Accessibility and accommodations.
Why clients don't receive our emails and how to fix it.

chunks.heading: Checks
chunks.text:
- Is the email address on file correct and verified? (Ask the client to tell you the address.)
- Spam or junk folders; add noreply@bobsmutualfunds.com to safe senders.
- Corporate or school email filters.
- Did the client unsubscribe from that type of email? Security alerts and document notifications can't be unsubscribed, but marketing can.
- Bounced emails: if our emails bounce, paperless delivery is switched to paper and the client is notified by mail.

chunks.heading: Password reset emails
chunks.text: Reset links expire after 30 minutes and only the latest link works. See Password resets.

chunks.heading: Statement and tax form notifications
chunks.text: Paperless clients receive a notification email when documents are ready. If they missed one, the document is still available online at My Account → Statements & Documents. Offer to send the link.

chunks.heading: Security codes by email
chunks.text: Some verification codes are sent by email. Codes expire after 10 minutes; ask the client to request a new one and to check that they are looking at the newest message.

chunks.heading: Changing the email address
chunks.text: If the client's email address has changed, they can update it at My Account → Profile and confirm the code sent to the new address. See Email and phone changes.

chunks.heading: Phishing caution
chunks.text: Clients sometimes find an email that looks like ours in their spam folder and are unsure whether it is genuine. Our emails never ask for passwords and never contain account numbers. If in doubt, they should sign in directly rather than clicking a link. See Phishing and investment scams.
Problems clients and agents have with chat itself, and how to recover.

chunks.heading: Client side
chunks.text:
Problem: Messages not sending; Fix: Check connection; reload the page (the chat resumes)
Problem: Chat disappeared after navigating; Fix: Chat persists per browser tab; returning to the site in the same tab resumes it. A new tab starts a new chat
Problem: Can't find the chat; Fix: It may be minimized to the bar at the bottom of the screen
Problem: Card "Your approval is required" not visible; Fix: Scroll down in the chat; reload if needed
Problem: Transcript download didn't work; Fix: Allow downloads for the site; the chat history menu also has transcripts for 3 months

chunks.heading: Agent side
chunks.text:
Problem: Workspace disconnected banner; Fix: Refresh; chats reattach
Problem: AI suggestions not loading; Fix: Continue manually; suggestions resume when the service recovers
Problem: Autopilot stopped with an error; Fix: Read the note, resume when ready, or continue manually
Problem: Proposed Action failed; Fix: Check whether it partially completed before retrying. See The Proposed Action card
Report persistent issues with the build stamp from the browser console. See The agent workspace at a glance.

chunks.heading: Example
chunks.text:
Client: "My chat keeps disappearing when I go to another page."
Agent: "The chat stays with your browser tab. If you open a page in a new tab, it starts fresh. Navigate within the same tab and our conversation will stay right here, and you can minimize it to the bar at the bottom of your screen."
The situations that require escalation, to whom, and how fast.

chunks.heading: Escalation map
chunks.text:
Situation: Suspected fraud or unauthorized activity; Escalate to: Fraud and Security, via team lead; Urgency: Immediate
Situation: Suspected elder exploitation or diminished capacity; Escalate to: Senior Investor Protection; Urgency: Immediate
Situation: Client asks for a supervisor; Escalate to: Team lead / supervisor; Urgency: Immediate
Situation: Formal complaint, regulator or attorney mentioned; Escalate to: Supervisor and Compliance; Urgency: Immediate
Situation: Death of an account holder; Escalate to: Estate Services; Urgency: Same day
Situation: Investment advice requested; Escalate to: Licensed professional callback; Urgency: At the client's chosen time
Situation: Complex IRA issue (excess contribution, recharacterization, 72(t)); Escalate to: Retirement Specialists; Urgency: Within 1 business day
Situation: Missing money (wire, ACH, check); Escalate to: Money Movement Operations; Urgency: Same day
Situation: Tax form error; Escalate to: Tax Reporting; Urgency: Within 2 business days
Situation: Our processing error; Escalate to: Team lead, for correction approval; Urgency: Same day
Situation: Legal documents (subpoena, court order, garnishment); Escalate to: Legal; Urgency: Same day; never handle in chat
Situation: Technical defect; Escalate to: Technical support log; Urgency: As appropriate

chunks.heading: How
chunks.text: Use the escalation tools in the workspace or notify your team lead. Always tell the client who will contact them, how, and when. Document the escalation in ACW.

chunks.heading: What escalation is not
chunks.text: Escalation is not a way to avoid a difficult conversation. Handle what you can; escalate what requires someone else's authority or expertise.
How to handle a client who asks for a supervisor.

chunks.heading: Steps
chunks.text:
1. Don't resist or delay. "Of course. I'll get a supervisor for you."
2. Briefly ask what the client would like the supervisor to help with, so the supervisor is prepared. Don't make the client justify the request.
3. Notify your team lead with a one- or two-line summary.
4. Keep the client informed: "I've asked a supervisor to join. It may be a few minutes."
5. If no supervisor is available within 5 minutes, offer a supervisor callback within 1 business day.

chunks.heading: While waiting
chunks.text: Stay present. Don't argue the client's points. If the client asks you to continue helping in the meantime, do so.

chunks.heading: Example
chunks.text:
Client: "I want to talk to your supervisor."
Agent: "Of course. I'll ask a supervisor to join. So they can help you right away, could you tell me in a sentence what you'd like them to look at?"
Client: "Your company lost my rollover check."
Agent: "Thank you. I've asked a supervisor to join and given them that summary. It may take a few minutes; I'll stay here with you."

chunks.heading: Documenting
chunks.text: Record the request, the reason, and the outcome in ACW. If a complaint was made, also follow Handling complaints.
Which specialist team handles which request, and how to hand off cleanly.

chunks.heading: Teams and what they handle
chunks.text:
Team: Licensed professionals; Requests: Investment advice, portfolio reviews, planning conversations
Team: Retirement Specialists; Requests: Excess contributions, recharacterizations, 72(t), complex rollovers, RMD calculation disputes, prior-year recoding
Team: Estate Services; Requests: Deaths, inherited accounts, estate accounts, survivorship
Team: Account Services; Requests: Registration changes, trust and custodial matters, POA review, name changes, address-unknown flags
Team: Money Movement Operations; Requests: Wires, ACH issues, checks, stop payments, returned items
Team: Tax Reporting; Requests: Corrected forms, cost basis issues
Team: Fraud and Security; Requests: Unauthorized activity, compromised accounts
Team: Senior Investor Protection; Requests: Exploitation, diminished capacity
Team: Client Records; Requests: Older documents and transcripts
See also Internal department directory.

chunks.heading: A clean handoff
chunks.text:
1. Summarize the client's request and what you've already confirmed.
2. Tell the client which team, how they'll be contacted, and when.
3. Make sure your ACW captures the referral (Referral wrap-up code where the referral is the main outcome).

chunks.heading: Choosing between a referral and a callback
chunks.text:
- Referral (internal): the specialist team works the request behind the scenes and contacts the client (excess contribution removals, stop payments, tax form corrections).
- Callback: the client wants a conversation (licensed advice, complex estate discussions).

chunks.heading: Avoiding ping-pong
chunks.text: Before referring, make sure the request truly belongs to that team. If you're unsure, ask your team lead. A client bounced between teams has a bad experience even if every team was helpful.
How callbacks are scheduled through chat, availability, time zones, and what to confirm.

chunks.heading: How
chunks.text:
Switch the column to the callback scope, or the client can schedule from the virtual assistant. The flow:
1. Opens with why a callback is the right next step (for example, licensed guidance).
2. Asks for the client's preferred day and time.
3. Checks availability and resolves the time correctly (callbacks are scheduled in Eastern Time; the server converts times safely, including across daylight saving changes).
4. Confirms the phone number to call.
5. Confirms the appointment.

chunks.heading: Availability
chunks.text: Callbacks are available during phone service hours: Monday–Friday 8:00 AM–8:00 PM ET and Saturday 9:00 AM–5:00 PM ET, excluding holidays. Licensed professional callbacks may have narrower availability. The flow offers only available slots.

chunks.heading: Time zones
chunks.text: Always state the time in the client's time zone and Eastern: "Thursday at 2:00 PM Eastern, which is 11:00 AM your time."

chunks.heading: What happens next
chunks.text: A dossier is prepared for the phone agent from the real conversation. See The phone callback console. The client receives a confirmation.

chunks.heading: Changes
chunks.text: See Procedure: Cancel or Reschedule Callback (chat).

chunks.heading: Example
chunks.text:
Agent: "I'd suggest a call with one of our licensed professionals for this. What day and time works for you?"
Client: "Tomorrow after 3."
Agent: "I have 3:30 PM or 4:00 PM Eastern tomorrow. You're in Chicago, so that's 2:30 or 3:00 your time. Which do you prefer?"

chunks.heading: Phone number
chunks.text: Confirm the number to call. If the client wants a number not on file, note it for the callback only; changing their profile phone is a separate request.
Step-by-step chat procedure for changing an arranged callback.

chunks.heading: What the task collects
chunks.text:
Field: Action; Options or format: Cancel, Reschedule
Field: New time; Options or format: The new day and time (for Reschedule)

chunks.heading: Procedure
chunks.text:
1. Identify the callback: date and time currently scheduled.
2. Let the task expert collect the action and, for a reschedule, the new time.
3. Confirm the new time in both Eastern and the client's time zone, and the phone number.
4. Submit and confirm.

chunks.heading: Tips
chunks.text:
- If the client wants to cancel because they no longer need help, ask if there's anything you can help with now.
- If the client wants an earlier time, check availability; same-day slots may be limited.

chunks.heading: Example
chunks.text:
Client: "Can we move my call tomorrow to Friday morning?"
Agent: "Of course. Your call is set for tomorrow, Wednesday, at 2:00 PM Eastern. For Friday morning, would 10:00 AM Eastern work?"
After confirming: "Done. Your call is now Friday at 10:00 AM Eastern at the number ending in 0192."

chunks.heading: If the original time has passed
chunks.text: If the client missed a callback, schedule a new one rather than rescheduling. The phone agent will have noted the missed attempt.
How to transfer a chat or hand off to a colleague so the client doesn't have to repeat themselves.

chunks.heading: Principles
chunks.text:
- The client should never have to repeat their story.
- The receiving person should know what's been done and what's needed.

chunks.heading: How
chunks.text:
1. Tell the client: "I'm going to connect you with our estate team, who handle this. I'll share what you've told me so you won't have to repeat it."
2. Send a short internal summary: client, request, facts confirmed, actions taken, what's needed.
3. Stay with the client until the handoff is complete, or until the callback is confirmed.

chunks.heading: Continued chats
chunks.text: If a client returns later, the "Continue this chat" feature loads prior context. See Continued chats.

chunks.heading: What a good internal summary looks like
chunks.text: "Client: Maria Lopez. Wants to roll over a Fidelity 401(k) (~$85k, pre-tax and Roth portions) into Bob's. Has a Traditional IRA (acc-201) but no Roth IRA. Confirmed: she has requested paperwork from Fidelity. Needs: help opening a Roth IRA for the Roth portion and our receiving details. Prefers phone after 5 PM ET."

chunks.heading: What to tell the client
chunks.text: Tell the client what you've shared, who will contact them, and when. Clients who have had to repeat themselves are often frustrated; this sentence prevents that.
What clients can do outside live-agent hours and how the virtual assistant handles requests.

chunks.heading: Available after hours
chunks.text:
- The virtual assistant (24/7): answers, links, starting some tasks, scheduling callbacks.
- The portal and app: almost all self-service, including trades (priced at the next NAV).
- Secure messages (answered next business day).
- Phone service on Saturdays 9:00 AM–5:00 PM ET.

chunks.heading: Urgent after-hours issues
chunks.text:
- Suspected fraud: clients can lock their online access from My Account → Security (or by repeated failed logins) and call when lines open. The virtual assistant provides fraud guidance.
- Lost or stolen device with the app: remove trusted devices online.

chunks.heading: Setting expectations
chunks.text: When a client chats near closing time, tell them honestly if their request can't be completed today and schedule a callback or note the follow-up.

chunks.heading: Example
chunks.text: A client chats at 7:50 PM ET wanting to change beneficiaries. You can complete it before closing if the details are simple. If not, tell them: "We close at 8:00 PM Eastern. I can schedule a callback for tomorrow morning, or you can update beneficiaries any time online at My Account → Beneficiaries."

chunks.heading: Trades after hours
chunks.text: Orders placed after 4:00 PM ET receive the next business day's NAV whether placed in chat, online, or on the weekend. Make this clear to clients chatting in the evening.
Opening messages for new, escalated, and continued chats.

chunks.heading: Principles
chunks.text: Greet by name, show you know why they're here, and move to the task. The suggested greeting is drafted from the intent; edit as needed.

chunks.heading: Templates
chunks.text:
Escalated from the virtual assistant (intent known): "Hi Maria, I'm Jordan. I see you'd like to roll over a 401(k) from a previous employer. I can help with that. Do you already have an IRA with us you'd like it to go into?"
Intent unclear: "Hi Sam, I'm Jordan from Bob's Mutual Funds. How can I help you today?"
Continued chat: "Welcome back, David. Last time we set up your monthly investment into BF500. How can I help today?"
After a wait: "Hi Priya, thanks for your patience. I'm Jordan, and I'm here to help with your RMD question."

chunks.heading: Avoid
chunks.text: "How may I assist you?" when the intent is already known. Long introductions. Asking the client to repeat what they told the virtual assistant.

chunks.heading: Matching the client's energy
chunks.text: If the client's first message to the virtual assistant was terse or frustrated, keep your greeting short and get to the point. If they were chatty, a little warmth goes a long way.

chunks.heading: Using pronouns and names
chunks.text: Use the name the client uses for themselves in the chat. If their profile lists pronouns, use them when referring to the client in notes or handoffs.
Language for additional identity verification that feels protective, not suspicious.

chunks.heading: Templates
chunks.text:
Before a high-risk request: "Before I make this change, I need to verify a couple of details to protect your account. Could you tell me the ZIP code on file and the last four digits of your Social Security number?"
Third party: "I'm glad to help with general questions. For account-specific information, I can only speak with the account owner or someone they've authorized. If your mother would like you to have access, she can add you as an authorized user."
Verification failed: "For your security, I'm not able to make changes in chat right now. Please call us at 1-800-BOB-FUND so we can verify your identity by phone."

chunks.heading: Avoid
chunks.text: Saying which detail was wrong. Reading out personal information for the client to confirm.

chunks.heading: Example: a request to change email and withdraw
chunks.text: "I can help with both. Because you're updating your email and taking money out in the same conversation, I need to verify a couple of extra details first. This is to protect your account. Could you tell me your date of birth and the ZIP code we have on file?"

chunks.heading: Example: the owner is present and asks you to speak with a family member
chunks.text: "I'm happy to talk with your son about your account while you're here in the chat. Just so I have it on record, you'd like me to discuss your account with him today, is that right?"
Messages for when you need time to research or a process takes longer than expected.

chunks.heading: Templates
chunks.text:
Researching: "Good question. I want to give you an exact answer, so let me check. This will take about two minutes."
Still checking: "Thanks for bearing with me. I'm still confirming this and should have an answer in a minute or two."
Need to follow up later: "I want to get this exactly right, so I'm going to confirm with our retirement specialists. You'll hear back from me by secure message by 3:00 PM Eastern tomorrow."
Process delay (for example, a transfer): "I can see the transfer request is still with your previous firm. These usually complete within 5 to 7 business days. If it hasn't arrived by Friday, let us know and we'll follow up with them."

chunks.heading: Avoid
chunks.text: Disappearing without a message. Vague promises ("soon"). Blaming other teams.

chunks.heading: Long waits
chunks.text: If research will take more than 5 minutes, give the client a choice: "This will take a bit longer to confirm. Would you like to wait, or should I send you the answer by secure message within the hour?"

chunks.heading: Explaining delays outside our control
chunks.text: "Your previous employer's plan has to release the money first. Once they send it, it typically arrives within 5 to 15 business days. I'll note your account so we watch for it."
Compassionate language for conversations about a death.

chunks.heading: Templates
chunks.text:
Opening: "I'm so sorry for the loss of your father. I'm here to help, and we'll take this one step at a time."
Explaining next steps: "Here's what happens next: we'll protect your father's accounts while we review documents, and our Estate Services team will contact you within two business days. They'll send a checklist of what's needed, which usually starts with a certified copy of the death certificate. You don't need to decide anything today."
Information you can't share yet: "I understand you'd like to know what's in the account. Once Estate Services has the documents confirming your role, they'll be able to go over everything with you."
Closing: "Please take care of yourself. If anything comes up before Estate Services reaches you, you can message us any time."
See Communicating with grieving clients.

chunks.heading: When the caller is also grieving the client's spouse
chunks.text: "I'm so sorry about Robert. I know this is a lot to handle. Let's take care of what's most urgent for you today, and we'll connect you with our Estate Services team for the rest."

chunks.heading: When the client needs money urgently
chunks.text: "I understand you need funds for expenses right now. Let's look at your own accounts first. For Robert's accounts, Estate Services can explain what can be released and how quickly."

chunks.heading: When the caller is upset by a requirement
chunks.text: "I know asking for a death certificate feels like one more burden right now. It's how we make sure his assets go exactly where he intended, and it protects you and your family."
Language for acknowledging frustration, gathering facts, logging complaints, and escalating.

chunks.heading: Templates
chunks.text:
Acknowledge: "I'm sorry this happened, and I understand why you're frustrated. I want to make this right, so let me make sure I understand exactly what happened."
Gather facts: "Can you tell me when you placed the order and what you expected to happen?"
Fix within your authority: "I see the problem: the automatic investment wasn't paused as you asked. I've paused it now, and I've requested a refund of the $20 returned-payment fee."
Log a complaint: "I've recorded your complaint so our team can review it. You'll receive a response within five business days."
Supervisor request: "Of course. I'll get a supervisor for you right away."

chunks.heading: Avoid
chunks.text:
"Calm down." Arguing. Admitting legal fault or promising compensation without approval. Blaming the client or another team.
See Handling complaints.

chunks.heading: Example: a fee complaint
chunks.text:
Client: "This is ridiculous. You charged me $20 for nothing."
Agent: "I understand, and I'm sorry this was frustrating. Let me look at what happened. The fee is for a returned automatic investment on March 3. Your bank returned it marked 'account closed'. If that account was closed, let's update your plan to your current bank so it doesn't happen again. I can also ask whether we can waive this one."

chunks.heading: Example: a service complaint
chunks.text:
Client: "I've been waiting three weeks for my transfer and nobody calls me back."
Agent: "I'm sorry. Three weeks is too long, and you shouldn't have to chase us. I'm recording this as a complaint so it's reviewed, and I'm checking the transfer status right now."
Language that declines investment advice warmly and offers real help instead.

chunks.heading: Templates
chunks.text:
General: "That's an important decision, and it depends on your whole financial picture, so I'm not able to recommend a specific investment. I can explain how the options work, or set up a call with one of our licensed professionals who can give you personalized guidance. Which would you prefer?"
"What would you do?": "I appreciate you asking! I'm not able to give personal recommendations, but I can walk you through the facts on each fund side by side."
Choosing between funds: "Here's how BF500 and BFTM compare on cost, holdings, and history. Which fits your goals is something a licensed professional can help you decide; I'm happy to set up that call."
Timing the market: "No one can reliably predict where markets will go next. I can share how the fund has behaved historically, and if you'd like guidance on your strategy, I can schedule a call with a licensed professional."
Roth vs. Traditional: "Both have advantages, and the right choice depends on your tax situation now versus in retirement. I can explain how each works, or arrange a call with a licensed professional."
See The investment advice boundary.
Messages for ending chats, including summaries of what was done and next steps.

chunks.heading: Templates
chunks.text:
After a completed task: "You're all set: your $2,000 purchase of BF500 is placed (reference REF-48213). It'll be priced at today's close. Is there anything else I can help with?"
Final close: "Thanks for chatting with us today, Maria. Have a great afternoon."
After a referral: "Your call with a licensed professional is set for Thursday at 2:00 PM Eastern. They'll have a summary of today's conversation. Thanks for reaching out!"
Idle client: "It looks like you may have stepped away. I'll close this chat for now, but you can start a new one any time, and you can continue this conversation from the chat menu for the next week."

chunks.heading: Closing after a multi-task chat
chunks.text: "Here's a summary of what we did today: your beneficiary on the Roth IRA is updated (REF-48213), your monthly investment into BF500 increased to $300 starting October 15 (REF-48214), and your tax form request is submitted (REF-48215). Anything else I can help with?"

chunks.heading: Closing a difficult chat
chunks.text: "Thank you for your patience today. I know this wasn't easy. Estate Services will contact you within two business days, and you can reach us any time in the meantime."
Language for anxious clients during market declines.

chunks.heading: Templates
chunks.text:
Acknowledge: "It's completely understandable to feel uneasy when you see your balance drop."
Explain factually: "Stock funds broadly declined this week, and BF500 follows the 500 largest U.S. companies, so it moved with them."
Context: "Markets have gone through many declines; for example, BF500 fell 18.2% in 2022 and then rose 26.3% in 2023. Of course, past performance doesn't guarantee future results."
Offer options: "If you'd like to talk through your strategy, I can schedule a call with a licensed professional. If you've decided on a change, I can help you make it."

chunks.heading: Avoid
chunks.text:
"It'll come back." "Don't sell." "Now's a buying opportunity." Any prediction.
See Talking with clients during market downturns.

chunks.heading: Client asks "Should I sell?"
chunks.text: "That's a personal decision, and I can't recommend whether to sell. What I can do is explain how a sale would work, including any tax effects, or set up a call with a licensed professional who can talk through your plan. Which would help most?"

chunks.heading: Client is clearly distressed
chunks.text: Slow down. Lead with empathy, offer the callback, and do not rush any transaction. If the client still wants to sell, confirm clearly and process it.
Language for clients reporting suspicious activity or scams.

chunks.heading: Templates
chunks.text:
Client reports unauthorized activity: "Thank you for letting us know right away. I'm going to help you secure your account now and get our security team involved."
Phishing: "That email didn't come from us. We'll never ask for your password or a security code. Please don't click any links in it. If you entered your password anywhere, let's reset it now."
Pausing a suspicious request: "This request needs an additional security review before it can be completed. Our security team will contact you at the phone number on file, usually within one business day."
Wire scam warning: "Our wire instructions never change by email. If you received a message saying they changed, please don't send money to that account."
See Suspected account takeover or unauthorized activity and Phishing and investment scams.

chunks.heading: Client already sent money to a scammer
chunks.text: "I'm sorry this happened. Let's act quickly. I'm escalating to our security team now to see what can be done, and I'd recommend you also contact your bank right away and report the scam to the authorities."

chunks.heading: Client can't tell whether a call was from us
chunks.text: "If you're ever unsure whether a call is really from us, hang up and call 1-800-BOB-FUND directly. We'll never be offended."
Language for helping clients with website, app, or chat problems.

chunks.heading: Templates
chunks.text:
First steps: "Sorry for the trouble. Could you try refreshing the page, or opening it in a private window? That often clears it up."
Workaround: "While we look into that, I can make the change for you here in chat. Would that help?"
Escalation: "I've reported this to our technical team with the details you gave me. Thanks for your patience."
See Website and app errors.

chunks.heading: Gathering details
chunks.text: "So our technical team can fix this, could you tell me what device and browser you're using, and what exactly you see on the screen when it happens?"

chunks.heading: When the client is frustrated
chunks.text: "I'm sorry the website is giving you trouble, especially when you're trying to get something done. Let me take care of it for you here, and I'll report the problem."

chunks.heading: Example: the app crashes when opening statements
chunks.text: "Thanks for letting me know. While our team looks into it, you can view and download the same statements on the website at My Account → Statements & Documents. I'll log the app issue with the details you gave me."
How to recap a task before submitting so the client's confirmation is clear and complete.

chunks.heading: The rule
chunks.text: Before any action is submitted, recap every material detail in one message and get a clear yes. The evidence highlighting uses this confirmed recap.

chunks.heading: Templates
chunks.text:
Purchase: "To confirm: buy $2,000 of BobsFunds 500 Index (BF500) in your Roth IRA, funded from your linked bank account ending in 4421, as a 2026 contribution. Shall I place it?"
Sale: "To confirm: sell $5,000 of BobsFunds Growth (BFGR) in your taxable account, with the proceeds kept as cash in the account. Is that right?"
Exchange: "To confirm: exchange $3,000 from BFGR into BobsFunds Bond Income (BFBI) in your Traditional IRA. Shall I go ahead?"
Beneficiary: "To confirm, after this change your Roth IRA's primary beneficiaries will be David Chen (spouse) at 60% and Maria Chen (daughter) at 40%, with no secondary beneficiaries. Is that correct?"
Distribution: "To confirm: withdraw $5,000 from your Traditional IRA, withhold 10% federal tax, and deposit $4,500 to your linked bank. Shall I submit it?"

chunks.heading: Avoid
chunks.text: Recapping only part of the details. Treating "ok" to a different question as confirmation. Submitting after the client changes a detail without a fresh recap.
Language for routing a client to another team or a callback.

chunks.heading: Templates
chunks.text:
Specialist team: "Our retirement specialists handle excess contribution corrections, because they calculate the exact earnings. I've sent them your details, and they'll contact you within one business day."
Callback: "I've scheduled a call for Tuesday at 10:00 AM Eastern (7:00 AM your time) at the number ending in 0192. You'll get a confirmation shortly."
Phone route: "For this, please call 1-800-BOB-FUND and say 'inherited account'. You'll reach our estate team directly, Monday to Friday, 8:00 AM to 7:30 PM Eastern."

chunks.heading: Example: Estate Services by callback
chunks.text: "I'll arrange for our Estate Services team to call you. Would tomorrow morning work, around 10:00 AM Eastern? They'll have everything you've told me today."

chunks.heading: Example: licensed professional
chunks.text: "For advice on how to invest your rollover, I'll schedule a call with one of our licensed professionals. They'll be able to look at your full situation. What day works best?"

chunks.heading: Example: Retirement Specialists
chunks.text: "Correcting an excess contribution involves calculating the exact earnings, so our retirement specialists handle it. I've sent them your account and the amount, and they'll contact you within one business day to confirm the numbers before anything is withdrawn."

chunks.heading: Example: Fraud team
chunks.text: "I've escalated this to our security team as a priority. They'll call you at the number on file, usually within one business day, and they may contact you sooner."
Definitions of terms beginning A through D.

chunks.heading: A
chunks.text:
ACAT:
Automated Customer Account Transfer. The industry system for moving brokerage accounts between firms, started by the receiving firm. See Incoming ACAT transfers.
ACH:
Automated Clearing House. The U.S. electronic bank transfer network; free, 2–3 business days. See ACH transfers.
ACW (after-chat work):
The wrap-up code, summary, and coaching generated when a chat ends, reviewed and submitted by the agent. See After-chat work (ACW).
Agent (under a POA):
The person authorized to act for another under a power of attorney. See Power of attorney.
AML:
Anti-money-laundering. Laws and programs to detect and report suspicious financial activity. See Anti-money-laundering red flags.
Annualized return:
The average yearly return over a multi-year period. See How performance is reported.
Asset allocation:
The division of investments among stocks, bonds, and cash. See Asset allocation.
Authorized user:
A person given view-only, limited, or full access to a client's account by the owner. See Authorized users and access levels.
Autopilot:
The agent-workspace feature that sends AI-drafted messages on a timer, within a scope. See Autopilot: what it is and when to use it.
Average cost:
The default cost basis method: the average price of all shares owned. See Cost basis methods.

chunks.heading: B
chunks.text:
Backdoor Roth:
A nondeductible Traditional IRA contribution followed by a Roth conversion. See The "backdoor Roth" strategy.
Backup withholding:
24% withholding required when a client's TIN is missing or incorrect. See Form W-9 and backup withholding.
Basis (cost basis):
What was paid for shares, used to calculate gains and losses. For IRAs, basis means nondeductible contributions.
Beneficiary:
A person or entity designated to receive an account at the owner's death. See Beneficiaries: overview.
Benchmark:
The index a fund tracks or is measured against. See Benchmarks and tracking.
Beta:
A measure of how much a fund has moved relative to the S&P 500.
Bond:
A loan to a government or company that pays interest. See Bonds and interest rates.

chunks.heading: C
chunks.text:
Capital gain distribution:
A fund's payout of net realized gains, usually in December. See Capital gain distributions.
Catch-up contribution:
The additional IRA contribution allowed at age 50+ ($1,100 for 2026). See Catch-up contributions.
CIP:
Customer Identification Program; identity verification for new accounts. See Identity verification for new accounts (CIP).
Contingent beneficiary:
A secondary beneficiary who inherits if all primary beneficiaries have died. See Primary and contingent beneficiaries.
Conversion (Roth):
Moving pre-tax IRA money to a Roth IRA, a taxable event. See Roth conversions: overview.
Covered shares:
Shares acquired since 2012 whose basis we report to the IRS. See Covered and noncovered shares.
Custodial account:
An account held for a minor under UTMA or UGMA. See Custodial accounts (UTMA/UGMA).
Cutoff:
4:00 PM ET; orders received before it get that day's NAV. See Trade cutoff and NAV pricing.

chunks.heading: D
chunks.text:
Designated beneficiary:
An individual named as an IRA beneficiary; most are subject to the 10-year rule. See Options for non-spouse beneficiaries.
Direct rollover:
A rollover paid directly from a plan to an IRA. See Direct rollovers.
Distribution (fund):
A payment of dividends or capital gains by a fund. See Fund distributions overview.
Distribution (IRA):
Money taken out of an IRA. See IRA distributions overview.
Diversification:
Spreading investments to reduce the impact of any single holding. See Diversification.
Dollar-cost averaging:
Investing a fixed amount at regular intervals. See Dollar-cost averaging.
DRIP:
Dividend reinvestment; distributions buy more shares automatically. See Dividend reinvestment (DRIP).
Duration:
A bond fund's sensitivity to interest-rate changes, in years. See Duration.
Definitions of terms beginning E through L.

chunks.heading: E
chunks.text:
Early withdrawal penalty:
The 10% additional tax on IRA distributions before 59½, unless an exception applies. See The 10% early-withdrawal penalty.
Eligible designated beneficiary (EDB):
A beneficiary who may stretch inherited IRA payments over life expectancy. See Eligible designated beneficiaries.
ESG:
Environmental, social, and governance criteria used to screen investments; BFESG applies such screens.
Escheatment:
Turning dormant property over to a state. See Dormant accounts and unclaimed property.
Evidence highlighting:
Transcript highlights showing where each Proposed Action value came from. See Evidence highlighting.
Excess contribution:
An IRA contribution above the allowed amount, subject to 6% annual excise tax. See Excess contributions and how to fix them.
Exchange:
Moving money from one fund to another in the same account. See Exchanges overview.
Ex-dividend date:
The date a fund's NAV drops by a distribution. See Record, ex-dividend, reinvestment, and pay dates.
Expense ratio:
A fund's annual operating cost as a percentage of assets. See Expense ratios.

chunks.heading: F
chunks.text:
FIFO:
First in, first out; a cost basis method selling the oldest shares first.
FINRA:
The Financial Industry Regulatory Authority, which regulates broker-dealers.
Form 1099-B, 1099-DIV, 1099-R, 5498:
Tax forms we issue. See Tax center overview.
Frequent trading policy:
Restricts purchases after a round trip within 30 days. See Frequent trading (market timing) policy.
Full redemption:
Selling all shares of a fund in an account. See Partial and full redemptions.

chunks.heading: G–H
chunks.text:
Good order:
An order with all information needed to process it.
Growth (style):
Companies with above-average expected earnings growth. See How the lineup is organized.
Holding period:
How long shares were held; over one year is long-term.

chunks.heading: I
chunks.text:
In kind:
Moving securities as-is rather than selling for cash.
Index fund:
A fund that tracks an index. See Index funds and active funds.
Indirect rollover:
A 60-day rollover in which the client receives the money first. See Indirect (60-day) rollovers.
Inherited IRA:
An IRA held for a beneficiary after the owner's death. See Inherited IRA.
Intent label / intent summary:
The AI-generated description of why a client is chatting, shown at escalation. See Incoming contacts and the alert card.
Interested party:
A person who receives duplicate statements. See Duplicate statements and interested parties.

chunks.heading: J–L
chunks.text:
JTWROS:
Joint tenants with rights of survivorship; the survivor inherits automatically. See Joint accounts.
Letters Testamentary / of Administration:
Court documents authorizing an executor or administrator. See Documents needed after a death.
Limited access:
An authorized-user level allowing trades and payments back to the owner only.
Linked bank account:
A verified bank account used for electronic transfers. See Linking bank accounts.
Long-term capital gain:
A gain on shares held more than a year, taxed at lower rates. See Capital gains tax rates.
Definitions of terms beginning M through R.

chunks.heading: M
chunks.text:
MAGI:
Modified adjusted gross income; used for Roth eligibility and deductibility.
Medallion signature guarantee:
A stamp from a financial institution guaranteeing a signature. See Medallion signature guarantees.
Micro-deposits:
Two small deposits used to verify a bank account. See Bank verification methods.
Mutual fund:
A pooled investment owned by its shareholders. See Mutual funds explained.

chunks.heading: N
chunks.text:
NAV:
Net asset value per share; a mutual fund's daily price. See NAV: how fund prices work.
Net investment income tax:
A 3.8% tax on investment income above certain income levels.
Noncovered shares:
Shares whose cost basis we don't report to the IRS. See Covered and noncovered shares.

chunks.heading: O–P
chunks.text:
OFAC:
The Treasury office that administers sanctions. See Sanctions screening (OFAC).
Paperless:
Electronic delivery of documents. See Paperless delivery.
Per stirpes:
A designation passing a deceased beneficiary's share to their descendants. See Per stirpes designations.
POA:
Power of attorney. See Power of attorney.
Primary beneficiary:
A beneficiary who inherits first. See Primary and contingent beneficiaries.
Pro-rata rule:
Conversions are taxed in proportion to pre-tax and after-tax money across all IRAs. See How conversions are taxed.
Proposed Action:
The structured card a task expert prepares for agent approval. See The Proposed Action card.
Prospectus:
A fund's legal disclosure document. See The prospectus.

chunks.heading: Q
chunks.text:
QCD:
Qualified charitable distribution from an IRA at 70½+. See Qualified charitable distributions (QCDs).
QDRO:
Qualified domestic relations order dividing an employer plan in divorce. See QDRO versus divorce decree.
Qualified dividend:
A dividend taxed at long-term capital gain rates. See Qualified dividends.
Qualified distribution (Roth):
A tax-free Roth withdrawal meeting the age and five-year tests. See Roth IRA distribution rules.

chunks.heading: R
chunks.text:
Recharacterization:
Treating a contribution as made to the other IRA type. See Recharacterizations.
Record date:
The date that determines who receives a distribution.
Redemption:
Selling fund shares. See Selling shares: overview.
Redemption hold:
A hold on proceeds from recently purchased shares until payment clears. See Holds on redemption proceeds.
Reference number:
The REF-XXXXXX identifier for actions submitted in chat. See Reference numbers.
Required beginning date:
April 1 of the year after reaching RMD age. See Timing the first RMD.
Risk level:
The five-step rating on each fund's profile. See Published risk levels.
RMD:
Required minimum distribution. See RMDs: overview.
Rollover:
Moving retirement money from one plan or IRA to another. See Rollovers and transfers: overview.
Round trip:
A purchase followed by a sale of the same fund within 30 days.
Definitions of terms beginning S through Z.

chunks.heading: S
chunks.text:
SAI:
Statement of Additional Information. See Statement of Additional Information (SAI).
SEC:
The Securities and Exchange Commission.
SECURE Act / SECURE 2.0:
Federal laws (2019, 2022) that changed RMD ages, inherited IRA rules, and more.
SEP-IRA:
Simplified Employee Pension IRA for self-employed people and small businesses. See SEP-IRA.
SEPP / 72(t):
Substantially equal periodic payments avoiding the early-withdrawal penalty. See Substantially equal periodic payments (72(t)).
Settlement:
The completion of a trade, T+1 for mutual funds. See Settlement and when money is available.
SIPC:
Securities Investor Protection Corporation. See SIPC and the safety of client assets.
Specific identification:
A cost basis method in which the client chooses which shares to sell.
Spousal IRA:
An IRA funded based on a working spouse's income. See Spousal IRA.
Standard deviation:
A measure of how widely returns have varied.
Step-up in basis:
Resetting cost basis to the date-of-death value for inherited taxable assets. See Inheriting taxable accounts.
Suggested reply:
The AI-drafted next message in the agent's support panel. See Suggested replies, Change to, and Magic.
Systematic withdrawal plan (SWP):
Recurring withdrawals on a schedule. See Systematic withdrawal plans.

chunks.heading: T
chunks.text:
T+1:
Settlement one business day after the trade date.
Task expert:
An AI specialist that collects the details for one service task. See Task experts and the task menu.
TOD:
Transfer on death registration for taxable accounts. See Transfer on death (TOD) for taxable accounts.
Total return:
Price change plus reinvested distributions. See Total return versus price change.
Trusted contact person:
Someone we may contact about exploitation or if we can't reach the client. See Trusted contact person.
Turnover:
The share of a fund's holdings replaced in a year.

chunks.heading: U–Z
chunks.text:
UTMA / UGMA:
Uniform Transfers/Gifts to Minors Acts governing custodial accounts.
Uniform Lifetime Table:
The IRS table used for most owners' RMDs. See Uniform Lifetime Table.
Value (style):
Companies that appear inexpensive relative to fundamentals.
Wash sale:
A loss disallowed because the same security was bought within 30 days. See The wash-sale rule.
Wire:
A same-day bank transfer. See Incoming wires and Outgoing wires.
Wrap-up code:
The code classifying a chat's primary topic. See Wrap-up codes.
Yield:
Income relative to price. See Yields.
